overview.summary: A rare, noble, and tirelessly agile large French pointing dog from the Ariège region of southwestern France, prized for its lean muscular stamina, bright white-and-orange ticked coat, and stable, sociable, easily trained hunting character.
overview.description: The Ariège Pointer—known in its French homeland as the Braque de l'Ariège—is a robust, athletic braccoid gun dog that pairs commanding bone and prominent dry musculature with unmistakable elegance and lightness of movement. Slightly longer than tall in balanced medium proportions, it carries a broad, deep oval chest reaching elbow level, a straight muscled back, a powerful slightly convex loin, and straight lean legs propelling an extended, supple, energetic stride. Its long, cleanly sculpted head—narrow across the cheekbones with gently divergent skull and muzzle planes and a pronounced occiput—features an orange-to-pale-brown nose (never black), fine neatly closing lips, gentle frank amber-to-brown eyes, and long, fine, inward-curling drop ears set at eye level and held slightly away from the cheeks. Clad in a short, glossy, well-provided coat predominantly white with extensive pale-to-vivid orangy fawn or light brown patches and ticking over supple skin, the Ariège Pointer adapts seamlessly to every style of upland and woodland hunting—especially partridge and quail—while proving stable, docile, and sociable with humans and other dogs when its vigorous daily exercise needs are met.
overview.history: Originating in southwestern France—historically known regionally as the Braque de Toulouse or Braque du Midi before taking the name of the Ariège department where its earliest dedicated breeders lived—the Ariège Pointer descends from old French pointing hounds crossed during the nineteenth century with white-and-orange southern pointers to gain greater lightness, speed, and liveliness. Devastated by both World Wars, the breed dwindled so severely that no puppies were registered in France's national studbook after 1964, surviving solely because a handful of traditional Ariège hunters continued working local lines in the field. Definitive international recognition had already been granted in June 1955, and in 1990 a determined team of enthusiasts met in Toulouse to rescue the breed from oblivion—locating dogs of authentic type, breeding a foundation litter whose first two puppies became the earliest national registrations since 1964, founding a dedicated French preservation society that same year, and implementing a structured breeding recovery plan in 1991. With an updated written blueprint established in August 2023, the Ariège Pointer has steadily rebounded in French field trials and exhibitions while remaining rare outside France.
overview.originalPurpose: Locating, pointing, and retrieving upland game birds—especially partridge and quail—and small game across the plains, hills, and woodlands of southwestern France.
currentRoles: Versatile upland pointing and retrieving hunting dog (especially on partridge and quail)
Field-trial and hunting-test sporting competitor
Active rural companion for outdoor-oriented hunting households

physical.coatType: Short, rather thick, dense, well-provided, glossy single-style coat lying smoothly over moderately thick, supple skin (not overly loose, and finer on the head). Hair grows finer and smoother over the head and ear leathers.
coatColors: White with very extended or invasive patches of pale to vivid orangy fawn (with or without ticking or mottling)
White with extended light brown patches (with or without ticking or mottling)
Predominantly white heavily ticked or mottled with pale orangy fawn or light brown
Black spots in the coat, black nose pigment, or black patches on mucous membranes are strictly disqualified
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; the short, thick, glossy coat sheds lightly throughout the year with moderate seasonal increases
physical.droolingLevel: Low; quite fine lips with a folded, non-droopy corner that close neatly and only a modest neck dewlap keep drooling minimal
distinctiveFeatures: Braccoid, robust, vigorous continental pointer preferring lean legs, prominent muscles, and crisp well-defined lines without excessive heaviness (females usually lighter)
Height at the withers of 58 to 65 cm for males (preferred 61 cm, ± 2 cm tolerance) and 54 to 63 cm for females (preferred 59 cm, ± 2 cm tolerance)
Working adult weight of 25 to 30 kg
Medium proportions with body length slightly exceeding height at the withers and skull length closely matching muzzle length (within 1 cm)
Long, well-sculpted head narrow at the zygomatic arches, slightly rounded skull, gently divergent skull and muzzle planes, quite pronounced occiput, and lightly marked stop

Orange to pale-brown nose (never black) with wide nostrils, long straight or slightly convex muzzle, fine non-droopy lips closing neatly, and scissor bite (pincer bite and absence of two PM1 or one PM2/PM3 tolerated; bite gap over 1 mm disqualified)
Well-open, slightly oval amber-to-brown eyes harmonizing with coat colour and projecting a gentle, frank, expressive gaze (excessive eyelid depigmentation disqualified)
Quite fine, long, inward-curling drop ears set at eye level, held slightly away from the head, reaching the nose without stretching (flat or high-set ears disqualified)
Medium-length strong neck with a slight dewlap, broad deep oval chest reaching elbow level, straight muscular back, slightly convex loin, and gently rising belly
Tail continuing the croup line, carried horizontally never above topline (traditionally docked by 6/10 where permitted; natural long tail admitted)
Straight muscular forelegs, compact slightly slender tight-toed feet with well-cushioned resistant pads, and an extended, supple, energetic gait

traits: Stable, balanced, and reliably sociable with both humans and other dogs
Docile, cooperative, and easy to train when given clear, consistent guidance
Lively, energetic, and lightly independent in the field—adapted to every style of hunting with high physical resistance
Deeply enthusiastic bird hunter with a strong pointing drive, especially on partridge and quail
Affectionate and pleasant indoors once its substantial daily physical and scenting energy is spent
Sensitive to erratic or overly harsh handling, responding best to calm firmness and steady leadership

exercise.level: High; an energetic, all-terrain French pointing breed built for sustained upland stamina that demands generous daily countryside running, vigorous walks, and purposeful scent or field work
activities: Upland bird hunting and pointing fieldwork—especially for partridge and quail
Organised continental pointing field trials and hunting tests
Long daily countryside trail hikes, running, or bikejoring in safe rural areas
Structured scent tracking, retrieve games, and off-leash exploration inside a large, securely fenced rural property

grooming.brushing: Easy-care short, dense, glossy coat—brush once a week with a rubber grooming mitt or soft bristle brush to clear loose hairs and field dust.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally when visibly muddy or odorous after countryside runs, using a mild canine shampoo.
notes: Because the long, fine, inward-curling drop ears easily collect moisture, grass seeds, and field debris, inspect and dry them weekly—and after every wet outing—to prevent ear infections.
Check the compact, slightly slender feet, well-cushioned pads, and supple skin after brush hunting for thorns, burrs, cuts, or ticks.
Trim strong nails regularly whenever rough outdoor terrain does not wear them down naturally.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate; docile, intelligent, and readily trained, though its lively energy and lightly independent hunting streak call for firm, calm, consistent leadership started early
tips: Begin obedience, recall, and calm impulse control in early puppyhood using clear, firm, reward-based consistency—combining steady boundaries with positive encouragement.
Channel its intense upland bird-hunting passion into field training, retrieve games, or structured nosework so pent-up drive does not cause restlessness.
Proof recall thoroughly on a long line around birds, hares, and open meadows before granting off-leash freedom.
Acclimate puppies early to everyday noises and calm indoor settling if they will live as household companions.
training.socialization: Early, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, children, rural and urban environments, and routine ear handling supports its naturally stable, frank, and sociable disposition.

climates: Temperate, sunny, and four-season southern European countryside climates, matching southwestern France and the Pyrenean foothills

Warm climates are handled well during active work when strenuous runs are scheduled during cooler morning or evening hours with reliable shade, fresh water, and sun awareness for pale white skin areas
Cold winter weather is tolerated comfortably during vigorous movement, though its short single-style coat needs warm, dry indoor shelter during freezing rest periods
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; sociable with people and other dogs and driven to work actively outdoors, an Ariège Pointer left isolated all day without daily exercise quickly grows restless.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for large, high-endurance sporting and hunting breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age on a controlled large-breed growth formula to support healthy skeletal and joint development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain upland hunting endurance and help reduce acute stomach distension.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for reduced activity and joint health.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately to maintain the breed's lean, dry, prominently muscled working frame without excess weight over its joints. Increase caloric and protein density during strenuous autumn and winter hunting seasons and scale back during quieter off-season months. Divide daily adult rations into two smaller meals, allow calm rest before and after eating, and provide cool, fresh drinking water continuously.
considerations: Because the Ariège Pointer is a large pointer with a broad, deep chest reaching elbow level, divide adult meals into two portions and avoid vigorous sprinting immediately before or after eating as a precaution against gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat).
Feed growing puppies a balanced large-breed growth diet with controlled energy and calcium to support sound hip and elbow development.
Count all training treats inside the daily calorie budget and transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Caloric requirements vary substantially between active hunting-season pointers and off-season adults. Consult a veterinarian to establish individual feeding portions.

health.overview: Because the Ariège Pointer is a very rare breed whose modern registered population was rebuilt from a tiny founder base starting in 1990, no large peer-reviewed breed-wide epidemiological health surveys, mandatory breed-specific genetic test panels, or verified actuarial lifespan datasets have been published to date. Practical veterinary care therefore focuses on careful multi-generation pedigree management to preserve genetic diversity alongside standard precautions for large, deep-chested, long-eared continental pointers—specifically pre-breeding radiographic hip (and elective elbow) screening, weekly drop-ear hygiene, bloat (GDV) mealtime precautions, and woodland parasite and fieldwork injury protection.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia — general developmental orthopaedic precautions recommended for large, athletic continental pointers standing 54 to 65 cm at the withers (radiographic evaluation protocols are available in France through official reading schemes)
Otitis externa (outer ear infections) — general conformation-linked precaution associated with long, fine, inward-curling drop ears that can retain moisture, wax, or woodland grass seeds
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — general acute, life-threatening stomach distension and twisting precaution relevant to large pointers with broad, deep chests reaching elbow level

Small-population genetic-diversity vulnerability — the 1964–1990 national registration gap and small modern population make thoughtful multi-generation pedigree planning essential to avoid inbreeding depression
Fieldwork trauma, tick-borne exposure, and sun sensitivity — paw pad wear, brush cuts, ticks from upland cover, and mild sunburn risk on pale white-and-orange skin or lightly pigmented nose leather
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for documented multi-generation pedigrees, parental veterinary wellness records, and any available radiographic hip and elbow dysplasia evaluations.
Inspect and dry the long, inward-curling drop ears weekly—and after every damp field outing—to prevent moisture-driven ear infections.
Divide daily adult meals into two portions, enforce calm rest around mealtimes, and know emergency bloat warning signs (unproductive retching, swollen tight abdomen, severe restlessness).

Keep the dog lean and well-conditioned, inspect feet and coat for thorns or ticks after every hunt, and maintain consistent vaccinations and year-round parasite prevention alongside annual veterinary exams.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation (and elective radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation) prior to breeding as a prudent large-pointer orthopaedic precaution
Careful multi-generation pedigree analysis to maintain genetic diversity within a small global population
Routine veterinary ophthalmic, dental, and cardiac checks during annual wellness examinations
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental checks to keep the scissor bite (or tolerated pincer bite) and gums healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the long, fine, inward-curling drop ears weekly—and after every wet hunting walk—for moisture, wax buildup, grass seeds, odour, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Check the supple skin and short glossy coat after every countryside outing for ticks, burrs, thorns, minor brush scratches, or sun irritation on pale white areas.

idealFor: Upland game hunters (especially partridge and quail hunters) looking for a resistant, agile, biddable French continental pointer
Very active rural or countryside families with spacious, securely fenced grounds who enjoy long daily trail hikes, running, or scent work
Multi-dog rural households wanting a stable, sociable pointer that gets along smoothly with other dogs and requires minimal coat grooming
Conservation-minded sporting-dog enthusiasts supporting a rare heritage French pointing breed
notIdealFor: City apartment dwellers or sedentary households unable to provide 60 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily countryside exercise
First-time or passive owners unwilling to provide firm, consistent training for a lively, lightly independent hunting dog
Homes with free-roaming pet birds or small prey animals without strict management
People who leave an active, people-sociable pointer isolated alone all day

funFacts: Before adopting the name of the Ariège department in southwestern France, the breed was historically known regionally as the 'Braque de Toulouse' and the 'Braque du Midi.'

After World War II, the Ariège Pointer vanished from France's national studbook completely—with zero new registrations between 1964 and 1990—until a small team of enthusiasts met in Toulouse in 1990, tracked down surviving local hunting dogs of true type, and revived the breed from scratch.

Strict pigmentation rules define the Ariège Pointer's pale-to-vivid orange-and-white look: its nose must range from orange to pale brown matching its coat, while a black nose, black coat spots, or black patches on mucous membranes are strictly disqualified.
Its long, fine drop ears curl gently inward ('papillotées') and are carried slightly away from the cheeks rather than pressed flat against the head—a signature French braccoid trait.
Among French hunters in the Pyrenean foothills, the Ariège Pointer is especially prized for its nimble endurance when hunting wild partridge and quail across varied terrain.

faq.question: What is an Ariège Pointer?
faq.answer: The Ariège Pointer (Braque de l'Ariège) is a rare, lean, muscular large French continental pointing dog from the Ariège department of southwestern France, prized for its glossy white-and-orange ticked coat, tireless upland hunting skill, and stable, sociable nature.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an Ariège Pointer?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 58 to 65 cm at the withers (ideally 61 cm, with a 2 cm tolerance) and adult females stand 54 to 63 cm (ideally 59 cm, with a 2 cm tolerance). Working adults typically weigh 25 to 30 kg, with females usually lighter in build.

faq.question: How long does an Ariège Pointer live?
faq.answer: No official lifespan range or peer-reviewed actuarial longevity study is published for the Ariège Pointer due to its very small global population, though healthy lean care and preventive veterinary attention support longevity typical of large sporting pointers.

faq.question: Can an Ariège Pointer live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Although stable and docile when properly exercised, it is a large, high-energy countryside hunting pointer that needs 60 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily outdoor movement and scent work, thriving best in a rural or spacious home with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: What coat colours do Ariège Pointers come in?
faq.answer: The coat is predominantly white with extensive patches or ticking in shades ranging from pale to vivid orangy fawn and light brown. Black coat spots, black noses, and black pigment patches on mucous membranes are not permitted.

faq.question: How much grooming does an Ariège Pointer need?
faq.answer: Coat upkeep is minimal: weekly brushing with a rubber mitt or soft brush keeps its short, glossy coat clean, with baths only when muddy. However, its long, fine, inward-curling drop ears need regular weekly inspection and drying to prevent ear infections.

faq.question: Are Ariège Pointers good with families, other dogs, and training?
faq.answer: Yes, in active outdoor homes. They are stable, sociable with both humans and other dogs, docile, and easy to train—though their lively hunting drive and slight independence benefit from firm, consistent, positive training started early.

faq.question: What health precautions should Ariège Pointer owners keep in mind?
faq.answer: No breed-specific genetic diseases are formally documented due to its small modern population, so practical care focuses on general large drop-eared pointer precautions: pre-breeding hip (and elective elbow) radiographs, careful pedigree diversity planning, weekly drop-ear care, bloat (GDV) mealtime safety, and woodland parasite prevention.

overview.summary: The Ariegeois is an elegant, medium-sized French scent hound originating in the Midi-Pyrénées region. Bred to hunt hare and deer in difficult mountain terrain, it combines a fine scenting nose, an active bell-like voice, and notable stamina. In addition to its hunting heritage, its calm and affectionate nature makes it an agreeable companion for households with the time and dedication to provide daily physical activity and scent-focused mental stimulation.
overview.description: Lightly constructed yet robustly framed, the Ariegeois presents an aristocratic appearance characterised by clean, dry contours, a slightly arched muzzle, and long, supple, curled ears attached low. Its short, dense coat is predominantly pure white with well-defined jet-black patches, occasional subtle black ticking, and soft tan points on the cheeks and above the eyes. Built for swiftness and endurance rather than brute force, this medium-sized hound moves with smooth, effortless strides and carries its sabre-curved tail proudly. While dedicated and focused when pursuing a scent trail, it is gentle, companionable, and sociable when resting among humans and other hounds.
overview.history: Originating in the rugged department of Ariège in southwestern France at the beginning of the twentieth century, the breed was established by crossing local briquet hounds with larger traditional French scent hounds, notably the Grand Bleu de Gascogne and Grand Gascon-Saintongeois. The intention was to develop a lighter, swifter hound capable of navigating rocky Pyrenean foothills while retaining the superb scenting accuracy and resonant voice of its larger forebears. Formal international acceptance followed in 1954, securing its position as a distinctive medium-sized pack hound primarily valued for hunting hare.

funFacts: The Ariegeois was created in the Ariège department of southwestern France at the foot of the Pyrenees mountains.
The breed is grouped among medium-sized scent hounds suited for trailing game across varied ground.
Its ancestry combines the local Briquet hound with larger French hounds, specifically the Grand Bleu de Gascogne and Grand Gascon-Saintongeois.
Bred primarily for trailing hare, it is renowned for its light step, fast pace, and ringing musical voice during the chase.
Its white coat with sharply defined black markings and optional pale tan eye spots gives it an easily recognisable appearance in the field.

faq.question: What was the Ariegeois originally bred for?
faq.answer: The Ariegeois was developed in southern France as a versatile scent hound specialised in hunting hare, as well as tracking larger game such as deer and wild boar over rugged terrain.

faq.question: How big does an Ariegeois get?
faq.answer: Typical height at the withers ranges from 52 to 58 cm for males and 50 to 56 cm for females. While no official weight range is published in standard documentation, working adults generally weigh between 25 and 30 kg.

faq.question: What does the coat of an Ariegeois look like?
faq.answer: It has a short, fine, and dense coat that is predominantly white with crisp jet-black patches, occasional subtle black flecking, and delicate pale tan points on the cheeks and above the eyes.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Ariegeois require?
faq.answer: As an energetic working hound, it requires substantial daily physical activity, including long walks, jogging, or scent-tracking games in secure environments to channel its natural stamina.

faq.question: Is the Ariegeois suitable for apartment living?
faq.answer: Because of its high energy, strong tracking instincts, and vocal tendencies, an apartment is generally challenging unless an owner provides extensive daily outdoor exercise and enrichment.

faq.question: What is the life expectancy of an Ariegeois?
faq.answer: Documented breed profiles report a typical lifespan of 10 to 12 years when provided with appropriate nutrition, preventive veterinary care, and regular exercise.

faq.question: Does the Ariegeois have any known breed-specific health issues?
faq.answer: There are currently no formal epidemiological studies establishing common inherited conditions for the breed. Like all long-eared hunting dogs, regular attention should be paid to ear hygiene, skin checks, and maintaining athletic conditioning.

overview.summary: A sturdy, compact medium-sized northern French scent hound of classic briquet build, prized for its cold-trailing nose on hare, roe deer, and wild boar, its nearly flat hanging ears, and its dark-fawn tricolour coat.
overview.description: The Artois Hound (Chien d'Artois, historically called the Picard or Briquet d'Artois) is a well-constructed, muscular, medium-sized French pack hound built for methodical stamina and scenting precision rather than sheer speed. Standing 53 to 58 cm at the withers (with a ±1 cm tolerance) and weighing 28 to 30 kg on average, it embodies the compact, nearly square 'briquet' format (withers height to body length between 10:10 and 10:11). Its broad, strong, rounded skull with a flattened top and accentuated stop is slightly longer than its straight muzzle (roughly a 10:8 skull-to-muzzle ratio), whose overhanging upper lips give the tip of the foreface a square profile. Unlike Anglo-French hounds with narrower skulls and lower-set curled ears, the Artois Hound is distinguished by wide-set round dark brown eyes with a gentle, melancholic expression and broad, fairly thick, almost flat ears set at eye level and reaching the base of the black nose. Its short, thick, flat coat is always dark-fawn tricolour with a hare- or badger-like shading, a mantle or large patches, and a fawn head sometimes overlaid with black. Renowned as a meticulous 'closer' (rapprocheur) capable of puzzling out cold trails up to six hours old and giving voice in a high-pitched, melodious cry, it is a peaceful, gregarious pack mate and an affectionate, calm companion off duty.
overview.history: Originating in the historic northern French provinces of Artois and Picardy as a smaller descendant of the black Saint-Hubert hound, hounds of Artois are recorded as early as 1394 and 1410 ('valets de chiens d'Artois') in the hunting accounts of the Dukes of Burgundy Philip the Bold and John the Fearless, and in a 1431 chronicle of King Henry VI of England's coronation entry into Paris. Highly prized during the reigns of Henry IV and Louis XIII (who hunted hare, fox, and wild boar with his 'petits chiens d'Artois' between 1608 and 1610, and whose father received a prized pack from Prince Charles-Alexandre de Croÿ in 1609), the breed—also known as the Chien Picard—was celebrated by Jean de Sacquépée, seigneur de Sélincourt, in Le Parfait Chasseur (1683) for trailing a hare that had passed an hour earlier in dry weather. In Manuel de Vénerie Française (1890), Count Jean-Emmanuel Le Couteulx de Canteleu noted that although pure specimens had grown scarce through crossbreeding with Norman and English hounds, the Artois remained one of the finest hare hounds and placed examples in the Paris Jardin d'Acclimatation. Around 1888, Picardy breeder Ernest Levoir at the Château du Plouy in Domqueur (Somme) founded the Rallye-Scardon pack (motto: 'Chasse droit, Briquet d'Artois') to restore the ancestral type without English or heavy Norman blood, while Auguste and Albert Mallart in Barly (Pas-de-Calais) bred a competing line until 1932. In 1930, French hunting authorities dropped the term 'Briquet' in favour of 'Chien d'Artois', and the breed received definitive international recognition on 18 October 1963. Nearly extinct after the Second World War, the breed was rescued in the early 1970s by farmer-hunter André Audréchy of Buigny-lès-Gamaches in the Somme ('du Parc à Biches' kennel), joined around 1975 by Joseph Mancini in the Var and breeder Josette Pilat in Oise ('La Meute Saint-Louis' kennel and 'Piqu'Artois Saint-Louis' pack), leading to the modern standard published in July–November 1996.

physical.coatType: Short, thick, dense, and fairly flat single coat over fairly thick, moderately loose skin, with a few longer, coarser, slightly off-standing hairs ('épiée' / like ears of grain) along the underside of the tail toward the tip.
coatColors: Dark-fawn tricolour (fawn, black, and white) with a hare-toned or badger-toned ('poil de lièvre ou de blaireau') shading, carried as a mantle (blanket) or large patches

Fawn head, sometimes with a black overlay ('charbonnée'; bicolour white-and-orange coats without black/badger hair are not accepted, and invasive ticking or mottling on the white areas is a disqualifying fault)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; weekly brushing removes dead hairs and field debris.
physical.droolingLevel: Low (despite well-developed upper lips that give the muzzle tip a square profile, the skin is only moderately loose with very little throat dewlap).
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, muscular, nearly square 'briquet' outline (withers height to body length between 10:10 and 10:11, and chest depth equal to half the withers height) built for steady endurance rather than high speed
Strong, broad, rather short skull rounded at the sides and flattened on top (skull width to head length ~5:9) with an inconspicuous occipital peak and an accentuated stop

Straight, moderately elongated muzzle slightly shorter than the skull (muzzle-to-skull ratio ~8:10), with overhanging upper lips giving the muzzle tip a distinct square profile, clean cheeks, a strong black nose with wide nostrils, and a square-set scissor bite
Round, dark brown eyes set well apart and level with the head surface with concealed lower-lid conjunctiva, conveying a soft, melancholic expression
Broad, somewhat thick, almost flat hanging ears set at eye level with rounded tips, reaching the beginning of the nose (a key hallmark distinguishing it from Anglo-French hounds)
Moderately long, powerful neck with very little dewlap, broad well-supported back, slightly arched loin, deep chest reaching the elbows with well-sprung ribs, and full flanks

Strong, fairly long tail carried sickle-fashion (never falling forward over the back) and furnished toward the tip with slightly longer, coarser off-standing hairs like ears of grain ('épiée' / 'espiée')
Strong, vertical, round-boned limbs ending in tight, slightly elongated 'cat-like' feet with tough, compact black pads, and an even, effortless gait

Withers height of 53 to 58 cm with a ±1 cm tolerance (52–59 cm; French breed commentary favours 52–56 cm in males and 48–53 cm in females to preserve true briquet proportions) and average adult weight of 28 to 30 kg across both sexes

traits: Vigorous, hardy, and tireless in the field across plains, woods, and thickets
Exceptionally fine nose ('rapprocheur') capable of unravelling cold trails up to six hours old
Gregarious, peaceful, and non-quarrelsome in a pack (entering the pack from 6 months of age and coexisting peacefully with same-sex hounds)
Balanced, gentle, and affectionate with its handler, actively seeking petting and cuddles
More biddable, cooperative, and easy to lead than many other scent hounds
High-pitched, melodious hunting voice audible from afar (often preceded by soft 'meowing' whimpers when working a cold trail), yet quiet and rarely a nuisance barker off duty
Dislikes being tied or chained and requires space and regular field or outdoor exercise
Never aggressive or timid (aggression or shyness is a disqualifying fault)

exercise.level: High. Bred as an all-terrain endurance hound, it needs long daily country walks or runs, spacious enclosed turnout, and regular scent-tracking or hunting work—and must never be kept tied up.
activities: Small-pack or shooting-party scent hunting (chasse à tir / petite vénerie) on hare, wild boar, or roe deer
Cold-trail tracking, blood trailing, and structured nose-work games
Long, brisk daily country walks or hikes (ideally twice daily) on a leash or long line
Free movement and social interaction with packmates in a spacious, securely fenced rural enclosure
Recall, horn/whistle conditioning, and handler-focus exercises

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a rubber hound mitt or soft bristle brush to remove dead hair, dust, and plant debris and keep the short, thick coat clean.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when dirty or malodorous using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, rinsing thoroughly and drying the coat and hanging ears completely afterward.
notes: Inspect the long, broad, nearly flat hanging ears systematically after every outing in woods or brambles to remove burrs, grass awns, or ticks and check for moisture, redness, or odour.
Examine the short coat, skin, and tough black paw pads after field work for thorns, cuts, or external parasites.
Trim the nails whenever natural wear does not keep them short.
Brush the teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste to prevent tartar accumulation.

training.difficulty: Moderate for experienced hound handlers. National breed guidance notes that the Artois Hound is intelligent, gentle, and more obedient and easier to lead than many other scent hounds, though dominant individuals require a 'firm hand in a velvet glove' and early recall training.
tips: Begin recall conditioning and basic obedience early in puppyhood, combining calm firmness with kindness ('an iron hand in a velvet glove') so the dog's natural willingness to please develops.
For working hounds, gentle scent-search initiation can begin at 4 to 5 months of age in a safely enclosed brushy paddock, and young hounds can integrate into an adult pack from 6 months of age.
Never tether or chain an Artois Hound, and always use a leash or secure fencing in open areas where a fresh game trail can override recall.
Provide structured olfactory enrichment—such as laid scent trails or tracking games—if the dog is not actively hunted.
training.socialization: Bred to live and hunt harmoniously in packs—including peacefully with hounds of the same sex—the Artois Hound is naturally dog-sociable. Introduce puppies early and positively to household routines, varied people, children, handling, and rural environments, while supervising around small non-canine pets due to its strong hunting instinct.

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low when isolated alone. As a deeply gregarious pack hound that loves living with fellow hounds and stays closely attached to its owner, the Artois Hound thrives in a spacious rural enclosure with packmates or attentive human company and does poorly if isolated or tied up.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality commercial diet (or a veterinarian-supplemented home-prepared ration with added calcium and vitamins) tailored to life stage, body condition, and seasonal hunting workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Two substantial measured meals daily until the dog finishes growing at around 12 months of age.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete, balanced industrial diet suited to growth and adult maintenance—or, if feeding a traditional home-prepared ration, supplement with appropriate vitamins and calcium under veterinary guidance. Because the Artois Hound continues growing until about 12 months of age, provide two substantial measured meals per day throughout its first year. In adulthood, increase daily rations during active hunting seasons to match higher energy expenditure, then return to maintenance portions during the off-season so the dog stays lean and muscular around 28 to 30 kg. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Provide two substantial measured meals daily during the growth period up to 12 months of age.
If using a home-prepared (ménagère) diet rather than complete commercial food, add veterinary-recommended vitamin and calcium supplementation.
Increase energy intake during active hunting seasons and reduce portions in the off-season to prevent excess weight.
Allow rest before and after meals rather than feeding immediately before or after intense field runs.
Monitor body condition regularly so the flanks remain full without obesity.
nutrition.note: While two substantial meals daily during the first year of growth are recommended for puppies, adult and senior meal frequencies and exact calorie targets should be individualized with a veterinarian.

health.overview: A hardy, rustic, and solid working hound (with typical longevity estimates ranging from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years), the Artois Hound has no documented breed-specific hereditary disease prevalence profile or mandatory genetic testing panel. Conformation and breeding rules mandate that only functionally and clinically healthy dogs with breed-typical morphology be used for reproduction, and explicitly disqualify any dog exhibiting a detectable disabling hereditary defect, anatomical anomaly, frail limbs, overshot or undershot jaw (prognathism), very light eyes, or behavioural abnormality. As with other active, drop-eared pack hounds worked across fields, woods, and brambles, everyday veterinary care centres on post-outing ear canal hygiene, parasite and infectious-disease prevention, dental care, and field-injury checks.
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding stock is functionally and clinically healthy, free of disqualifying hereditary or anatomical defects, and has a normal scissor bite.
Inspect the long, broad hanging ears, short coat, and black paw pads after every outing in woods, fields, or thickets to remove ticks, grass awns, burrs, or thorns and prevent otitis externa.
Keep vaccinations, deworming, and external parasite prevention strictly up to date—especially for hounds living in packs or working in wildlife areas.
Maintain a lean, athletic body weight (typically 28–30 kg) by adjusting food intake between hunting and rest seasons.
Brush the teeth frequently with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary wellness and oral examinations.
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth frequently with dog-specific toothpaste and have the mouth examined at routine veterinary visits. Conformation rules require a regular scissor bite with the upper incisors closely overlapping the lower incisors and set squarely in the jaws, while overshot or undershot jaws (prognathism) are disqualifying faults.
health.earCare: Inspect the broad, nearly flat hanging ears after every field outing and during weekly brushing for plant debris, parasites, excess wax, redness, or foul odour. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and dry the ears thoroughly after wet weather.
health.skinCare: Examine the short, dense tricolour coat, fairly thick skin, and compact black paw pads during weekly brushing and after runs through brambles or forest cover for scratches, ticks, burrs, or interdigital foreign bodies.

idealFor: Hunters (including novice hare hunters as well as wild-boar and roe-deer hunters) seeking a steady, biddable, cold-trailing pack or shooting hound
Active rural households with a large, securely fenced garden or spacious enclosure
Scent-work and tracking enthusiasts who can provide long daily countryside outings
Multi-dog homes or pack-hound keepers seeking a peaceful, non-quarrelsome hound that gets along well with peers
notIdealFor: Urban or apartment dwellers—national breed guidance states that this country hunting hound is not made for city life or narrow quarters
Anyone who would tie or chain a dog or leave a single hound isolated without companionship or space
Sedentary households unable to provide long daily walks and scent-based outlets
Owners expecting reliable off-leash recall in unfenced wildlife areas without dedicated training

funFacts: Records of 'valets de chiens d'Artois' appear as early as 1394 and 1410 in the hunting accounts of the Dukes of Burgundy (Philip the Bold and John the Fearless), and in 1431 a live stag hunt with Artois hounds was staged along the streets of Paris during the coronation entry of young King Henry VI of England.

Formerly called the Picard or Chien Picard, the breed was a favourite of Kings Henry IV and Louis XIII; in 1683, royal huntsman Jean de Sacquépée, seigneur de Sélincourt, marvelled at seeing these hounds puzzle out the trail of a hare that had passed an hour earlier in dry weather.

Around 1888, Picardy breeder Ernest Levoir established the famous 'Rallye-Scardon' pack at the Château du Plouy in the Somme under the rhyming French motto 'Chasse droit, Briquet d'Artois' ('Hunt straight, Briquet of Artois').

Feared extinct after the Second World War, the breed was rescued in the 1970s by Somme farmer André Audréchy (in the very same Gamaches area where seventeenth-century authors had praised Picard hounds), joined by Joseph Mancini and Josette Pilat.

Renowned as a cold-trail specialist ('rapprocheur') able to pick up trails up to six hours old, an Artois Hound often emits high-pitched whimpers—humourously described by breeder Josette Pilat as 'meowing' ('miauler')—when working a cold scent before bursting into full, resonant voice once the trail is hot.

A matched pack of just six to eight tricolour Artois Hounds is traditionally considered sufficient to delight the most demanding huntmaster, and although bred for hare, roughly three-quarters of working Artois Hounds in France today are used on wild boar.

faq.question: Where does the Artois Hound come from, and what are its historical names?
faq.answer: The Artois Hound (officially the Chien d'Artois) originates from the Artois and Picardy regions of northern France. Historically, it was also known as the Picard, Chien Picard, and—until French hunting authorities dropped the term 'Briquet' in 1930—the Briquet d'Artois.

faq.question: What was the Artois Hound bred to do, and how is it used today?
faq.answer: It was bred as a medium-sized 'briquet' scent hound for hunting with the gun (chasse à tir) and in small packs (petite vénerie) of six to eight hounds. Prized for its fine nose and steady endurance as a cold-trail finder ('rapprocheur' capable of following trails up to six hours old), it outwits hare on open plains, drives roe deer through open woods, and flushes or holds wild boar in thickets. Today, roughly three-quarters of working Artois Hounds in France hunt wild boar, and the breed is also appreciated in Greece, Italy, and Spain for hare hunting.

faq.question: How large is an adult Artois Hound?
faq.answer: Conformation rules specify a withers height of 53 to 58 cm (with a ±1 cm tolerance, or 52 to 59 cm) and an average weight of 28 to 30 kg for both males and females. In France, an ideal working height of 52 to 56 cm for males and 48 to 53 cm for females is favoured to preserve the breed's compact, nearly square 'briquet' proportions.

faq.question: How can you tell an Artois Hound apart from an Anglo-Français de Petite Vénerie?
faq.answer: The Artois Hound is more compact and cobby, with a broader, rounded skull flattened on top, a muzzle slightly shorter than the skull (about an 8:10 ratio) squared off at the tip by overhanging upper lips, and broad, thick, almost flat ears set at eye level. By contrast, the Anglo-Français de Petite Vénerie has a narrower skull equal in length to the muzzle (1:1), drier lips, and lower-set, thinner, slightly curled ears.

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted in the Artois Hound?
faq.answer: The short, thick, flat coat must always be dark-fawn tricolour (fawn, black, and white) with a hare-toned or badger-toned shading, carried as a mantle or large patches, with a fawn head that is sometimes overlaid with black ('charbonnée'). Bicolour white-and-orange coats without black/badger hair are not accepted, and heavy ticking or mottling on the white areas is a disqualifying fault.

faq.question: Is the Artois Hound suitable for city or apartment living?
faq.answer: No. This country hunting hound is not suited to urban or apartment living, dislikes confined spaces, and must never be kept tied up. It needs a rural home with a large, securely fenced enclosure or kennel, ideally with canine companions, and long daily country outings.

faq.question: What is the Artois Hound's temperament like with people and other dogs?
faq.answer: Off the hunting field, the Artois Hound is calm, gentle, affectionate, and fond of cuddles, and barks very little at home. It is more obedient and easier to lead than many other scent hounds—making it popular even with novice hare hunters—and is exceptionally sociable and non-quarrelsome with other dogs, integrating into packs from 6 months of age and living peacefully with same-sex kennelmates.

faq.question: Does the Artois Hound have known hereditary diseases or a fixed lifespan?
faq.answer: A breed-specific list of hereditary diseases and a single definitive lifespan range have not been established (so those structured fields are kept empty or null), though typical longevity estimates in France range from 10 to 13 or 12 to 14 years. Breeding rules disqualify any dog with a detectable disabling hereditary defect, anatomical anomaly, or bite malocclusion, and routine care focuses on ear checks after field outings, dental hygiene, parasite prevention, and balanced nutrition.

overview.summary: A compact, hard-muscled Australian cattle-driving dog built for long-distance outback endurance, known for its rain-repelling blue or red speckled double coat, upright prick ears, sharp problem-solving mind, and intense loyalty.
overview.description: Shaped for arduous stock work across open ranges and tight yards, the Australian Cattle Dog packs dense muscle, agility, and staying power into a balanced frame slightly longer than it is tall. Its smooth, odor-free double coat pairs a close, dense undercoat with straight, hard outer guard hairs that shed rain, appearing in blue, blue-mottled, or blue-speckled patterns with tan markings, or in an even red speckle. A broad skull narrows cleanly to a strong, deep muzzle beneath wide-set, thick pointed prick ears, while dark brown oval eyes carry a keen, watchful look around strangers. At home, the breed bonds closely with its people and thrives when given structured daily work, sport, or vigorous exercise.
overview.history: As cattle stations expanded across New South Wales and Queensland in the nineteenth century, settlers found that imported British herding dogs struggled with Australia's heat, vast distances, and semi-wild horned herds. In the 1830s and 1840s, pastoralist Thomas Hall crossed smooth blue-merle Scottish Highland Collies with native Australian Dingoes to create quiet, tireless cattle drivers known as Hall's Heelers. Later breeders in Sydney, including Jack and Harry Bagust, refined the type by introducing Dalmatian lines—contributing to the breed's affinity for horses and protective loyalty—and black-and-tan Australian Kelpie blood for sharper working focus. Robert Kaleski wrote down the earliest formal breed description in 1893, which gained approval in Australia in 1903. Today, the breed continues to work livestock while excelling worldwide in dog sports and active family homes.

health.overview: The Australian Cattle Dog is a hardy, long-lived working breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 16 years. Scientifically established hereditary concerns include progressive rod-cone degeneration (prcd-PRA, caused by an autosomal recessive PRCD gene mutation), primary lens luxation (PLL), and congenital sensorineural deafness associated with white piebald pigmentation—all of which can be screened via DNA or hearing tests—alongside hip and elbow dysplasia.
commonConditions: Progressive rod-cone degeneration (prcd-PRA) — a scientifically established autosomal recessive retinal disease caused by a PRCD gene mutation that leads to progressive vision loss; preventable in litters through DNA testing
Primary lens luxation (PLL) — an inherited weakening of the fibers holding the eye's lens in place, risking painful lens dislocation and glaucoma, screenable via DNA test
Congenital sensorineural deafness — hereditary partial or complete hearing loss linked to piebald coat genetics, detectable early in puppies via Brainstem Auditory Evoked Response (BAER) testing
Hip dysplasia — developmental hip joint malformation that can lead to arthritis, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Elbow dysplasia — developmental elbow joint abnormalities that can cause forelimb lameness, screened radiographically prior to breeding
Athletic soft-tissue injuries — occasional knee ligament or paw injuries in high-drive working or sport dogs, reduced by lean conditioning and sensible warm-ups
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have completed BAER hearing tests, DNA tests for prcd-PRA and PLL, radiographic hip and elbow evaluations, and specialist ophthalmologist eye exams.
Keep adult weight lean and muscular to reduce joint stress during running and jumping.
Check erect ears regularly for debris or wax and brush teeth consistently.
Maintain annual veterinary wellness visits, vaccinations, and year-round parasite control.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Specialist veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination
Brainstem Auditory Evoked Response (BAER) hearing evaluation
DNA test for Primary Lens Luxation (PLL)

health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary dental checks to protect the strong scissor bite and gums.
health.earCare: Check the wide-set prick ears weekly for dust, foreign debris, or wax buildup, wiping gently with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser when needed.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin beneath the dense double coat during weekly brushing for ticks, burrs, or trail scrapes, avoiding frequent bathing that strips natural weather-resistant oils.

funFacts: Australian Cattle Dog puppies are born white—except for any solid head or body patches—with their signature blue mottling or red speckling starting to appear around three weeks of age.
Puppies start life with folded drop ears that stand upright gradually, sometimes taking up to six or seven months to perk fully.
Many individuals carry a small white star or streak on the forehead known as the Bentley Mark, linked in breed lore to an early Australian foundation stud owned by Tom Bentley.

A female Australian Cattle Dog named Bluey from Rochester, Victoria, lived 29 years and 5 months (1910–1939) while working cattle and sheep for nearly twenty years, remaining one of the oldest verified dogs on record.
When working cattle, the breed silently nips low at the weight-bearing hind hoof and immediately crouches flat so any retaliatory kick sails safely overhead.
Despite popular myths, blue and red Australian Cattle Dogs belong to the exact same breed and show no difference in temperament.

faq.question: What kind of dog is an Australian Cattle Dog?
faq.answer: Also called a Blue Heeler, Red Heeler, or Queensland Heeler, it is a medium-sized, compact, hard-muscled herding breed developed in Australia to drive cattle across rugged terrain, prized for its stamina, sharp intelligence, and fierce loyalty.

faq.question: What is the difference between a Blue Heeler and a Red Heeler?
faq.answer: Only their coat color. Both are the exact same breed—the Australian Cattle Dog—with identical structure and temperament; blues carry black hairs mixed through white with tan markings, while reds are evenly red-speckled.

faq.question: How tall and heavy does an Australian Cattle Dog get?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 46 to 51 cm at the withers and females stand 43 to 48 cm, with adults typically weighing 35 to 50 lb in lean, muscular working condition.

faq.question: How long do Australian Cattle Dogs live?
faq.answer: They are known for strong longevity, typically living 12 to 16 years with lean conditioning, regular exercise, and routine veterinary care.

faq.question: How much grooming and shedding should I expect?
faq.answer: Their smooth, odor-free double coat needs only a quick weekly brush and an occasional bath, though they blow their dense undercoat once or twice a year and need brushing every few days during shedding seasons.

faq.question: Can an Australian Cattle Dog live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Their intense stamina, alertness, and need for a daily job and 90 to 120 minutes of vigorous activity fit much better in a house with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Are Australian Cattle Dogs good with children?
faq.answer: They can be loyal companions in active, experienced families with older, respectful children, but early training is essential to redirect natural heel-nipping instincts away from running feet.

faq.question: Why are Australian Cattle Dog puppies born white?
faq.answer: White birth coloration (apart from solid head or body patches) comes from piebald spotting genetics inherited from Dalmatian crosses in the breed's history; their blue or red speckling begins showing at about three weeks old.

faq.question: How much daily exercise does an Australian Cattle Dog need?
faq.answer: Plan on 90 to 120 minutes of vigorous physical and mental activity every day, such as running, hiking, herding, agility, obedience, or scent games.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for breeding Australian Cattle Dogs?
faq.answer: Core pre-breeding checks include hip and elbow radiographic evaluations, a specialist ophthalmologist eye exam, BAER hearing testing for congenital deafness, and DNA tests for prcd-PRA and primary lens luxation (PLL).

overview.summary: A lithe, athletic, and seemingly tireless medium-sized Australian sheepdog prized for razor-sharp independent livestock control, effortless sudden turns at full speed, and loyal, eager devotion to an active handler.
overview.description: The Australian Kelpie is a supple, hard-muscled, medium-sized herding dog built for relentless all-day work across sprawling, sun-baked pastures and crowded livestock yards alike. Slightly longer than tall in a classic 10:9 ratio, its clean, refined bone and deep, muscular chest carry zero coarseness or bulk, allowing it to pivot sharply at full speed and leap effortlessly across the backs of tightly packed sheep. Its cleanly chiselled, slightly fox-like head pairs a broad, gently rounded skull and pronounced stop with tight lips, a strong scissor bite, eager almond-shaped brown eyes, and wide-set, fine-tipped prick ears angled outward. Cloaked in a short, dense, rain-resisting double coat—measuring 2 to 3 cm over the body with a protective neck ruff, light thigh breeching, and a well-brushed low-set tail reaching the hock—it appears in black, black and tan, red, red and tan, fawn, chocolate, or smoke blue. Mild, tractable, and deeply devoted to its owner, the Kelpie flourishes when given purposeful daily physical and mental tasks, settling peacefully indoors after hard work yet growing restless or stressed in an under-stimulated home.
overview.history: As nineteenth-century pastoral expansion opened vast sheep stations across New South Wales and Victoria—some spanning millions of acres with flocks numbering in the hundreds of thousands—Australian graziers required a tough, heat-tolerant herder able to work huge mobs of sheep with minimal human direction. Early settlers drew on black-and-tan working collies imported from Scotland, selectively breeding for endurance, independence, and grit. Around 1872, stockman Jack Gleeson acquired a black-and-tan female puppy from George Robertson's Warrock Station near Casterton, Victoria, naming her 'Kelpie' after the water spirit of Celtic folklore. Mated to Caesar, a son of imported Scottish collies Brutus and Jennie, Gleeson's Kelpie produced a black-and-tan daughter known as King's Kelpie, who famously won or tied the prestigious Forbes sheepdog trial in New South Wales during the 1870s. Demand for 'Kelpie's pups' swept rural Australia, while a standout black descendant named Barb inspired the longtime nickname 'Barb' for solid black Kelpies. The breed's first written blueprint appeared in 1902, and definitive international recognition arrived in September 1973. Over the twentieth century, Australian Kelpies diverged into exhibition/companion lines and dedicated Working Kelpie strains, while gaining widespread international acclaim—especially in Scandinavia—as elite herding, tracking, rescue, obedience, and agility dogs.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate; exceptionally sharp, eager to work, and fast to learn—requiring an engaged owner because it learns unwanted habits just as quickly as polished cues
tips: Use upbeat, fast-paced, reward-based training paired with purposeful jobs such as agility, obedience, rally, or scent work to satisfy its busy mind.
Explicitly teach a calm 'settle' cue and off-switch habits from early puppyhood so high drive does not spiral into chronic stress.
Tailor puppy walks to age-appropriate lengths even though agile Kelpie puppies look like miniature adults.
Redirect instinctive herding impulses around running children, cyclists, or pets early into structured games and rock-solid recall.
training.socialization: Early, calm, structured exposure to busy environments, unfamiliar people, friendly dogs, children, and quiet resting drills helps build a confident, stress-resilient adult partner.

climates: Warm, dry, and sun-exposed climates—engineered for long working days across Australia's hot pastoral plains (still requiring shade, rest breaks, and cool water during peak heat)
Temperate four-season climates with active outdoor access
Cool, rainy climates are handled well during active work thanks to its flat rain-resisting double coat, though warm indoor shelter is needed in freezing rest periods
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; prefers active partnership and company over spending entire days locked alone indoors, quickly developing restlessness or stress when left isolated without daily jobs.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for medium-sized, high-energy working and herding breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age to support steady, lean skeletal and muscular growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain high daily energy and steady digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for reduced activity and joint and cardiac wellness.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately to maintain the Kelpie's hard, lithe, athletic working build without excess fat over its joints. High-output working farm dogs and agility competitors require higher caloric and protein density than moderately active household dogs. Divide adult food into two daily meals, monitor training-treat calories closely, and keep clean, fresh drinking water continuously available.
considerations: Count all training rewards inside the daily calorie budget to prevent weight gain during intensive obedience or agility training.
Keep growing puppies lean on a balanced medium-breed growth formula to support sound hip and elbow development.
Puppies diagnosed with inborn lipid malabsorption (ILM / lipase 1 deficiency) require specialized veterinary nutritional support and pancreatic enzyme supplementation during early growth.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric demands differ substantially between working station sheepdogs and sport-companion Kelpies. Consult a veterinarian to establish individual feeding quantities.

health.overview: The Australian Kelpie is widely regarded as a hardy, athletic, and generally healthy medium-sized herding breed with a typical life expectancy of 10 to 13 years (and working lines often reaching 12 to 15 years). Peer-reviewed veterinary genetics research and European breed-health monitoring identify three key hereditary priorities for breeding stock: autosomal-recessive Cerebellar Abiotrophy (CA, linked in 2022 research to two major risk loci on CFA20 and CFA9 including a VMP1 candidate variant), congenital Inborn Lipid Malabsorption (ILM / lipase 1 deficiency in young puppies, with a validated Kelpie DNA test), and Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA / NHEJ1 deletion confirmed in certain European lines). Routine breeding oversight also tracks hip dysplasia (low-to-moderate incidence, averaging roughly 12% in Swedish 2011–2015 screened cohorts and mostly mild), occasional elbow dysplasia and patellar luxation, and acquired adult mitral valve heart disease.
commonConditions: Cerebellar Abiotrophy (CA) — a progressive, incurable autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disorder causing cerebellar neuron loss, tremors, and severe ataxia/loss of balance; a 2022 University of Sydney genomic study identified two major risk loci in Working Kelpies—an early-onset form on CFA20 visible within days to weeks of birth and a later-onset form on CFA9 associated with a candidate VMP1 missense variant (p.P160Q)—with marker/risk DNA testing used to guide breeding in both Working and Australian Kelpies

Inborn Lipid Malabsorption (ILM / Lipase 1 deficiency) — a congenital autosomal-recessive digestive defect documented in Australian Kelpies in Australia and Europe where newborn puppies lack functional lipase 1 for early fat absorption, causing stunted growth until lipase 2 activates around 12 weeks of age; preventable via a breed-validated DNA test and often manageable with early veterinary enzyme and dietary support

Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA, NHEJ1-related) — a congenital developmental eye defect (choroidal hypoplasia) confirmed via DNA testing for the 7.8-kb NHEJ1 deletion in a Polish Australian Kelpie breeding line, underscoring the value of puppy eye exams and DNA screening in international lines

Hip dysplasia (HD), elbow dysplasia (ED), and patellar luxation — developmental orthopaedic conditions occurring at relatively low rates (Swedish 2011–2015 screened cohorts averaged ~12% HD, mostly mild, with isolated ED and patellar luxation cases), monitored through pre-breeding radiographic evaluations

Acquired cardiac disease (myxomatous mitral valve insufficiency / endocardiosis) — Swedish veterinary insurance data notes slightly above-average heart-disease diagnoses in Australian Kelpies (though lower cardiac mortality than average), supporting routine veterinary auscultation in adult and senior years
Fieldwork trauma and heat stress — paw pad wear, thorn injuries, sprains, and overexertion during intense hot-weather herding or dog sports
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for documented parental health records, including official radiographic hip (and ideally elbow) evaluations, specialist veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams, and breed-validated DNA testing for Cerebellar Abiotrophy (CA), Inborn Lipid Malabsorption (ILM), and Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA).
Be cautious with unvalidated multi-breed commercial DNA panels that test markers not established in Kelpies; prioritize tests validated specifically for the breed.
Keep the dog lean, build sports and running fitness gradually, and avoid over-exercising young puppies while joints mature.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness exams (including cardiac auscultation in middle-aged and senior dogs) and keep vaccinations and year-round parasite prevention current.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation (and elective elbow dysplasia evaluation) prior to breeding
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
DNA test for Inborn Lipid Malabsorption (ILM / lipase 1 deficiency)
DNA marker/risk test for Cerebellar Abiotrophy (CA)
DNA test for Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA / NHEJ1 deletion), particularly in European or internationally imported lines
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental checks to keep the sound, evenly spaced scissor bite and gums healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the wide-set, hair-furnished erect ears weekly for dust, excess wax, grass seeds, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Run hands over the short, flat double coat after pasture or woodland outings to catch ticks, burrs, thorns, or minor scrapes early.

idealFor: Sheep, cattle, and livestock farmers needing a tough, independent, heat-hardy herding dog capable of working open plains and crowded yards
Highly active runners, hikers, and dog-sport enthusiasts competing in agility, obedience, rally, flyball, disc, tracking, or search-and-rescue
Committed active families with spacious fenced yards and older, respectful children who enjoy daily structured training and exercise
Handlers who value a low-grooming, weatherproof short double coat and an intensely loyal, razor-sharp working partner
notIdealFor: Apartment dwellers or sedentary households hoping for a low-energy casual pet—the breed requires space and real daily jobs
First-time or passive owners unprepared to teach calm off-switch habits and channel relentless herding drive
Households leaving an active dog confined alone all day without physical or mental engagement
Families with unsupervised toddlers or loose small pets that may trigger strong herding and chasing instincts

funFacts: One of the Kelpie's signature livestock-yard manoeuvres is 'backing': leaping effortlessly onto the backs of tightly packed sheep and running right across the flock to break up jams from the far side.

The breed takes its name from 'Kelpie,' a black-and-tan puppy acquired around 1872 in Victoria and named after the shapeshifting water spirit of Scottish folklore—and her daughter, King's Kelpie, launched the breed's fame by excelling at the prestigious Forbes sheepdog trial in New South Wales.
Solid black Kelpies were long nicknamed 'Barbs' after a celebrated early black male named for The Barb, a champion black racehorse that won Australia's Melbourne Cup in 1866.

Despite a persistent nineteenth-century legend claiming Kelpies carried Australian Dingo blood for their upright ears and tawny-red coats, a 2019 University of Sydney genomic study of external morphology traits found no shared dingo genetic basis for those coat and ear features.
In rural Australia, a classic tribute sums up the breed's economic value to the wool industry: a single skilled Kelpie working a sheep mob is said to do the work of two riders on horseback.

faq.question: What is an Australian Kelpie?
faq.answer: The Australian Kelpie is a lithe, tireless medium-sized herding dog developed in nineteenth-century Australia from working Scottish collies to muster and control massive sheep flocks across open plains and stockyards.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an Australian Kelpie?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 46 to 51 cm at the withers and adult females stand 43 to 48 cm, with adults typically weighing between 35 and 50 pounds.

faq.question: How long does an Australian Kelpie live?
faq.answer: With balanced nutrition, vigorous daily exercise, and routine veterinary care, the Australian Kelpie has a typical life expectancy of 10 to 13 years.

faq.question: Can an Australian Kelpie live in an apartment or purely as a casual pet?
faq.answer: No. Although a well-exercised Kelpie has a calm indoor 'off switch,' its almost limitless working stamina and intense need for daily physical and mental jobs make it unsuited to apartment living or sedentary companion-only homes.

faq.question: Are Australian Kelpies good family dogs?
faq.answer: They are loyal, mild-tempered, and affectionate in very active families who love training and outdoor sports. Supervision is important around young children and other pets because strong herding instincts can prompt circling or nipping at running heels.

faq.question: How much grooming and shedding should I expect from an Australian Kelpie?
faq.answer: Grooming is minimal: weekly brushing or combing clears dead hair from its short, flat, rain-resisting double coat (which sheds moderately), paired with occasional baths, nail trims, and weekly ear checks.

faq.question: Are Australian Kelpies easy to train?
faq.answer: Yes—they are exceptionally intelligent, responsive, and eager for a job in agility, obedience, rally, tracking, or herding. Because they learn so quickly and can grow stressed if mismanaged, consistent positive training and early calm-relaxation habits are essential.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for an Australian Kelpie?
faq.answer: Generally a healthy, rugged breed, its main documented hereditary priorities include Cerebellar Abiotrophy (CA), congenital Inborn Lipid Malabsorption (ILM / lipase 1 deficiency in puppies), Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA) in certain European lines, mild-to-moderate hip dysplasia, isolated elbow or patella issues, and adult mitral valve heart monitoring.

overview.summary: A compact, spirited Australian toy terrier distinguished by its straight, glossy blue-and-tan silky coat and keen, alert expression, packing genuine terrier energy into a small frame.
overview.description: Moderately low-set and slightly longer than tall, the Australian Silky Terrier wears a fine, straight, parted coat in crisp shades of blue and tan. Though sized as a household companion, it carries the bold curiosity, quickness, and rodent-hunting heritage of its terrier forebears. Owners should expect daily interactive play, consistent reward-based training, and frequent brushing to keep the silky coat tangle-free.
overview.history: Bred in Australia—historically around Sydney, earning the early nickname Sydney Silky—the breed emerged from crosses between local Australian Terriers and imported Yorkshire Terriers in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Breeders aimed to pair the Yorkshire Terrier's glossy blue-and-tan coat with sturdier terrier substance, achieving a unified national breed type by the mid-twentieth century.
overview.originalPurpose: A small companion terrier capable of keeping homes and yards clear of domestic rodents.

Obedience, agility, rally, and trick-training partner

Free, true movement without coat dragging on the floor

traits: Alert and keenly observant
Lively, playful, and curious

Affectionate and responsive with family members
Intelligent and quick to learn through positive reinforcement
Vocal watchdog with lingering small-prey chase instincts

exercise.level: Moderate — satisfied by daily walks, interactive toy play, sniffing, and brief training games tailored to age and fitness.
activities: Daily leashed walks on a well-fitted harness
Interactive indoor fetch and puzzle-toy play
Reward-based trick, obedience, or nose-work sessions
Supervised yard exploration inside secure fencing

grooming.level: High when kept in full coat; moderate with a shorter pet trim
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb several times a week—ideally daily in full coat—paying close attention behind the ears, under the legs, and around harness contact points.
grooming.bathing: Bathe periodically with a gentle canine shampoo, conditioning and drying carefully while combing out tangles before they set.
notes: Check skin, ears, eyes, and paws during routine brushing.
Keep nails trimmed and brush teeth regularly.
A practical puppy or pet trim reduces daily combing while altering the traditional long silhouette.

training.difficulty: Moderate — bright and eager to engage, though terrier independence benefits from upbeat consistency.
tips: Keep sessions short, varied, and reward-based.
Teach a calm 'quiet' cue early to manage alert barking.
Practise recall in secure spaces before trusting off-leash cues around small animals.
training.socialization: Provide gradual, positive exposure to varied people, calm dogs, grooming handling, and everyday noises from puppyhood.

climates: Adapts well to most climates indoors with appropriate shelter.
Provide shade, fresh water, and cooler walking hours in hot weather.
Dry the fine single coat thoroughly after rain or cold, damp outings.
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate when conditioned gradually — prefers regular company and enrichment, as prolonged boredom can trigger barking.

nutrition.dietType: A complete and balanced commercial diet formulated for small-breed dogs according to life stage and body condition.
nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily portions by body condition score rather than guesswork, keeping treats modest and fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Small-breed formulas offer appropriately sized kibble and calorie density.
Avoid overfeeding, as excess weight strains knees and joints.
Introduce food transitions gradually and consult a veterinarian for persistent digestive signs.
nutrition.note: No universal meal frequency or gram ration applies to every Australian Silky Terrier; tailor portions with veterinary guidance.

health.overview: Australian Silky Terriers are generally long-lived companions, though breed profiles note concerns involving the kneecaps, hip joints, eyes, and teeth. These represent potential risks to monitor rather than inevitable conditions, so routine veterinary exams and responsible breeder health checks are essential.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation — slipping of the kneecap reported as a concern in small terriers.
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease — a developmental hip-joint disorder noted in toy breeds.
Eye disorders including juvenile cataracts — monitored through veterinary eye exams.
Dental and periodontal disease — common in small breeds without regular oral care.
preventiveCare: Schedule routine veterinary wellness exams, vaccinations, and parasite control.
Ask breeders about parental patella and eye health history.
Maintain lean body weight and seek veterinary care promptly for skipping gaits, limping, or eye cloudiness.

Periodic veterinary eye examination
Review of parental and close-relative health records
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week with canine toothpaste and arrange periodic professional veterinary dental cleanings.
health.earCare: Inspect the small upright ears regularly for wax, redness, or odour, seeking veterinary advice if irritation appears.
health.skinCare: Check the skin beneath the parted coat during brushing for tangles, harness rubbing, redness, or itching.

funFacts: The Australian Silky Terrier was developed in Australia and was known early on as the Sydney Silky.
Puppies are born black and tan, gradually developing their signature blue-and-tan adult coat by around 18 months of age.
Though grouped with toy breeds, it retains the alert confidence and rodent-hunting spirit of a true terrier.
Despite its glamorous silky coat, the breed is built for free, unobstructed movement rather than floor-length dragging hair.

faq.question: Is the Australian Silky Terrier suited to apartment living?
faq.answer: Yes—its compact size and moderate exercise needs fit apartment life well when paired with daily walks, play, and gentle quiet-cue training.

faq.question: How much grooming does an Australian Silky Terrier need?
faq.answer: A full-length coat requires frequent—often daily—brushing and combing to stay tangle-free, though a shorter pet trim simplifies upkeep.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an Australian Silky Terrier?
faq.answer: Males typically stand 23–26 cm at the withers (with females slightly smaller), and adults generally weigh around 3.5–5 kg.

faq.question: What is the breed's expected lifespan?
faq.answer: Australian Silky Terriers typically live about 10–15 years with attentive veterinary and dental care.

faq.question: Do Australian Silky Terriers shed heavily?
faq.answer: No—they are generally low shedders, though their fine single coat still needs regular brushing to prevent mats.

faq.question: Are Australian Silky Terriers good with children?
faq.answer: They can be affectionate family companions when children are taught gentle handling and interactions are supervised to protect their small frame.

faq.question: Which health issues should owners watch for?
faq.answer: Watch for skipping or limping (which can signal patellar luxation or hip issues), eye cloudiness, and dental tartar buildup, scheduling regular veterinary checkups.
