overview.summary: A massive, noble, and powerfully built scent hound originating from the Ardennes of Belgium, world-renowned for its unmatched cold-trail scenting ability, long velvety curling ears, abundant head and neck folds, and gentle, sensitive nature at home.
overview.description: The Bloodhound—officially known in continental Europe as the Chien de Saint-Hubert and historically celebrated as the 'Sleuth Hound'—is the most powerful and substantial of all scent hounds. Built on a harmonious rectangular outline (roughly a 10:9 ratio of body length to withers height, with chest depth equal to half the withers height), it combines heavy, round bone and strong muscle with a solemn, dignified bearing and a free, elastic, slightly rolling trot capable of covering ground effortlessly for hours. Its majestic head—measuring 30 cm (12 inches) or more in adult males and 28 cm (11 inches) or more in females—is narrow relative to its length, crowned by a pronounced occipital peak, and draped in thin, supple skin that falls into deep forehead and cheek ridges and a pronounced double dewlap when the nose is lowered to the ground. Extremely long, low-set, velvety ears curl inward and backward past the tip of the nose, working alongside the loose facial folds to funnel and trap scent particles. Off duty, the Bloodhound is a gentle, placid, and affectionate companion that gets along well with people and other dogs, yet on a trail it becomes single-minded and unstoppable. Prospective owners must be prepared for heavy drooling (including 15-foot 'slobber missiles' when the dog shakes its head), a resonant baying voice, a high physical fence, leashed exercise, and daily cleaning of the ears and facial folds.
overview.history: One of the oldest scent-hunting breeds, the modern Bloodhound traces its primary lineage to the Ardennes forest region of Belgium, where black and black-and-tan pack hounds were bred from the seventh century onward by the monk Hubert (later Bishop of Liège and canonised as Saint Hubert, the patron saint of hunters) and maintained for centuries by monks at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert to hunt wild boar and stag. In 1066, William the Conqueror brought Saint-Hubert hounds—alongside white hounds of similar type known as Talbots—to England, where the breed was recorded by around 1300 and acquired the English name 'Bloodhound', derived from 'blooded hound' (meaning a hound of pure, aristocratic breeding kept carefully recorded) or from its skill in tracking wounded, bleeding game. Along the Anglo-Scottish border through the sixteenth century, these hounds were known as 'sleuth hounds' and were used to track cattle raiders ('reivers'), with law dictating that anyone who barred a sleuth hound on a hot trail was deemed an accomplice. By the seventeenth century, scientist Robert Boyle documented a Bloodhound trailing a quarry seven miles along busy thoroughfares to an upstairs room, and in 1805 the Thrapston Association for the Prevention of Felons in England recorded the first organized law-enforcement use of a Bloodhound to catch poachers and thieves. Exported to North America by the nineteenth century (where the breed was formally registered in 1885 and where trailing evidence from a proven Bloodhound is accepted in courts of law, though historical records also note its misuse in the antebellum American South), North American and continental lines later helped replenish British stock after the breed nearly died out in Britain during the Second World War.
overview.originalPurpose: Trailing large game (such as wild boar and deer) and tracking wounded animals as a leash hound, as well as long-distance human scent-trailing (mantrailing) in law-enforcement and search-and-rescue operations.
currentRoles: Law-enforcement, search-and-rescue, and forensic human mantrailing dog
Leash hound for tracking wounded game and blood-scenting trials
Competitive mantrailing, tracking, and scent-work participant
Devoted family and household companion
Active leashed hiking and walking partner

physical.coatType: Short, dense, close-lying, and weatherproof single coat that is quite harsh on the body, very short, soft, and velvety on the head and ears, and slightly longer and coarser (about 5 cm / 2 inches) along the underside of the tapering tail.
coatColors: Black and tan (bicolour with either a predominant black mantle or a more limited dorsal black saddle, sometimes interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs)
Liver and tan (bicolour in mantle or saddle pattern with brown/liver nose and lip pigment, sometimes interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs)

Red (unicolour ranging from light red/blond to deep red; across all three colours, a small amount of white on the forechest, toes/feet, and tip of the tail is permissible, whereas widespread white reaching the wrists/hocks or white patches on the muzzle or blaze are disqualifying faults)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate year-round, with heavier seasonal shedding twice a year in late spring and late autumn.
physical.droolingLevel: High
distinctiveFeatures: Most powerful and massive of all scent hounds, built on a rectangular 10:9 body-length-to-height ratio with a deep, oval chest forming a prominent keel between the forelegs (chest depth equal to half the withers height)

Majestic, narrow, flat-sided head (measuring 3/7 of body length, or at least 30 cm [12 in] in males and 28 cm [11 in] in females) with a very pronounced occipital peak ('cone head'), slight stop, and deep, square-profiled muzzle equal in length to the skull

Abundant, thin, supple skin over the forehead and cheeks that falls into deep pendulous ridges and wrinkles when the head is carried low, blending into long upper lips (hanging about 5 cm below the lower jaw) and a pronounced double dewlap (less marked in females)
Extremely long, thin, velvety ears ('leathers') set at or below eye level, falling in graceful inward- and backward-curling folds that reach well beyond the tip of the nose

Moderate-sized, oval dark brown or hazel eyes (amber to yellow in liver-and-tan or red hounds without a black saddle/mantle) conveying a solemn, wise, and dignified expression; conformation standards emphasize that loose skin and eyelid shape must never obscure vision or allow eyelashes to irritate the cornea
High-set, thick, tapering tail ('stern') furnished with ~5 cm harsher hair underneath and carried high in a graceful sabre/scimitar curve on the move without curling over the back
Elastic, swinging, ground-covering trot with a characteristic slight roll, strong rear drive, and straight, heavy-boned legs ending in compact, well-knuckled cat feet

Adult withers height of 68 cm ideal (64–72 cm with ±4 cm tolerance) for males and 62 cm ideal (58–66 cm with ±4 cm tolerance) for females in international standards—or 63–69 cm (25–27 in, average 66 cm / 26 in) for males and 58–63 cm (23–25 in, average 61 cm / 24 in) in British and American standards—with weights of 46–54 kg (101–119 lbs) for males and 40–48 kg (88–106 lbs) for females internationally (41–50 kg [90–110 lbs] for males and 36–45.5 kg [80–100 lbs] for females in British and American standards, and tall individuals occasionally exceeding 55–60 kg / 120–130+ lbs)

traits: Gentle, placid, and kind-hearted ('nature's gentleman') indoors
Deeply affectionate and strongly bonded to its owner and family
Sociable, courteous, and non-quarrelsome with people, kennelmates, and other dogs
Relentless, single-minded, and independent once locked onto a scent trail
Equally sensitive to praise and correction
Somewhat reserved or shy, yet never aggressive
Stubborn and inclined to test boundaries if not guided with patient consistency
Rarely barks like a guard dog, but communicates with a resonant, melodious bay or howl ('rooooo')
Curious mouth-explorer and counter-surfer capable of reaching standard kitchen tables without lifting its paws

exercise.level: Moderate to high. Despite a laid-back indoor demeanour, the Bloodhound was bred to follow a scent trail for hours and requires daily sustained leashed walks, safe enclosed play, and regular nose-work enrichment.
activities: Long daily walks and hikes on a strong leash and harness where the dog can safely sniff
Mantrailing (human scent trailing), tracking trials, and blood-scenting games
Structured nose work and hidden-scent search games in the yard or home
Supervised play and romping with other dogs in a securely fenced enclosure
Jogging, swimming, or rally/obedience exercises for skeletally mature adult hounds

grooming.brushing: Brush weekly with a rubber grooming mitt, hound glove, or medium-bristle brush to remove dead hair and distribute natural skin oils; increase brushing frequency during spring and autumn coat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed (every few weeks to months, or when smelly) using a mild dog-safe shampoo, rinse thoroughly, and dry all facial, neck, and dewlap folds completely so moisture is never trapped against the skin.
notes: Inspect and wipe the facial wrinkles, lip folds, and neck dewlap daily with a warm damp cloth or pet-safe wipe, then dry thoroughly to prevent moisture, food debris, and skin-fold dermatitis.

Check the long, heavy hanging ears ('leathers') daily—and clean them regularly with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser—because they dip into food and water bowls, sweep the ground, and trap warmth and moisture.
Keep 'slobber cloths' (towels) handy around the house and when travelling: a head shake can fling ropes of saliva 15 feet across furniture, walls, and clothing.
Check the eyes daily for dust, debris, redness, or irritation from eyelid folds.
Trim toenails regularly and inspect the compact cat feet after outdoor walks.
Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Affectionate and capable of remarkable focus in scent work, yet independent-minded, quick to become set in its ways, and deeply sensitive to harsh handling.
tips: Start puppy socialization and basic obedience classes early so polite leash manners and household rules are established before the dog reaches 40 to 54+ kg.

Be firm, patient, and kind, using positive reinforcement (high-value food rewards and warm praise); Bloodhounds are equally sensitive to kindness and correction and will shut down or resist under harsh methods.
Never trust a Bloodhound off-leash in an unenclosed area—even obedience-titled hounds will ignore recall when they strike a compelling scent and have no road or traffic sense.
Enclose yards with a sturdy 5- to 6-foot (1.5–1.8 m) above-ground fence and guard against digging under the fence line.

Do not rely on electronic ('invisible') underground fences: a Bloodhound's high pain threshold, thick loose neck skin, and intense scent drive allow it to charge right through the shock zone and never return.

Dog-proof counters, tables, and rubbish bins: an adult Bloodhound stands tall enough to rest its chin on a 29-inch dining table with all four feet on the floor and is notorious for swallowing non-food items.
Channel the dog's natural nose into mantrailing or tracking games, which build a strong cooperative bond between handler and hound.
training.socialization: Provide early, calm, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, children, surfaces, and veterinary/grooming handling. Because Bloodhounds are gentle pack hounds that enjoy canine company but are often unaware of their own bulk, supervise interactions with young children (particularly toddlers under 5 years old who can be accidentally knocked over by a wagging tail or playful nudge).

livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. As pack-oriented hounds that bond closely with their families, Bloodhounds left isolated alone for long periods often become bored, bay loudly enough to disturb neighbours, or chew furniture and household objects.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced, high-quality large-breed dog food (commercial or veterinarian-formulated home-prepared diet) matched to life stage (large-breed puppy, adult, or senior), body condition, and workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Several smaller measured meals daily using a large-breed puppy formula to support steady, controlled skeletal growth, adjusted with veterinary guidance.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two to three smaller meals daily rather than a single large meal to help reduce the risk of life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
feedingFrequency.senior: Two to three smaller daily meals tailored to body condition, mobility, dental health, and veterinary advice.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions appropriate for a large, deep-chested hound (typically 4 to 8 cups of dry food daily for an 80- to 110-pound adult depending on calorie density, age, and activity level, confirmed with a veterinarian). Divide the daily ration into two or three smaller meals, avoid elevated food bowls unless specifically directed by a veterinarian, and restrict vigorous exercise for at least an hour before and after mealtimes to help minimize gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV) risk. Keep clean, fresh water available at all times (wiping the ears and flews after drinking).
considerations: Feed a dedicated large-breed puppy diet during growth so bone and joint development proceed at a steady pace without excess weight.
Divide daily food into two or three smaller meals and avoid strenuous exercise immediately before or after eating to reduce bloat (GDV) risk.

Discuss prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking' surgery, often performed during spaying or neutering) with your veterinarian, as epidemiological studies rank the Bloodhound among the breeds at highest risk of GDV.
Keep all non-food objects, socks, rocks, corn cobs, and rubbish strictly out of reach; Bloodhounds are notorious for indiscriminate ingestion leading to gastrointestinal foreign-body obstruction.
Monitor body condition score regularly and deduct training treats from the daily food ration so excess weight does not overload the hips and elbows.
Consult a veterinarian before adding joint supplements (such as omega-3 fatty acids, glucosamine, or chondroitin).
nutrition.note: Exact caloric needs vary widely across individuals ranging from 36 to over 54 kg (80 to 130+ lbs) and between working mantrailing hounds and family companions; establish portion sizes and bloat-prevention routines with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Bloodhound has an average life expectancy of 10 to 12 years, and health priorities centre on risks linked to its large, deep-chested build, heavy bone, abundant skin folds, and long pendulous ears. In both British breed-health surveys and a peer-reviewed UK epidemiological study of 15,881 deceased and 36,006 living pedigree dogs across 165–169 breeds (Evans & Adams, 2010), gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) and cancer were identified as the two leading causes of mortality, with the Bloodhound ranking among the breeds at greatest risk of both GDV mortality and GDV morbidity. Orthopaedic, cardiac, ocular, and neurological screening data are tracked in North American and British health registries: in cumulative North American orthopaedic registry evaluations through December 2014, 25.4% of 2,941 hip evaluations were graded abnormal (72.6% normal), 14.2% of 1,224 elbow evaluations were abnormal (85.3% normal), 0.7% of 732 cardiac evaluations were abnormal (98.1% normal), 2.7% of 150 patellar evaluations were abnormal (97.3% normal), 5.7% of 159 thyroid panels were abnormal with 19.5% equivocal, and among 311 dogs DNA-tested for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1), 49.5% tested clear/normal, 44.1% carriers, and 6.4% genetically at-risk/affected (figures reflecting tested cohorts rather than random population prevalence). Conformation-related concerns include eyelid abnormalities (entropion, ectropion, prolapsed third-eyelid gland ['cherry eye'], and keratoconjunctivitis sicca ['dry eye']), recurrent otitis externa, and skin-fold dermatitis or atopic dermatitis, though careful selective breeding has reduced severe skin and eyelid exaggerations (reflected in the breed's reclassification from Category 3 to Category 2 in the United Kingdom effective 1 January 2025, alongside a reported breed-average inbreeding coefficient of 10.0%).
commonConditions: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / gastric torsion / bloat) — a sudden, life-threatening emergency in which the stomach distends with gas and twists on its axis; UK epidemiological research (Evans & Adams, 2010) and breed mortality surveys identify the Bloodhound as one of the breeds at highest risk of GDV morbidity and mortality.

Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia — developmental joint malformations causing osteoarthritic pain and lameness; in North American registry statistics, 25.4% of 2,941 tested Bloodhounds showed hip dysplasia and 14.2% of 1,224 showed elbow dysplasia.

Eyelid and ocular surface disorders — entropion (inward-rolling eyelid causing eyelashes to rub the cornea), ectropion (outward-sagging lower lid exposing the conjunctiva), prolapsed gland of the third eyelid ('cherry eye'), and keratoconjunctivitis sicca ('dry eye') linked to loose facial skin and heavy flews.

Recurrent otitis externa (ear canal infections) — the long, heavy, low-set ears ('leathers') restrict airflow and trap moisture, wax, and debris, predisposing the ear canals to bacterial and yeast overgrowth.

Skin-fold dermatitis (intertrigo), atopic dermatitis, and eczema — trapped moisture, saliva, and friction within the deep forehead, cheek, lip, and neck folds can cause bacterial or yeast skin infections.

Gastrointestinal foreign-body ingestion and obstruction — Bloodhounds are notorious for swallowing non-food objects, rocks, clothing, or household items, frequently requiring emergency veterinary intervention.
Neoplasia (cancer) — identified alongside gastric torsion as one of the two leading causes of death in British breed health surveys, a risk shared across many large and giant breeds.

Degenerative myelopathy (DM) — a late-onset (typically 8+ years) progressive spinal cord neuropathy associated with the SOD1 gene; in North American DNA-testing statistics of 311 Bloodhounds, 44.1% were carriers and 6.4% tested genetically at risk.

Congenital cardiac disease, autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), and patellar luxation — monitored through pre-breeding cardiac auscultation/echocardiography, thyroid antibody panels, and knee examinations.
preventiveCare: Learn the emergency warning signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV)—distended or tight abdomen, unproductive retching, restlessness, stretching in pain, pale gums, or sudden collapse—and seek immediate emergency veterinary care if suspected.
Feed two to three smaller meals daily rather than one large meal, avoid vigorous exercise before and after eating, and discuss prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking') with your veterinarian.
Inspect and clean the hanging ears and wipe and thoroughly dry the facial, lip, and neck folds daily, especially after drinking, eating, bathing, or swimming.

Verify documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents before acquiring a puppy, including hip and elbow radiographs, veterinary cardiac evaluation, eye examination, and degenerative myelopathy (SOD1) DNA status (as well as low pedigree inbreeding coefficient).
Keep counters, rubbish bins, laundry, and yard areas clear of swallowable objects to prevent foreign-body intestinal obstructions.
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition and avoid over-exercising or jogging growing puppies before skeletal maturity to protect the hips and elbows.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement; distraction-index hip evaluation is also used as an optional screening tool).
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation (core pre-breeding requirement).
Cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian—preferably a board-certified veterinary cardiologist or specialist, with echocardiography when indicated (core pre-breeding requirement).

Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist or accredited eye-scheme examiner (recommended in British breeding guidance and optional in North American health certification).
Degenerative myelopathy (DM / SOD1) DNA test from an approved laboratory (optional pre-breeding test in North American and British health programs).

Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation and laboratory thyroid panel (optional pre-breeding evaluations, alongside permanent microchip or tattoo identification and pedigree inbreeding-coefficient review).
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste and schedule periodic veterinary dental assessments. Conformation standards require strong jaws with complete dentition in a regular scissor bite (a pincer/level bite is also tolerated, whereas overshot, undershot, or wry jaws are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Inspect the long, velvety, low-set ears daily for redness, foul odour, excess wax, or discharge, and wipe them clean after meals and drinks. Clean the ear canals routinely—and after every bath or swim—using a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser, drying carefully without inserting cotton swabs deep into the canal.
health.skinCare: Check and wipe the facial wrinkles, hanging flews, and double dewlap daily with a damp cloth or pet-safe facial wipe, then dry every fold thoroughly so trapped saliva or water cannot cause skin-fold dermatitis. Monitor the rest of the short coat for parasites, hot spots, or allergic irritation.

idealFor: Active, patient owners and handlers who enjoy mantrailing, tracking, scent work, and long daily leashed hikes
Households with a securely fenced yard (5 to 6 feet high) and ample indoor space for a 40- to 54+ kg hound
People who are relaxed about housekeeping and comfortable with heavy drooling ('slobber cloths') and daily ear and wrinkle care
Families with children (ideally aged 5 and older, with adult supervision) or multi-dog homes seeking a gentle, pack-friendly companion
Owners financially prepared for the food, preventive gastropexy, and veterinary care costs of a large-to-giant breed
notIdealFor: Fastidious or house-proud owners bothered by ropes of drool on walls, ceilings, furniture, and clothing
Apartment dwellers or densely packed urban neighbourhoods sensitive to deep, resonant baying and howling
Owners seeking reliable off-leash recall in unfenced areas or expecting an Electronic/Invisible fence to contain a scent hound
People who want an aggressive property guard dog rather than a friendly, non-quarrelsome pack hound
Sedentary households or homes where the dog is left isolated alone for long workdays

funFacts: The word 'blood' in Bloodhound does not refer to bloodthirstiness: it derives from 'blooded hound', meaning a hound of pure, aristocratic breeding whose lineage was carefully preserved (along with its historic work tracking wounded game).
So legendary is the breed's nose—estimated to contain roughly 250 to 300 million olfactory receptors—that trailing evidence from a proven Bloodhound is admissible in courts of law.

The Bloodhound's long, velvety ears ('leathers') and loose facial wrinkles are functional scent-tracking tools: as the dog lowers its head, the ears sweep scent particles up from the ground while the skin folds trap them near the nostrils.
In 1805, the Thrapston Association for the Prevention of Felons in England recorded the first organized law-enforcement use of a Bloodhound, acquiring a hound to track down poachers and thieves.

Along the Scottish border up to the late sixteenth century, the Bloodhound was known as the 'sleuth hound' (the origin of the modern word 'sleuth' for a detective), and anyone who refused entry to a sleuth hound pursuing a cattle thief was legally considered an accomplice.

In the seventeenth century, pioneering chemist Robert Boyle documented a trial in which a Bloodhound followed a person's scent trail for seven miles along busy footpaths and located the quarry in an upstairs room.

Standing up to 68–72 cm (27+ inches) at the shoulder, an adult male Bloodhound can rest its chin directly on a standard 29-inch dining table and help itself to dinner without lifting a single paw off the floor.
In 2022, a Bloodhound named Trumpet made dog-show history by winning Best in Show at the 146th Westminster Dog Show—the first Bloodhound ever to take the top prize.

faq.question: Where does the Bloodhound originate, and why is it also called the Chien de Saint-Hubert?
faq.answer: The breed originates from the Ardennes region of Belgium, where black and black-and-tan scent hounds were bred from the seventh century onward by the monk Hubert (later Bishop of Liège and canonised as Saint Hubert, patron saint of hunters) and maintained for centuries at the Abbey of Saint-Hubert. In French-speaking Europe and international standards, the breed is still officially named the Chien de Saint-Hubert.

faq.question: Where do the names 'Bloodhound' and 'Sleuth Hound' come from?
faq.answer: After Saint-Hubert hounds were brought to Britain following the Norman Conquest of 1066, their descendants became known as 'blooded hounds'—meaning hounds of pure, aristocratic blood—as well as hounds used to track wounded, bleeding game. In medieval Scotland and northern England, they were called 'sleuth hounds' (from the Old Norse word slóð, meaning 'trail' or 'track'), which gave English the modern word 'sleuth' for a detective.

faq.question: How big does an adult Bloodhound get?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify an ideal withers height of 68 cm for males and 62 cm for females, with a tolerance of ±4 cm (64 to 72 cm for males; 58 to 66 cm for females), and typical weights of 46 to 54 kg (101–119 lbs) for males and 40 to 48 kg (88–106 lbs) for females. British and American standards specify a height range of 25 to 27 inches (63–69 cm, average 26 in / 66 cm) for males and 23 to 25 inches (58–63 cm, average 24 in / 61 cm) for females, and weights of 90 to 110 pounds (41–50 kg) for males and 80 to 100 pounds (36–45.5 kg) for females, though large individuals frequently reach 120 to 130+ pounds (54–59+ kg).

faq.question: What coat colours are accepted in the Bloodhound?
faq.answer: Three colours are recognized: black and tan, liver and tan, and solid red. In the bicolour varieties (black and tan or liver and tan), the darker colour may form either a full mantle (where black or liver predominates) or a smaller dorsal saddle with more extensive tan, and darker areas may be interspersed with lighter or badger-coloured hairs. Red dogs range from light golden-blond red to deep red. A small amount of white is permitted on the forechest, toes/feet, and tip of the tail.

faq.question: How long does a Bloodhound typically live?
faq.answer: The average lifespan is 10 to 12 years.

faq.question: Does a Bloodhound drool and make a lot of noise?
faq.answer: Yes to both. Because of its square muzzle, long hanging upper lips (flews), and loose neck folds, the Bloodhound drools heavily—especially after drinking, eating, or sniffing—and a single head shake can fling saliva 15 feet across a room. While Bloodhounds rarely bark like guard dogs, they have a deep, resonant, melodious bay ('rooooo') when excited or on a scent trail.

faq.question: Is a Bloodhound a good family dog or guard dog?
faq.answer: Bloodhounds are gentle, placid, and deeply affectionate with their families and get along well with other dogs and children. Because of their sheer size and wagging tails, interactions with toddlers and children under 5 years old should always be supervised. However, they are terrible guard dogs: they may bay when someone approaches, but their friendly, non-aggressive nature means they are more likely to welcome an intruder than guard property.

faq.question: Can a Bloodhound be let off-leash or kept behind an electronic ('invisible') fence?
faq.answer: No. Once a Bloodhound catches an interesting scent, its tracking instinct overrides recall commands and road awareness—even in obedience-titled dogs. Electronic underground fences are ineffective because the breed's high pain threshold, thick loose neck skin, and scent drive allow it to bolt right through the shock boundary. Always walk a Bloodhound on a leash and enclose yards with a sturdy 5- to 6-foot physical fence.

faq.question: How much daily grooming and ear care does a Bloodhound need?
faq.answer: The short coat needs only a weekly brushing with a hound glove or rubber mitt (more often during spring and autumn sheds), but the ears and facial wrinkles require daily attention. Because the long ears dip into food and water bowls and trap warm moisture, inspect them daily and clean them regularly with a veterinary ear cleanser. Wipe the facial, lip, and neck folds daily with a damp cloth and dry them thoroughly to prevent skin-fold dermatitis.

faq.question: Why is bloat (GDV) such an important concern in Bloodhounds, and how can risk be reduced?
faq.answer: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV, or gastric torsion/bloat) occurs when the deep, narrow stomach fills with gas and twists, cutting off blood flow. Epidemiological studies in pedigree dogs rank the Bloodhound among the breeds at highest risk of GDV morbidity and mortality. Owners can help reduce risk by feeding two to three smaller meals daily instead of one large meal, avoiding vigorous exercise around mealtimes, avoiding elevated food bowls unless advised by a vet, discussing prophylactic gastropexy ('stomach tacking' surgery) with their veterinarian, and seeking immediate emergency care if abdominal swelling, unproductive retching, or restlessness occurs.

faq.question: What pre-breeding health screenings should I ask a breeder for?
faq.answer: Ask for documented results of the three core pre-breeding evaluations—hip dysplasia radiographs, elbow dysplasia radiographs, and a veterinary cardiac examination (ideally by a veterinary cardiologist)—along with optional screenings such as a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exam, patellar luxation check, thyroid panel, and DNA testing for degenerative myelopathy (SOD1).

overview.summary: A small, square-built Italian toy companion of the bichon family, prized for its pure white flocky coat, dark expressive eyes, calm demeanor, and deep devotion to its people.
overview.description: The Bolognese is a compact, sturdy toy dog with a square outline in which body length from shoulder to buttock equals height at the withers. Its signature feature is a long, airy, pure white coat that stands off the body in loose, fluffy flocks rather than hanging flat or forming straight fringes, contrasted by a large black nose, dark-rimmed lips, and round dark eyes. High-set hanging ears are firm enough at the base to stand slightly away from the skull, giving the head a broad, expressive frame. Quiet, observant, and deeply attached to its household, the Bolognese prefers staying close to its family and adapts smoothly to calm indoor life.
overview.history: Named for the northern Italian city of Bologna, the Bolognese shares ancient Mediterranean ancestry with the Maltese and other white bichon lapdogs mentioned by Aristotle as Canes Melitenses. Valued in Italy as early as the 11th and 12th centuries, the breed reached peak prestige during the Renaissance as a favored companion and diplomatic gift among European courts. Cosimo de' Medici carried eight puppies to Brussels as gifts for Belgian noblemen, and King Philip II of Spain—after receiving two from the Duke d'Este—wrote that they were the most royal gift one could present to an emperor. Artists such as Titian, Pieter Bruegel the Elder, and Goya painted Bolognese dogs in noble portraits, and Flemish weavers featured them in 17th-century tapestries. Later Italian breeders preserved the breed's classic type through the 20th century, and it entered Britain in 1989.

health.overview: The Bolognese is generally a healthy, sturdy toy breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years. No breed-wide severe conformational exaggerations affect the breed, and health screening focuses on orthopedic and eye conditions monitored in small companion dogs—especially patellar luxation and inherited retinal or lens disorders—alongside routine dental care for compact toy jaws.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation — slipping of the kneecap out of its normal groove, a primary orthopedic screening focus in toy breeds
Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA-prcd) and other inherited eye anomalies — monitored through genetic testing and routine veterinary eye exams
Hereditary cataracts — lens clouding screened through periodic ophthalmologist examinations
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease — a hip-joint bone blood-supply condition occasionally reported in small toy dogs
Periodontal disease — tartar accumulation and gum inflammation common in crowded toy mouths without regular brushing
Tear staining (epiphora) — brownish staining beneath the eyes caused by tearing on white facial hair, managed through routine wiping
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for documented clearances on patella evaluations, veterinary eye exams, and PRA-prcd genetic testing.
Brush teeth regularly and schedule routine veterinary dental checks.
Maintain a healthy, lean weight to protect knees and hips, and keep up with annual wellness exams and parasite prevention.

health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week—ideally daily—using dog-safe toothpaste, and schedule routine veterinary dental exams to keep small jaws healthy.

health.skinCare: Part the flocky white coat during regular combing to inspect the skin for tangles, dryness, redness, or parasites.

funFacts: During the Renaissance, Cosimo de' Medici brought eight Bolognese puppies to Brussels as gifts for Belgian noblemen.
After receiving two Bolognese from the Duke d'Este, King Philip II of Spain wrote to thank him, calling them the most royal gift one could bestow upon an emperor.
Venetian master Titian painted Duke Federico Gonzaga caressing his Bolognese, and the breed also appears in works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, Francisco Goya, and 17th-century Flemish tapestries.
Unlike the Bichon Frise, whose coat is blown out and scissored into rounded shapes, the Bolognese is traditionally presented in its natural, untrimmed flocky tufts.
High-set ears that stand slightly stiff at the base create the optical illusion that a Bolognese's head is broader than it actually is.

faq.question: How is a Bolognese different from a Bichon Frise?
faq.answer: Both are small white companions in the bichon family, but the Bolognese has a long, airy, flocky coat worn naturally untrimmed and a calmer, more serene temperament, whereas the Bichon Frise is typically scissored into a rounded plush silhouette.

faq.question: How big does a Bolognese get?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 27 to 30 cm at the withers and females stand 25 to 28 cm, with a typical weight of 2.5 to 4 kg.

faq.question: Can a Bolognese be left alone during a full workday?
faq.answer: No. Bolognese form a very close bond with their people and are prone to separation anxiety, so they thrive best in homes where someone is around much of the day.

faq.question: Do Bolognese dogs shed much?
faq.answer: They shed very little onto furniture, though loose hair catches inside their flocky coat and must be combed out several times a week to prevent matting.

faq.question: Are Bolognese good apartment dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. Their compact size, calm indoor habits, and modest exercise needs make them well suited to apartment living when paired with daily walks and indoor play.

faq.question: What health tests are recommended for Bolognese breeding stock?
faq.answer: Recommended screenings include a patella evaluation, a PRA-prcd DNA test, a veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination, and routine cardiac checks.

overview.summary: A highly energetic, athletic, and fiercely intelligent sheepdog famous for its intense, hypnotic stare used to control livestock, making it a premier working dog and canine sports champion.
overview.description: The Border Collie is a well-balanced, medium-sized working dog that radiates grace, agility, and immense stamina. Built specifically for tireless activity, it possesses a lithe, muscular frame capable of sudden bursts of speed and remarkable changes of direction. The breed is most famous for its 'intense eye'—a deeply focused, hypnotic stare it uses while crouching low to the ground to silently command and move flocks of sheep. It comes in two distinct coat varieties (rough and smooth), both featuring a dense, weather-resisting undercoat. While black and white is the most iconic coloration, they appear in a wide array of patterns and colors. Renowned worldwide as perhaps the most intelligent and trainable of all canine breeds, the Border Collie is a workaholic that absolutely demands a purposeful 'job' to remain mentally and physically stable. It is an affectionate and incredibly observant companion, but its explosive energy and deeply hardwired herding instincts require a highly active, dedicated handler.
overview.history: The Border Collie was forged in the rugged, hilly landscape along the border of Scotland and England, an environment that demanded an exceptionally resilient and intelligent sheepdog. For centuries, local shepherds relied on agile, medium-sized collies to gather and manage large flocks over vast, unfenced moorlands. The modern breed's lineage is often traced back to a single legendary progenitor named Old Hemp, a quiet, intensely focused working dog born in 1893 who perfectly demonstrated the breed's signature 'eye' and stealthy, crouching herding style. Recognizing their unparalleled utility, shepherds favored performance and working ability above all else, ensuring the breed remained largely unchanged by the cosmetic exaggerations of the conformation show ring for many decades. Today, the Border Collie remains the world's premier sheep-herding breed and dominates high-level canine sports such as agility, obedience, and flyball across the globe.
overview.originalPurpose: Gathering, controlling, and moving flocks of sheep over rugged terrain using a specialized crouching stance and an intense, hypnotic stare.
currentRoles: Premier livestock herding dog
Elite canine sports competitor (agility, flyball, obedience)
Search and rescue dog
Highly active household companion

physical.coatType: Exists in two varieties: Rough (medium length and flat) and Smooth (short). Both feature a dense, weather-resisting undercoat and a close-fitting outer coat. Rough coats feature a noticeable mane, breeches, and a plumed tail.
coatColors: Any color is acceptable, but white should never be the predominant color
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high; the dense double coat sheds steadily year-round and requires regular brushing to manage the heavier seasonal 'blow' of the undercoat
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tightly fitting lips prevent excessive drooling
distinctiveFeatures: Athletic, slightly rectangular build (the body is slightly longer than the height at the withers)
Height typically ranges from 19 to 22 inches for males and 18 to 21 inches for females
Weight generally falls between 30 and 55 pounds, kept in lean, hard working condition
Broad, flat skull with a distinct stop and a strong, moderately short muzzle
Complete, powerful scissor bite
Medium-sized, oval eyes set wide apart, projecting a highly intense, intelligent, and piercing expression (often blue in merle dogs)
Medium-sized, highly mobile ears carried erect or semi-erect (tipped over)
Deep chest reaching the elbows, accommodating massive lung capacity for endurance
Low-set, moderately long tail featuring an upward swirl at the tip, never carried tightly over the back
Smooth, effortless, and highly stealthy gait with minimum lifting of the feet

traits: Incredibly intelligent, highly focused, and intensely driven to work
Eager to learn and remarkably responsive to complex commands
Extremely energetic and athletic, possessing virtually limitless stamina
Deeply loyal and affectionate with its immediate family
Can be reserved, aloof, or cautious with strangers, making an alert watchdog
Possesses a profound, hardwired herding instinct, often attempting to corral children, pets, or even moving vehicles
Highly sensitive to sound, motion, and its handler's body language
Prone to obsessive-compulsive behaviors (like staring at lights or shadows) if chronically bored or under-exercised

exercise.level: Very high; a true workaholic that requires massive amounts of vigorous physical exertion and complex mental challenges to remain sane and balanced
activities: Long-distance trail running, intense hiking, or biking alongside a handler
Advanced canine sports training (agility, flyball, competitive obedience)
Herding clinics and livestock management tasks
Interactive fetch and frisbee sessions in large open spaces
Complex problem-solving puzzles and continuous trick training

grooming.brushing: Brush two to three times a week using a slicker brush and metal comb to remove dead undercoat, prevent tangles in the feathering (for rough coats), and distribute healthy skin oils.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when visibly dirty; the weather-resistant coat naturally repels mud and dirt once it dries.
notes: Pay special attention to the feathering on the legs, belly, and tail to prevent painful matting.
Inspect the ears weekly for dirt, debris, or wax buildup.
Trim fast-growing nails every two weeks to support their agile, quick-turning movements.
Brush teeth several times weekly with canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging; while they are exceptionally quick learners, their intense intelligence means they also learn bad habits instantly and require an expert, active handler to provide constant direction
tips: Provide a concrete 'job' every single day; without purposeful work, they will invent their own (often destructive or obsessive) jobs.
Use positive, reward-based training with high-value toys or fetch as the primary motivator.
Actively manage their extreme herding instinct; they must be taught from puppyhood that chasing cars, bicycles, or children is strictly forbidden.
Incorporate advanced trick training and obedience to thoroughly exhaust their highly active minds.
training.socialization: Extensive, continuous socialization is absolutely mandatory. Because they are hyper-aware of environmental changes and movement, early positive exposure to diverse sounds, people, and objects is necessary to prevent them from becoming sound-sensitive or neurotically reactive.

climates: Temperate climates
Cool climates, where the dense double coat provides excellent insulation
Warm climates are tolerated, but intense exercise must be strictly limited to cooler morning or evening hours to prevent heat exhaustion
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low; they are deeply devoted to their handlers and require nearly constant physical and mental engagement. Leaving a Border Collie isolated and bored in a backyard is a recipe for severe behavioral problems.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for highly active, medium-sized working breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady digestion and fuel intense activity.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations strictly using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup. Adjust amounts based on their daily work output; active competing athletes require significantly higher caloric and protein density than a standard household pet. Provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a strictly lean, athletic body condition to minimize mechanical stress on joints during high-speed turns and jumping.
Account for all training treats within the total daily caloric allowance.
Performance dogs may benefit from diets specifically enriched with omega-3 fatty acids for coat health and joint lubrication.
Avoid feeding a large meal immediately before strenuous exercise to mitigate the risk of gastric issues.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs fluctuate dramatically based on exercise intensity, age, and training schedule. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Border Collie is a robust and highly athletic breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 15 years. However, they are predisposed to several inherited genetic conditions, particularly concerning their eyes and neurological systems. Dedicated breeding programs utilize extensive DNA testing and orthopedic screening to minimize the prevalence of these diseases.
commonConditions: Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA) — an inherited, congenital condition causing defects in the formation of the eye, ranging from mild to severe vision loss; completely screenable via DNA testing
Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints leading to osteoarthritis, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Trapped Neutrophil Syndrome (TNS) — a fatal hereditary disease where the bone marrow cannot release white blood cells into the bloodstream, impairing the immune system; screenable via DNA testing
Multidrug Resistance 1 (MDR1) mutation — a genetic sensitivity to certain common veterinary medications (like ivermectin), requiring DNA testing to prevent toxic reactions
Epilepsy — inherited neurological seizure disorders that typically manifest in early adulthood and require lifelong veterinary management
Congenital deafness — occasionally associated with the merle or excessive white coat patterns, verifiable through BAER testing
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified DNA clearances for CEA, TNS, and MDR1, along with clinical clearances for hips and eyes.
If the dog's MDR1 status is unknown or affected, strictly avoid certain anti-parasitic medications and anesthetics as advised by a veterinarian.
Maintain a lean, well-muscled body condition to minimize mechanical wear on the hips and elbows during high-impact sports.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: DNA marker test for Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA)
DNA marker test for Trapped Neutrophil Syndrome (TNS)
DNA marker test for MDR1 medication sensitivity
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (CAER)
Brainstem Auditory Evoked Response (BAER) hearing evaluation for puppies
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has powerful jaws and a complete scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve long-term gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the highly mobile ears weekly for dirt, wax buildup, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution.
health.skinCare: Part the dense double coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, ticks, or burrs sustained during outdoor work.

idealFor: Highly active individuals, runners, and hikers willing to commit massive amounts of time to daily exercise
Experienced dog owners familiar with managing extreme working drive, high intelligence, and obsessive behaviors
Canine sports enthusiasts heavily involved in agility, flyball, herding, or competitive obedience
Rural households, ranches, or farms with expansive, securely fenced acreage and actual livestock to manage
notIdealFor: First-time dog owners or passive handlers unequipped to manage extreme intelligence and boundless energy
Apartment, condominium, or dense urban dwellers where unavoidable noise and lack of space will cause the dog immense stress
Households looking for a calm, low-energy indoor pet or a highly submissive lap dog
Families with toddlers or young children who may be frightened by the dog's hardwired instinct to nip at heels and herd them

funFacts: The Border Collie is widely considered by canine behavioral scientists and experts to be the most intelligent dog breed in the world, capable of learning hundreds of distinct words and commands.
A famous Border Collie named Chaser achieved global recognition for successfully learning and identifying the names of over 1,000 different toys.

Unlike other herding breeds that nip and bark to move livestock, the Border Collie uses a unique predatory crouch and a hypnotic, intense stare known as 'the eye' to silently intimidate and control sheep.

The modern breed traces almost its entire lineage back to a single dog named Old Hemp, born in Northumberland in 1893, who possessed a brilliant, quiet herding style that revolutionized the working sheepdog.

Because they are so intensely driven by motion, a bored Border Collie will often try to 'herd' moving objects like bicycles, cars, or even shadows, which can lead to dangerous situations if unmanaged.

faq.question: What is a Border Collie?
faq.answer: The Border Collie is a medium-sized, highly athletic working sheepdog from the Anglo-Scottish border, globally recognized as the most intelligent and energetic breed, famous for its intense herding stare.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Border Collie?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 19 to 22 inches at the withers, while females stand 18 to 21 inches. Both sexes are kept in lean, athletic condition and typically weigh between 30 and 55 pounds.

faq.question: How long does a Border Collie live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, extensive daily exercise, and preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 15 years.

faq.question: Do Border Collies shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They are moderate to high shedders. Their dense, weather-resistant double coat requires brushing two to three times a week to prevent matting in the longer feathering and to manage seasonal shedding.

faq.question: Can a Border Collie live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Absolutely not. They are hyper-active workaholics that require vast amounts of open space, vigorous running, and constant mental stimulation; they will become highly destructive and neurotic in a small apartment.

faq.question: Are Border Collies good with children?
faq.answer: They can be, provided the children are older and respectful. However, their intense hardwired herding instinct often drives them to chase and nip at the heels of running toddlers, making them less suited for families with very young children.

faq.question: Are Border Collies hard to train?
faq.answer: They are exceptionally easy to train for complex tasks because of their brilliance, but they are difficult to live with if you are inexperienced. Because they learn so quickly, they also learn bad habits instantly and require an expert, deeply engaged handler.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Border Collie?
faq.answer: Primary health concerns include genetic eye disorders like Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA), medication sensitivity (MDR1 mutation), Trapped Neutrophil Syndrome (TNS), epilepsy, and hip dysplasia.

overview.summary: An aristocratic, swift, and silky-coated giant Russian sighthound once kept by imperial nobility to course wolves, hares, and foxes across open steppes, admired today for its quiet, dignified indoor composure and breathtaking bursts of speed outdoors.
overview.description: The Borzoi—known in Russia as the Russkaya Psovaya Borzaya and formerly called the Russian Wolfhound—is a tall, lean, narrow-bodied sighthound built for explosive agility and graceful coursing power. Slightly elongated in outline (with females marginally longer than males), it pairs a deeply dropped yet fairly narrow chest, a smoothly arched muscular loin, and blade-like straight forelegs with a long, slender, gently domed head inclined toward a subtle Roman nose and scarcely visible stop. Large, obliquely set dark almond eyes lined in black convey soft intelligence, complemented by small, thin, mobile ears folded neatly back toward the nape in repose. Its hallmark coat is long, supple, and silky—lying flat, wavy, or loosely curled over the body with short smooth hair on the head, ears, and front legs, a curly frill around the neck, and abundant feathering down the chest, hindquarters, and low-carried curved tail. Quiet, clean, and almost cat-like in calm indoor dignity, the Borzoi transforms instantly outdoors into a lightning-fast sprinter capable of 35 to 40 miles per hour whenever fleeing game catches its eye.
overview.history: The ancestry of the Borzoi stretches back at least to the fifteenth century in Russia, shaped across the open steppes by blending swift, long-coated local coursing dogs with Greyhound, Mountain (Gorsky), and Crimean sighthound blood to create an agile, cold-hardy hunter. By the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, the breed was firmly established among the Russian aristocracy, who maintained grand country kennels and staged elaborate hunts where matched pairs of Borzoi coursed hares, foxes, and wolves across open terrain—holding wolves pinned until mounted hunters arrived. Known internationally as the Russian Wolfhound until 1936, the breed took its modern name from the Russian word for 'swift.' Following the Russian Revolution of 1917, many imperial kennels were lost, and the breed's global survival owed much to dogs previously gifted to Western European and American fanciers. Definitive international recognition followed in January 1956. Today, the Borzoi excels in lure coursing, oval-track racing, and conformation while living peacefully in calm homes as a serene, independent companion.
overview.originalPurpose: Coursing wild game by sight—principally hare and fox, and historically wolves in matched pairs—across open Russian terrain.
currentRoles: Calm, dignified household companion
Lure-coursing and sighthound-racing athlete
Conformation and calm therapy-dog partner

physical.coatType: Long, supple, silky coat (never woolly or harshly bristled) that lies flat, wavy, or in loose large curls over thin, elastic, fold-free skin. Hair on the head, ears, and fronts of the legs is short and smooth, while a profuse curly frill frames the neck and long silky feathering drapes the chest, backs of the forelegs, hindquarters, and long tail.
coatColors: Any colour or combination of colours—solid or patched on a white ground—including white, gold, sable, red, grey, brindle, and black with tan points

Nose, lips, and eyelid rims must always carry black pigment regardless of coat shade (brown/chocolate, blue, lilac/isabella, and dilute coats with non-black noses are not accepted under international guidelines)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high; sheds steadily throughout the year and drops large amounts of long silky hair during seasonal shedding periods (roughly once or twice a year)
physical.droolingLevel: Low; thin, elastic, fold-free skin and tight, clean black-edged lips free of pendulous flews keep drooling minimal
distinctiveFeatures: Tall, narrow, lean, aristocratic giant sighthound built slightly longer than tall (ideal body length 5 to 10 percent greater than withers height; females longer than males)
Desirable height at the withers of 75 to 85 cm for males and 68 to 78 cm for females (elbow height sits slightly above half of height at the withers)
Adult weight typically ranging from 75 to 105 pounds for males and 60 to 85 pounds for females
Long, narrow, oval-shaped skull almost flat or slightly domed in profile with pronounced occiput, scarcely perceptible stop, and a long, deep muzzle inclined toward a subtle Roman nose
Large, prominent always-black nose, flat cheeks, tight lips, and strong clean jaws meeting in a scissor or even bite
Large, obliquely set dark brown almond eyes with tight black-edged lids projecting a soft, intelligent gaze (never round, bulging, or light)
Small, thin, mobile pointed ears clad in short hair, set above eye level and folded close and backward toward the nape in repose (lifting when attentive)
Long, lean, muscular, laterally flattened slightly arched neck flowing into an unpronounced withers, smoothly arched muscular back and loin, and deeply tucked belly
Narrow yet very deep brisket, blade-like flattened straight forelegs, long muscular hindquarters wider than the forequarters, and hare-shaped feet with arched tight toes
Long, low-set, profusely feathered tail carried low in a graceful curve
Effortless, flowing, ground-covering trot that converges toward the centreline at speed and shifts into an explosive coursing gallop

traits: Calm, serene, dignified, and remarkably quiet indoors—rarely barking without cause
Gentle, affectionate, and deeply devoted to its immediate family, often showing an endearing cat-like independence
Naturally reserved, polite, or mildly aloof around unfamiliar strangers without nervous shyness or aggression
Clever, observant, and self-willed rather than mechanically eager to please, responding best to respectful partnership
Expressive in canine body language and generally harmonious living alongside other sighthounds or large respectful dogs
Possesses a powerful, lightning-fast visual chasing instinct triggered instantly by running rabbits, squirrels, cats, or small dogs outdoors
Delicate and sensitive around roughhousing, making calm supervision essential around young children

exercise.level: Moderate; calm, graceful, and happy lounging indoors for much of the day, adult Borzoi need daily brisk leashed walks paired with safe, regular opportunities to sprint in large, securely fenced enclosures
activities: Brisk daily leashed walks across quiet neighbourhoods or open trails (always on leash outside secure fences)
Short, exuberant full-speed sprints inside a very large, high-fenced paddock or yard
Organised lure coursing and straight or oval sighthound racing for fit adults
Calm, low-pressure obedience, trick enrichment, and relaxed indoor lounging

grooming.brushing: Despite its regal length, the silky coat is surprisingly manageable—brush and comb thoroughly two to three times a week (and daily during the heavy seasonal shedding weeks) with a pin brush and wide-toothed comb, focusing behind the ears, neck frill, armpits, chest, hindquarter feathering, and tail to prevent mats.
grooming.bathing: Bathe periodically with a mild canine shampoo—and add an extra bath or two during heavy seasonal coat blows to loosen and clear dead hair quickly.
notes: Trim excess hair cleanly around the hare-shaped paw pads for sure footing and keep strong nails clipped regularly.
Check the small folded ears weekly for wax buildup, dirt, or redness.
Provide soft, thick, supportive bedding to cushion lean sighthound joints and prevent elbow calluses.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging; intelligent and gently well-mannered, yet deeply independent and easily bored by repetitive drills—and its hardwired visual chase drive makes off-leash recall unreliable near moving wildlife
tips: Enrol in calm, positive puppy socialization and obedience classes early using patience, consistency, and appealing food rewards; harsh pressure causes this sensitive aristocrat to withdraw.
Keep training sessions brief, upbeat, and varied rather than drilling mechanical repetitions.
Never allow a Borzoi off-leash in unfenced parks, roadsides, or open fields—flying at 35 to 40 miles per hour after a squirrel or rabbit can carry it out of earshot in seconds.
Use a snug Martingale collar or well-fitted sighthound harness on walks, as the narrow head and sleek neck slip easily out of ordinary flat buckle collars.
training.socialization: Early, unhurried, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, everyday noises, and veterinary handling builds quiet confidence while respecting its naturally reserved sighthound dignity.

climates: Cool, crisp, and snowy climates—bred for open Russian winters, where its silky double-layering coat keeps it comfortable during vigorous outdoor exercise
Temperate four-season climates with spacious indoor resting areas
Warm climates are handled well indoors with air conditioning; schedule sprinting and brisk walks during cool early-morning or evening hours with constant shade and cool water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate; calm, clean, and quiet indoors once exercised, though many Borzoi enjoy the quiet company of their household or another compatible sighthound.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced large- or giant-breed dog food, using a controlled-growth large-breed puppy diet during rapid skeletal development.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three measured meals daily during rapid early growth (growing Borzoi puppies consume significantly more calories than mature adults).
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily (important for lowering acute stomach distension in a deep-chested giant sighthound).
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for slower metabolism, cardiac support, and joint wellness.

nutrition.guidelines: Adult Borzoi often eat less than people expect for a dog of their towering height, whereas fast-growing puppies require carefully balanced nutrition to support rapid bone growth without excess weight. Measure every meal accurately so the dog keeps a lean, hard-muscled coursing frame with visible rib contours and deep tuck-up. Divide daily adult food into two smaller meals, enforce strict calm rest for at least an hour before and after eating, and provide cool fresh drinking water continuously.
considerations: Because the Borzoi has a very deep, narrow chest, strictly avoid vigorous running immediately before or for a couple of hours after meals to help reduce the risk of life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat), and discuss prophylactic gastropexy with a veterinarian.
Keep growing puppies lean on a balanced large-breed growth formula—rapid growth combined with high-speed puppy running increases developmental orthopaedic and injury risk.
Count all training treats inside the daily calorie budget and transition gradually between diets over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs differ substantially between rapidly growing puppies, coursing athletes, and serene indoor adults. Consult a veterinarian familiar with giant sighthounds to tailor feeding quantities.

health.overview: The Borzoi is generally a robust, athletic giant sighthound with a typical life expectancy of 9 to 14 years (a 2021 Swedish owner survey reported a mean age of 8.8 years overall—7.4 years in males and 9.8 years in females—reflecting giant-breed mortality patterns). Peer-reviewed veterinary cardiology, genetics, and ophthalmology studies identify five key breed health priorities: cardiac arrhythmias and Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM, with a 2023 multicenter study of 152 Borzoi documenting ventricular arrhythmias in 19%—76% without major structural changes—and recommending echocardiographic and ECG/Holter screening), acute gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), autosomal-recessive Degenerative Myelopathy (SOD1:c.118G>A allele frequency 0.17 across 787 tested Borzoi), familial autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis (hypothyroidism), and multifocal chorioretinopathy ('Borzoi retinopathy'), alongside giant-breed osteosarcoma risk and sighthound anaesthetic sensitivity.
commonConditions: Cardiac arrhythmias, Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM), and sudden cardiac death — a 2023 multicenter retrospective study of 152 Borzoi across 14 cardiology centres detected ventricular arrhythmias in 19% (25/131, of which 76% had minimal or no structural heart disease) alongside DCM (n = 13), mostly mild myxomatous mitral valve disease (n = 12), tricuspid valve dysplasia (n = 6), and sudden death in 5% (3/55) with follow-up; a 2024 study established breed-specific echocardiographic reference values and urged routine cardiac screening

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — sudden, life-threatening gas distension and twisting of the stomach requiring immediate emergency surgery; a top non-testable emergency concern in this very deep-chested giant sighthound

Degenerative Myelopathy (DM, SOD1-related) — a late-onset, progressive, painless spinal cord degeneration (typically starting around age 8) associated with homozygosity for the SOD1:c.118G>A variant (found at an allele frequency of 0.17 across 787 tested Borzoi, with incomplete penetrance); preventable through pre-breeding DNA screening

Autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis (primary hypothyroidism) — a well-documented familial endocrine disorder studied across four generations of Borzoi, causing lethargy, coat thinning, or weight gain and managed with thyroid hormone replacement; monitored via pre-breeding thyroid panels

Multifocal chorioretinopathy ('Borzoi retinopathy') and other hereditary eye disorders — focal chorioretinal lesions documented in Borzoi (distinct from Progressive Retinal Atrophy) alongside cataracts, monitored through periodic specialist veterinary ophthalmologist examinations
Osteosarcoma (bone cancer) and other senior cancers — a major non-testable cause of senior mortality in giant sighthounds (owner surveys note cancer predominantly in older adults)

Sighthound anaesthetic sensitivity and rapid-growth musculoskeletal injuries — lower body-fat stores and sighthound drug metabolism increase sensitivity to certain anaesthetics, while rapid giant puppy growth heightens vulnerability to developmental or high-speed running injuries
preventiveCare: Verify documented pre-breeding health clearances for both parents: veterinary cardiac examination (ideally cardiologist echocardiogram plus ECG/Holter screening where available), board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination, thyroid panel, and Degenerative Myelopathy (SOD1) DNA testing.

Divide daily adult meals into two portions, avoid vigorous exercise right before and for a couple of hours after eating, learn emergency warning signs of bloat (unproductive retching, swollen tight abdomen, restlessness), and discuss prophylactic gastropexy with a veterinarian.
Always remind veterinarians prior to surgery or dental procedures that sighthounds such as Borzoi have heightened anaesthetic sensitivity and unique sighthound blood-chemistry baselines.
Protect rapidly growing Borzoi puppies from excessive forced jumping or uncontrolled collisions during high-speed play, and schedule annual veterinary wellness exams including cardiac auscultation.
recommendedScreenings: Cardiac evaluation by a board-certified veterinary cardiologist (echocardiogram using breed-specific reference values and ECG / 24-hour Holter monitoring for arrhythmias and DCM)
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (screening for Borzoi multifocal chorioretinopathy and cataracts)
Thyroid panel evaluation prior to breeding
DNA test for Degenerative Myelopathy (SOD1:c.118G>A)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental evaluations to keep the long, powerful jaws and scissor or even bite healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the small, thin, backward-folded ears weekly for wax buildup, dirt, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Part the long silky coat during regular brushing to check the thin, elastic skin for mats behind the ears or feathering, ticks, scrapes from sprinting, or pressure calluses on bony elbows.

idealFor: Calm, spacious homes with a very large, securely fenced yard seeking a quiet, serene, cat-like giant companion
Sighthound enthusiasts interested in lure coursing, oval racing, or showcasing an aristocratic long-coated hound
Quiet families with older, respectful children who appreciate a gentle, dignified, low-barking household dog
Owners willing to provide regular silky-coat brushing, strict on-leash safety, and proactive cardiac and bloat vigilance
notIdealFor: Small apartments or households lacking safe, spacious fenced areas for high-speed sighthound sprinting
Owners wanting an off-leash hiking dog or instant, mechanical obedience in distracting outdoor environments
Homes with free-roaming cats, rabbits, small rodents, or boisterous roughhousing toddlers
People seeking a loud, fiercely territorial guard dog or unwilling to manage seasonal long-coat shedding

funFacts: The Russian word 'borzoi' translates directly to 'swift'—and in full stride across open ground, a fit Borzoi can accelerate to 35 to 40 miles per hour.

Until 1936, the breed was officially known in the English-speaking world as the 'Russian Wolfhound,' reflecting imperial hunts where matched pairs of Borzoi coursed wolves across the Russian steppes and pinned them until mounted hunters arrived.
Before the 1917 Russian Revolution, Russian aristocrats kept immense country estates devoted to Borzoi hunting packs—often celebrating successful hunts with lavish ceremonial feasts in field tents.

Despite its towering 75 to 85 cm male frame and flowing silky coat, the Borzoi is famously quiet, tidy, and serene indoors—often likened to an oversized aristocratic cat that may flatly refuse to step outside on a rainy day.

Because sighthounds have uniquely proportioned athletic hearts, veterinary cardiologists published dedicated Borzoi-specific echocardiographic reference values in 2024 to help screen accurately for dilated cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias.

faq.question: What is a Borzoi?
faq.answer: The Borzoi (Russkaya Psovaya Borzaya, formerly called the Russian Wolfhound) is a tall, lean, silky-coated giant Russian sighthound historically bred by the aristocracy to course hares, foxes, and wolves across open terrain.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Borzoi?
faq.answer: Desirable height at the withers is 75 to 85 cm for males and 68 to 78 cm for females, with adult males typically weighing 75 to 105 pounds and adult females typically weighing 60 to 85 pounds.

faq.question: How long does a Borzoi live?
faq.answer: The breed's typical life expectancy is 9 to 14 years (though giant-breed owner surveys report an average age around 9 years, with females often living slightly longer than males).

faq.question: Can a Borzoi live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Although remarkably quiet, clean, and calm indoors, its giant size and need for safe, spacious fenced areas to sprint at full speed make a large house with a big, securely fenced yard far more practical.

faq.question: Do Borzoi shed a lot, and how much grooming do they need?
faq.answer: They shed moderately year-round and drop substantial amounts of long hair during seasonal shedding periods (once or twice a year). Thorough brushing two to three times a week—and daily plus extra baths during heavy shedding—keeps the silky coat tangle-free.

faq.question: Are Borzoi good with children and other pets?
faq.answer: They are gentle, calm, and affectionate with older, respectful children (always supervised, as they dislike roughhousing) and generally live harmoniously with other large, polite dogs. Because of their intense visual chasing instinct, however, they should never be trusted loose around small running animals or unfamiliar outdoor cats.

faq.question: Are Borzoi easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent and polite, but deeply independent rather than eager to please through repetitive obedience drills. Patient, positive, short sessions work best—and they must always be walked on a leash outside secure fences because running prey instantly triggers their chase instinct.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Borzoi?
faq.answer: Major breed health priorities include ventricular arrhythmias and Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM, screened via cardiologist echo and ECG/Holter monitoring), acute bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus), Degenerative Myelopathy (SOD1 DNA-screenable), autoimmune hypothyroidism, multifocal chorioretinopathy ('Borzoi retinopathy'), senior bone cancer (osteosarcoma), and sighthound anaesthetic sensitivity.
