funFacts: The word 'belton'—used exclusively to describe the flecked coat pattern of the English Setter—comes from a village in Northumberland, England, and was popularized by nineteenth-century breeder Edward Laverack.

Before hunting firearms existed, early British setters were trained to creep forward and lie flat ('set') on their bellies when they scented partridge or quail so hunters could throw a large net right over the crouching dog and the birds.

In 1570, royal physician John Caius wrote the earliest detailed account of the setting dog in 'De Canibus Britannicis', referring to the breed by the Latin name 'Index' for the way it silently pointed out game.

Modern English Setters are often seen in two complementary types: the taller, more heavily feathered bench or 'Laverack' type, and the slightly smaller, lighter-coated field or 'Llewellin' type bred for upland hunting and field trials.

The English Setter competed at the very first formal British dog show held at Newcastle upon Tyne on 28 January 1859 and was one of the nine original charter breeds registered in the United States in 1878.

faq.question: What does the term 'belton' mean in English Setters?
faq.answer: Belton refers to the breed's signature coat pattern of coloured flecking or ticking blended through a white coat, occurring in blue (black on white), orange, lemon, liver, or tricolour. Named after a village in Northumberland, England, the term was popularized by nineteenth-century breeder Edward Laverack.

faq.question: What is the difference between a Laverack and a Llewellin English Setter?
faq.answer: Both belong to the same English Setter breed, but they reflect different nineteenth-century British breeding lines. Laverack lines form the foundation of modern conformation or show-type dogs, which are typically larger with longer, more profuse feathering, whereas Llewellin lines were developed by R. Purcell Llewellin for field trials and upland hunting and tend to be slightly lighter in frame and coat.

faq.question: Are English Setters good family dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. English Setters are widely known for a gentle, merry, and affectionate nature with family members, children, strangers, and other dogs. As with any medium-to-large active breed, interactions with young children should be supervised and the dog's daily exercise needs must be met.

faq.question: How much exercise does an English Setter need?
faq.answer: Adult English Setters generally need 60 to 120 minutes of daily physical activity and scent enrichment, such as brisk walks, hikes, or running in a securely fenced area. Once thoroughly exercised, they typically settle calmly indoors. High-impact exercise should be avoided until skeletal maturity around two years of age.

faq.question: Why is BAER hearing testing important for English Setter puppies?
faq.answer: English Setters carry a predisposition to congenital sensorineural deafness associated with white piebald and roan pigmentation. A Brainstem Auditory Evoked Response (BAER) test—typically performed on puppies from 5 to 7 weeks of age onward—accurately identifies whether a puppy hears normally in both ears or has unilateral or bilateral deafness.

faq.question: What health screenings should I ask an English Setter breeder about?
faq.answer: Prospective owners should ask for documented hip and elbow radiographic evaluations, an autoimmune thyroiditis panel, and BAER hearing test results for both parents and puppies, as well as DNA test status for late-onset progressive retinal atrophy (rcd4-PRA) and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL8) where applicable.

overview.summary: A compact, athletic British flushing gundog with long feathered ears, a weather-resistant double coat, and a cheerful, eager-to-please nature that thrives both in the field and as an active family companion.
overview.description: The English Springer Spaniel is a symmetrical, muscular medium-sized gundog standing highest on the leg among native British land spaniels. Built to work long days pushing birds from dense cover and retrieving cleanly over land and water, it moves with a smooth, free-swinging stride driven cleanly from the hocks. Its close, straight, flat double coat resists wet weather and carries moderate feathering along the ears, chest, legs, and underside, classically patterned in liver and white, black and white, or either combination with tan points. The finely modeled head frames medium almond-shaped dark hazel eyes with a kind, attentive expression and long lobular ears set in line with the eyes. Indoors, this people-oriented spaniel is affectionate, polite, and playful, though it needs generous daily activity and companionship to stay content.
overview.history: Britain's land spaniels share ancient roots as flushing dogs that sprang birds into nets or for falcons long before sporting firearms became widespread. For generations, larger 'springers' and smaller 'cockers' were born in the same litters and sorted simply by size and hunting task. During the nineteenth century, selective breeding stabilized distinct types—including a liver-and-white strain popularly linked to the Duke of Norfolk and known for a time as the Norfolk Spaniel. Formal recognition as a separate breed arrived in Britain in 1902, followed by recognition in the United States in 1910 and international recognition in 1954. Over the twentieth century, field-bred working lines (lighter-boned with shorter feathering and intense hunting drive) and show-bred lines (heavier-boned with fuller feathering) diverged in appearance while retaining the breed's signature biddability and stamina.

grooming.bathing: Bathe every four to six weeks or after muddy field outings using a gentle dog shampoo, drying the ears and feathering thoroughly.

Check and dry the long, lush drop ears regularly—especially after swimming—to prevent moisture buildup and ear infections.

Brush teeth often with dog-safe enzymatic toothpaste.

Provide structured retrieving games so mouthy energy goes into toys rather than household items.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal and factor training treats into the daily calorie budget so this food-loving spaniel stays lean and athletic. Avoid cooked bones and high-fat table scraps, use narrow spaniel bowls if needed to keep long ear fringes dry, and keep fresh water available continuously.
considerations: Keep weight lean to protect hip and elbow joints over a long active life.
Limit treats and fatty table scraps to prevent weight gain and digestive upset.
Use narrow bowls or ear snoods at mealtime if long ear fringes get wet or soiled.
Transition between food formulas gradually over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Calorie needs vary noticeably between active field-trial dogs and quieter household pets. Consult a veterinarian if you have questions about weight or diet.

health.overview: English Springer Spaniels are generally healthy, vigorous gundogs with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years. Responsible breeding focuses on radiographic hip and elbow screening, annual ophthalmologist exams, and DNA testing for inherited disorders documented in the breed—most notably delayed-onset cone-rod dystrophy 1 progressive retinal atrophy (cord1-PRA, linked to an RPGRIP1 variant), alongside breed-club screening for phosphofructokinase (PFK) deficiency, fucosidosis, and familial nephropathy—while routine home care prioritizes ear hygiene.
commonConditions: Cone-rod dystrophy 1 progressive retinal atrophy (cord1-PRA / RPGRIP1 variant) — a well-established, highly prevalent inherited retinal degeneration in the breed that typically causes delayed-onset photoreceptor loss and visual decline; screenable via DNA testing and ophthalmic exams
Hip dysplasia — developmental looseness of the hip joint that can progress to osteoarthritis, monitored via pre-breeding radiographic hip evaluations
Elbow dysplasia — developmental abnormality of the elbow joint causing forelimb lameness, screened radiographically prior to breeding
Otitis externa (outer ear infections) — a frequent conformational risk in long, lush drop-eared spaniels when moisture or wax accumulates in the ear canal
Phosphofructokinase (PFK) deficiency — an autosomal recessive metabolic enzyme deficiency causing exercise-induced muscle cramping and hemolytic episodes, preventable through DNA screening
Fucosidosis — a rare autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder (FUCA1 gene) causing progressive neurological signs, preventable through DNA screening
Hereditary eye disorders — including cataracts and retinal anomalies, monitored through periodic veterinary ophthalmologist examinations
preventiveCare: Confirm breeding parents have completed radiographic hip and elbow clearances, specialist eye evaluations, and cord1-PRA DNA testing (plus PFK and fucosidosis DNA tests where recommended).
Inspect and gently dry the long drop ears regularly, especially after swimming or bathing.
Maintain a lean, athletic weight to reduce strain on hips and elbows.
Brush teeth often with canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental and wellness exams.
Keep year-round parasite prevention against ticks, fleas, and heartworm up to date.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip evaluation prior to breeding

Periodic veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination

health.skinCare: Part the feathered double coat during weekly brushing to inspect for ticks, burrs, grass seeds, or damp-skin irritation.

funFacts: Historically, larger 'springers' and smaller 'cockers' were born in the same British land-spaniel litters and sorted purely by size and hunting task before being separated into distinct breeds in 1902.
The breed's name comes from its classic hunting style of 'springing' forward into dense undergrowth to flush game birds into nets or into the air.
At one point the breed was widely called the Norfolk Spaniel because of a celebrated liver-and-white strain linked to the Duke of Norfolk.
Among all native British land spaniels, the English Springer Spaniel stands highest on the leg, giving it the smooth, ground-covering stride needed for full days in rough cover.

Modern English Springer Spaniels often reflect two distinct lines—leaner, shorter-coated field-bred dogs selected for hunting trials and fuller-feathered show-bred dogs—though both share the same eager-to-please spirit.

faq.question: What is an English Springer Spaniel?
faq.answer: The English Springer Spaniel is a medium-sized British flushing gundog known for its compact athletic frame, long feathered ears, weather-resistant double coat, and friendly, playful, trainable personality.

faq.question: How does an English Springer Spaniel differ from an English Cocker Spaniel?
faq.answer: They share the same British land-spaniel roots, but the English Springer Spaniel is taller and racier (standing around 51 cm and weighing roughly 20 to 25 kg for males), whereas the English Cocker Spaniel is smaller and lower on leg.

faq.question: What is the difference between field-bred and show-bred English Springer Spaniels?
faq.answer: Field-bred lines are selected for hunting and field trials and typically have shorter coats, lighter bone, and intense drive, while show-bred lines tend to have fuller feathering, heavier bone, and a slightly calmer household pace.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an English Springer Spaniel?
faq.answer: Target height is approximately 51 cm at the withers (typically 48 to 53 cm for males and 46 to 51 cm for females), with working weights around 22.5 kg (typically 20 to 25 kg for males and 16 to 23 kg for females).

faq.question: How long does an English Springer Spaniel live?
faq.answer: With good nutrition, regular exercise, and routine veterinary care, English Springer Spaniels typically live 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: How much grooming does an English Springer Spaniel need?
faq.answer: Brush at least once or twice weekly with a slicker brush and metal comb to keep the feathering mat-free, neaten hair around the feet, neck, and tail periodically, check the long drop ears regularly, trim nails, and brush teeth often.

faq.question: Can an English Springer Spaniel live in an apartment?
faq.answer: While adaptable indoors if given plenty of daily exercise, a house with a large, securely fenced yard is generally much better suited to their high energy and love of outdoor exploration.

faq.question: Are English Springer Spaniels good family dogs and good with children?
faq.answer: Yes. They are famously polite, gentle, playful, and people-oriented, getting along well with children and other dogs when properly socialized and exercised.

faq.question: How much daily exercise does an English Springer Spaniel need?
faq.answer: Plan on at least 60 to 90 minutes of daily activity—such as brisk walks, hikes, swimming, fetch, or dog sports—plus mental enrichment.

faq.question: Which health screenings are recommended for breeding English Springer Spaniels?
faq.answer: Recommended pre-breeding screenings include radiographic hip and elbow evaluations, periodic veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams, and DNA testing for cord1-PRA (RPGRIP1), along with parent-club DNA tests for PFK deficiency and fucosidosis.

overview.summary: A miniature, finely boned British toy terrier celebrated for its sleek black coat, sharply etched mahogany-tan markings, erect candle-flame ears, and alert, affectionate disposition.
overview.description: The English Toy Terrier (Black & Tan) is an elegant, compact companion that combines the sharp wit and rapid reactions of an ancient ratter with the gentle devotion of a toy companion. It presents a refined, wedge-shaped head, small almond-shaped eyes, distinctive pointed prick ears, and a smooth, glistening single coat. Despite its dainty stature, it possesses genuine terrier spirit, remaining intensely observant and curious about household activity. Thriving in urban flats as well as suburban homes, it requires thoughtful daily interaction, reward-based training, and gentle handling to protect its delicate skeletal framework.
overview.history: Developed in nineteenth-century England from the Black and Tan Terrier—the same root stock that produced the Manchester Terrier—this breed was selectively bred down in size to excel in Victorian rat pits and serve as an elegant parlor pet. Known historically as the Miniature Black and Tan, it enjoyed immense popularity in early British dog shows before evolving into a devoted companion. Today, it is recognized as a vulnerable native heritage breed in Great Britain, where dedicated preservationists maintain its historic bloodlines and sound genetic health.

tips: Employ positive reinforcement with tiny, low-calorie soft treats and enthusiastic verbal praise.
Keep lessons short, varied, and entertaining to sustain focus.
Introduce gentle handling and cooperative nail trimming from early puppyhood.
Avoid punitive or heavy-handed methods that cause sensitive toy terriers to lose trust.

Factor all training treats into the total daily caloric intake.
Ensure continuous access to fresh drinking water.

health.overview: The English Toy Terrier (Black & Tan) is generally a hardy toy breed with an average lifespan of 12 to 13 years. Breed clubs recommend pre-breeding health screening for patellar luxation, juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy (JDCM), and xanthinuria. Prospective owners should review parental screening documentation and maintain routine veterinary care.
commonConditions: Patellar luxation (slipping kneecaps)
Juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy (JDCM), an inherited cardiac condition managed via DNA screening
Xanthinuria, an inherited metabolic defect that can predispose dogs to xanthine urinary stones
Periodontal disease common among toy canines
Bone fractures resulting from falls or rough handling
preventiveCare: Verify parental health clearances for patellas, JDCM, and xanthinuria before obtaining a puppy.
Establish consistent oral hygiene with daily tooth brushing and periodic veterinary scalings.
Protect against household falls by discouraging jumping from high sofas or beds.
Schedule yearly wellness check-ups including auscultation of the heart.
recommendedScreenings: Patellar luxation veterinary clinical evaluation

health.dentalCare: Small dogs can be prone to dental plaque and periodontal problems. Brush the teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and arrange veterinary dental checks; professional cleaning should be guided by clinical need.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears routinely for redness, odour, discharge or persistent scratching. Clean only as advised by a veterinarian and do not insert cotton swabs deeply into the ear canal.
health.skinCare: The short coat needs little maintenance. Check for irritation, parasites, wounds or unusual hair loss during grooming and seek veterinary advice if signs persist.

funFacts: The breed's traditional black-and-tan pattern is expected to have sharply defined boundaries between the two colours.
Its distinctive upright prick ears curve gracefully to resemble the silhouette of a flickering candle flame.
The English Toy Terrier descends from British black-and-tan ratting terriers.
It is designated as a vulnerable native breed in Great Britain due to low annual puppy registration numbers.

faq.question: How big does an English Toy Terrier get?
faq.answer: Ideal height measures 25 to 30 cm at the withers, accompanied by a target adult body weight of 2.7 to 3.6 kg.

faq.question: What colours can an English Toy Terrier have?
faq.answer: The only accepted colour pattern is ebony black with rich chestnut-tan points, with crisp boundaries separating the two colours.

faq.question: Is the English Toy Terrier suitable for an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes. Their small stature, moderate exercise needs, and tidy habits make them well-suited to apartment living, provided they receive daily outdoor strolls and loving interaction.

faq.question: How much grooming does it need?
faq.answer: Very little. Weekly wiping with a rubber mitt or soft brush, regular nail trims, and daily dental care are all that is required to maintain its glossy short coat.

faq.question: What health tests should prospective breeders discuss?
faq.answer: Responsible breeders screen prospective parents for patellar luxation, juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy (JDCM), and xanthinuria.

faq.question: Is the English Toy Terrier good with children?
faq.answer: It can be a delightful companion for gentle, considerate older children. Because of its delicate toy frame, supervision is essential to avoid rough handling or accidental drops.

overview.summary: The Épagneul Bleu de Picardie, or Blue Picardy Spaniel, is a medium-sized French pointing dog bred for versatile field work. Its signature blue-grey coat comes from fine black-and-white speckling, often accented with black patches. Gentle, affectionate, and athletic, it adapts well to active family homes while keeping strong sporting and scenting instincts.
overview.description: This sturdy, continental spaniel-type pointer has a slightly elongated, muscular frame and a broad, oval skull with a long, fairly wide muzzle, dark expressive eyes, and low-set pendulous ears framed in wavy, silky hair. Its flat or slightly wavy coat shows longer feathering on the legs and tail, and gets its distinctive bluish tone from black-and-white ticked hairs with or without solid black patches. Calm and even-tempered indoors, it thrives when given consistent training, early socialization, and daily outlets for its sporting energy.
overview.history: Originating in northern France's Picardy region, the breed grew out of nineteenth-century black and black-and-white northern spaniels crossed with setter bloodlines, including English and Gordon Setters. By the early twentieth century it was recognized separately from the Picardy Spaniel, distinguished primarily by its blue-speckled coat. Valued for close-range pointing and retrieving—especially for woodcock and marsh game—it remains a working sporting breed.

health.overview: Available breed standards establish conformation and temperament but do not provide population-wide disease prevalence or a formal screening protocol. Use positive handling so the dog stays comfortable during grooming and veterinary checks.
Seek veterinary evaluation for any persistent changes in appetite, stamina, mobility, or hearing.
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with canine toothpaste and arrange periodic veterinary oral checks. Have bad breath, bleeding gums, or chewing difficulty assessed promptly.
health.earCare: Check the long, pendulous ears weekly for redness, odour, moisture, or head shaking. Clean gently with a veterinarian-recommended solution only when needed.
health.skinCare: Inspect skin during brushing and after outdoor runs for ticks, grass seeds, hotspots, or persistent itching.

idealFor: Active owners who enjoy daily walks, hiking, and outdoor routines
Handlers interested in scent games, pointing work, or field sports
Households ready to provide consistent training, companionship, and enrichment
Owners prepared to manage strong wildlife and scenting instincts safely
notIdealFor: Sedentary households wanting a low-activity companion
Owners unable to commit time to daily exercise and training

funFacts: Its blue-grey coat effect comes from finely intermingled black and white ticked hairs rather than a solid blue pigment.
Woodcock hunting in northern France's marshes and woodlands was one of its signature traditional roles.
Closely related to the Picardy Spaniel, it is distinguished primarily by its blue-grey speckled colouring.
Classified among continental pointing dogs of the spaniel type, it remains subject to a field working trial.

faq.question: Where does the Épagneul Bleu de Picardie come from?
faq.answer: It comes from Picardy in northern France, where it was developed as a versatile sporting dog for pointing and retrieving small game.

faq.question: Why is it called the Blue Picardy Spaniel?
faq.answer: Its name reflects the bluish-grey cast produced by a dense mixture of black and white speckled hairs, often paired with black patches.

faq.question: How tall is the Épagneul Bleu de Picardie?
faq.answer: Adult males typically measure 57 to 62 cm at the withers and females 55 to 60 cm, with a ± 2 cm tolerance considered undesirable.

faq.question: How much does the breed weigh?
faq.answer: Typical adult weight is around 19.5 to 22.7 kg, depending on sex, build, and conditioning.

faq.question: Is it a good family dog?
faq.answer: Typically gentle, calm indoors, and affectionate, it adapts well to active family homes when given adequate exercise, early socialization, and supervision around children.

faq.question: How much exercise does it need?
faq.answer: As an athletic pointing breed, it needs daily walks plus regular mental stimulation such as scent games, retrieving, or field training, tailored to age and fitness.

faq.question: What health problems is the breed known for?
faq.answer: No comprehensive breed-wide disease prevalence list is established in the consulted standards. Ask breeders for documented parental health checks and keep up routine veterinary care, especially for its long pendulous ears.

overview.summary: The Estrela Mountain Dog is a powerful, rustic mastiff-type livestock guardian native to the Serra da Estrela highlands of central Portugal, bred in both long-haired and short-haired varieties and recognised for its goat-hair-textured double coat, dark facial mask, hooked scimitar tail, and steadfast devotion to its flock and household.
overview.description: Built on a well-proportioned, athletic molossoid frame that combines substance with quick, nimble movement, the Estrela Mountain Dog is engineered to confront predators across steep, rocky terrain. Its thick, resilient coat—comparable in feel to goat hair—comes in two varieties, long-haired and short-haired, both backed by a dense, fine, lighter-coloured undercoat and shaded in fawn, wolf grey, yellow, or brindle with a characteristic dark mask over the muzzle and skull. The strong, elongated head carries medium-sized oval amber eyes, small rose-folded triangular ears, and a long, well-feathered tail that hangs in a scimitar curve ending in a distinct hook at the tip. Docile and deeply attached to its shepherd or family, this self-assured guardian is naturally wary of strangers and decisive when defending its charges.
overview.history: One of the oldest indigenous breeds of the Iberian Peninsula, the Estrela Mountain Dog developed in the granite highlands of the Serra da Estrela—mainland Portugal's highest mountain range—where shepherds relied on formidable flock guardians during seasonal transhumance migrations. For centuries these dogs accompanied sheep and goat herds between high summer pastures and lowland winter valleys, wearing spiked iron collars ('carrancas') to shield their throats from Iberian wolves. Special working and conformation trials ('concursos') began between 1908 and 1919 to preserve the mountain stock, followed by a preliminary written description in 1922 and the first formal standard in 1933. Internationally recognised on a definitive basis in January 1955, the breed continues to work as a flock and estate guardian in Portugal and abroad.
overview.originalPurpose: Guarding flocks of sheep and goats against wolves and livestock thieves in the Serra da Estrela mountains, as well as watching rural homesteads and pulling light carts.
currentRoles: Working livestock guardian for sheep, goats, and cattle
Rural estate and homestead watchdog
Devoted family guardian for experienced handlers
Patrol and security working dog

physical.coatType: Strong, very abundant, slightly coarse outer coat resembling goat hair in texture, lying flat or slightly wavy over a dense, fine, short, lighter-coloured undercoat; bred in both a long-haired variety (with a thick neck ruff, forearm and hindlimb feathering, and bushy tail) and a short-haired variety (with short, dense outer hair and no feathering).
physical.coatLength: Two recognised varieties: Long-haired (long on trunk, neck ruff, breeches, and tail; short and smooth on head and front of legs) and Short-haired (short, dense, and even without feathering).
coatColors: Solid fawn, wolf grey, or yellow
Brindle (fawn, wolf grey, or yellow ground striped with blackish brindling)
Typical dark or black cranio-facial mask
White markings permitted only on the tips of the fore and hind feet and a small patch on the lower neck and chest
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate to high; sheds year-round with heavy seasonal moulting of the dense undercoat in spring and autumn
physical.droolingLevel: Low to moderate; well-developed upper lips overlap without being thick or pendulous, and the mouth corners stay tight
distinctiveFeatures: Athletic, rustic mountain molossoid standing 65 to 73 cm in males and 62 to 69 cm in females (with an upper tolerance of +2 cm)
Working weight of 45 to 60 kg in males and 35 to 45 kg in females
Two distinct coat varieties—long-haired and short-haired—both carrying a goat-hair-textured outer coat over a lighter undercoat
Dark cranio-facial mask contrasting with a fawn, wolf-grey, yellow, or brindle coat
Long, strong, slightly convex head with almost parallel skull and muzzle axes, a gentle stop, and a slightly convex nasal bridge near the tip
Large, well-opened black nostrils and firm, non-pendulous lips with black mucous membranes
Horizontal, oval, medium-sized dark amber eyes with tight black-rimmed lids and a calm, intelligent expression
Small, thin, triangular ears with rounded tips, set at medium height and falling backward and laterally against the head (rose-type carriage)
Short, straight, thick neck well set into the shoulders with a slight, unexaggerated dewlap on the throat
Long, uncut scimitar-shaped tail reaching the hock, well feathered in the long-haired variety, and ending in a characteristic hook at the tip

traits: Inseparable, loyal, and docile toward its shepherd and household
Fearless, resolute defender of flocks and property against predators and thieves
Naturally wary and aloof toward strangers
Calm, dignified, and observant with a vivid, expressive gaze
Independent decision-maker bred to assess threats on its own
Protective and gentle with family children when properly socialised
Deep, resonant warning bark when patrolling boundaries

exercise.level: Moderate to high. Built for long days patrolling mountain pastures, the Estrela Mountain Dog needs daily country walks and space to patrol inside a securely fenced property.
activities: Daily country or hill walks on a sturdy lead
Supervised perimeter patrolling in a large, securely fenced yard or paddock
Livestock guarding duties on rural holdings
Scent-tracking and nosework games

grooming.brushing: Brush the long-haired variety two to three times a week (and the short-haired variety once a week) with a pin brush and undercoat rake, increasing to daily raking during the spring and autumn undercoat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when heavily soiled, using a mild canine shampoo so the coarse goat-like outer coat retains its natural weather resistance.
notes: Pay special attention to the thick neck ruff, behind the ears, and the hindlimb breeches on long-haired dogs to prevent tangles or trapped burrs.
Never shave the double coat, which shields the dog from both winter mountain cold and summer sun.
Inspect the small, folded ears weekly for wax, moisture, or grass seeds.
Trim strong nails every few weeks if they do not wear down naturally.
Brush teeth several times a week with canine toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Challenging. Intelligent and devoted to its owner, yet bred for centuries to work and make guarding decisions independently—requiring calm, steady leadership and early socialisation.
tips: Use calm, consistent, reward-based training rather than harsh force or repetitive mechanical drills.
Establish reliable lead manners and household rules early in puppyhood before the dog reaches 35 to 60 kg.
Enclose the property with secure fencing at least 1.8 metres high, as the breed is a dedicated territorial guardian.
Supervise introductions to visitors calmly so the dog sees that guests are welcomed by the owner.
training.socialization: Expose puppies thoroughly and positively from an early age to varied people, sights, sounds, veterinary handling, and calm dogs so their natural aloofness toward strangers matures into steady, discerning composure.

climates: Cool and mountain climates where its dense double coat thrives
Temperate climates
Warm weather when ample shade, cool indoor rest, fresh water, and early-morning or evening walks are provided
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate when given a secure outdoor territory or flock to watch over, though companion dogs still need daily interaction with their family.

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced large- or giant-breed diet formulated to support steady skeletal growth in puppies and lean muscle in adults.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three measured meals daily until six months of age on a controlled-calcium large-breed puppy formula, then two daily meals.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady digestion and reduce the risk of gastric torsion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored to lower energy output and joint health.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure rations to keep the dog in fit, muscular condition without obesity, which is explicitly faulted and strains the hips and elbows. Divide daily food into two meals, rest the dog for at least an hour before and after exercise around mealtimes, and provide clean water at all times.
considerations: Use a large-breed puppy diet with appropriate calcium-to-phosphorus balance so bone growth is steady rather than overly rapid.
Keep adult weight lean so the dog remains agile and light on its feet.
Avoid vigorous activity immediately before and after meals to help prevent gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
Adjust portions between cold winter work and warmer summer months.
nutrition.note: General large-breed nutrition guidance; consult a veterinarian to tailor daily portions to age and workload.

health.overview: The Estrela Mountain Dog is a hardy, rustic mountain breed with a typical life expectancy of 10 to 14 years. Peer-reviewed veterinary studies and breed club records identify hip and elbow dysplasia, dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) with occasional sinoatrial conduction abnormalities, gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), and eyelid conformation issues as the principal health considerations.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia — heritable coxofemoral joint laxity and malformation studied extensively in the breed, where early passive hip laxity testing between 4 and 12 months and adult radiographic scoring help identify affected dogs

Dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) and sinoatrial dysfunction — myocardial dilation and conduction disorders documented in clinical veterinary cardiology studies of the breed and monitored via echocardiography and electrocardiography
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — acute, life-threatening stomach distension and twisting in deep-chested large breeds
Entropion or ectropion — inward- or outward-rolling eyelid margins that can irritate the cornea
preventiveCare: Select puppies from parents with official hip and elbow radiographic clearances and recent veterinary cardiac evaluations (echocardiogram and ECG/Holter).
Consider early veterinary hip laxity evaluation in growing dogs alongside standard adult radiographic hip scoring prior to breeding.
Raise puppies on a controlled large-breed growth diet and avoid excessive high-impact jumping before skeletal maturity.
Feed two smaller daily meals and rest the dog before and after exercise to lower bloat risk.
Check ears, eyes, and coat regularly after country walks for ticks and grass awns.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness and cardiac examinations.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip evaluation prior to breeding (including early passive hip laxity assessment where available)
Radiographic elbow evaluation prior to breeding
Specialist cardiac evaluation (echocardiography and electrocardiography / Holter monitoring) for dilated cardiomyopathy and sinoatrial conduction disorders
Ophthalmic examination
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week with canine toothpaste and check the strong scissor or pincer bite and gums during annual veterinary visits.
health.earCare: Inspect the small, folded triangular ears weekly for wax, moisture, or plant debris and clean gently with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser.
health.skinCare: Brush and rake the double coat regularly during seasonal moults so dead undercoat does not mat and trap moisture against the skin.

notIdealFor: First-time dog owners unaccustomed to large, independent territorial guardians

funFacts: Named after the Serra da Estrela ('Star Mountain Range'), the highest mountain range in mainland Portugal, where granite peaks rise to nearly 2,000 metres.
At rest, the breed's long scimitar tail hangs to the hock with a signature upward hook at the very tip.

Unlike many mountain guardians that exist in only one coat length, the Cão da Serra da Estrela has both a long-haired and a short-haired variety—and historically the short-haired type was widely favoured by working shepherds.
Early twentieth-century preservation began with rural working trials called 'concursos' between 1908 and 1919, leading to a first draft description in 1922 and the 1933 standard.
When guarding flocks on wolf-inhabited mountain pastures, working dogs traditionally wore heavy iron-spiked collars ('carrancas') to protect their necks.
Aside from guarding herds, the breed has even served as a patrol dog with the Portuguese Marines (Fuzileiros).

faq.question: What is an Estrela Mountain Dog?
faq.answer: The Estrela Mountain Dog (Cão da Serra da Estrela) is an ancient Portuguese molossoid flock guardian from the Serra da Estrela mountains, bred in both long-haired and short-haired varieties and known for its dark facial mask, hooked tail tip, and loyal protective nature.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Estrela Mountain Dog?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 65 to 73 cm at the withers (with a tolerance of +2 cm) and weigh 45 to 60 kg, while females stand 62 to 69 cm (+2 cm tolerance) and weigh 35 to 45 kg.

faq.question: What is the typical lifespan of an Estrela Mountain Dog?
faq.answer: The breed typically lives 10 to 14 years.

faq.question: What is the difference between the two coat varieties?
faq.answer: Both varieties have a resilient outer coat with a goat-hair texture over a dense, lighter-coloured undercoat. The long-haired variety has longer body hair, a thick neck ruff (especially in males), feathered limbs, and a bushy tail, while the short-haired variety has a short, dense, even coat with no feathering.

faq.question: What coat colours are permitted?
faq.answer: Only solid fawn, wolf grey, and yellow, or brindle on a fawn, wolf-grey, or yellow ground are permitted, accompanied by a typical dark cranio-facial mask. White markings are allowed only on the tips of the feet and a small area on the lower neck and chest.

faq.question: Can an Estrela Mountain Dog live in an apartment?
faq.answer: No. Its large size, strong territorial guarding instinct, and deep warning bark require a home with a spacious, securely fenced yard or rural land.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for the breed?
faq.answer: Breeding dogs should be screened with hip and elbow radiographs, a specialist cardiac evaluation (echocardiogram and ECG) for dilated cardiomyopathy and conduction disorders, and an eye examination.

overview.summary: A self-assured, calm, and even-tempered medium-sized German Spitz breed developed specifically as a devoted household companion.
overview.description: The Eurasier is a balanced, well-constructed medium-sized Spitz-type dog with prick ears, a wedge-shaped head, a dense double coat, and a bushy tail carried lying forward over the back, bent slightly sideways, or rolled up. The body is slightly longer than the height at the withers, with medium bone and a coat length that still reveals the dog's natural outline. Calm, poised, and watchful without being noisy, the Eurasier bonds to its entire family rather than a single person and displays a dignified reserve toward strangers without fear or aggression. To develop its characteristic even temperament, the breed requires close daily indoor contact with its household, gentle and consistent guidance, and regular outdoor walks.
overview.history: The breed originated in Weinheim, Germany, in 1960 when Julius Wipfel, joined by Charlotte Baldamus and other dedicated breeders, crossed Wolfspitz females with Chow Chow males to create a family-oriented Spitz with primitive canine traits. This initial cross was known as the Wolf-Chow. In 1972, Samoyed blood was introduced through the male Cito von Pol to broaden genetic diversity and enhance a friendly, cooperative disposition. In 1973, the breed was renamed Eurasier—reflecting its combined European and Asian heritage—and gained official national and international recognition. Ethologist Konrad Lorenz acquired a Eurasier in 1972 and praised the breed's character and devotion.

exercise.level: Moderate. Calm and composed indoors, yet active and energetic outdoors during daily walks and play.
activities: Daily walks, including off-leash outings in secure areas once recall is reliable
Interactive play and chasing games with family members or familiar dogs
Agility, rally, and obedience activities
Scent games and varied mental enrichment
Swimming or water play for individuals that enjoy water

grooming.level: Moderate overall; low maintenance for most of the year, increasing to high daily maintenance during seasonal undercoat shedding.
grooming.brushing: Thorough combing and brushing once a week to once every two weeks normally, increasing to daily brushing for roughly three weeks once or twice a year when the undercoat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Infrequent, only as needed; the coat has very little doggy odour and naturally sheds dirt.
notes: Use a pin brush and metal comb to reach through the dense undercoat, paying attention to feathering on the forelegs, hind-leg breeches, and behind the ears.
Daily brushing during the once- or twice-yearly coat blow prevents loose undercoat wool from matting or collecting indoors.
Spaying or neutering can cause the coat to become noticeably thicker, longer, softer, and more labour-intensive to groom.
Avoid shaving or clipping the double coat unless medically required, as it provides insulation and skin protection.
Check eyes, ears, paw pads, and nails (especially dewclaws) during weekly grooming sessions.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Intelligent and eager to please its family, though capable of independent thought and easily bored by repetitive drills.
tips: Rely on affectionate, reward-based positive reinforcement and calm, consistent leadership.
Avoid harsh corrections or heavy-handed pressure, which can shut down a sensitive dog.
Keep training sessions varied, purposeful, and engaging rather than repeating the same exercise.
Focus on chase games and interactive rewards rather than repetitive ball retrieving, which many individuals find tedious.
Practise reliable recall in enclosed spaces before allowing off-leash freedom.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, positive exposure to varied people, sights, sounds, and other animals early in puppyhood and continue into adulthood. Because the breed naturally assesses unfamiliar people at its own pace, allow the dog to approach strangers voluntarily rather than forcing physical contact.

climates: Cold and snowy climates
Cool climates
Temperate climates
Warm climates when provided with shade, air-conditioned or cool tile resting areas, fresh water, and exercise during cooler hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. The breed requires close indoor contact with its household and must never be kept in a kennel or isolated outdoors. Adult dogs can handle short periods alone after gradual training, but routine long hours of daily isolation cause distress and may lead to destructive behaviour.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced diet appropriate for the dog's life stage, activity level, and health.
nutrition.guidelines: Provide a high-quality commercial or veterinary-approved diet suited to the dog's age and activity level. Relative to their medium build, many Eurasiers are light or selective eaters that regulate their own intake and rarely overeat. Rotating flavours or incorporating safe variety can help keep picky eaters interested, and fresh water should always be available.
considerations: Many individuals have modest appetites for their size and may seem finicky if fed the same food indefinitely.
Introduce new foods or rotational variety gradually to avoid digestive upset.
Monitor body condition and adjust portions so the dog remains lean, supporting joint health.
Be aware of the signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) and discuss feeding routines with a veterinarian.
Consult a veterinarian if appetite changes suddenly or if digestive issues persist.
nutrition.note: Consulted breed sources do not prescribe a fixed daily meal count for puppies, adults, or seniors; portion sizes and feeding schedules should be tailored with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Eurasier is generally a sturdy, long-lived breed with an average lifespan of 12 to 14 years, supported by strict breed-club health screening protocols prior to breeding. The most frequently recorded hereditary concern in health registries is autoimmune thyroiditis (leading to hypothyroidism), followed by orthopedic conditions such as patellar luxation, elbow dysplasia, and hip dysplasia, as well as eyelid and eyelash abnormalities. A breed-specific autosomal recessive neurological disorder, Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM), has a validated genetic test (`VLDLR` gene) that enables breeders to prevent affected puppies. Other conditions such as exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, gastric dilatation-volvulus, primary ciliary dyskinesia, and rare pedigree-specific recessive disorders have been reported less frequently.
commonConditions: Autoimmune thyroiditis and resulting hypothyroidism, the most frequently recorded condition in breed health registries (reported in roughly 14%–20% of tested dogs, typically manifesting between 2 and 7 years of age)
Patellar luxation, the most common orthopedic finding in breed screening statistics (affecting about 7.6% of evaluated dogs)
Elbow dysplasia, an inherited joint abnormality recorded in approximately 5.2% of screened dogs
Hip dysplasia, an inherited joint malformation recorded in approximately 3.2% of screened dogs
Ophthalmic disorders including distichiasis (extra eyelashes), entropion, ectropion, glaucoma, and progressive retinal atrophy

Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM), an autosomal recessive congenital cerebellar hypoplasia caused by a VLDLR gene deletion (c.1713delC) that produces non-progressive cerebellar ataxia from puppyhood

Additional reported risks and isolated pedigree-specific conditions: gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI), primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), and rare autosomal recessive polioencephalopathy (PE) and epidermolysis bullosa simplex (EB)
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents of a puppy have completed required pre-breeding screenings for hips, patellas, eyes, thyroid function, and Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM).
Consider periodic veterinary thyroid blood panels (including thyroglobulin autoantibodies) during adulthood, especially between 2 and 7 years of age.
Maintain a lean body condition and avoid excessive high-impact jumping during skeletal growth to protect hips, elbows, and patellas.
Monitor the eyes for tearing, squinting, or irritation caused by distichiasis or eyelid conformation.
Learn the emergency signs of gastric dilatation-volvulus (unproductive retching, distended abdomen, restlessness) and seek immediate veterinary care if they occur.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation (radiographic screening at 24 months or older, or distraction-index evaluation)
Patella evaluation (veterinary examination at 12 months or older)
Ophthalmic evaluation by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Annual thyroid panel (including thyroglobulin autoantibodies, tested within 12 months before breeding)
Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM) DNA test (VLDLR c.1713delC mutation)
Optional additional screenings: radiographic elbow evaluation (at 24 months or older) and adult dentition count
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule veterinary dental checks. The breed standard requires a complete scissor or pincer bite of 42 teeth, and missing incisors, canines, third or fourth premolars, or first or second molars are disqualifying faults in conformation.
health.earCare: Inspect the erect triangular ears during weekly grooming for wax buildup, redness, parasites, or odour, and clean gently only when needed with a veterinarian-approved ear cleaner.
health.skinCare: Part the dense double coat during weekly brushing to check the skin for burrs, ticks, hot spots, or dryness, and check the hair between the paw pads for trapped debris or ice balls in winter.

idealFor: Families and households that include their dog in daily indoor life and activities
Owners seeking a calm, quiet indoor companion that enjoys daily outdoor walks and play
People who appreciate a dog that is polite and reserved rather than effusive with strangers
Households prepared to brush a thick double coat and manage heavy twice-yearly seasonal shedding
notIdealFor: People who leave a dog alone for long workdays or intend to keep a dog in a kennel or backyard
Owners looking for an aggressive guard dog or a dog that greets every stranger as an instant best friend
Those unwilling to deal with heavy seasonal undercoat shedding twice a year
Handlers who use harsh, repetitive, or forceful training methods

funFacts: The breed began in 1960 in Weinheim, Germany, as the 'Wolf-Chow' before Samoyed ancestry was added in 1972 and the name 'Eurasier' was adopted in 1973 to reflect its European and Asian roots.
Nobel Prize-winning ethologist Konrad Lorenz acquired a Eurasier female in 1972 and described her as one of the finest dogs he had ever owned.
Reflecting its Chow Chow heritage, a Eurasier's tongue can be solid blue-black, solid pink, or spotted with both colours.

From the beginning of the breeding program, founder Julius Wipfel prioritized sound temperament and health over coat colour, allowing almost all colours and combinations except pure white and piebald.
Many Eurasiers love games of chase and tag with their families or other dogs, but quickly lose interest in repetitive ball-fetching.

faq.question: Is the Eurasier a one-person dog or a family dog?
faq.answer: The Eurasier bonds with its entire household, including children and extended family members it knows well, rather than attaching exclusively to a single person. When raised with gentle guidance and supervision around young children, it is an affectionate, tolerant family companion.

faq.question: How much does an adult Eurasier weigh and measure?
faq.answer: Males stand 52 to 60 cm at the withers and weigh 22 to 30 kg, with an ideal of 56 cm and 26 kg. Females stand 48 to 56 cm and weigh 18 to 26 kg, with an ideal of 52 cm and 22 kg.

faq.question: Does the Eurasier shed heavily or require difficult grooming?
faq.answer: For most of the year, the coat is relatively low maintenance and needs only a thorough weekly or bi-weekly brushing, as it has little odour and sheds dirt easily. However, once or twice a year the breed blows its entire undercoat over about three weeks, requiring daily brushing during that period.

faq.question: How does a Eurasier behave around strangers and other dogs?
faq.answer: Toward strangers, the Eurasier is calm, discerning, and reserved without being fearful or aggressive, preferring to approach new people at its own pace. Around other dogs, it is typically polite and non-confrontational, backing away from conflict rather than initiating fights.

faq.question: Can a Eurasier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes. Because it is calm indoors and barks only when warranted rather than incessantly, the Eurasier adapts well to apartments of sufficient size, provided it receives daily outdoor walks, mental enrichment, and close companionship with its family.

faq.question: What inherited health conditions and screenings are most important for Eurasiers?
faq.answer: Prospective owners should ask breeders for health clearances covering autoimmune thyroiditis (annual thyroid panel), patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, ophthalmic examinations, and the DNA test for Dandy-Walker-like malformation (DWLM, caused by a VLDLR gene mutation). Elbow radiographs and dentition records are also commonly tracked.

faq.question: How does the Eurasier handle hot or cold weather?
faq.answer: With its thick double coat, the Eurasier thrives in cool and snowy weather. It can also live comfortably in warmer climates when given shade, cool indoor flooring or air conditioning, fresh water, and walks during the cooler hours of the day. The double coat should never be shaved.

overview.summary: A noble, silky-coated, and quietly dignified rare British sporting spaniel crafted for unhurried endurance in rough shooting, uniting a soulful expression and tender, docile family devotion with an independent, thoughtful working mind.
overview.description: The Field Spaniel is a medium-sized, well-balanced, upstanding British flushing and retrieving spaniel prized as a harmonious blend of elegance and practical countryside utility. Moderately longer than tall in an approximate 7:6 ratio, it carries strong flat bone, a deep ribcage extending two-thirds of body length, a level muscular back, and a long, unhurried, driving stride built for all-day stamina rather than frantic sprinting. Its unmistakably noble head features a cleanly chiselled skull with a distinct occiput, slightly raised eyebrows, a long lean curved-under muzzle, tight lips free of heavy flews, wide-open dark hazel almond eyes radiating a grave yet gentle gaze, and moderately long, wide, low-set feathered drop ears. Clad in a dense, weatherproof, flat, glossy silky single coat—abundant in setter-like feathering along the chest, underbody, and backs of the legs yet tidy from hock to ground—the breed appears predominantly in solid liver or black, as well as roan and tan-pointed variations. Unusually docile, calm, and sensitive indoors, the Field Spaniel is slightly more independent and dignified than its busier spaniel cousins, politely reserved around strangers while deeply faithful and fun-loving with its own household.
overview.history: Sharing ancient British land-spaniel ancestry with the English Cocker, Sussex, and English Springer Spaniels, the Field Spaniel began separating into a distinct type during the mid-to-late nineteenth century—when British land spaniels were initially sorted largely by weight (under 25 pounds classed as Cockers, over 25 pounds as Fields, inspiring the old joke 'before breakfast a Cocker, after breakfast a Field'). During the late 1800s, Victorian exhibition trends led by breeder Phineas Bullock pushed the breed toward extreme, heavy-boned, low-slung proportions caricatured by contemporary writers as resembling a 'caterpillar'—undermining its hunting soundness and driving its popularity into steep decline. By the mid-twentieth century, the Field Spaniel stood on the brink of extinction. Dedicated British enthusiasts revived the breed during the 1950s and 1960s through carefully planned outcrosses—principally with English Springer Spaniels—restoring its balanced, athletic hunting frame while introducing roan coat colours alongside traditional liver and black. Definitive international recognition arrived in December 1954. Today, the Field Spaniel remains a rare heritage sporting breed officially designated as a vulnerable native breed in the United Kingdom, treasured by hunters, dog-sport competitors, and country families.
overview.originalPurpose: Finding, flushing, and retrieving upland and wetland game birds and small furred game from dense cover and water during rough countryside shooting.
currentRoles: Working flushing and retrieving rough-shooting gundog
Devoted, adaptable country and active-family companion
Versatile canine-sports competitor (nosework, tracking, rally, obedience, agility, and hunting tests)
Therapy and service dog

physical.coatType: Moderately long, flat (or very slightly wavy), dense, weatherproof, glossy silky single coat—never curly, short, or wiry. Setter-like feathering adorns the chest, underbody, backs of the legs, buttocks, and underside of the tail, while the pasterns and lower hind legs from hock to ground remain clean. Presented naturally without body clipping.
coatColors: Liver (most common modern colour) and liver and tan
Liver roan and liver roan and tan
Blue roan and blue roan and tan
In solid-coloured dogs, white or roan markings on the chest are acceptable (clear black-and-white, clear liver-and-white, orange, red, golden, and sable are unacceptable)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; the glossy silky single coat sheds steadily throughout the year and benefits from weekly brushing and combing
physical.droolingLevel: Low; close-fitting, clean lips covering the lower jaw without pendulous heaviness keep drooling low (though owners note messy drinking around the mouth)
distinctiveFeatures: Well-balanced, noble, upstanding medium sporting spaniel built slightly longer than tall (approximate length-to-height ratio of 7:6)
Height at the withers of approximately 46 cm for both males and females
Adult working weight between 18 and 25 kg for both males and females

Cleanly chiselled, noble head lean beneath the eyes with a distinct occiput, slightly raised eyebrows, moderate stop, long lean curving-under muzzle, large open-nostril nose, close-fitting lips, and complete scissor bite
Wide-open almond-shaped dark hazel to dark brown eyes with tight lids showing no haw and a grave, gentle, intelligent expression
Moderately long and wide, low-set, supple rounded-tip drop ears hanging close and heavily feathered
Long, strong, muscular neck enabling game retrieval without undue fatigue, level muscular back, deep ribcage spanning two-thirds of body length, and short strong loin with minimal tuck-up
Low-set feathered tail never carried above back level, moving with lively action (natural tails reach roughly to the hocks; docked by one-third where historically practiced)
Straight flat-boned legs with oblique well-laid-back shoulders, well-let-down hocks, and large, round, tight webbed feet with strong pads driving a long, unhurried, powerful stride
Slow physical and mental maturation—females typically reach full maturity around 2 to 3 years of age and males closer to 4 years

traits: Unusually docile, calm, peaceful, and even-tempered indoors—less frenetic than many other sporting spaniels
Sweet, deeply affectionate, loyal, and fun-loving with its family, thriving on close inclusion in daily activities
Emotionally soft and sensitive to tone and atmosphere, responding poorly to harshness
Carries a quiet, dignified integrity—naturally reserved or discerning around unfamiliar strangers without nervous shyness
Intelligent, independent problem-solver that can be noticeably more stubborn than busier spaniel cousins when unmotivated
Rarely barks excessively, though many individuals 'talk' expressively with soft vocalizations
Vigorous, persistent, and deeply scent-driven outdoors—working methodically to flush birds and locate wounded game

exercise.level: High; an enduring, active countryside flushing spaniel that settles peacefully indoors once exercised yet needs vigorous daily walks, scent tracking, or swimming alongside mental challenges
activities: Countryside rough shooting, upland flushing, and water retrieving
Long daily woodland walks, hikes, and swimming in safe rural settings
Structured nosework, wildlife tracking, rally, obedience, and agility
Interactive retrieve games and backyard exploration inside a securely fenced garden

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly at least once or twice a week using a pin brush and metal comb—paying close attention to the long feathered ears, chest, underbody, and leg furnishings—to keep the silky single coat shiny, mat-free, and clean.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed when muddy or after swampy outdoor romps using a mild canine shampoo, detangling beforehand and drying completely.
notes: Never body-clip the silky, weatherproof coat short; limit routine tidy trimming to excess hair around the feet, pasterns, and inside the ears roughly once a month.
Because the long, wide, low-set feathered drop ears restrict airflow and readily trail through wet brush and bowls, inspect and dry them weekly to prevent ear infections.
Keep nails neatly trimmed and brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate; a smart, food-motivated 'thinking dog' that excels across obedience, tracking, and hunting tests when guided patiently, yet carries a sensitive, slightly stubborn independent streak
tips: Use warm, clear, reward-based training with measured food treats and praise—Field Spaniels are famously food-motivated ('Food Spaniels') and blossom with positive encouragement, whereas harsh corrections shut them down.
Start calm, consistent foundations in early puppyhood and stay patient through their slow physical and mental maturation (2 to 4 years).
Keep lessons engaging and varied; mechanical repetition invites quiet spaniel stubbornness.
Proof recall thoroughly on a long line around birds and woodland scents before granting off-leash freedom in safe rural areas.
training.socialization: Early, unhurried, positive exposure to varied visitors, friendly dogs, children, and new environments ensures their natural dignified reserve matures into poised, confident sociability rather than shyness.

climates: Cool, damp, and temperate maritime countryside climates, matching its British rough-shooting heritage
Four-season climates with outdoor woodland and garden access; its dense, weatherproof silky coat resists rain and brush well
Warm climates require shifting brisk exercise and swimming to cooler morning or evening hours with reliable shade and cool fresh water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply devoted to its household and eager to stay near its people, a Field Spaniel can become unhappy or restless if isolated alone for long stretches without daily mental and physical engagement.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced medium-breed dog food with high nutrient bioavailability tailored to an active sporting dog.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age to support steady, unhurried skeletal development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily on a consistent schedule to sustain countryside endurance without excess weight.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for slower metabolism, thyroid wellness, and joint comfort.

nutrition.guidelines: Field Spaniels adore meals and treats—so much so that devotees fondly nickname them 'Food Spaniels.' Measure every portion accurately with a scale or measuring cup and feel beneath the silky coat weekly so ribs stay easily palpable without excess fat, protecting developing and mature hip joints. Count all training treats inside the daily calorie budget, avoid fatty table scraps and cooked bones, and keep clean fresh water continuously available.
considerations: Keep growing puppies lean on a balanced medium-breed growth formula to minimise environmental stress on hip and elbow joints.
Watch for sudden unexplained weight gain accompanied by coat thinning or lethargy, which can signal hypothyroidism—a relatively common, treatable endocrine condition in the breed.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric requirements differ markedly between active rough-shooting gundogs and quieter companion adults. Consult a veterinarian to establish individual feeding portions.

health.overview: The Field Spaniel is generally a hardy, reasonably long-lived sporting spaniel with a typical life expectancy of 11 to 15 years, though its twentieth-century population bottleneck means most dogs share close ancestry and disciplined pre-breeding health screening is essential. Documented breed priorities include polygenic hip dysplasia, autoimmune thyroiditis (hypothyroidism, noted as fairly common and linked to broader autoimmune vigilance including rare autoimmune hemolytic anemia), ocular findings (retinal folds, entropion, ectropion, and very rare Progressive Retinal Atrophy), congenital and acquired cardiac defects (leading North American health programmes to elevate pre-breeding cardiac screening to cardiologist echocardiography), and late-onset seizure disorder (actively under ongoing data collection). Additionally, a 2025 peer-reviewed clinical report documented lysosomal acid lipase (LAL) deficiency causing Cholesterol Ester Storage Disease (CESD) in two unrelated Field Spaniels—an isolated finding rather than an established breed-wide prevalence.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — polygenic developmental laxity and malformation of the hip joints that can lead to painful osteoarthritis; actively screened prior to breeding in both UK and North American programmes

Hypothyroidism (autoimmune thyroiditis) — a fairly common endocrine condition in Field Spaniels causing weight gain, lethargy, or sparse coat growth, readily managed with daily veterinary hormone replacement; screened via pre-breeding thyroid blood panels alongside vigilance for broader autoimmune disorders (such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia and skin allergies)

Hereditary eye disorders (retinal folds, ectropion, entropion, and rare PRA) — eyelid conformation issues (saggy or inward-rolling eyelids) and retinal folds (which sometimes resolve by age one without severe vision impact), monitored via periodic specialist veterinary ophthalmologist exams
Cardiac defects — heart murmurs and structural cardiac abnormalities monitored via pre-breeding veterinary cardiologist echocardiography (preferred over auscultation alone to catch subtle murmurs)

Late-onset seizure disorder / epilepsy — idiopathic or cryptogenic seizures actively tracked in ongoing breed health data collection; suspected polygenic with no predictive DNA test currently available

Elbow dysplasia and otitis externa (outer ear infections) — developmental elbow incongruity included in UK Best Practice radiographic screening, plus conformation-linked ear infections tied to long, wide, low-set feathered drop ears

Cholesterol Ester Storage Disease (CESD / Lysosomal Acid Lipase deficiency — rare isolated clinical evidence) — a peer-reviewed 2025 veterinary internal medicine case report documented LAL deficiency and hepatic lipid accumulation in two unrelated Field Spaniels; breed-wide prevalence is not established
preventiveCare: Verify documented pre-breeding clearances for both parents: official radiographic hip (and ideally elbow) evaluations, annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination, thyroid panel, and board-certified veterinary cardiologist echocardiogram.
Keep puppies and adults strictly lean and avoid over-exercising young joints during their slow maturation period to help reduce hip-dysplasia severity.
Inspect and thoroughly dry the long, low-set feathered drop ears weekly—and after every swim or damp countryside walk—to prevent ear infections.

Schedule annual veterinary wellness exams (including cardiac auscultation and periodic thyroid blood screening in adulthood) alongside regular toothbrushing, vaccinations, and year-round parasite prevention.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding (and radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation in UK Best Practice guidance)
Periodic ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Thyroid panel / autoimmune thyroiditis blood evaluation prior to breeding
Advanced cardiac evaluation (echocardiogram) by a board-certified veterinary cardiologist prior to breeding
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth often—several times weekly—using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental evaluations to keep the strong jaws and complete scissor bite healthy.
health.earCare: Check and gently dry the moderately long, wide, low-set feathered drop ears weekly—and after every wet field outing—for odour, moisture, wax buildup, burrs, or redness, trimming excess inner-ear hair monthly.
health.skinCare: Part the glossy silky single coat during weekly brushing to check for burrs, ticks, hidden mats in the feathering, or signs of allergic skin irritation.

idealFor: Active country or suburban families with a securely fenced garden wanting a calm, sweet, dignified, and deeply devoted sporting companion
Rough-shooting hunters and dog-sport fans seeking a methodical, scent-driven partner for flushing, tracking, nosework, rally, or obedience
Patient, sensitive owners (including committed first-time sporting-dog owners) willing to use gentle food-motivated positive training and embrace slow maturation
Conservation-minded dog lovers interested in supporting a rare, vulnerable heritage British spaniel
notIdealFor: Dense city apartments or sedentary households unable to provide 60 to 120 minutes of daily countryside walks and mental enrichment
Handlers who use loud, harsh, or impatient training corrections that crush this soft, sensitive spaniel
Owners wanting a zero-grooming, zero-shedding coat or unwilling to check long feathered ears weekly
Households leaving a family-oriented companion isolated alone all day

funFacts: In 1900, British Cocker Spaniels and Field Spaniels were still separated chiefly by a 25-pound weight line—giving rise to the wry saying, 'before breakfast a Cocker, and after breakfast a Field.'

During the late nineteenth century, Victorian show-ring exaggeration bred Field Spaniels so long and low to the ground that a writer compared the dog to 'a cucumber or a caterpillar,' nearly ending the breed before 1950s–1960s outcrosses restored its athletic hunting frame.
Today the Field Spaniel is officially listed among the United Kingdom's Vulnerable Native Breeds due to its small annual puppy registrations, making it far rarer than its Cocker and Springer cousins.
Unlike fast-maturing small spaniels, Field Spaniels grow up remarkably slowly both physically and mentally—females generally mature around 2 to 3 years of age and males closer to 4 years.
Because they are so joyfully enthusiastic about meals and treats, breed devotees affectionately joke that they actually own 'Food Spaniels'—a handy trait for upbeat reward-based training.

faq.question: What is a Field Spaniel?
faq.answer: The Field Spaniel is a rare, noble, medium-sized British flushing and retrieving gundog sharing heritage with Cocker, Sussex, and Springer Spaniels, admired for its glossy silky coat, soulful gaze, and docile, dignified family nature.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Field Spaniel?
faq.answer: Adult males and females stand approximately 46 cm at the withers and weigh between 18 and 25 kg.

faq.question: How long does a Field Spaniel live?
faq.answer: Generally a hardy, well-balanced sporting spaniel, the Field Spaniel has a typical life expectancy of 11 to 15 years with lean nutrition and preventive veterinary care.

faq.question: Can a Field Spaniel live in a city apartment?
faq.answer: No. Designed as an active countryside rough-shooting spaniel with strong daily exercise and scent-work needs, it is poorly suited to city apartment living and thrives best in a house with a securely fenced garden and rural trail access.

faq.question: How much grooming and shedding should I expect from a Field Spaniel?
faq.answer: Its glossy, silky single coat sheds moderately year-round and needs thorough brushing and combing at least once or twice a week, baths as needed, and light monthly tidying around the feet and inner ears—never body-clipping the coat short.

faq.question: Are Field Spaniels good with children and other dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. They are sweet, calm, peaceful, and affectionate with respectful children and generally sociable with other dogs, though their natural dignified reserve around unfamiliar strangers benefits from calm early socialization.

faq.question: Are Field Spaniels easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent, sensitive, food-motivated problem-solvers that excel in nosework, tracking, rally, obedience, and fieldwork using gentle positive rewards—though they mature slowly (2 to 4 years) and can show a mild stubborn streak under harsh or boring drills.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Field Spaniel?
faq.answer: Key documented health priorities include hip dysplasia, hypothyroidism (autoimmune thyroiditis), hereditary eye findings (retinal folds, ectropion, entropion, and rare PRA), cardiac defects (screened via cardiologist echocardiogram), late-onset seizures, elbow dysplasia, and drop-ear infections.

overview.summary: A formidable, heavy-boned, and extraordinarily loyal giant Brazilian mastiff-type guardian distinguished by loose, thick skin, a characteristic rolling camel-like pace, proverbial devotion to its household, and intense natural aloofness toward strangers.
overview.description: The Fila Brasileiro—widely known in English as the Brazilian Mastiff—is a massive yet surprisingly agile molossoid working dog shaped over centuries on sprawling Brazilian estates and cattle ranches. Built on a rectangular, compact frame roughly 15 percent longer than tall, it carries a distinctive silhouette in which the croup rises slightly higher than the withers, supporting an unusual, elastic two-beat 'camel's pace' where both legs on the same side advance together. Its huge, heavy head—resembling a pear set inside a trapezoid when viewed from above—features a prominent occiput, almost imperceptible front stop, broad deep muzzle with a black nose, almond-shaped eyes harmonized to the coat, and large, thick, V-shaped hanging ears. Draped in thick, remarkably loose, supple skin forming pronounced neck dewlaps beneath a short, soft, dense, close-lying coat in solid or brindle shades, the Fila Brasileiro balances two stark temperamental poles: serene, affectionate, deeply devoted docility toward its own family and children, paired with fierce territorial vigilance and ingrained suspicion toward unfamiliar strangers. Because of its sheer power and intense guarding instinct, ownership is strictly restricted or banned by law in several countries and demands highly experienced, responsible rural management.
overview.history: The Fila Brasileiro evolved in colonial Brazil starting in the sixteenth century from large European working dogs brought across the Atlantic by Portuguese and Spanish settlers—primarily ancient mastiffs, bloodhounds, and Portuguese cattle-driving dogs—which adapted to harsh tropical ranchlands and forests. Its name derives from the Portuguese verb 'filar,' meaning to seize and hold fast, reflecting its historic role as a catch and holding dog. Across colonial plantations and vast interior ranches, Filas were relied upon to drive unruly cattle, track and confront jaguars and other large predators, and guard remote homesteads—as well as being used during Brazil's slavery era to track and recapture escaped enslaved people on sugar plantations before abolition. Organized breeding and formal written breed documentation began in Brazil in 1946, followed by definitive international recognition in January 1960. Recent mitogenomic research published in 2026 underscores a complex historical formation behind Brazil's two internationally recognized native breeds. Today, the Fila Brasileiro remains a prized property guardian and cattle dog in Brazil while facing strict legal restrictions or outright prohibitions in several jurisdictions worldwide, including the United Kingdom under Section 1 of the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991.
