Small white markings are permissible only on the feet, chest, and tip of the tail (white coats, mouse-grey, dappled/merle, black-and-tan, and blue coats are strictly disqualified)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; the short, dense, closely laid coat sheds lightly throughout the year with moderate seasonal increases
physical.droolingLevel: High; thick, pendulous upper lips and abundant loose skin with heavy neck dewlaps produce generous drool after drinking, eating, or warm activity
distinctiveFeatures: Massive, heavy-boned, rectangular yet compact molossoid build displaying clearly perceived concentrated agility and strong sexual dimorphism
Height at the withers of 65 to 75 cm for males and 60 to 70 cm for females
Minimum adult working weight of 50 kg for males and 40 kg for females
Body length from sternum to buttock exceeds height at the withers by 15 percent, with the croup rising slightly higher than the withers (a croup lower than the withers is disqualified)

Characteristically elastic, rolling 'camel's pace' (both legs on the same side moving forward together at a walk, shifting into a smooth trot and powerful gallop; absence of camel's pace is disqualified)

Huge, heavy head shaped like a pear inside a trapezoid from above, with muzzle slightly shorter than skull, prominent occiput (especially in puppies), almost non-existent front stop, broad black nose, and deep muzzle
Significantly wider-than-long teeth in powerful jaws (overshot bite, visible-teeth undershot bite, or missing canine/molar other than M3 are disqualified)
Medium-to-large almond-shaped eyes ranging from dark brown to yellow in harmony with coat colour (blue/china eyes disqualified)
Large, thick, tapered V-shaped pendant ears that hang close or fold backward exposing the interior depending on alertness (cropped ears or docked tails are strictly disqualified)
Exceptionally thick, loose, supple skin forming pronounced dewlaps along the neck beneath a short, soft, dense coat

traits: Extraordinarily courageous, determined, calm, and deeply self-confident—unperturbed by unfamiliar noises or strange surroundings
Proverbially faithful, docile, obedient, and affectionate—even clingy—toward its owner and immediate household
Traditionally noted for strong tolerance and protective devotion toward children within its own family (always requiring vigilant adult supervision given its massive strength)
Defined by strong natural aloofness, suspicion, and aversion toward unfamiliar strangers—especially on its own territory—requiring disciplined, controlled handling
Intensely territorial and driven by hardwired instincts for property guarding, cattle handling, and big-game tracking
Independent and imposing enough that it strictly requires a calm, knowledgeable, experienced owner—never suited to novice handlers or careless management

exercise.level: Moderate to high; a powerful, agile working mastiff with strong stamina that needs steady daily countryside walks, property patrolling, and structured obedience or tracking—while rapidly growing puppies require strict exercise moderation to protect developing giant joints
activities: Calm, controlled daily leashed walks in low-congestion rural or countryside areas
Structured scent-tracking, obedience, and controlled boundary exercises
Supervised patrolling and free movement inside a tall, heavy-duty, securely fenced rural property
Working cattle herding and ranch guarding in rural environments where appropriate

grooming.brushing: Easy-care short, soft, dense coat—brush once a week with a rubber hound mitt or soft bristle brush to lift dead hair and dust.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when genuinely dirty or odorous using a mild canine shampoo, drying skin folds and dewlaps thoroughly afterward.
notes: Wipe drool and moisture daily from the heavy flews, facial folds, and pronounced neck dewlaps to prevent moist skin-fold dermatitis.
Inspect the large, thick, pendulous V-shaped ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, odour, or redness.
Provide thick, supportive bedding to prevent pressure calluses on heavy giant elbows and hocks.
Trim strong nails regularly and brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Challenging; deeply loyal and obedient to a respected family leader, yet its massive strength, sharp independence, and ingrained suspicion of strangers demand skilled, calm, unwavering management from puppyhood
tips: Raise a Fila Brasileiro puppy with calm affection, clear structure, and consistent boundaries from day one—never use harsh dominance or erratic handling, which undermines trust and stability.
Teach dependable stationing ('go to your bed'), impulse control, and calm leash manners early so visitors can be managed safely and respectfully without treating separate confinement as punishment.
Understand and respect its innate stranger aloofness: focus socialization on calm neutrality around everyday sights, sounds, and polite distance rather than forcing strangers to pet the dog.

Always check national and local breed legislation before acquiring a Fila Brasileiro, as ownership, breeding, and importation are banned or heavily regulated in multiple countries (including the United Kingdom).
training.socialization: Calm, structured, positive exposure from early puppyhood to diverse environments, everyday noises, and controlled veterinary handling builds poised self-assurance and manageable public neutrality—without expecting a Fila to become indiscriminately friendly with strangers.

climates: Warm, tropical, and temperate rural climates, mirroring Brazil's interior pastures and estates (still requiring deep shade and cool fresh water during peak midday heat)
Four-season climates with spacious indoor living areas
Cold winter climates require warm, dry indoor shelter during rest periods, as its short single-style coat offers minimal cold insulation
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply attached to its owners and insisting on their company, a Fila Brasileiro should live as an integrated family guardian rather than being isolated permanently away from its household.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced giant-breed dog food, strictly using a controlled-calcium, moderate-calorie giant-breed puppy diet throughout its slow skeletal growth.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured meals daily during slow giant-breed growth to promote steady, lean bone and joint development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain massive muscular condition and reduce acute stomach distension.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for slower giant-breed metabolism, cardiac support, and joint comfort.

nutrition.guidelines: Like other giant mastiff-type dogs, the Fila Brasileiro grows slowly and has high nutritional demands during development alongside a serious vulnerability to orthopaedic stress if overfed. Measure every meal accurately so ribs remain palpable beneath the thick, loose skin without excess body fat. Divide daily adult food into two smaller meals, enforce calm rest before and after eating, and provide cool fresh drinking water continuously.
considerations: Feed growing puppies a balanced giant-breed growth diet with controlled energy and calcium—never add unprescribed calcium supplements, which can worsen developmental hip and elbow disorders.

Because this massive, deep-chested giant is vulnerable to life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat), divide daily adult rations into two meals, avoid vigorous exertion around mealtimes, and discuss prophylactic gastropexy with a veterinarian.
Avoid high-impact jumping, forced running, and repetitive steep stair climbing until giant growth plates close around 18 to 24 months.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Giant-breed puppy growth nutrition and adult joint/bloat feeding routines should always be tailored with a veterinarian.

health.overview: Although no peer-reviewed breed-wide actuarial lifespan studies or mandatory breed-specific genetic disease panels are established for the Fila Brasileiro, veterinary registries and national kennel health monitoring identify developmental orthopaedic disease—especially hip dysplasia—as the breed's most prominent documented health concern. In one North American radiographic registry dataset of 228 evaluated Fila Brasileiros, 32.5% were graded dysplastic and 67.5% normal (reflecting a screened cohort rather than universal population prevalence). Additional giant-molossoid veterinary priorities include elbow dysplasia, acute gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), eyelid conformation disorders (entropion/ectropion) and skin-fold dermatitis linked to its abundant loose skin, and routine cardiac vigilance (an isolated 2022 peer-reviewed case report documented left-dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy in a single Fila Brasileiro).
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the hip joints leading to painful osteoarthritis in heavy-boned giants; documented in Swedish national breed monitoring and in North American radiographic registry statistics (32.5% dysplastic among 228 screened Fila Brasileiros, a screened-cohort rate rather than universal prevalence)
Elbow dysplasia — developmental elbow-joint incongruity and osteoarthritis monitored alongside hip radiographs in giant mastiff-type breeding programmes

Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — sudden, life-threatening gas distension and twisting of the stomach requiring immediate emergency surgery, a major emergency risk in deep-chested giant breeds

Eyelid conformation disorders (entropion / ectropion), skin-fold dermatitis, and otitis externa — conformation-linked risks associated with heavy loose facial skin, pronounced neck dewlaps, and large pendulous drop ears

Cardiac abnormalities (isolated case evidence) — an isolated 2022 veterinary cardiology case report described left-dominant arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with fibroadipose myocardial replacement in one Fila Brasileiro; breed-wide cardiac prevalence is not established, though routine auscultation and pre-breeding heart checks remain prudent for giant molossoids
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for documented parental radiographic hip and elbow dysplasia clearances alongside veterinary ophthalmic and cardiac evaluations.

Protect developing giant joints during the first 18 to 24 months by keeping the puppy strictly lean on a giant-breed growth formula and avoiding forced running, high jumping, or frequent steep staircases.

Divide daily adult rations into two meals, enforce calm rest around mealtimes, know emergency bloat warning signs (unproductive retching, swollen tight abdomen, restlessness), and discuss prophylactic gastropexy with a veterinarian.
Wipe drool from lip folds and neck dewlaps daily, inspect and dry the heavy drop ears weekly, and maintain strict year-round parasite prevention alongside annual veterinary wellness exams.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Routine veterinary ophthalmic evaluation (checking eyelids for entropion/ectropion) and baseline cardiac evaluation for giant breeding stock
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental evaluations to keep the powerful jaws and wide teeth healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the large, thick, pendulous V-shaped ears weekly for moisture, excess wax, odour, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Wipe moisture and drool daily from the heavy flews, facial folds, and pronounced neck dewlaps to prevent skin-fold irritation, and check elbows and hocks for giant-breed pressure calluses.

idealFor: Highly experienced, calm, responsible large-guardian handlers living in spacious rural properties with heavy-duty perimeter fencing (strictly where legal)
Farm, ranch, and estate owners needing a deeply faithful, courageous property guardian and cattle-working dog
Owners who understand and respect natural stranger aloofness, commit to structured management around guests, and welcome intense family devotion
notIdealFor: First-time dog owners, casual pet households, or anyone unprepared for a massive, fiercely protective giant guardian
Urban apartments, crowded cities, busy off-leash dog parks, or households hosting frequent unannounced visitors
Families with unsupervised young children or people bothered by heavy drool and giant-breed food and veterinary costs
Residents of countries or regions where ownership, breeding, or importation of the Fila Brasileiro is legally prohibited or heavily restricted (such as the United Kingdom)

funFacts: In Brazil, the breed's legendary devotion inspired the famous national saying 'Fiel como um Fila'—'As faithful as a Fila.'

Unlike almost all other dog breeds, the Fila Brasileiro naturally moves at an elastic, rolling 'camel's pace' (passo de camelo), advancing both legs on the same side simultaneously—a trait so essential that its absence is a disqualifying fault.
Another anatomical rarity is its topline: the croup rises slightly higher than the withers, and a croup lower than the withers is strictly disqualified.
Its name comes from the ancient Portuguese verb 'filar' ('to seize and hold'), reflecting its historic role as a holding dog for cattle and big game.

Because of its immense power and intense territorial guarding instincts, the Fila Brasileiro is one of the specific dog types prohibited from private ownership, breeding, or sale in the United Kingdom under Section 1 of the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991, and faces legal restrictions in several other countries.

faq.question: What is a Fila Brasileiro?
faq.answer: The Fila Brasileiro (Brazilian Mastiff) is a giant, heavy-boned Brazilian molossoid guardian and cattle dog shaped from sixteenth-century European mastiffs and hounds, celebrated for its thick loose skin, rolling camel-like gait, intense family loyalty, and natural aloofness toward strangers.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Fila Brasileiro?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 65 to 75 cm at the withers and weigh a minimum of 50 kg, while adult females stand 60 to 70 cm and weigh a minimum of 40 kg (no official upper weight limit is specified).

faq.question: How long does a Fila Brasileiro live?
faq.answer: No official lifespan range or peer-reviewed actuarial longevity study is published by primary registries for the Fila Brasileiro; as with other giant molossoids, longevity depends heavily on lean weight control, joint care, bloat prevention, and attentive veterinary care.

faq.question: Are Fila Brasileiros banned or legally restricted in some countries?
faq.answer: Yes. Because of their immense size and powerful territorial guarding instincts, Fila Brasileiros are prohibited or strictly regulated in several countries—for example, ownership, breeding, gifting, and sale are banned in the United Kingdom under Section 1 of the Dangerous Dogs Act 1991. Always check local and national laws before considering the breed.

faq.question: Can a Fila Brasileiro live in an apartment or with first-time owners?
faq.answer: No. It is a rural estate guardian poorly suited to dense urban apartments, high noise, and busy crowds, and its massive strength, independence, and strong suspicion of strangers make it strictly unsuitable for first-time dog owners.

faq.question: How do Fila Brasileiros behave with family versus strangers?
faq.answer: They are famously docile, affectionate, deeply faithful, and protective with their own family, yet display strong, natural aloofness and suspicion toward unfamiliar strangers—especially on home territory—requiring disciplined management whenever guests visit.

faq.question: How much grooming and drooling should I expect from a Fila Brasileiro?
faq.answer: Coat care is simple—weekly brushing keeps its short, soft, dense coat clean, with baths only as needed. However, its thick loose skin, heavy flews, and pronounced neck dewlaps produce copious drool and require daily fold wiping alongside weekly ear checks.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Fila Brasileiro?
faq.answer: The main documented health priorities are hip dysplasia (recorded at 32.5% in a screened North American radiographic cohort of 228 dogs), elbow dysplasia, acute bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus), eyelid and skin-fold issues tied to its loose skin, and routine cardiac monitoring.

overview.summary: The Finnish Hound, known natively as the Suomenajokoira, is a medium-sized tricoloured scent hound bred in Finland to track hare and fox across rugged Nordic woodlands and snow. Celebrated for exceptional scenting ability, stamina, and a melodious hunting voice, it pairs a passionate working drive in the field with a peaceful, calm demeanor at home.
overview.description: Noticeably longer in body than it is tall at the withers, the Finnish Hound combines athletic substance with clean, efficient movement. A dense, weatherproof double coat carries a bold black saddle over rich tan shading, accented by crisp white markings on the muzzle, chest, feet, and tail tip. Long, hanging ears, dark expressive eyes, and a purposeful ground-scenting style reflect its deep working background. In the field, it is renowned for hunting independently over long distances, using resonant baying to signal the quarry's path. At home, once given sufficient physical exercise and scent-tracking outlets, it is gentle, composed, and affectionate with its family, though its powerful hunting instinct requires secure fencing and reliable leash management around small wildlife.
overview.history: Systematic breeding of the Finnish Hound began following the establishment of a national kennel club in Finland in 1889, driven by hunters seeking a tracking hound uniquely adapted to deep snow and cold Nordic terrain. By interbreeding regional Finnish hounds with selected Russian, French, German, and Swedish scent hounds, breeders crafted a sturdy dog possessing both endurance and a clear, carrying bark. The breed's distinct tricolour pattern and physical conformation were consolidated in the early twentieth century, establishing the hound as one of the most popular and culturally cherished working breeds in Finland and Scandinavia.
overview.originalPurpose: Tracking and pursuing hare and fox by scent over snowy and forested Nordic terrain, working independently and baying to guide the hunter.

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice weekly with a rubber curry comb or firm bristle brush to clear loose undercoat, increase circulation, and remove field debris after outdoor excursions.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when dirty or after muddy tracking work, using a gentle canine shampoo that preserves the natural protective oils of the weatherproof coat.

Inspect the paws, pads, and between the toes after runs through brambles, frozen crust, or rocky ground.
Trim nails regularly to prevent toe splay and maintain sound footing.
Brush teeth multiple times weekly using canine-formulated toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging; very friendly and cooperative, but selective hearing can emerge once an enticing scent trail is picked up.
tips: Use positive, high-value reward-based methods and avoid harsh reprimands that diminish enthusiasm.
Establish reliable recall foundation early, keeping the hound on lead or long line in unenclosed rural areas where game scent abounds.
Channel instinctual tracking drive into organized nosework and search activities rather than attempting to suppress it.
Teach polite leash manners early to counter strong pulling when following scent lines.
training.socialization: Provide early and varied exposure to diverse environments, livestock, friendly dogs, and household visitors to cultivate an unshakeable, friendly adult demeanor.

climates: Cool and cold climates with snowy winters
Temperate climates
Warm climates with air conditioning, shaded yards, and exercise scheduled during cool morning and evening hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate when adequate daily physical exercise and mental tracking enrichment are provided; under-stimulated hounds may bay or dig out of boredom.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality commercial dry kibble, wet food, or veterinary-formulated working dog diet rich in protein and healthy fats for endurance.

feedingFrequency.puppy: 3 to 4 measured meals daily during growth, transitioning to 2 meals daily around six months of age
feedingFrequency.adult: 2 measured meals per day, adjusted upward during rigorous hunting seasons and downward during rest periods

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily portions based on workload and body condition score, regularly feeling for the ribs beneath the dense coat to ensure the hound stays lean and athletic.
considerations: Increase calorie and fat intake during active hunting autumn and winter months, reducing portions in the off-season to avoid excess weight.
Account for all training rewards within the daily calorie allowance.
Ensure continuous access to fresh, clean drinking water, especially after arduous outdoor tracking sessions.
Avoid feeding large meals immediately before or after strenuous field work.
nutrition.note: Calorie needs vary dramatically between working hunting hounds and companion pets; consult a veterinarian for individualized feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Finnish Hound is generally a robust and healthy working breed with a typical lifespan of 11 to 14 years. Breed-health programs in Finland focus on radiographic hip evaluation via breeding indices, alongside DNA screening for hereditary cerebellar ataxia (a severe neurodegenerative condition caused by an autosomal recessive SEL1L mutation).
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: developmental laxity of the hip joints monitored closely through national hip-index breeding databases.

Cerebellar ataxia (Finnish Hound type): an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by a mutation in the SEL1L gene, causing early-onset progressive incoordination; detectable via DNA testing.
Ear canal irritation (otitis externa): inflammation related to moisture retention beneath long hanging ear leather.
Hunting-related field injuries: minor pad abrasions, bramble cuts, or sprains sustained while traversing rough terrain.
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has been DNA-tested for cerebellar ataxia (SEL1L gene) and evaluated for hip dysplasia.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, core vaccinations, and appropriate parasite control.
Inspect ears, eyes, and foot pads thoroughly after tracking through brush or snow crust.
Maintain a lean, muscular body condition to prevent unnecessary joint stress.
recommendedScreenings: Cerebellar ataxia (SEL1L gene) DNA test
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accepted screening scheme
Regular veterinary ear and ocular examinations
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic paste to prevent tartar and maintain healthy oral tissues.
health.earCare: Lift and inspect the hanging ears weekly, wiping clean and ensuring the canals dry completely after outdoor rain or wet snow.
health.skinCare: Examine the skin and coat after field work for ticks, grass burrs, or scratches; treat any minor cuts promptly.

idealFor: Hunters and outdoor sportsmen seeking an exceptional, cold-hardy scent tracking partner
Active rural or suburban households with a securely fenced yard and time for long daily hikes
Enthusiasts of blood tracking, search-and-rescue, and competitive nosework sports
Families looking for an affectionate, even-tempered, and calm indoor companion between adventures
notIdealFor: Sedentary owners seeking a low-energy lap dog or apartment pet
Households expecting 100% off-leash reliability in open country near wildlife
Homes unwilling to provide substantial daily physical exercise and mental scent stimulation
Dense urban environments sensitive to loud, carrying baying barks

funFacts: The Finnish Hound, or Suomenajokoira, consistently ranks among the most registered and beloved native dog breeds in Finland.
Bred specifically to navigate thick snow, the hound possesses tight, arched cat-like paws that minimize snow clumping between the toes.
While tracking hare and fox, Finnish Hounds produce a melodious, carrying bay that echoes across dense Nordic forests, allowing handlers to track their progress from miles away.
Despite their fierce determination on a scent trail, Finnish Hounds are famously gentle, friendly, and placid family companions indoors.
Breed development began formally in 1889 following the founding of the Finnish Kennel Club, creating a hound capable of withstanding sub-zero Scandinavian winters.

faq.question: What was the Finnish Hound originally bred to do?
faq.answer: The Finnish Hound was developed in Finland to hunt hare and fox by scent, following trails independently across forests and deep snow while baying melodiously to guide the hunter.

faq.question: How big do Finnish Hounds get?
faq.answer: According to official measurements, males stand 55 to 61 cm at the withers and weigh about 20 to 29 kg, while females measure 52 to 58 cm and weigh about 20 to 25 kg.

faq.question: Are Finnish Hounds good family pets?
faq.answer: Yes, they are known for their calm, affectionate, and friendly nature in the home. They get along well with children and other dogs, provided their high exercise and scent-tracking needs are met daily.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Finnish Hound need daily?
faq.answer: A healthy adult Finnish Hound needs 60 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily physical activity. Long walks on tracking lines, hiking, and nosework games are ideal for keeping their minds and bodies engaged.

faq.question: What health tests should I look for in a Finnish Hound?
faq.answer: Prospective owners should ensure that both parent dogs have documented DNA testing for cerebellar ataxia (SEL1L gene) and certified hip evaluations.

faq.question: Can a Finnish Hound live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Their high energy, intense scent drive, and loud carrying bay make apartment living challenging, and they thrive best in homes with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Do Finnish Hounds shed a lot?
faq.answer: They are moderate shedders. Their dense double coat sheds hair continuously and blows coat seasonally, requiring weekly brushing with a rubber curry mitt to remove loose undercoat.

faq.question: What colors do Finnish Hounds come in?
faq.answer: The classic coloration is tricolour, consisting of a rich black saddle over the back and neck, warm tan on the head and limbs, and white markings on the muzzle, chest, feet, and tail tip.

faq.question: How long do Finnish Hounds typically live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy for a healthy Finnish Hound is 11 to 14 years when supported by proper nutrition, regular exercise, and preventive veterinary care.

overview.summary: Finland's national dog: a square, fox-like red spitz bred to find forest birds and hold them in place by barking, lively and brave in the field and friendly at home.
overview.description: The Finnish Spitz is a square-built Nordic hunting dog whose body is as long as it is tall, with a chest reaching just under half its height. Its fox-like head carries small, pointed, very mobile ears that stand erect, dark almond-shaped eyes with a bright, alert look, and a small jet-black nose. The stand-off coat is bright red or golden red over the back, paler on the cheeks, chest, belly and inner legs, with a short, soft, light-coloured undercoat; the hair is stiffer and longer over the neck and shoulders, most noticeably in males. A plumed tail curls forward over the back and drops against the thigh. In the forest it works independently, locating game and announcing it with persistent barking. At home it is lively, energetic and sociable with its family, a little reserved with strangers but never vicious, and quick to learn, though its independent streak calls for consistent training.
overview.history: Dogs of this type were used for hunting all kinds of game throughout Finland for hundreds of years. When the Finnish kennel club was founded in 1889, the forester Hugo Sandberg wrote a description of the native barking bird dog and proposed its breed characteristics, while fellow forester Hugo Roos set about breeding the dogs and testing their hunting ability in Lapland and Kainuu. The first breed standard and the first show for the breed followed in 1892, with a revised standard and the name Finnish Spitz adopted in 1897, the same year as the first bird-hunting trial. The breed was declared Finland's national dog in 1979. In 2006 the Finnish and Russian kennel organisations agreed to treat the Karelian-Finnish Laika and the Finnish Spitz as one breed under a shared standard.

nutrition.guidelines: Weigh or measure meals and feel for the ribs under the thick coat, which can hide weight gain. Feed more during active hunting seasons and less in quiet periods, and keep fresh water available.

health.overview: Finland's national kennel club regards this as one of the healthiest breeds and has run a compulsory knee and eye screening scheme for it since 1994. Epilepsy is the condition most studied in the breed. A large Finnish survey of owners in 2003–2004 found that about 5% of dogs were affected; the seizures usually started on one side of the brain, most dogs did not get worse over time, and most were easily controlled with medication. Inheritance appears to involve many genes, one of which, ADAM23, raises risk only modestly. Current estimates put the rate at roughly 1–2%. Diabetes, missing teeth or bite faults, and bloody diarrhoea are also noted in the breed.
commonConditions: Idiopathic epilepsy: recurring seizures with no other cause found; about 5% of dogs in a 2003–2004 survey, now estimated at 1–2%
Patellar luxation: a kneecap that slips out of place; screened before breeding, with about 96% of recently tested dogs free of it
Hereditary eye disease such as cataract or progressive retinal atrophy: screened before breeding, with about 94% of recently examined dogs clear
Diabetes mellitus
Missing teeth and bite faults
Bloody diarrhoea

Brush the teeth several times a week.
Book a yearly veterinary check-up.
recommendedScreenings: Patellar luxation examination at 12 months of age or older
Eye examination for hereditary eye disease (repeat every two years for dogs examined under age 3)
Review of epilepsy in the pedigree before mating

health.earCare: Check the erect ears weekly and wipe away visible dirt if needed.
health.skinCare: Part the coat while brushing to check for ticks and skin irritation, especially after time in the forest.

funFacts: It was named Finland's national dog in 1979.
The breed's first show, held in Oulu in 1892, drew 93 dogs.
Its original Finnish name translates as 'Finnish barking bird dog'; it took the name Finnish Spitz in 1897.
In the forest it pins a bird in a treetop by barking until the hunter arrives.

Finland's Finnish Spitz club made the first Saturday of August the breed's own flag day, first celebrated in 2023.

faq.question: Why does the Finnish Spitz bark so much?
faq.answer: It was bred to find birds and hold them in place by barking until the hunter arrives, so barking is part of its job. Early training helps keep it under control at home.

faq.question: How big is a Finnish Spitz?
faq.answer: Males stand 44 to 50 cm at the withers and females 39 to 45 cm. In Finland males usually weigh 15 to 17 kg and females 10 to 12 kg.

faq.question: How long does it live?
faq.answer: Typically 12 to 15 years.

faq.question: What colour is it?
faq.answer: Bright red or golden red on the back, paler underneath. A small white chest spot and small white marks on the feet are allowed.

faq.question: Is it a good family dog?
faq.answer: Yes. It is sociable with its own people and suits families, including first-time owners who are ready to train it, especially those who enjoy outdoor life.

faq.question: Can it live in a town?
faq.answer: It can, if its barking is trained and it is well socialised from puppyhood. It still needs plenty of daily exercise.

faq.question: What health problems should I ask about?
faq.answer: Ask breeders for knee and eye results on both parents and about epilepsy in the family line. Epilepsy is the condition most studied in the breed, and most affected dogs respond well to treatment.

overview.summary: A crisp, athletic British earthdog with a flat, mostly white smooth coat, neatly folded V-shaped ears, keen energy, and bold hunting spirit.
overview.description: The Fox Terrier (Smooth) packs bone, stamina, and quickness into a neat, short-backed frame designed to cover ground smoothly without looking heavy or leggy. Its long, flat, moderately narrow head tapers toward strong jaws with a complete scissor bite, bright dark circular eyes, and small V-shaped ears folding forward close to the cheeks. The straight, hard, dense coat sits flat over the body—including the belly and inner thighs—and is predominantly white with black, tan, or black-and-tan patches. Alert, cheerful, and fearless, this lively terrier makes an engaging companion and keen watchdog for households ready to match its energy.
overview.history: Developed in England during the 18th and 19th centuries for traditional foxhunts, the Smooth Fox Terrier ran alongside hound packs or rode in saddle panniers until a fox went to ground, where the terrier entered the burrow to drive it out. Early working terriers were often dark or black-and-tan, so breeders blended them with the now-extinct Old English White Terrier, Bull Terrier, Beagle, and Greyhound lines to create a mostly white dog that hunters would not confuse with a red fox. Fox Terriers entered early British dog shows in the 1860s—with foundational dogs Old Jock, Old Tartar, and Old Trap competing at Birmingham in 1863—and a dedicated club wrote the first written description of the breed in 1876. Though Smooth and Wire varieties were long treated as coat types of one breed in some regions, they were formally separated into distinct breeds in the late 20th century.
overview.originalPurpose: Accompanying mounted foxhunts to bolt foxes from underground dens and controlling farm vermin.

health.overview: Fox Terriers (Smooth) are generally sturdy, energetic dogs with a typical lifespan of 12 to 15 years. Two inherited conditions have scientifically confirmed causal genetic mutations in the breed or closely related terrier lines: spinocerebellar ataxia with myokymia and seizures (linked to the KCNJ10 gene) and primary lens luxation (linked to the ADAMTS17 gene). Responsible breeding programs also screen for patellar luxation, heart conditions, inherited eye disorders, and congenital deafness.
commonConditions: Spinocerebellar ataxia with myokymia and seizures (SCA / SAMS) — an established autosomal recessive neurological disorder caused by a KCNJ10 gene mutation confirmed in Smooth-Haired Fox Terriers, leading to progressive incoordination, muscle twitching, and seizures

Primary lens luxation (PLL) — an inherited eye disorder linked to an autosomal recessive ADAMTS17 gene mutation in terrier breeds that causes the eye lens to dislocate and can trigger painful glaucoma
Patellar luxation — slipping of the kneecap out of its normal groove, monitored through veterinary orthopedic exams
Cardiac conditions — congenital heart anomalies and murmurs evaluated through specialist heart screenings
Congenital sensorineural deafness — unilateral or bilateral hearing loss reported in some predominantly white lines, checked with hearing (BAER) testing
Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease — a hip-joint bone blood-supply disorder occasionally reported in young small terriers
Cataracts and other ocular disorders — monitored through periodic veterinary eye examinations
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have documented clearances for patellar luxation, cardiac health, eye exams, and DNA tests for spinocerebellar ataxia (KCNJ10) and primary lens luxation (ADAMTS17).
Keep the dog at a lean, athletic weight to protect knees and hips.
Maintain regular dental brushing, weekly ear checks, parasite prevention, and annual veterinary wellness visits.

health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary dental exams to keep teeth and gums clean.
health.earCare: Inspect the small forward-folding ears weekly for wax, dirt, or redness and wipe gently with a veterinarian-approved cleaner.
health.skinCare: Check the skin during weekly brushing for scratches, burrs, dryness, or parasites, especially after outdoor digging or trail walks.

funFacts: In 1863 at Birmingham, three early Fox Terriers—Old Jock, Old Tartar, and Old Trap—helped shape the breed, and within ten years Fox Terrier classes there drew 276 entries.
A Smooth Fox Terrier named Ch. Warren Remedy won top honors at a premier New York championship dog show three consecutive years in 1907, 1908, and 1909—a streak that remains unmatched.
U.S. President Herbert Hoover kept two Fox Terriers named Big Ben and Sonnie.
Predominantly white coats were deliberately favored by 19th-century foxhunters so terriers bolting out of underground dens would never be mistaken for red foxes.
Despite sharing ancestry with the Wire Fox Terrier, the Smooth has a slightly more V-shaped head and a flat coat that needs only weekly brushing instead of hand-stripping.

faq.question: How is a Smooth Fox Terrier different from a Wire Fox Terrier?
faq.answer: Both share similar size, proportions, and lively hunting drive, but the Smooth has a short, flat, low-maintenance coat and a slightly more V-shaped head, while the Wire has a harsh, wiry coat with facial furnishings that requires stripping.

faq.question: How big does a Fox Terrier (Smooth) get?
faq.answer: Males stand up to 39 cm at the withers and weigh 7.5 to 8 kg, while females are slightly smaller at 36 to 38 cm and weigh 7 to 7.5 kg.

faq.question: Can a Smooth Fox Terrier live happily in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes, as long as it gets brisk daily walks and active play. Because the breed is an alert watchdog, teaching a reliable quiet cue early helps in close-neighbor living.

faq.question: Can Smooth Fox Terriers be trusted off-leash?
faq.answer: No. Their strong instinct to chase squirrels, rabbits, and other small animals means they should stay on a leash or inside a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: How much grooming does the smooth coat require?
faq.answer: Very little—weekly brushing with a firm brush or rubber hound glove, monthly baths or rinses after muddy digging, regular nail trims, and weekly ear checks are usually enough.

faq.question: What health tests matter most for Smooth Fox Terriers?
faq.answer: Key screenings include patella and cardiac evaluations, veterinary eye exams, hearing (BAER) checks where relevant, and DNA tests for spinocerebellar ataxia (KCNJ10) and primary lens luxation (ADAMTS17).

overview.summary: A compact, sharp-witted British terrier with a crisp, broken wire coat, a mostly white body with darker patches, and an eager, ready-for-anything attitude.
overview.description: The Wire Fox Terrier is a small, square-built working terrier that packs plenty of bone and muscle into a neat frame. Seen from the side it should look short in the back and balanced, with the height at the shoulder roughly matching the length of the body. Its signature feature is the coat: a dense, harsh, twisting outer layer over a shorter, softer undercoat, longest along the back and quarters and shortest on the shoulders, with crisp hair on the muzzle that gives the face a strong, bearded look. White is the main colour, broken up by black, tan, or black-and-tan patches. Small folded ears, dark keen eyes, a nearly flat skull and a high, upright tail complete the picture. At home it is friendly, outgoing and full of energy, but it keeps the quick reactions, curiosity and courage that suited it to hunting work.
overview.history: The breed grew out of the rough-coated working terriers used by British fox hunts, dogs expected to keep pace with the hounds and push a fox out of its earth. In the early days of dog shows, fox terriers of different coat types were exhibited together. During the 1870s wire-coated dogs were given their own classes, and breeding between the wire and smooth coats was discouraged from then on. Early breeders had sometimes used smooth-coated dogs to bring more white and a cleaner head into the wire line, but that practice ended long ago. The smooth type was established first and was the more popular of the two until around 1920, after which the Wire overtook it. In the 1930s a Wire Fox Terrier playing the dog Asta in the Thin Man films made the breed a fashionable family pet. The breed was accepted on a definitive basis by the international federation in 1955, and in the United States the Smooth and Wire were formally recognised as separate breeds in 1985. Today the Wire is best known as a companion and as a highly successful show dog, though the work involved in keeping its coat in show trim has made it less common than it once was.

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb through the coat more than once a week, paying attention to the beard and leg hair where knots form.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when needed; frequent washing softens the harsh coat. Wipe the beard after meals to keep it clean.
notes: The traditional wire texture is kept by hand-stripping, which pulls out dead outer hair so new harsh coat can grow.
Clipping is easier but leaves the coat softer and can change its colour and texture over time.
Many owners use a professional groomer who knows terrier stripping, especially for a show-style outline.
Trim the nails every few weeks and check the pads after outdoor play.
Check the folded ears each week for dirt, wax or redness.

tips: Use rewards, play and short, varied sessions rather than repetition.
Start recall training early, but keep the dog on a lead or in a fenced area near wildlife and roads.
Teach a calm 'quiet' cue to manage alert barking.
Give digging and chasing urges a legal outlet such as tunnel games or a sand pit.
Stay consistent with household rules; terriers notice and use any gaps.
Avoid harsh handling, which tends to make a terrier more stubborn, not more cooperative.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy to many people, calm adult dogs, everyday noises and handling from an early age. Supervised, positive meetings with other dogs help reduce the scrappy reactions some terriers show towards dogs they do not know.

health.overview: The Wire Fox Terrier is generally a sturdy, long-lived small breed, with a typical lifespan of more than 12 years. In a large owner survey from the UK, skin, coat and ear problems were the most frequently reported issues, mostly allergic skin disease, followed by lumps and tumours, digestive problems and eye conditions. Cancer was the most common cause of death in that survey, and degenerative myelopathy, a progressive disease of the spinal cord in older dogs, was also an important cause. Breed-specific inherited conditions include van den Ende-Gupta syndrome, a skeletal disorder present from birth, and primary lens luxation. DNA tests exist for both, and for the gene variant linked to degenerative myelopathy. Kneecap problems and heart checks are also part of recommended screening for breeding dogs.
commonConditions: Allergic skin disease (atopic dermatitis): itchy, inflamed skin, often with recurring ear infections; the most reported problem in a UK breed survey
Ear inflammation (otitis externa), frequently linked with skin allergies
Lumps and tumours, including benign fatty lumps (lipomas) and cancers; cancer was the leading cause of death in the UK survey, with the bladder the most often reported tumour site

Degenerative myelopathy: a slowly progressive spinal cord disease of older dogs causing hind-limb weakness; a DNA test identifies dogs carrying the SOD1 risk variant, but not every at-risk dog develops the disease
Van den Ende-Gupta syndrome: an inherited (autosomal recessive) skeletal disorder caused by a SCARF2 mutation, seen in puppies as a severe underbite and severe kneecap displacement
Patellar luxation: the kneecap slips out of place, causing skipping or lameness
Primary lens luxation: an inherited eye condition in which the lens moves out of position and can cause painful glaucoma; reported rarely in recent testing of the breed
Digestive problems, including food intolerance and pancreatitis
Arthritis in older dogs
Dental disease
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for DNA results for van den Ende-Gupta syndrome, primary lens luxation and degenerative myelopathy, and for kneecap, heart and eye checks on the parents.
Book an urgent vet visit for a suddenly red, painful or cloudy eye, which can signal lens luxation.
Treat itching and ear problems early, and work with a vet to find allergy triggers.
Check the skin regularly for new lumps and have any new or growing lump examined.
Keep the dog lean to protect the knees and joints.
Brush the teeth regularly and schedule dental checks.
Keep up yearly health checks, vaccinations and parasite control.
recommendedScreenings: Patella (kneecap) evaluation
Cardiac examination
Eye examination under an official eye scheme or by a veterinary ophthalmologist
DNA test for van den Ende-Gupta syndrome (SCARF2)
DNA test for primary lens luxation (ADAMTS17)
DNA test for degenerative myelopathy risk (SOD1)
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week with dog toothpaste and have the mouth checked at each vet visit. Watch for a puppy whose lower jaw is clearly longer than the upper, which should be checked by a vet.
health.earCare: Check the small folded ears weekly for wax, smell or redness and clean only with a vet-approved cleaner. Repeated ear infections are often a sign of an underlying skin allergy.
health.skinCare: Part the coat during grooming to look for redness, scratching marks, lumps or parasites. Ongoing itching, licking of the paws or recurring hot spots are worth discussing with a vet, as allergic skin disease is common in the breed.

funFacts: The Wire Fox Terrier has won Best in Show at Westminster 15 times, more than any other breed; the first Wire winner was Ch. Matford Vic in 1915.
A Wire Fox Terrier named Caesar, owned by King Edward VII of Britain, walked in the king's funeral procession in 1910.
A Wire Fox Terrier played Asta in the 1930s Thin Man films, and the breed's popularity as a family pet soared as a result.
In post-war Britain, many toddlers learned to walk holding a toy Wire Fox Terrier on a wheeled frame.
In the United States, Smooth and Wire Fox Terriers were registered as one breed for a century before being recognised as separate breeds in 1985.

faq.question: How big does a Wire Fox Terrier get?
faq.answer: Males should stand no more than 39 cm at the withers, with females slightly smaller. The ideal show weight for a male is 8.25 kg, and females are a little lighter.

faq.question: How long do Wire Fox Terriers live?
faq.answer: They are a long-lived breed, typically living more than 12 years with good care.

faq.question: What is the difference between the Wire and Smooth Fox Terrier?
faq.answer: They share the same build, size and character. The Wire has a harsh, broken coat with a beard and leg furnishings that needs regular stripping, while the Smooth has a short, flat coat that is much easier to care for.

faq.question: Does a Wire Fox Terrier need professional grooming?
faq.answer: The coat needs brushing more than once a week, plus stripping every so often to remove dead hair. Many owners use a groomer experienced with terriers. Clipping is simpler but softens the coat and can fade its colour.

faq.question: Do Wire Fox Terriers shed?
faq.answer: Yes, they do shed. Regular brushing and stripping remove dead hair before it ends up around the house.

faq.question: Are Wire Fox Terriers good with children?
faq.answer: They are friendly and playful and can be great with respectful older children. Their energy and quick reactions mean play with toddlers should always be supervised.

faq.question: Can a Wire Fox Terrier live with cats or small pets?
faq.answer: They were bred to hunt, so most have a strong urge to chase. Some live peacefully with a cat they were raised with, but they are not a safe match for rodents, rabbits or birds.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Wire Fox Terrier need?
faq.answer: Plan on up to about an hour of activity a day, combined with training games or puzzles to keep the mind busy.

faq.question: What health tests should a breeder do?
faq.answer: Good breeders check the kneecaps, heart and eyes of parent dogs and use DNA tests for van den Ende-Gupta syndrome, primary lens luxation and degenerative myelopathy.

faq.question: What health problems are most common in the breed?
faq.answer: Itchy, allergic skin and ear problems are the issues owners report most. Lumps and tumours, digestive upsets, eye conditions and spinal cord disease in older age also occur.

overview.summary: An elegant, muscular, and exceptionally calm French pointing dog known for its beautiful brown-and-white feathered coat, steadfast hunting ability, and gentle, affectionate devotion to its family.
overview.description: The French Spaniel is a medium-sized, harmoniously built continental pointing dog that radiates both noble elegance and robust athleticism. Sporting a slightly rectangular silhouette, it is covered by a dense, flat, and silky coat of white and brown (liver), characterized by distinct patches and moderate feathering on the ears, legs, and tail. The head features a sculpted, noble profile with dark amber eyes that express profound gentleness and intelligence. Well-developed drop ears frame the face, lying close to the cheeks. In the field, it is a persistent, close-working hunter that points staunchly and retrieves gracefully from both land and water. In the home, however, it transforms into an incredibly docile, calm, and sociable companion that bonds intensely with its owners. Uncomplicated and deeply sensitive, the French Spaniel strikes a perfect balance between an untiring gundog and a peaceful domestic pet.
overview.history: The Epagneul Français boasts a truly ancient lineage, descending directly from the 'Chien d'Oysel', the venerable bird dogs used in the Middle Ages for netting and falconry across Europe. During the seventeenth century, these dogs were highly favored by the French royal court in Versailles for their exceptional scenting abilities and elegant appearance. As English pointing breeds surged in popularity during the nineteenth century, the traditional French Spaniel faced a sharp decline and near extinction. Fortunately, dedicated French breeders in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries led a meticulous revival, rescuing the authentic working bloodlines and standardizing the breed. Father Fournier, a prominent French priest and cynologist, was instrumental in this recovery, helping establish the first formal guidelines for the breed in 1891. While it remains somewhat rare outside of France and Canada, it is deeply cherished today by hunters and families who value its rustic endurance, beautiful coat, and exceptionally sweet nature.
overview.originalPurpose: Pointing and retrieving game birds across diverse terrain, often working in tandem with falconers or net hunters.
currentRoles: Versatile pointing and retrieving gundog
Canine athlete in field trials and tracking
Devoted household companion
Therapy dog (due to its gentle and calm disposition)

physical.coatType: Dense, flat, and silky single coat with substantial feathering on the ears, back of the legs, and tail. A slight waviness is permissible, particularly on the ears and tail.
coatColors: White and brown (ranging from cinnamon to dark liver)
Features irregular brown patches and varying degrees of brown roaning or ticking
A white blaze on the forehead is highly desirable
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; sheds consistently year-round, requiring regular brushing to manage loose hairs in the feathering
physical.droolingLevel: Low to moderate; cleanly fitted lips prevent excessive drooling, though panting during vigorous work may cause slight moisture
distinctiveFeatures: Elegant, muscular, and slightly rectangular silhouette (body length slightly exceeds height at the withers)
Height at the withers of 56 to 61 cm for males and 55 to 59 cm for females, with a tolerance of 2 cm above and 1 cm below these limits
Working weight typically ranging from 23 to 27 kg for males and 20 to 25 kg for females
Dense, silky white-and-brown coat featuring beautiful, long feathering
Noble, sculpted head with a moderately pronounced stop and a slightly convex muzzle profile
Complete, regular scissor bite (a pincer bite is tolerated)
Large, oval-shaped amber or dark amber eyes expressing profound gentleness and intelligence
Long, supple drop ears set at eye level, heavily fringed with wavy hair and hanging close to the cheeks
Deep, broad chest reaching down to the elbows with well-sprung ribs
Tail set slightly below the topline, tapering at the tip, carried horizontally or slightly curved in action, heavily feathered
Strong, well-boned limbs ending in oval, tight-knit toes with thick, dark pads

traits: Exceptionally gentle, docile, and affectionate with its family
Calm, composed, and quiet in domestic environments
Intelligent, eager to please, and highly cooperative during training
Sociable and polite with unfamiliar strangers, never aggressive or shy
Patient and sweet-natured with children
Enthusiastic, persistent, and focused when working outdoors in the field or water
Very peaceable with other dogs and household pets
Highly sensitive to harsh corrections or negative tone of voice
Deeply bonded to its primary handlers, often requiring close physical proximity

exercise.level: High; an athletic pointing breed requiring daily vigorous physical activity and mental stimulation, though it settles very calmly indoors afterward
activities: Daily brisk leashed walks or long trail hikes
Free running in a securely fenced, open field
Water retrieving and swimming in safe environments
Scent tracking, hunt tests, and interactive fetch games
Canine sports including agility and rally obedience

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly two to three times a week using a pin brush and metal comb to detangle the long, silky feathering on the ears, legs, and tail.
grooming.bathing: Bathe occasionally—every six to eight weeks or when visibly muddy—using a mild, moisturizing canine shampoo.
notes: The fine feathering is prone to collecting burrs and twigs; inspect and brush the coat immediately after woodland walks.
Inspect the long, heavily feathered drop ears weekly, wiping the canals gently with a veterinary-approved cleanser to prevent trapped moisture and infections.
Trim the hair between the foot pads regularly to prevent mud impaction and ensure solid traction.
Trim fast-growing nails every two to three weeks.
Brush teeth several times weekly with canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy; highly intelligent, naturally cooperative, and eager to please, making them highly responsive to positive reinforcement
tips: Use exclusively positive, reward-based training; they are exceptionally sensitive and will shut down completely if yelled at or treated harshly.
Begin basic obedience and leash training early to build confidence and establish a strong communicative bond.
Channel their natural pointing and retrieving instincts into structured play to keep their minds engaged.
Although they are generally reliable, practice recall relentlessly to manage their hunting drive in unfenced areas.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy early, gradually, and positively to diverse people, friendly dogs, and novel environments. Their naturally sweet and gentle disposition blossoms with proper early exposure, ensuring a confident adult.

climates: Temperate climates
Cool climates, where the dense, silky coat provides adequate insulation
Warm climates, provided shade, cool indoor shelter, and fresh water are available, with exercise restricted to cooler hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; they form deep, sensitive bonds with their human family and are prone to separation anxiety or depression if left isolated for long workdays without companionship.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for active medium-to-large sporting breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady energy and digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations strictly using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup, adjusting amounts to maintain a lean, athletic body silhouette where the ribs are easily felt. Divide daily food into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous running immediately before and after eating to mitigate bloat risk, and provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a strictly lean, well-muscled body condition to minimize mechanical stress on the joints.
Account for training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to prevent obesity.
Rest the dog before and after meals to mitigate the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
Increase protein and caloric density during active autumn hunting seasons.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary significantly based on exercise intensity, age, and outdoor temperature. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The French Spaniel is a generally healthy, robust, and athletic sporting breed with a typical life expectancy of 10 to 13 years. Health priorities focus on maintaining orthopedic soundness and screening for a breed-specific genetic neurological disorder known as Acral Mutilation Syndrome (AMS). Strict breeding protocols utilizing DNA and radiographic screening have helped minimize these conditions.
commonConditions: Acral Mutilation Syndrome (AMS) — a rare but severe inherited sensory neuropathy causing insensitivity to pain in the paws, leading to self-mutilation; completely preventable through DNA testing
Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints leading to osteoarthritis and stiffness, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Chronic otitis externa — bacterial and yeast ear infections promoted by heavy, feathered drop ears that restrict canal ventilation and trap moisture
Ocular conditions — occasional reports of entropion (inward rolling eyelids) or ectropion (outward sagging eyelids), requiring veterinary monitoring
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — an acute, life-threatening twisting of the stomach, requiring emergency veterinary care
Traumatic outdoor injuries — minor cuts, sprains, or thorn punctures sustained during vigorous fieldwork
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified DNA clearances for Acral Mutilation Syndrome (AMS), radiographic hip clearances, and specialist eye examinations.
Thoroughly dry the heavily feathered drop ears after swimming, bathing, or wet weather walks to prevent moisture-induced ear infections.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition throughout life to minimize mechanical wear on joints.
Feed two smaller meals daily and avoid vigorous running immediately before or after eating to mitigate bloat risk.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms, especially for dogs active in rural woodlands.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: DNA marker test for Acral Mutilation Syndrome (AMS)
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong jaws with a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the long, heavily feathered drop ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the flat, silky coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, ticks, or brush scratches. The coat is largely self-cleaning, but regular brushing prevents mats in the feathering.

idealFor: Active individuals and families seeking an exceptionally calm, gentle, and highly affectionate sporting companion
First-time dog owners willing to provide consistent daily exercise to a highly biddable, eager-to-please breed
Hunters or outdoor enthusiasts looking for a dedicated pointing and retrieving partner
Homes with a securely fenced yard providing ample space for supervised running
Households looking for a peaceable dog that integrates very well with children and other pets
notIdealFor: Sedentary individuals looking for a low-maintenance, low-energy indoor lap dog
Apartment dwellers without access to extensive outdoor running space
Owners who leave a dog home alone in isolation for long workdays, risking separation anxiety
Handlers who rely on harsh training methods or heavy-handed corrections
People seeking a fierce territorial guard dog

funFacts: The French Spaniel is one of the direct descendants of the ancient 'Chien d'Oysel', making it one of the oldest pointing spaniel breeds in Europe.
During the seventeenth century, the breed was a favorite of French royalty and was extensively used at the court of Versailles for falconry and net hunting.

The breed is renowned for its remarkable 'on/off switch'—it is a tireless, passionate worker in the field, but immediately transforms into an incredibly calm, docile, and unobtrusive companion indoors.
Unlike many other spaniels that are strictly flushing dogs, the French Spaniel is a true pointing breed, known for freezing and indicating the location of game before retrieving it.

In the late nineteenth century, Father Fournier, a French priest, spearheaded the effort to save the breed from extinction by gathering the remaining purebred specimens and helping to draft the first formal guidelines.

faq.question: What is a French Spaniel?
faq.answer: The French Spaniel (Epagneul Français) is an elegant, medium-to-large pointing and retrieving gundog from France, celebrated for its beautiful brown-and-white feathered coat, steadfast working ability, and exceptionally calm, affectionate nature.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a French Spaniel?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 56 to 61 cm at the withers and typically weigh 23 to 27 kg, while adult females stand 55 to 59 cm and weigh 20 to 25 kg, presenting a robust yet elegant silhouette.

faq.question: How long does a French Spaniel live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular rigorous exercise, and preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 10 to 13 years.

faq.question: Do French Spaniels shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They are moderate shedders. Their dense, flat, and silky coat requires brushing two to three times a week to prevent tangles in the feathering on the ears, legs, and tail, along with regular ear cleaning.

faq.question: Can a French Spaniel live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. While they are famously calm and quiet indoors, their high physical energy and need for vigorous daily exercise make them better suited to a house with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Are French Spaniels hard to train?
faq.answer: No, they are highly intelligent, cooperative, and very eager to please, making them easy to train. However, they are deeply sensitive and require gentle, positive reinforcement, as harsh corrections will severely damage their trust.

faq.question: Are French Spaniels good family pets and good with children?
faq.answer: Yes, they are outstanding family pets. They are exceptionally docile, sweet-natured, and patient, making them wonderful, peaceable companions for children and other household pets.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a French Spaniel?
faq.answer: Primary health concerns include a rare genetic neurological condition called Acral Mutilation Syndrome (AMS) which can be prevented with DNA testing, as well as hip dysplasia and ear infections due to their heavy drop ears.

overview.summary: An ancient Spanish sighthound built for chasing hares across open country: lean, long-legged and fast, with a very long hooked tail and a calm, reserved manner at rest.
overview.description: The Galgo Español is a good-sized sighthound with a long, narrow head, a deep chest, a strongly tucked-up belly and a flexible, slightly longer-than-tall body. One of its most recognisable features is the tail: very long, low-set and sickle-shaped, ending in a marked hook that almost reaches the ground when held between the legs. The loin is arched and can stand higher than the withers, and the croup slopes steeply, giving the breed a different outline from the English Greyhound. There are two coat types: a fine, short, dense smooth coat, and a harder, semi-long rough coat that often forms a beard, moustache and eyebrows. Any colour is allowed, with brindles and fawns among the most typical. Its natural fast gait is the gallop. In temperament it is serious and somewhat reserved, quiet and gentle at home, yet keen and energetic when it sights quarry.
overview.history: Sighthounds of this type have been part of Spanish life for many centuries; the breed was known in Roman times and is traditionally thought to descend from ancient sighthounds of Asian origin, although its earliest beginnings cannot be traced with certainty. Medieval Spanish literature already describes the galgo catching hares. Between the 16th and 18th centuries large numbers were taken to England and Ireland, and the breed is regarded as one of the ancestors of the English Greyhound. Hare coursing on open land has always been its main job, though it was once also used on rabbits, foxes and wild boar. The breed received definitive international recognition in 1971, and in the United States it was recognised by one registry in 2006 but remains too rare there for national breed club status. Many galgos in Spain are still kept for hunting. The end of the hunting season is among the main reasons dogs enter Spanish shelters, and Spain's 2023 national animal welfare law excludes hunting dogs from its scope, which has kept their treatment a subject of public debate.

grooming.brushing: Smooth coats need only a weekly brush or rub with a grooming mitt. Rough coats need brushing once or twice a week, with extra care for the beard and leg hair.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when needed. Dry thoroughly and keep the dog warm afterwards, because the smooth coat gives little insulation.
notes: Check the thin skin regularly for cuts and scrapes, especially after running.
Trim the nails regularly; long nails can affect the feet of a fast-running dog.
Soft bedding helps prevent pressure sores on the bony elbows and hips.
Smooth-coated dogs often need a coat or jumper in cold or wet weather.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging; gentle and sensitive but independent, and the urge to chase moving animals can override commands
tips: Use gentle, reward-based training; harsh handling makes sensitive sighthounds shut down.
Keep sessions short and pleasant.
Assume recall will fail if the dog sees prey; let it run free only in fully fenced areas.
Use a well-fitting martingale or harness, as the narrow head can slip out of a flat collar.
Give dogs from shelters or hunting backgrounds time to learn house routines, stairs and household noises.
training.socialization: Introduce the dog calmly to people, other dogs and everyday situations. Any introduction to cats or small pets should be slow, muzzled at first and closely supervised, as many galgos have a strong chase instinct.

feedingFrequency.senior: Two smaller meals a day, adjusted for activity and body condition.

nutrition.guidelines: Sighthounds are naturally lean: hip bones and a few ribs may be faintly visible in a fit dog. Weigh the dog regularly and adjust portions to keep that athletic shape. Keep fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Underweight newly adopted dogs should regain weight gradually under veterinary guidance.
Avoid strenuous running just before and after meals.
Raised bowls are not needed for most dogs; ask a vet if your dog eats awkwardly.
Change foods gradually over about a week.
nutrition.note: Calorie needs vary with age, activity and neutering status. A vet can advise on a healthy target weight for the individual dog.

health.overview: Breed-specific health research on the Galgo Español is limited, and no breed health survey or official screening scheme was found. Studies show that healthy galgos normally have higher red blood cell counts, haemoglobin and packed cell volume, and lower platelet counts, than most other breeds; these results are normal for the breed and should not be mistaken for illness. Like other sighthounds, they may also have naturally lower thyroid hormone values and can process some anaesthetic drugs more slowly, so it helps to choose a vet familiar with sighthounds. Dogs that lived in Spain may have been exposed to diseases spread by sandflies and ticks: a 2026 study of 160 galgos in central Spain found antibodies to Leishmania in 13.1%, Anaplasma in 10% and Ehrlichia in 3.1%.
commonConditions: Leishmaniosis (exposure to Leishmania infantum, spread by sandflies): antibodies found in 13.1% of galgos tested in central Spain; can cause skin, kidney and other disease
Anaplasmosis (tick-borne Anaplasma phagocytophilum): antibodies found in 10% of galgos tested in central Spain
Ehrlichiosis (tick-borne Ehrlichia canis): antibodies found in 3.1% of galgos tested in central Spain
preventiveCare: Tell every vet that your dog is a sighthound, so blood results and anaesthetic drugs are chosen and interpreted accordingly.
For dogs from Spain or other areas where Leishmania is present, ask your vet about testing and about sandfly and tick protection.
Check the thin skin after exercise and treat cuts promptly.
Provide warmth and padded bedding, especially for smooth-coated dogs.
Keep up yearly health checks, vaccinations and parasite control.
recommendedScreenings: Leishmania testing for dogs that have lived in or travel to areas where it occurs
Tick-borne disease testing (Ehrlichia, Anaplasma) for dogs imported from Spain
Baseline blood tests interpreted with sighthound reference values
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week with dog toothpaste and have the mouth checked at each vet visit.
health.earCare: Check the ears weekly for wax, redness or smell and clean only with a vet-approved cleaner when needed.
health.skinCare: The thin skin tears easily during play or running, so check for cuts and scrapes regularly. Unexplained hair loss, scaling or sores in a dog from Spain should be checked by a vet, as they can be signs of leishmaniosis.

faq.question: How big is a Galgo Español?
faq.answer: Males stand 62–70 cm at the withers and females 60–68 cm, with up to 2 cm more allowed for perfectly proportioned dogs. The breed standard does not set a weight.

faq.question: What is the difference between a Galgo and a Greyhound?
faq.answer: Both are sighthounds, and the Galgo is considered one of the Greyhound's ancestors. The Galgo has a longer, hooked tail, an arched loin that can be higher than the withers, a more sloping croup and comes in both smooth and rough coats.

faq.question: Can a Galgo live with cats?
faq.answer: Some can, but many have a strong instinct to chase small animals. Any introduction should be slow, supervised and preferably done with a dog already assessed as cat-safe.

faq.question: Can a Galgo be let off the lead?
faq.answer: Only in a fully fenced area. Once a galgo sees something to chase, it may not respond to recall and can reach high speeds very quickly.

faq.question: Why are my galgo's blood test results unusual?
faq.answer: Healthy galgos normally have higher red blood cell counts and lower platelet counts than most breeds, and sighthounds often show lower thyroid values. A vet familiar with sighthounds will take this into account.

faq.question: Should an adopted galgo from Spain be tested for diseases?
faq.answer: Yes, it is sensible to ask your vet about testing for leishmaniosis and tick-borne diseases, which a recent study found in a notable share of galgos in Spain.

faq.question: Do Galgos feel the cold?
faq.answer: Smooth-coated galgos have little body fat and a thin coat, so most need a coat in cold or wet weather and warm, soft bedding indoors.

faq.question: How long do Galgos live?
faq.answer: No reliable lifespan figure has been published for the breed. Good weight control, parasite prevention and regular vet checks support a long, healthy life.

overview.summary: The Gascon Saintongeois is an athletic French scenthound prized for its acute nose, resonant voice, steady endurance, and natural pack-working drive. Recognised in two size varieties—the larger Grand and the medium-sized Petit—it wears a short, dense white coat marked with black patches and pale tan points. While composed, gentle, and responsive with its handlers, its deep-rooted trailing instincts require dedicated daily exercise, scent-based enrichment, and secure outdoor containment.
overview.description: Combining muscular substance with refined French hound lines, the Gascon Saintongeois has a slightly rectangular build with a height-to-body-length ratio of 10 to 10.5. The head features divergent skull and muzzle planes of equal length, a domed and narrow skull with a pronounced occipital peak, a slight stop, a strong slightly arched nasal bridge, and oval brown eyes with a gentle, trusting expression. Thin, inward-curling ears are set well below eye level and reach at least to the tip of the black nose. A deep, broad chest extending to the elbows, firm back, well-muscled hindquarters, and sabre-carried tapering tail support effortless, regular movement across rough terrain. The short, tight coat is white with black patches—sometimes moderately ticked—accompanied by pale tan cheek and eyebrow markings and an occasional dead-leaf 'roebuck mark' on the lower thigh. The Grand variety is a large pack and tracking hound, whereas the Petit variety is a compact, versatile medium hound.
overview.history: In the mid-19th century, Count Joseph de Carayon-Latour of Château de Virelade in Gironde sought to save the nearly extinct Chien de Saintonge, one of France's oldest royal pack hounds. Obtaining the last surviving Saintongeois dogs—recorded as two males and one female—he crossed them with Baron de Ruble's Grand Bleu de Gascogne hounds. This alliance established the Grand Gascon Saintongeois, though the pure Chien de Saintonge gradually vanished in the process. During the mid-20th century, hunters in southwestern France selected the smallest puppies from Grand Gascon Saintongeois litters—initially to pursue hare—and fixed a distinct, smaller variety known as the Petit Gascon Saintongeois.
overview.originalPurpose: Pursuing large game (such as roe deer, red deer, and wild boar) and hare by scent, with the Grand variety working in packs or individually as a tracking hound (limier) and the Petit variety developed as a hare specialist and versatile gun-hunting hound.
currentRoles: Pack and small-group hunting scenthound for large game and hare
Individual cold-trail tracking hound (limier)
Nosework, mantrailing, and scent-sport participant
Active rural companion for households experienced with working hounds

exercise.level: High. Bred for sustained field endurance, this scenthound requires substantial daily physical exercise paired with structured opportunities to use its nose. Because an active trail can override recall, off-leash running should take place only within securely fenced enclosures.
activities: Long, brisk countryside or trail walks tailored to age, variety, and physical conditioning
Structured mantrailing, tracking, and nosework games
Scent-puzzle foraging and hidden-object searches
