overview.summary: A rugged, shaggy-coated, and remarkably courageous medium-sized French scenthound from the historic Nivernais province, celebrated as an elite wild-boar specialist built for tireless endurance across dense brambles and cold wet terrain.
overview.description: The Griffon Nivernais is a rustic, tough, and distinctly tousled medium-sized French scenthound whose lean, dry limbs and sinewy musculature prioritize all-day stamina over sheer sprinting speed. Framed slightly longer than tall in a balanced rectangle, it wears a slightly wistful yet completely fearless expression framed by prominent eyebrows that leave its dark, penetrating eyes clearly visible, a small chin beard, well-pigmented moustaches, and medium-length, supple, hairy drop ears turning gently inward at the tips. Its hallmark is a long, rough, shaggy, weatherproof coat—known in French as 'Barbouillaud'—that sheds burrs cleanly and is always overlaid with dark hair tips across wolf-grey, wild-boar-grey, blue-grey, or hare-coloured shades. Specialized in locating and baying wild boar in small packs or solo across thorny thickets, the Griffon Nivernais combines an extraordinary nose and bold initiative with a resonant, carrying cry. Calm, friendly, and non-aggressive toward people around the home or kennel, it remains headstrong and intensely driven outdoors, demanding rural countryside access and consistent early leadership.
overview.history: Tracing its distant ancestry to the ancient Segusian hunting hounds (Canis Segusius) kept by the Gauls and to the famous Grey Dogs of Saint Louis ('Chiens Gris de Saint Louis') brought back from the East by King Louis IX in the mid-thirteenth century, the Griffon Nivernais lineage enjoyed two centuries of royal acclaim for wolf and wild-boar hunting through the reign of Louis XI. When King Francis I later favoured white royal packs, loyal country noblemen in the central French province of Nivernais (modern-day Nièvre) preserved the hardy grey hounds until the French Revolution of 1789 nearly erased the breed. Roughly a century later, local sportsmen reconstructed the breed—often called simply 'chien de pays' ('country dog')—from surviving regional dogs infused carefully with Vendéen, Foxhound, and Otterhound blood to restore its size, rough coat, and tracking grit. A dedicated French preservation society was founded in 1925 under the presidency of the Vicomte d'Anchald; after World War II reduced numbers sharply, the society was revitalized in 1969, building on definitive international recognition achieved in December 1959. Today, the Griffon Nivernais is highly esteemed across France and parts of Scandinavia as a premier wild-boar hound while remaining uncommon outside active hunting circles.
overview.originalPurpose: Trailing, closing in on, and baying wild boar (and historically wolves) to the gun—typically in small packs, though also individually—across thorny, rugged forests and wet terrain.
currentRoles: Specialist wild-boar hunting scenthound (small pack or solo)
Cold-trailing and scent-tracking countryside hound
Active rural working companion for dedicated hunting households

physical.coatType: Long, shaggy, bushy, rough, and strong outer coat ('Barbouillaud') that is never woolly or curly, naturally shrugging off thorns and mud. The belly and inner thighs are well coated, eyebrows are pronounced without obstructing vision, the chin bears a modest beard, and the lips are veiled by well-pigmented moustaches.
coatColors: Always black-overlaid (fawn hairs with tips darker than the base, never bright orange), spanning light to dark shades depending on the density of dark-tipped and interspersed white hairs
Wolf grey (black-overlaid sandy fawn) and wild-boar grey (dark smoky grizzle)
Blue grey (black-overlaid fawn with a bluish cast on the mantle)
A small white patch on the chest is tolerated; solid black, golden wheaten/orange, bright tricolour patterns, and white feet are not accepted
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; the rough, shaggy coat sheds modestly and holds dead hair until brushed out seasonally
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tight, well-pigmented lips that just cover the lower jaw without excess flews and a light, dry dewlap-free neck keep drooling minimal
distinctiveFeatures: Robust, hardy, shaggy medium-sized scenthound built slightly longer than tall with lean, dry limbs designed for endurance rather than pure speed
Height at the withers of 55 to 62 cm for males and 53 to 60 cm for females
Very dry, light yet well-proportioned head with parallel skull and muzzle lines, equal skull and muzzle lengths, a nearly flat skull, and a subtly marked stop

Well-marked black nose, gently converging non-pointed muzzle with a small chin beard, tight pigmented lips under strong moustaches, and robust jaws meeting in a scissor bite (pincer bite occasionally seen)
Dark, lively, penetrating eyes with well-pigmented rims and no visible haw, framed by pronounced eyebrows that never obscure vision
Supple, fairly thin, medium-width hairy drop ears set level with the upper eye line (roughly 3 cm wide at attachment), reaching the base of the nose and turning gently inward at the tips

Deep, long chest descending to the elbow—narrower in front and widening toward the rounder rear ribs—paired with a level topline, solid narrow back, slightly arched loin, and a slightly rising underline
Fairly high-set, medium-length tail bushiest in the middle, carried slightly below horizontal at rest and lifted upward in a sabre curve (sometimes curving toward the back at the tip) in motion
Straight, lean forelegs and slightly tucked-under stance at rest with slightly closed hock angles and elongated oval hare-like feet with tight toes and dark pigmented pads and nails
Supple, thick, tight, dewlap-free skin displaying black body spots beneath a shaggy black-overlaid coat

traits: Courageous, determined, and bold when baying wild boar—brave without reckless foolishness
Keenly scented, tenacious, and resourceful with strong initiative in dense brush and rugged terrain
Balanced, calm, friendly, and completely non-aggressive toward humans around the home or kennel
Deeply pack-oriented with a strong sense of social hierarchy and peaceful sociability toward other dogs
Independent, self-assured, and often stubborn when locked onto a scent trail, requiring patient yet firm guidance from puppyhood
Vocal during pursuit, driving game with a resonant, carrying, howling hunting cry
Affectionate and pleasant as a family dog when given genuine hunting or intensive tracking outlets

exercise.level: Very high; a tireless woodland wild-boar hound built for endurance over harsh terrain that demands extensive daily outdoor exercise alongside hunting or structured scent tracking
activities: Small-pack or solo wild-boar hunting and cold-trailing fieldwork
Structured mantrailing, blood tracking, and organised scenthound working trials
Long, vigorous daily forest hikes and rough countryside walks on a sturdy leash or long tracking line
Free outdoor movement inside a large, securely fenced rural property

grooming.brushing: Remarkably low-maintenance rough coat whose coarse texture naturally prevents burrs and debris from clinging—a thorough brushing and combing three to four times a year (or weekly during heavy seasonal shedding) removes dead hair cleanly.
grooming.bathing: Bathe infrequently, only when heavily soiled or strongly odorous after forest hunting, using a mild canine shampoo.
notes: Because the long, hairy, inward-turning drop ears are prone to collecting moisture and debris, inspect them weekly, gently pluck excess inner-ear hair when recommended by a veterinarian, and clean with a dog-safe ear cleanser.
Check the elongated hare-like feet, tight toes, pads, and hairy belly after rugged brush hunting for thorns, cuts, or ticks.
Trim dark nails regularly whenever rough outdoor ground does not wear them down naturally.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging; receptive and eager when trained on wild boar, yet dominant, independent, and stubborn around distracting scents—demanding calm, gentle firmness from early puppyhood
tips: Begin obedience, recall, and calm handler-leadership training very young using gentle yet unwavering consistency—neither harsh force nor permissive laxity works well with a dominant scenthound.
Channel its intense hunting passion early into structured wild-boar training, mantrailing, or tracking trials rather than expecting casual urban obedience.
Never trust off-leash reliability near unfenced roads or wildlife-heavy woods unless extensive recall and game-steadiness training has been achieved.
Respect its pack-oriented nature by fostering calm canine socialization while supervising around small non-canine pets.
training.socialization: Early, calm, positive exposure to varied people, other dogs, woodland environments, and routine ear handling ensures this courageous hound matures into a steady, trustworthy working companion.

climates: Cold, damp, and wet woodland climates—exceptionally hardy outdoors in winter cold, rain, and marshland thanks to its thick, rough, weatherproof coat
Temperate four-season countryside climates with forest access
Hot summer climates are more challenging than for smooth-coated hounds; restrict vigorous exercise to cool dawn or evening hours and provide reliable shade and cool fresh water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; accustomed to living and hunting in social packs, a Griffon Nivernais settles calmly in a rural kennel or home with canine companions after work but struggles with solitary city confinement.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for medium-sized, highly active working and hunting breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age to support steady, lean musculoskeletal growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily (preferred by veterinarians over a single large evening meal to help reduce bloat risk).
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for lower activity and joint wellness.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately according to age and seasonal hunting workload so the hound keeps its lean, dry, enduring working build. Traditional French hunting kennels often feed once in the evening after work, but splitting the daily ration into two smaller meals and enforcing strict calm rest after every meal is strongly advised to lower the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat). Provide cool, fresh drinking water continuously.
considerations: Always follow every meal with a calm rest period—and consider dividing daily adult food into two meals—specifically to help guard against gastric dilatation-volvulus (stomach torsion / bloat).
Adjust caloric density upward during strenuous autumn and winter wild-boar hunting seasons and scale back during quieter off-season months.
Keep growing puppies lean on a balanced medium-breed growth formula.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric requirements vary substantially between active forest-hunting hounds and off-season adults. Consult a veterinarian to establish individual feeding quantities.

health.overview: The Griffon Nivernais is widely regarded as an exceptionally hardy, rustic working hound with no formally established breed-specific congenital or hereditary disease predispositions and no verified actuarial lifespan range published by primary registries. Small registered populations outside France limit large-scale epidemiological surveys, though Nordic monitoring notes isolated cases of missing teeth and healthy radiographic hip findings among small screened numbers. Practical preventive veterinary care centres on mealtime precautions against gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), diligent ear hygiene for its hairy drop ears, heat awareness in warm weather, and protection against wild-boar hunting trauma and woodland parasites.
commonConditions: Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — acute, life-threatening stomach distension and twisting highlighted specifically in French breed-care guidance for deep-chested hunting hounds, mitigated by dividing meals and enforcing post-meal rest
Otitis externa (outer ear infections) — conformation-linked risk associated with long, hairy, inward-turning drop ears that retain moisture, wax, or woodland debris without regular cleaning
Fieldwork and wild-boar hunting trauma — tusk lacerations, thorn punctures, paw abrasions, and tick-borne exposure encountered during dense brush and big-game hunting
Heat sensitivity in warm weather — rough, shaggy-coated griffons tolerate heat less comfortably than smooth-coated hounds during strenuous summer exertion
Isolated missing teeth — occasional tooth-loss/oligodontia cases noted in Nordic breeding monitoring, warranting attention to dentition in breeding stock
preventiveCare: Divide daily adult meals into two smaller portions, enforce a calm rest period after every meal, and learn emergency warning signs of bloat (unproductive retching, swollen tight abdomen, restlessness).
Inspect, clean, and (where advised by a veterinarian) gently maintain hair around the hairy drop ears regularly to prevent ear infections.
Avoid strenuous exercise during hot midday weather and provide cool water and shade promptly.
Maintain regular deworming, core and lifestyle vaccinations, and strict year-round protection against ticks, fleas, and heartworm—especially for forest-hunting dogs.
Inspect skin, paws, and teeth regularly after hunts and ask breeders for documented parental veterinary health records and complete dentition.
recommendedScreenings: No mandatory national breed-specific genetic or radiographic screening panel is currently established (elective radiographic hip dysplasia checks and dental completeness evaluations may be discussed with a veterinarian for breeding stock)
Routine veterinary wellness, ear, and dental examinations
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental checks to keep the robust jaws, scissor bite, and dentition healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the long, supple, hairy, inward-turning drop ears weekly for moisture, wax buildup, grass seeds, odour, or redness, keeping them clean and gently ventilated with a veterinarian-approved solution.
health.skinCare: Check through the shaggy rough coat and thick pigmented skin after every forest hunt for ticks, burrs, thorn punctures, or boar scratches.

idealFor: Wild-boar hunters and countryside sportsmen seeking a brave, tough, cold-trailing scenthound that works eagerly in small packs or solo
Experienced scenthound handlers in rural homes with access to forests, trails, and organised tracking work
Multi-dog rural households appreciating a pack-social, calm-in-kennel, non-aggressive working hound
Active outdoorspeople wanting a hardy, all-weather rough coat that requires minimal routine grooming
notIdealFor: City or apartment dwellers—this active countryside pack hunter is explicitly unsuited to urban or apartment living
Households looking solely for a casual family pet without hunting or intensive scent-tracking outlets
First-time or passive owners unprepared for a dominant, stubborn, independent hunting drive
Homes with free-roaming small pets or warm-climate lifestyles lacking cool exercise hours

funFacts: The Griffon Nivernais descends from the legendary 'Chiens Gris de Saint Louis' (Grey Dogs of Saint Louis), brought to France from the East by King Louis IX after the Crusades in the thirteenth century and prized in royal hunts for 200 years.

In French cynological tradition, its famously rough, shaggy, tousled coat is affectionately described by the rustic word 'Barbouillaud,' and its texture is so coarse that forest burrs and brambles scarcely stick to it.

Rather than bright tricolour markings, every Griffon Nivernais wears a dark-tipped ('black-overlaid') coat described with evocative traditional French terms: 'wolf grey,' 'wild-boar grey,' 'blue grey,' and 'hare coat.'

Nearly wiped out by the French Revolution of 1789, the breed survived through rural dogs known simply as 'chiens de pays' ('country dogs') in the Nivernais region before careful nineteenth-century reconstruction.
Despite a slightly wistful, shaggy expression that looks deceptively mellow, the Griffon Nivernais is celebrated across France and Scandinavia as one of Europe's bravest wild-boar specialists.

faq.question: What is a Griffon Nivernais?
faq.answer: The Griffon Nivernais is an ancient, rugged, shaggy-coated medium-sized French scenthound from the Nivernais region, descended from medieval grey royal hounds and specialized in tracking and baying wild boar across dense forests.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Griffon Nivernais?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 55 to 62 cm at the withers and adult females stand 53 to 60 cm. No official weight range is published, as healthy working dogs maintain a dry, lean, muscular medium frame built for endurance.

faq.question: How long does a Griffon Nivernais live?
faq.answer: No official lifespan range or peer-reviewed actuarial longevity study is published by primary registries for the Griffon Nivernais, though it is widely regarded as a very rustic, hardy medium-sized working hound.

faq.question: Can a Griffon Nivernais live in a city or apartment?
faq.answer: No. It is an active, pack-oriented countryside hunting hound with strong tracking drive and a carrying baying voice; it is poorly suited to city life and especially unsuitable for apartment living.

faq.question: Are Griffon Nivernais good family dogs?
faq.answer: They are calm, friendly, sociable, and never aggressive toward people, making warm companions in rural hunting households—provided they receive genuine hunting or intensive scent-tracking work rather than being kept solely as inactive house pets.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Griffon Nivernais need?
faq.answer: Despite its long shaggy coat, upkeep is very easy: brushing and combing three to four times a year (or weekly during moulting) removes dead hair cleanly, with baths only when dirty. Its long, hairy drop ears, however, need regular weekly cleaning and inspection.

faq.question: Are Griffon Nivernais easy to train?
faq.answer: They learn wild-boar hunting eagerly and respond well to patient, consistent, gentle firmness started early in puppyhood, but their dominant, independent scenthound streak makes them stubborn when locked onto fresh scents.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Griffon Nivernais?
faq.answer: No breed-specific hereditary diseases are formally established, though small numbers outside France limit broad statistics. Practical health care focuses on preventing bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus) via divided meals and post-meal rest, regular ear hygiene, heat care in summer, and wild-boar fieldwork safety.

overview.summary: A medium-sized, rectangular Norwegian scenthound built for cold-climate hare, fox, and lynx tracking, recognized by its predominantly white tricolour coat, sturdy build, steady nerves, and quiet, affectionate home manners.
overview.description: The Halden Hound is a well-proportioned, rectangular, and strongly built yet light-footed Norwegian scenthound resembling a slightly lighter Foxhound in outline. Bred to hunt independently as a single-handed tracking dog across snowy Nordic forests and rugged terrain, it combines physical durability and parallel, ground-covering movement with a harsh, straight, weatherproof double coat and thick undercoat. Its coat is predominantly clean white marked with distinct black patches and warm tan shadings on the head, legs, and sometimes along the borders between black and white. Its dry, medium-sized head features a gently arched skull, understated stop and occiput, medium-set drop ears, and calm dark brown eyes. At home, the breed is notably sociable, trusting, and quiet in everyday life, saving its carrying voice for the trail.
overview.history: The Halden Hound's lineage traces back to the mid-nineteenth century in Norway's Østfold region around the border town of Halden, where local harehounds were crossed with imported English Foxhounds—along with some Harrier, Beagle, German, and Swedish hound ancestry—to create a swift, cold-hardy solo hunter. In the 1860s, Østfold farmer Hans Larsen Bisseberg bred early lines known as the 'Bisseberghund', while the Anker family of Rød Herregård in Halden gave rise to the name 'Ankerstøver'. The name 'Haldenstøver' came into use around 1938. After a canine distemper outbreak in 1931 and World War II nearly wiped out the narrow breeding base, dedicated Norwegian enthusiasts revived the breed and secured formal national approval in 1952, followed by international recognition in 1965. Today it remains critically rare, with only about 10 to 20 puppies registered annually in Norway.

health.overview: Despite its historically small breeding population, the Halden Hound is regarded as a notably healthy, hardy breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years and no widespread inherited disease burden recorded. Careful population management focuses on preserving genetic diversity alongside routine radiographic hip screening, weekly drop-ear care, and standard precautions for deep-chested working hounds.

funFacts: Before the name 'Haldenstøver' came into use around 1938, the breed was known locally as the 'Bisseberghund' (after Østfold farmer Hans Larsen Bisseberg in the 1860s) and the 'Ankerstøver' (after the Anker family at Rød Herregård in Halden).
Canine distemper in 1931 and World War II nearly wiped out the breed, but Norwegian enthusiasts rebuilt it and secured formal national recognition in 1952.

With only about 10 to 20 puppies registered each year in Norway, the Halden Hound is critically rare and carefully managed under a national breeding program that caps individual dogs at 20 offspring to protect genetic diversity.
Unlike many vocal pack hounds, most Halden Hounds are remarkably quiet in everyday family life, reserving their carrying voice for the hunting trail.
Its oval, tightly knit feet grow protective hair between the toes to help shield against freezing Nordic snow and rough forest ground.

faq.question: What is a Halden Hound?
faq.answer: The Halden Hound (Haldenstøver) is a rare, medium-sized Norwegian scenthound bred for solo hare, fox, and lynx tracking, known for its predominantly white tricolour coat, steady nerves, and gentle home manners.

faq.question: How does the Halden Hound differ from Norway's other native harehounds?
faq.answer: While the Halden Hound, Dunker, and Hygen Hound are all Norwegian harehounds, the Halden Hound is distinguished by its predominantly white tricolour coat with black patches and tan shadings, as well as its lighter Foxhound-like outline.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Halden Hound?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 52 to 60 cm at the withers (ideal 56 cm) and weigh roughly 23 to 29 kg, while adult females stand 50 to 58 cm (ideal 54 cm) and weigh roughly 20 to 26 kg.

faq.question: How long does a Halden Hound live?
faq.answer: With good nutrition, regular exercise, and routine veterinary care, the breed typically lives 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Halden Hound need?
faq.answer: Grooming is low-maintenance. Brush the harsh double coat weekly (more often during spring and autumn undercoat sheds), check the drop ears weekly, trim nails regularly, and brush teeth several times a week.

faq.question: Can a Halden Hound live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Although quiet indoors, its high endurance and daily exercise requirements make it far better suited to a rural or suburban house with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Are Halden Hounds good family dogs and good with children?
faq.answer: Yes, in active households. They are well known for steady nerves, friendliness, and gentle, trusting manners with children and other dogs, provided their outdoor exercise needs are met.

faq.question: How easy is it to train a Halden Hound?
faq.answer: They are intelligent, trusting, and cooperative with positive reinforcement, but strong wildlife-tracking instincts mean outdoor off-leash recall requires careful long-line training and secure fencing.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Halden Hound need each day?
faq.answer: Plan on at least 60 to 90 minutes of brisk daily activity, combining leashed walks, woodland hikes, secure yard running, and scent-tracking games.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for breeding Halden Hounds?
faq.answer: Radiographic hip dysplasia (HD) screening is recommended for all breeding dogs alongside careful genetic-diversity management and routine veterinary checkups.

overview.summary: The Hamiltonstövare is a well-proportioned, rectangular, medium-sized Swedish scent hound bred to trail hare and red fox solo across Nordic forests, distinguished by its crisp black-tan-and-white tricolour coat, calm household demeanour, and clear, far-carrying hunting voice.
overview.description: Built for strength and multi-day stamina without a trace of heaviness, the Hamiltonstövare presents a balanced, rectangular outline with well-developed muscle, clean bone, and parallel limb action. Its harsh, weather-resistant double coat lies close to the body and thickens in winter, patterned in a striking tricolour of a black mantle over the neck, back, and flanks, warm golden-to-reddish tan on the head and limbs, and symmetrical white markings on the muzzle, neck, chest, feet, and tail tip. The long, rectangular head carries dark brown eyes with a calm, friendly expression and soft, high-set hanging ears whose front edge turns slightly outward. In the forest, it works alone at a steady, accurate pace with a resonant voice that can be heard for miles; at home, it is remarkably even-tempered, gentle, and sociable.
overview.history: Scent hounds of continental type have been used in Sweden since the sixteenth century, brought home by soldiers returning from European wars. During the nineteenth century, Swedish breeders crossed these dogs with southern German (including Holsteiner) and Swiss hounds as well as English Foxhounds and Harriers. Foremost among these pioneers was Count Adolf Patrik Hamilton, who founded Sweden's national kennel club in 1889. At the country's first dog show in Stockholm in 1886, where 189 scent hounds were exhibited, Count Hamilton showed two influential tricolour hounds named Pang and Stella that became pillars of the breed. Originally called the Swedish Hound (Svensk stövare), the breed was renamed Hamiltonstövare in 1921 in Hamilton's honour and received definitive international recognition on 25 November 1954.
overview.originalPurpose: Solitary vocal scent-trailing and driving of hare and red fox (never deer or elk) across Scandinavian woodland and snow.
currentRoles: Solitary hunting scent hound for hare and red fox

Scale energy intake upward during active hunting or trial periods.
Allow rest before and after vigorous running around mealtimes.
Count training treats within the daily calorie budget.

health.overview: The Hamiltonstövare is widely regarded as a healthy, long-lived working breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years and decreasing inbreeding levels thanks to structured outcrossing guidelines. National breeding strategies require pre-breeding hip radiographs even though clinical hip symptoms are uncommon in the breed, and only low-frequency occurrences of epilepsy, allergic skin itching, tumours, cryptorchidism, and isolated cases of patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) are noted.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia (HD) — radiographic hip status must be recorded prior to breeding (with grades D and E excluded from breeding), though clinical hip lameness is rarely seen in the breed

Isolated hereditary or constitutional conditions — low-frequency cases of idiopathic epilepsy, allergic skin pruritus (itching), tumours, cryptorchidism, and occasional congenital patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) are monitored in national breed health strategies
Otitis externa — ear-canal irritation or infection associated with hanging ears after wet or brushy fieldwork
Field injuries — pad abrasions, small cuts, or snow and ice wear sustained during multi-hour forest hunts
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have recorded radiographic hip evaluations (grades A, B, or C, with C paired only to A or B) and low inbreeding coefficients.
Inspect and dry the hanging ears weekly and after wet woodland outings.
Check paw pads, nails, eyes, and skin after every hunting day or forest run.
Maintain routine tick, flea, and internal parasite prevention during active outdoor seasons.
Keep the hound in lean working condition and schedule annual veterinary check-ups, cardiac auscultation for puppies, and vaccinations.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip evaluation (HD screening required for breeding stock)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week with canine toothpaste and check the scissor bite and gums at routine veterinary visits.
health.earCare: Inspect the soft, hanging ears weekly for moisture, wax, or debris, and clean gently with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser when needed.
health.skinCare: Brush through the harsh double coat after forest outings to remove burrs, ticks, and snowballs, and monitor the skin for any signs of seasonal itching.

funFacts: Named in 1921 after Count Adolf Patrik Hamilton (1852–1910), who founded Sweden's national kennel club in 1889 and exhibited the foundational pair Pang and Stella among 189 scent hounds at the 1886 Stockholm dog show.
Before receiving the Hamiltonstövare name in 1921, the breed was simply called the Svensk stövare ('Swedish Hound').
Unlike British and French foxhounds that work in large packs, the Hamiltonstövare is bred to work strictly alone, trailing quarry at a calm, accurate pace without rushing the game.
A fit Hamiltonstövare is expected to work for at least five hours a day across two consecutive hunting days while keeping its clear, sharp voice audible from miles away.

Bicolour coats (yellow-and-white, black-and-white, or black-and-tan without white) and blue eyes are disqualifying faults because the crisp black-tan-and-white tricolour pattern is a hallmark of the breed.

faq.question: What is a Hamiltonstövare?
faq.answer: The Hamiltonstövare is Sweden's classic tricolour scent hound, developed in the late nineteenth century by Count Adolf Patrik Hamilton to trail hare and red fox solo across Nordic forests.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult Hamiltonstövare?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 53 to 61 cm at the withers (ideal 57 cm) and typically weigh 25 to 27 kg, while females stand 49 to 57 cm (ideal 53 cm) and weigh 23 to 25 kg.

faq.question: How long does a Hamiltonstövare live?
faq.answer: It is a hardy, long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: What coat colour is permitted in the Hamiltonstövare?
faq.answer: Only tricolour is permitted: a black mantle over the upper neck, back, trunk sides, and top of the tail; rich golden-to-reddish tan on the head, ears, chest, and legs; and white markings on the muzzle, throat/chest, lower legs and feet, and the tip of the tail.

faq.question: Does the Hamiltonstövare hunt in packs?
faq.answer: No. Like other Swedish stövare breeds, it is bred to hunt solo, trailing hare or fox on its own and using its clear, ringing voice to guide the hunter.

faq.question: Is the Hamiltonstövare a good family dog?
faq.answer: Yes, in an active outdoor household. Indoors it is famously calm, friendly, and gentle with children, provided its daily exercise and scent-work needs are met.

faq.question: What health screenings are required before breeding?
faq.answer: Breeding dogs must have an official radiographic hip evaluation on record (grades A, B, or C, with C dogs paired only with A or B partners), and breeders follow strict limits on litter numbers and inbreeding coefficients.

overview.summary: A medium-sized British scenthound bred for steady stamina and scent-tracking endurance, known for its smooth hound coat, friendly pack nature, and clear baying voice.
overview.description: The Harrier is a compact, strongly built, and well-balanced scenthound that sits squarely between the smaller Beagle and the larger English Foxhound in height and frame. Shaped by centuries of pursuing hares and rabbits across varied British terrain, it pairs solid bone and deep lung capacity with smooth, ground-covering movement. Its short, dense, weatherproof coat lies flat over a muscular, unexaggerated body with a deep chest reaching below the elbows, well-sprung ribs, a level topline with a slight arch over the loin, and straight, well-boned legs. The head is cleanly modeled with a fairly broad skull tapering gently toward a rectangular muzzle, bright oval eyes whose shade harmonizes with the coat, and drop ears hanging close to the cheeks. Indoors, this outgoing hound is cheerful, gentle, and eager for companionship, though its nose quickly takes charge once outdoors.
overview.history: Harriers belong to England's long tradition of pack scenthounds, with historical accounts tracing the Penistone pack in Yorkshire to Sir Elias de Midhope around 1260. The name itself stems from the Norman word 'harier', referring to a hunting hound. Over the centuries, British breeders refined medium-sized packs capable of working hares and rabbits steadily across open country, followed either on foot or on horseback; during the nineteenth century, some lines were crossed with Foxhounds to add pace for mounted followers. British packs were historically maintained in working hunting studbooks rather than conformation rings, leaving the breed relatively uncommon in modern British show entries even as dedicated breeders in France, continental Europe, and North America—where the hound has been used since colonial times—preserved its athletic build and friendly temperament.
overview.originalPurpose: Hunting hare and rabbit in organized packs across varied countryside by scenting and trailing quarry with steady stamina.

grooming.brushing: Brush weekly with a soft-bristle brush or rubber hound glove to sweep away loose hair and keep the short coat glossy.
grooming.bathing: Bathe occasionally—roughly every six to eight weeks or after muddy field outings—using a gentle canine shampoo.
notes: The short, flat coat sheds dirt easily and needs no clipping or professional trimming.
Check and gently clean the pendant ears once a week to prevent wax, debris, or trapped moisture.
Inspect paws, pads, and ear edges after brushy trail walks for thorns, burrs, or small scrapes.
Trim nails regularly so they stay short and do not interfere with the hound's stride.
Brush teeth frequently with dog-safe enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate; bright, eager for food rewards, and good-humoured, yet independent enough to require calm, consistent leadership
tips: Lead with positive reinforcement, tasty treats, and upbeat praise rather than harsh corrections.
Keep obedience lessons brief, varied, and engaging so the hound stays focused.
Rely on a sturdy leash or a securely enclosed yard outdoors; an intriguing trail can override recall.
Build recall habits early on a long training line in low-distraction areas before progressing outdoors.
Introduce a reliable 'quiet' cue early to channel vocal hound habits.
Channel scenting instincts constructively through nosework and tracking exercises.
training.socialization: Begin gentle, positive exposure during puppyhood to varied people, friendly vaccinated dogs, everyday noises, and unfamiliar outdoor settings. Early, steady socialization reinforces the breed's naturally outgoing, confident disposition.

climates: Temperate climates
Cool climates, where the dense, weatherproof coat offers reliable field protection during active movement
Warm climates, provided shade, fresh water, indoor cooling, and early or late exercise scheduling are maintained
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; bred to live and work in company, this hound can grow bored and noisy if left isolated for long stretches.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced commercial dog food formulated for active medium-sized breeds, tailored to life stage and daily workload.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until about six months of age, then transitioning to two measured meals per day.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals per day to maintain steady energy and comfortable digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily calibrated for lower caloric burn while preserving lean muscle.

nutrition.guidelines: Weigh or measure every meal rather than free-feeding, since food-driven scenthounds gain excess weight easily. Keep the dog in lean, athletic condition with an easily felt ribcage and visible waist. Splitting the daily ration into two meals and allowing quiet rest before and after eating helps support digestive safety in deep-chested dogs.
considerations: Keep weight lean to protect hip joints and maintain field endurance.
Count training treats toward the total daily calorie allowance.
Avoid vigorous running right before or after meals as a precaution against bloat.
Skip rich, greasy table scraps that can upset digestion.
Keep cool, fresh water readily available during and after active outings.
Switch diets gradually over five to seven days to avoid stomach upset.
nutrition.note: Daily calorie needs shift considerably between active trail seasons and quieter periods. Consult a veterinarian for an individualized feeding plan.

health.overview: The Harrier is generally a sturdy, long-lived hound with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 15 years and no major conformational exaggerations. Responsible breeding prioritizes orthopedic screening for hip dysplasia and regular specialist eye examinations, while everyday preventive care focuses on drop-ear hygiene, weight management, and bloat-aware feeding habits.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — an inherited developmental looseness of the hip joint that can progress to arthritis; screened via pre-breeding radiographic hip evaluations
Hereditary eye disorders — conditions such as cataracts or progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) are monitored through periodic examinations by a veterinary ophthalmologist
Otitis externa (outer ear infections) — a conformational risk shared by drop-eared hounds, as folded ear flaps restrict airflow and retain moisture
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — a life-threatening stomach distension and twisting risk seen across deep-chested breeds, requiring emergency veterinary treatment
Minor outdoor field injuries — scratches, paw pad cuts, or ear-tip nicks picked up while moving through brambles and rough cover
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have completed radiographic hip evaluations and current specialist eye examinations.
Inspect and dry the drop ears weekly, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
Keep body weight lean and well-muscled to reduce stress on joints over a long lifespan.
Divide daily food into two measured meals and schedule calm rest around mealtime.
Maintain year-round veterinary parasite prevention against ticks, fleas, and heartworm.
Book routine annual veterinary checkups and keep core vaccinations up to date.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip evaluation prior to breeding
Periodic eye examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Routine veterinary wellness and cardiovascular checkups
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week using dog-safe enzymatic toothpaste, and pair home care with routine veterinary oral exams to keep gums and teeth healthy.
health.earCare: Lift and inspect the hanging ears weekly for odour, redness, wax buildup, or dampness after wet walks, wiping gently with a veterinarian-recommended cleanser.
health.skinCare: Run a brush through the short coat weekly to inspect the skin for ticks, scrapes, or irritation, checking the undercarriage and ear margins closely after woodland walks.

funFacts: The breed's name traces back to the Norman word 'harier', meaning a hunting hound, reflecting centuries of pack work across the English countryside.
One of England's earliest documented packs was the Penistone Harrier pack in Yorkshire, founded by Sir Elias de Midhope in 1260.
Because the Harrier stands neatly between the Beagle and the English Foxhound, fans have long nicknamed it a 'Beagle on stilts' or a scaled-down Foxhound.
Historically, Harrier packs were versatile enough to be followed either on foot or on horseback, and they have also been used in North America since colonial times.
A Harrier's carrying, musical bay helped hunters track the pack's path through valleys and hedgerows even when the hounds were out of sight.
Despite being one of Britain's oldest native hound breeds, Harriers remain uncommon in modern pet homes compared with Beagles.

faq.question: What kind of dog is a Harrier?
faq.answer: The Harrier is a medium-sized British scenthound originally developed to hunt hares and rabbits in packs. It is known for its smooth coat, athletic stamina, friendly pack nature, and carrying bay.

faq.question: How does a Harrier differ from a Beagle and an English Foxhound?
faq.answer: Size and pace set them apart: the Harrier sits directly between the smaller Beagle and the taller English Foxhound, combining the Beagle's approachable, friendly outlook with a longer-legged, faster frame.

faq.question: How tall and heavy does a Harrier get?
faq.answer: Adults typically stand 48 to 55 cm at the withers and weigh 20 to 27 kg in lean, athletic condition.

faq.question: What is the average lifespan of a Harrier?
faq.answer: A well-cared-for Harrier typically lives 12 to 15 years.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Harrier require?
faq.answer: Grooming is straightforward. The short, dense coat sheds moderately and needs only weekly brushing with a soft brush or hound glove, alongside weekly ear checks, regular nail trims, and frequent tooth brushing.

faq.question: Are Harriers suited to apartment living?
faq.answer: Usually not. Their high exercise requirements, strong scenting drive, and resonant baying voice make them much better suited to a house with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Do Harriers get along with children and other dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. Bred to work harmoniously in packs, Harriers are typically outgoing, patient, and gentle with children and very sociable with other dogs, though small pet animals like rabbits can trigger their chase instinct.

faq.question: How easy is it to train a Harrier?
faq.answer: Harriers are bright and motivated by food rewards, which helps with positive-reinforcement training, but their independent nose means recall outdoors can be unreliable once they catch an exciting scent.

faq.question: How much daily exercise does a Harrier need?
faq.answer: Plan on roughly 90 to 120 minutes of daily activity—and often over two hours for high-drive individuals—combining brisk leashed walks, secure yard time, and sniffing or tracking games.

faq.question: Which health screenings are recommended for Harriers?
faq.answer: Pre-breeding health screening focuses on radiographic hip evaluations and periodic examinations by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, complemented by routine veterinary wellness care.

overview.summary: A medium-sized native Japanese hunting Spitz renowned for its endurance, bold courage, acute judgment, deep family loyalty, and weatherproof double coat built for severe winter cold.
overview.description: The Hokkaido Ken is a sturdy, medium-sized Japanese Spitz-type dog with strongly marked sexual dimorphism, small forward-inclining prick ears, dark triangular eyes, a high-set curled or sickle tail, and a harsh straight outer coat over a dense, insulating undercoat. Slightly longer in body than tall in a 11:10 ratio, the breed combines tough, clean-cut muscling with light, resilient movement and remarkable stamina in mountainous, snowy terrain. Devoted and affectionate with its household—often following family members from room to room and greeting them with expressive vocalizations—it is naturally watchful, bold, and independent. Because of its strong hunting drive and potential reactivity toward unfamiliar dogs and small animals, it thrives with an experienced, active handler who provides early socialization, positive structure, and purposeful daily outlets.
overview.history: One of Japan's six native Spitz breeds, the Hokkaido traces its heritage to ancient indigenous dogs of the Japanese archipelago and to medium-sized hunting dogs that accompanied migrants from the Tohoku region of Honshu to the northern island of Hokkaido during the Kamakura era in the 1140s. For centuries, the indigenous Ainu people bred these courageous dogs—which they called Seta—to track and hold brown bear, deer, and other game in rugged forests and heavy snow. When British zoologist Thomas Blakiston studied Hokkaido's fauna in 1869, he referred to the dogs as 'Ainu Ken'. In 1902, dogs of the breed assisted in searching for survivors after an Imperial Japanese Army regiment was caught in a catastrophic blizzard crossing the Hakkōda Mountains. In 1937, Japan designated the breed a Living Natural Monument under the name of its northern home region, and dedicated preservation societies formed in the mid-twentieth century to safeguard its working instincts and traditional type. In 2007, a white Hokkaido portraying the talking patriarch 'Otōsan' in a long-running Japanese television commercial series brought renewed public attention to this rare breed.

exercise.level: High. Requires vigorous daily physical exercise combined with structured mental work—a working 'job'—to prevent boredom, anxiety, and destructive habits.
activities: Brisk daily walks and long hikes on secure trails
Agility, rally, obedience, and trick-dog training
Tracking, nosework, and scent-detection games
Supervised outdoor play in mud, snow, or shallow creeks
Problem-solving puzzle toys and interactive games

grooming.level: Low to moderate for most of the year; high daily maintenance for several weeks roughly twice a year when blowing the undercoat.
grooming.brushing: Brush weekly during normal periods to remove dead hair and debris; increase to thorough daily brushing for several weeks twice a year during seasonal coat blows.
grooming.bathing: Infrequent, only as needed; natural skin and coat oils repel water and dirt, and the coat has virtually no doggy odour when fed a sound diet.
notes: Unlike some other native Japanese breeds that avoid puddles, many Hokkaido dogs love splashing in creeks, mud, and snow, though dried dirt brushes or falls off easily once dry.
Never shave or clip the double coat; shaving permanently damages the guard hairs and does not keep the dog cooler in summer.
Expect a heavy twice-yearly seasonal shed ('coat blow') lasting several weeks when the entire dense undercoat is released.
Keep nails trimmed short—ideally rounded with a rotary nail grinder—so they do not click on hard flooring.
Inspect the ears, teeth, and skin beneath the dense undercoat during routine grooming.

training.difficulty: Challenging for novice handlers; highly intelligent and quick to learn, yet independent, strong-willed, and vocal when given repetitive or unconvincing cues.
tips: Build a cooperative bond through reward-based positive reinforcement, clear boundaries, and mutual respect rather than heavy-handed punishment.
Channel the breed's problem-solving intelligence by giving the dog a structured job such as agility, tracking, or trick training.
Keep the dog on leash or within a securely fenced area featuring at least a 6-foot (1.8 m) fence, as the breed has a strong prey drive and is an agile jumper and climber.
Be prepared for expressive vocalizations—including howling, 'singing' greetings, rooing, and grumbling protests—and teach calm indoor manners early.

Allow roughly nine months for full housebreaking, using crate training and scheduled potty breaks at least every four hours during puppyhood while avoiding harsh reactions that could trigger submissive urination.
Supervise play closely and keep socks, rocks, sticks, and small household objects out of reach, as pica (chewing and swallowing non-food items) occurs in the breed.
training.socialization: Begin structured, positive socialization early in puppyhood and maintain it throughout adulthood. Introduce unfamiliar people, sights, sounds, and calm, well-mannered dogs gradually. Because dog reactivity—especially between intact males—and strong small-animal prey drive are common, supervise inter-dog interactions carefully and never force greetings.

climates: Cold and snowy climates
Cool climates
Temperate climates
Warm climates only with strict heat precautions, air conditioning or cool tiled floors, shade, fresh water, and exercise restricted to cool hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Hokkaido dogs bond closely with their families, follow their owners from room to room, and want to participate in daily household life. Prolonged isolation or lack of stimulation frequently leads to separation anxiety, vocalizing, destructive chewing, pica, or compulsive water drinking.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced canine diet formulated for the dog's life stage, activity level, and health.
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a high-quality, nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age, weight, and working or exercise demands, adjusting portions to maintain a lean, muscular body condition. Work with a veterinarian or breeder to establish an appropriate puppy and adult feeding schedule. Keep fresh water available while monitoring for compulsive overdrinking in anxious or bored individuals.
considerations: Adjust calorie intake to match seasonal activity levels and keep the dog lean to reduce stress on hips, elbows, and patellas.
Limit treats and table scraps to prevent obesity.
Supervise feeding and play environments carefully because familial pica (ingesting rocks, socks, sticks, or toys) is documented in the breed.
Monitor water consumption; compulsive drinking of large volumes of water followed by regurgitation (psychogenic polydipsia) has been observed in under-stimulated or anxious dogs.
Consult a veterinarian before introducing supplements or specialized therapeutic diets.
nutrition.note: Authoritative breed references do not prescribe a fixed daily meal count for puppies, adults, or seniors; meal frequency and portion sizes should be planned with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Hokkaido Ken is generally a hardy, cold-adapted breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 15 years, but its small global gene pool makes pre-breeding health screening essential. The most prevalent scientifically established hereditary condition in the breed is Collie eye anomaly (CEA), an autosomal recessive developmental eye defect associated with a 7.8-kb deletion in the NHEJ1 gene. Genotyping surveys indicate that roughly one-third of tested Hokkaido dogs are genetically affected and two-thirds are carriers, although the defect is non-progressive after eight weeks of age and nearly 90% of genetically affected dogs exhibit no clinical vision loss or only mild choroidal hypoplasia. Conversely, genetic screening has shown that tested Hokkaido dogs do not carry the MDR1 (ABCB1) ivermectin-sensitivity mutation. Other documented concerns tracked by preservation and breed clubs include hip dysplasia, cardiac murmurs, patellar luxation, idiopathic seizures, and stress- or drive-related behavioral syndromes such as pica and psychogenic polydipsia.
commonConditions: Collie eye anomaly (CEA / NHEJ1-related choroidal hypoplasia), the most prevalent hereditary disorder in the breed (autosomal recessive 7.8-kb deletion in the NHEJ1 gene on chromosome 37, with genotyping studies reporting roughly one-third affected and two-thirds carriers, though ~90% of genetically affected dogs have normal functional vision or only mild non-progressive fundus changes)
Hip dysplasia, a multifactorial orthopedic malformation identified in North American and European dogs and targeted by mandatory pre-breeding radiographic screening
Heart murmurs and cardiac abnormalities (systolic, diastolic, or continuous murmurs graded I–VI), reported in Japanese and international lines and subject to mandatory pre-breeding cardiac evaluation
Idiopathic seizures (epilepsy of unknown cause), reported in some dogs in North America and overseas with typical onset between 6 months and 6 years of age
Additional orthopedic and ophthalmic screening targets: patellar luxation, elbow dysplasia, and progressive retinal atrophy (PRA)

Behavioral and ingestive conditions observed in the breed: familial pica (chewing and swallowing non-food items such as rocks, socks, and sticks, sometimes requiring emergency surgery), psychogenic polydipsia (compulsive water drinking followed by vomiting excess liquid), and separation anxiety
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have completed mandatory pre-breeding clearances for hips, cardiac health, ophthalmic examination, and the Collie eye anomaly (NHEJ1) DNA test.
Schedule veterinary ophthalmic examinations early in puppyhood and periodically throughout adulthood to evaluate ocular health.
Maintain a lean body weight and age-appropriate exercise routine to protect developing and adult joints.
Provide abundant daily physical exercise, mental enrichment, and companionship to reduce the risk of anxiety, psychogenic polydipsia, and destructive behaviour.
Keep floors and yards clear of swallowable objects (rocks, socks, stick fragments, small balls) and supervise chewing closely to prevent pica-related gastrointestinal obstructions.
Protect the dog from heat stress in warm weather by providing shade, cool indoor floors or air conditioning, and fresh water, and never shave the insulating double coat.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic screening at 12 months of age or older for preliminary evaluation or 24 months for final certification, or distraction-index evaluation)
Cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (at 12 months of age or older for breeding stock, plus puppy eye screening)
Collie Eye Anomaly (CEA) DNA test (NHEJ1 7.8-kb intronic deletion)
Optional additional clearances: patellar luxation evaluation, elbow dysplasia evaluation, thyroid evaluation, progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) DNA test, and degenerative myelopathy (DM) DNA test
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with dog-safe toothpaste and schedule routine veterinary dental examinations. The breed standard requires strong jaws with a complete, evenly spaced scissor bite.
health.earCare: Inspect the small, erect triangular ears weekly for debris, wax buildup, redness, or odour, and clean gently only when needed using a veterinarian-recommended ear cleaner.
health.skinCare: Part the dense undercoat regularly to check the skin for ticks, burrs, hot spots, or irritation, keep nails trimmed short with a grinder or clippers, and inspect the thick paw pads after hikes on rough or icy terrain.

idealFor: Experienced handlers who understand independent, strong-willed primitive and hunting Spitz breeds
Active individuals and families who enjoy daily hiking, trail exploring, tracking, agility, or trick training
Households where the dog is included indoors as a constant companion rather than left isolated for long workdays
Homes with a securely fenced yard (at least 6 feet / 1.8 m high) and cool or temperate weather
Owners prepared for expressive vocalizations ('singing', howling, rooing) and heavy twice-yearly coat blows
notIdealFor: First-time or passive dog owners seeking an effortlessly biddable, low-energy pet
Apartment dwellers or noise-sensitive households where loud vocal greetings and howling would cause conflict
Households that leave dogs alone for long hours each day
Multi-dog homes expecting automatic compatibility with unfamiliar dogs (especially intact males) or small pets
Owners in hot climates who cannot provide indoor cooling and careful heat management

funFacts: In 1902, Hokkaido dogs assisted search parties looking for survivors of an Imperial Japanese Army regiment stranded in a catastrophic blizzard in the Hakkōda Mountains.
The indigenous Ainu people of northern Japan called these dogs 'Seta' and relied on them to track and hold brown bears and deer in deep mountain snow.
British zoologist Thomas Blakiston coined the name 'Ainu Ken' in 1869 before the breed was designated a Living Natural Monument of Japan in 1937 and named after the island of Hokkaido.
Like several other native Japanese breeds, the Hokkaido frequently has blue-black spots or pigmentation on its tongue, which is explicitly permitted by the breed standard.
Unlike the fastidious Shiba Inu that often avoids puddles, many Hokkaido dogs love splashing in creeks, swimming, and rolling in mud, though dried mud falls quickly off their harsh guard coat.
Since 2007, a white Hokkaido portraying the talking family father 'Otōsan' in a famous Japanese mobile-phone commercial campaign has made the breed a household icon in Japan.

faq.question: What is a Hokkaido Ken?
faq.answer: The Hokkaido Ken (also called the Hokkaido Inu or Ainu Ken) is a medium-sized native Japanese Spitz breed historically developed on the northern island of Hokkaido to hunt bear and deer in snowy mountain terrain. Today it is kept primarily as a devoted household companion, watchdog, and outdoor sporting partner.

faq.question: How big does a Hokkaido Ken get?
faq.answer: It is a sturdy medium-sized dog, though height ranges differ slightly between standards. Japanese preservation and North American breed-club standards specify 48.5 cm ± 3 cm (45.5–51.5 cm, or 18–20 inches) for males and 45.5 cm ± 3 cm (42.5–48.5 cm, or 17–19 inches) for females, whereas international conformation standards list 48.5–51.5 cm for males and 45.5–48.5 cm for females. Typical adult weight is 20–30 kg (44–66 lbs), though some preservation lines weigh roughly 13.6–25 kg (30–55 lbs).

faq.question: How long does a Hokkaido Ken live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 12 to 15 years when supported by responsible genetic screening, a lean diet, and routine veterinary care.

faq.question: What is Collie eye anomaly (CEA) in the Hokkaido Ken?
faq.answer: Collie eye anomaly is an autosomal recessive developmental eye condition associated with a 7.8-kb deletion in the NHEJ1 gene. Genotyping studies in Hokkaido dogs have found that roughly one-third are genetically affected and two-thirds are carriers. However, the condition is non-progressive after eight weeks of age, and nearly 90% of genetically affected Hokkaido dogs show either no vision loss or only mild choroidal hypoplasia. Responsible breeders use DNA testing and ophthalmic exams to avoid producing clinically impaired puppies while preserving genetic diversity.

faq.question: Is the Hokkaido Ken good for first-time dog owners?
faq.answer: Generally no. While deeply loyal and intelligent, the Hokkaido has a bold, independent working character, a strong prey drive, expressive vocal habits, and a tendency toward dog reactivity (particularly in intact males). It does best with an experienced handler committed to early socialization and daily mental and physical engagement.

faq.question: Does the Hokkaido Ken get along with other dogs and pets?
faq.answer: Because of its hunting heritage, the breed has a strong prey drive toward small animals and can display dog aggression or selectivity, especially between intact males. Early, carefully managed socialization helps, but compatibility with unfamiliar dogs or small pets should never be assumed.

faq.question: Is the Hokkaido Ken a quiet breed or a vocal breed?
faq.answer: It is a very vocal, expressive breed. Hokkaido dogs are famous for bursting into loud, multi-minute 'songs' when their owners return home, rooing at visiting friends, and howling or grumbling in protest when given a cue they would rather ignore.

faq.question: How much grooming and shedding should owners expect?
faq.answer: Outside of shedding season, grooming is straightforward: weekly brushing keeps the weatherproof coat clean, and the breed has almost no doggy odour even when it swims or plays in mud. Roughly twice a year, however, the dog blows its entire dense undercoat over several weeks, requiring daily brushing. The double coat must never be shaved.

faq.question: What are pica and psychogenic polydipsia in Hokkaido dogs?
faq.answer: Pica—chewing and swallowing non-food items such as rocks, socks, sticks, or toys—appears to have a familial tendency in the breed and has caused veterinary emergencies in multiple dogs. Psychogenic polydipsia (compulsive drinking of large quantities of water followed by regurgitating the excess) has also been observed, often linked to high drive, boredom, or anxiety. Keeping non-edible objects out of reach and providing ample daily exercise and enrichment are essential precautions.

faq.question: Is the Hokkaido Ken suitable for apartments or hot climates?
faq.answer: Apartment living is generally unsuitable because the breed is vocal, energetic, and thrives with a securely fenced yard (at least 6 feet high). Because its thick double coat is built for subzero snow, living in a hot climate requires indoor air conditioning or cool tiled floors, shade, plenty of water, and restricting outdoor exercise to the coolest hours of the day.
