overview.summary: A powerful, medium-to-large German working and estate-guarding breed with a long, slightly wavy weather-resistant coat in black and gold, black, or blond, prized for its even nerve, fine scenting ability, defensive watchfulness, and deep family devotion.
overview.description: The Hovawart is a powerful, medium-to-large long-haired working dog built on a slightly rectangular frame whose body length exceeds withers height by 10 to 15 percent. Marked sexual dimorphism distinguishes the broader-headed, more substantial male from the finer female. Developed to watch over German farmsteads and estates rather than herd stock, the breed combines an even-tempered, stress-resistant disposition with self-confidence, defensive watchfulness, and an exceptional sense of smell. Its dense, close-lying, slightly wavy coat—occurring in black and gold (black and tan), solid black, or medium blond, with all three colours able to appear in the same litter—has relatively sparse undercoat and longer feathering on the neck, chest, backs of the limbs, and bushy tail. Slow to mature and retaining playful puppy energy until at least two years of age, a Hovawart forms an intense bond with its family and must live indoors as part of the household rather than in a kennel, thriving when given patient, reward-based leadership and purposeful scent, tracking, rescue, or dog-sport work.
overview.history: The name Hovawart derives from the Middle High German words Hova (Hof, meaning yard, farm, or estate) and wart (Wächter, meaning watchman or guardian), a term recorded in medieval German law codes and chronicles for dogs that defended homesteads, castles, and livestock. By the early twentieth century, this traditional farm guardian survived only as scattered regional working dogs. Beginning in 1922 in Thale in the Harz Mountains, zoologist Kurt König—who founded the Hovawart-Verein für Deutsche Schutzhunde in January 1924—set out to reconstruct a thoughtful, naturally defensive estate guardian without predatory drive toward domestic stock. While older accounts listed outcrosses to German Shepherd Dogs, Newfoundlands, Leonbergers, and Kuvaszok, archival studbook research by Dr. Jens Kerl demonstrated that pre-war Kuvasz crosses were lost during the First World War and that all modern Hovawarts descend from the 1932 black-and-gold prototype sire Castor Meyer-Busch, whose pedigree combined roughly 65 percent regional farm dogs (Typenhunde from the Harz and Odenwald), 20.2 percent early German Shepherd Dogs, and 14.8 percent Newfoundland (through the von Qualitz litter brothers Barry Busch and Bob Busch). Officially recognised in Germany in 1936–1937, the breed suffered heavy losses during the Second World War before enthusiasts reorganised breeding in 1947, leading to definitive international recognition in November 1955 and German working-dog status in 1964. Systematic breeding selection for hip health since the 1960s has reduced hip dysplasia incidence to under 5 percent.
overview.originalPurpose: Guarding German farmsteads, estates, castles, and livestock independently through calm, defensive vigilance rather than herding.
currentRoles: Devoted family companion and defensive home or estate guardian
Search-and-rescue, mantrailing, and disaster-recovery dog
Tracking, scent-work, and working-trial competitor
Obedience, rally, agility, hoopers, canicross, and flyball partner
Therapy and service dog when appropriately selected and trained

physical.coatType: Long, thick, slightly wavy, close-lying weather-resistant coat with sparse undercoat; short on the head and fronts of the limbs, with longer feathering on the front of the neck, chest, belly, backs of the forelegs, backs of the thighs, and underside of the tail.
physical.coatLength: Medium to long over the body and tail, with short hair on the skull, muzzle, and fronts of both forelegs and hindlegs.
coatColors: Black and gold (black and tan / schwarzmarken): shiny black coat with clearly outlined medium-blond markings below the nasal bridge around the mouth corners into the throat, distinct points above the eyes, two adjacent or joined chest patches, and markings on the lower forelegs, hindlegs, and beneath the tail root
Black (schwarz): shiny deep black coat with black pigment on eyelids, lips, paw pads, and nails

Blond (blonde): shiny medium-blond coat that lightens toward the legs and belly, with black or dark pigment on eyelids, lips, and pads (seasonal snow nose is permissible; across all three colours, a few small white chest spots under 8 cm and single white hairs on the toes and tail tip are tolerated)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate overall because the undercoat is sparse compared with heavy double-coated mountain breeds, with heavier seasonal shedding when the coat changes.
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tightly fitting lips prevent heavy drooling.
distinctiveFeatures: Powerful, medium-to-large slightly rectangular body in which body length equals 110% to 115% of height at the withers (ratios under 100% or over 120% are disqualifying faults)
Pronounced sexual dimorphism in both head shape and body substance between males (63–70 cm, 30–40 kg) and females (58–65 cm, 25–35 kg)
Strong, clean head with a broad, arched forehead, a well-defined stop, and a straight muzzle equal in length to the skull (1:1 ratio) with parallel cranio-facial planes and tight lips
Complete 42-tooth dentition meeting in a strong scissor bite with teeth set vertically in the jaw (pincer bite is tolerated)
Medium-to-large triangular hanging ears set high so they visually broaden the skull, with gently rounded tips reaching the corner of the mouth and carried slightly forward when alert
Oval, medium-to-dark brown eyes with close-fitting eyelids conveying a calm, composed, and intelligent expression
Tightly fitting skin that shows a bluish shimmer in black-and-gold and black dogs and a pinkish shimmer in blond dogs
Bushy tail reaching below the hock joint without touching the ground, hanging low at rest and raised curved over the back when alert or moving

traits: Good-natured, even-tempered, and stress-resistant
Deeply devoted and loyal to its household ('pack')
Self-confident, courageous, and alert without nervousness
Defensive rather than aggressive guardian that assesses situations independently
Exceptional olfactory ability suited to tracking, mantrailing, and search-and-rescue
Slow-maturing, retaining lively puppy playfulness until at least two years of age
Reserved and discerning toward unfamiliar people until welcomed by the owner
Sensitive to handler trust; resists harsh compulsion and responds best to calm, consistent leadership

exercise.level: High. Requires substantial daily physical activity—typically at least one long walk of an hour or more plus several shorter outings, totalling two hours or more for mature adults—combined with nose-led mental work.
activities: Long daily countryside walks, woodland hikes, or canicross (once skeletally mature) totaling two hours or more per day for adults
Tracking, mantrailing, scent discrimination, and search-and-rescue exercises that harness the breed's keen nose
Working trials, reward-based obedience, rally, hoopers, and agility after joint growth plates close
Supervised free running and exploration in a large, securely fenced garden or paddock
Interactive problem-solving games and durable food puzzles (noting that some dogs prefer vigorous physical shaking over delicate pawing)
Carefully supervised play with compatible, resilient dogs, managing adolescent 'zoomies' and exuberant play styles

grooming.level: Moderate; the close-lying coat has sparse undercoat and does not mat easily overall, but feathered zones require thorough weekly combing.
grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly down to the skin two to three times per week using a long-pinned slicker brush and a rotating-tooth metal comb, paying close attention to mat-prone feathering behind the ears, around the elbows, and down the backs of the hindlegs.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when dirty using a mild, dog-safe shampoo, and dry wet coats and muddy paws thoroughly after winter or wet-weather walks.
notes: Accustom puppies from an early age to all-over handling, brushing, paw drying, ear inspection, and tooth cleaning before they grow into strong adolescents.
Inspect the ears and interdigital paw spaces after woodland or field walks for grass awns (seeds), burrs, ticks, or cuts.
Trim excess hair around the feet and beneath the ears if desired to reduce mud tracking and prevent grass seeds from lodging.
Keep the strong, fast-growing nails trimmed regularly with large nail clippers or a grinder to prevent splitting or splaying.
Never shave or clip the weather-resistant coat close to the skin unless medically required by a veterinarian.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging for novice handlers. Intelligent and versatile, yet strong-willed, slow to mature (taking about two years), and bred to make independent defensive decisions if left without clear direction.
tips: Build a relationship grounded in mutual trust, calm consistency, and positive reinforcement; harsh or confrontational methods undermine trust and provoke resistance.
Guide the dog's innate guarding instinct through structured exposure so it looks to the handler to decide how to respond to visitors rather than making autonomous guarding decisions.
Always greet guests at the door yourself rather than allowing visitors to walk in unannounced and surprise the dog.
Account for training treats within the daily food ration so reward-heavy training does not lead to excess weight.
Take young puppies to the veterinary clinic weekly for friendly weigh-ins and treats so adult veterinary examinations remain calm and stress-free.
Restrict high-impact jumping, repetitive stairs, and uncontrolled high-speed 'zoomies' during the first 18–24 months while bones and joints are maturing.
training.socialization: Begin broad, positive socialisation in puppyhood and continue throughout the two-year maturation period. Expose the young dog to varied people, household visitors, traffic, sounds, veterinary handling, and polite dogs. Because Hovawarts play exuberantly and can be wilful or dominant toward unfamiliar dogs of the same sex, supervise canine interactions closely.

climates: Cool, wet, and snowy temperate or continental climates (for which the all-weather coat is naturally suited)
Warm weather when provided with ample shade, cool indoor resting areas, fresh water, and exercise scheduled during cooler morning and evening hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate. Deeply attached to its family, the Hovawart must live indoors with its household and is completely unsuited to permanent kennel life, though a well-integrated adult can tolerate occasional short periods alone once exercised.

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced large-breed diet matched to the dog's life stage, growth rate, workload, and veterinary needs.

feedingFrequency.adult: Feed measured portions on a consistent daily schedule—typically divided into two smaller meals for adults—adjusted for workload, body condition, and training-treat intake.

nutrition.guidelines: Provide a high-quality, nutritionally complete large-breed ration in measured portions. Because Hovawart puppies grow rapidly and in uneven growth spurts, monitor body condition closely and adjust intake with veterinary guidance so the developing skeleton is not overloaded by excess weight. Deduct training treats from the daily calorie allowance, allow rest before and after meals to help reduce bloat risk, and keep clean water available at all times.
considerations: Adjust puppy rations carefully during growth spurts to maintain a lean, steady growth curve and protect developing hips and joints.
Do not add supplemental calcium, phosphorus, or vitamins to a balanced diet unless prescribed by a veterinarian.
Deduct training rewards from the daily meal portion, as training a working breed requires frequent food reinforcement.
Divide daily rations into smaller meals and avoid strenuous exercise immediately before or after eating to reduce the risk of gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV).
Monitor weight and thyroid health in adulthood, as unexplained weight gain despite a normal appetite can be an early sign of hypothyroidism.
nutrition.note: Specific numerical meal counts for puppies and seniors are not separately fixed; work with a veterinarian or breeder to set life-stage feeding frequency and portion sizes.

health.overview: With a typical lifespan of 10 to 14 years, the Hovawart is one of the healthier large working breeds, largely thanks to mandatory pre-breeding hip evaluations begun in the 1960s that have reduced hip dysplasia incidence to under 5 percent in screened populations (with a UK five-year median hip score of 8–9 out of 106). Primary hereditary and clinical health priorities focus on three areas covered by pre-breeding screening: autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis leading to hypothyroidism (shown in a pedigree study of 4,953 Finnish Hovawarts to have a moderate-to-high heritability of 0.47–0.62, and detected at 13 percent prevalence in a Swedish serological survey), degenerative myelopathy (a late-onset progressive spinal cord neuropathy associated with homozygosity for the SOD1:c.118G>A mutation, confirmed neuropathologically in affected Hovawarts aged 9–12 years), and hip dysplasia. As a large, deep-chested breed, the Hovawart is also at risk for acute gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
commonConditions: Autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis and hypothyroidism — the most common hereditary endocrine disorder in the breed (estimated heritability h² = 0.47–0.62 in a cohort of 4,953 dogs), typically presenting after 2 to 4 years of age with lethargy, weight gain without increased appetite, cold intolerance, dry skin, symmetrical trunk or 'rat-tail' hair loss, slow heart rate, or behavioural changes

Degenerative myelopathy (DM) — adult-onset (typically 9 to 12 years of age) painless, progressive degeneration of thoracic spinal cord pathways associated with homozygosity for the SOD1:c.118G>A (p.E40K) mutation, causing hindlimb wobble and ataxia that progress to paraparesis
Hip dysplasia — developmental coxofemoral joint laxity and osteoarthritis; kept below 5% in screened populations through decades of mandatory radiographic selection
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — life-threatening emergency in which the stomach fills with gas and twists on its axis, requiring immediate veterinary surgery
preventiveCare: Select puppies only from breeding parents that hold documented hip clearances, current full thyroid panels (including thyroglobulin autoantibodies), ophthalmic clearances, and SOD1 degenerative myelopathy DNA test results.
Plan matings using SOD1 DNA results so that two carriers or at-risk dogs are never bred together, preventing offspring homozygous for the mutated allele while preserving genetic diversity.

Monitor adult dogs from 2 years of age onward for subtle signs of hypothyroidism—such as unexplained weight gain, coat thinning on the tail or trunk, lethargy, or uncharacteristic anxiety or aggression—and request a full thyroid profile if signs appear.
Keep growing puppies lean, limit repetitive high-impact exercise until skeletal maturity at around 2 years of age, and maintain athletic body condition throughout life.
Learn the emergency warning signs of bloat (unproductive retching, distended abdomen, restlessness, collapse) and seek immediate emergency veterinary care if suspected.
Inspect ears, paws, skin, and teeth weekly, and avoid giving hard weight-bearing marrow bones that can slab-fracture canine or carnassial teeth.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding (such as national scoring schemes requiring an individual score of 20 or less and a combined parent score of 25 or less on a 0–106 scale, or a grade of Good or Excellent at 24 months of age or older)

Comprehensive pre-breeding thyroid blood panel—including Total T4, Free T4, canine thyroid-stimulating hormone (cTSH), and thyroglobulin autoantibodies (TgAA)—performed within 2 years prior to mating (tested midway between seasons in females and at least 30 to 45 days after any vaccination)
Degenerative myelopathy (SOD1:c.118G>A) DNA test prior to breeding so matings never produce homozygous at-risk (DM/DM) puppies
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist within 12 months prior to breeding
Formal breed temperament and conformation evaluation at 20 months of age or older prior to breeding
health.dentalCare: Brush the 42-tooth scissor bite regularly—ideally daily—beginning in puppyhood, inspect the mouth periodically for fractured teeth or hidden root abscesses (which can cause unexplained weight loss or subdued behaviour), and schedule veterinary dental checks as needed.
health.earCare: Inspect the high-set triangular drop ears weekly and after countryside walks for grass seeds, wax buildup, redness, or odour; chronic or recurrent ear infections should also prompt a veterinary check of thyroid function.
health.skinCare: Part the long, slightly wavy coat during brushing to check the skin (which naturally has a bluish shimmer in black and black-and-gold dogs and a pinkish shimmer in blond dogs) for ticks, grass awns, cuts, or dry patches, and dry the coat and feet thoroughly after wet walks.

idealFor: Experienced, active handlers who want a devoted working partner for tracking, mantrailing, search-and-rescue, working trials, obedience, or agility
Households with a spacious, securely fenced garden or rural access that include the dog indoors as a full family member
Owners who understand defensive guardian instincts and provide calm, consistent, reward-based leadership
People prepared to commit two hours or more per day to walking, training, and scent-based mental enrichment
notIdealFor: First-time dog owners unprepared for a strong, 25–40 kg slow-maturing guardian breed with independent judgement
Apartment dwellers or homes without adequate outdoor space and secure fencing
Anyone intending to keep a dog in an outdoor kennel or use it as an isolated, aggressive 'junkyard' guard dog
Households where visitors frequently walk in unannounced without the owner managing introductions at the door
Handlers who use harsh, confrontational, or physical punishment

funFacts: The name Hovawart comes directly from Middle High German: Hova (Hof, meaning farmstead, yard, or estate) and wart (Wächter, meaning watchman or guardian).
All three coat colours—black and gold, solid black, and blond—can be born in the very same litter, depending on the recessive alleles carried by the parents.
Beneath the coat, the skin itself differs by colour variety: black-and-gold and black Hovawarts have skin with a distinct bluish shimmer, whereas blond Hovawarts have skin with a pinkish shimmer.

Archival studbook research presented for the breed's centenary showed that every modern Hovawart traces back to a single black-and-gold male registered in 1932 named Castor Meyer-Busch, whose genetic makeup was roughly 65% regional German farm dogs (Typenhunde), 20.2% early German Shepherd Dog, and 14.8% Newfoundland.
Thanks to mandatory pre-breeding hip-dysplasia selection introduced in the 1960s, the Hovawart has achieved a hip dysplasia rate below 5%—one of the lowest among large working breeds.
Hovawarts are famous for taking at least two full years to mature, retaining their exuberant puppy playfulness and fondness for high-speed 'zoomies' well into young adulthood.

faq.question: Is the Hovawart suitable for a first-time dog owner?
faq.answer: Usually not. Because the Hovawart is a large, strong-willed, slow-maturing working dog with natural defensive guarding instincts and independent decision-making, it requires an owner who can provide calm, consistent leadership, early socialisation, and at least two hours of daily physical and mental activity.

faq.question: How big does a fully grown Hovawart get?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 63–70 cm (25–27.5 in) at the withers and typically weigh 30–40 kg (66–88 lb), while females stand 58–65 cm (23–25.5 in) and weigh 25–35 kg (55–77 lb), with some large North American males reaching 28 inches and 90–100 pounds. Males and females show a clear difference in head breadth and body substance.

faq.question: What coat colours occur in the Hovawart, and can they appear in one litter?
faq.answer: The three recognised colours are black and gold (shiny black with clearly defined medium-blond markings on the head, chest, legs, and under the tail), solid black, and medium blond (which pales softly toward the legs and belly). All three colours can be born in the same litter depending on the parents' genetics.

faq.question: How much daily exercise and mental stimulation does a Hovawart need?
faq.answer: A mature, healthy adult needs around two hours or more of daily exercise—such as a brisk walk or hike of at least an hour plus several shorter walks—combined with nose-led mental work like tracking, mantrailing, scent games, or obedience. Growing puppies require controlled, age-appropriate exercise to protect their developing joints.

faq.question: How does a Hovawart's guarding instinct work?
faq.answer: The breed was selected to guard homesteads and families from a calm, defensive posture rather than through unprovoked aggression. However, if an owner does not provide clear direction and socialisation, a Hovawart will assess situations on its own. Owners should socialise puppies thoroughly and always greet visitors at the door themselves.

faq.question: What health screenings should I ask a Hovawart breeder to provide?
faq.answer: Ask for written proof of pre-breeding hip scores (confirming low hip-dysplasia risk), a comprehensive thyroid blood panel (including Total T4, Free T4, cTSH, and TgAA autoantibodies tested within two years of mating), a degenerative myelopathy (SOD1) DNA test result ensuring no puppies are homozygous at-risk, a current veterinary ophthalmologist eye certificate, and a passed adult temperament evaluation.

faq.question: Is a Hovawart good with children and other dogs?
faq.answer: When raised in the family and properly socialised, a Hovawart is affectionate, loyal, and tolerant with its household's children, though adults must always supervise interactions because an exuberant 30–40 kg dog can accidentally knock over a small child. With other dogs, Hovawarts play very boisterously and can be wilful or dominant toward same-sex dogs if not well socialised.

overview.summary: A swift, deer-like rabbit hunter from Spain's Balearic Islands, instantly recognized by its tall, mobile ears, lean athletic frame, and remarkable standing-jump agility.
overview.description: Sleek yet muscular, the Ibizan Hound pairs a finely chiseled head and clear amber eyes with long limbs and large, stiffly upright ears that swivel toward every sound. Its slightly rectangular frame carries a deep chest and comes in two hard-textured coat varieties—smooth or wire-haired—in shades of white, red, or both combined. Affectionate and playful with its household yet often politely aloof with newcomers, this agile hunter combines sight, scent, and hearing to pursue fast-moving quarry, making high, secure fencing and dedicated recall training essential.
overview.history: Shaped over generations in Spain's Balearic Islands—especially Ibiza, Formentera, Mallorca, and Menorca—the breed is known locally as Podenco Ibicenco or Ca Eivissec. Island hunters relied on its speed, endurance, and extraordinary leaping ability to flush and catch rabbits across rocky, scrub-covered hillsides. While its silhouette echoes ancient Mediterranean hunting dogs, documented breed lineage centers on its sustained island development.

faq.question: What was the Ibizan Hound bred to do?
faq.answer: It was developed on Spain's Balearic Islands to hunt rabbits across rocky terrain using sight, scent, and hearing.

faq.question: How tall is an Ibizan Hound?
faq.answer: Males typically stand 23–27 inches at the withers and females 22–26 inches, though published ranges can vary slightly by region.

faq.question: How much does an Ibizan Hound weigh?
faq.answer: Adult males typically weigh 46–55 pounds and females 40–50 pounds, depending on individual build and body condition.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Ibizan Hound need?
faq.answer: Adult Ibizan Hounds generally need more than two hours of daily exercise and safe running opportunities, adjusted for age, health, and fitness.

faq.question: Does an Ibizan Hound need much grooming?
faq.answer: Smooth coats usually need only weekly brushing, while wire-haired coats benefit from extra combing to clear loose hair and field debris.

faq.question: Can an Ibizan Hound go off leash?
faq.answer: Its strong instinct to chase moving animals means off-leash running is safest inside tall, securely fenced enclosures.

faq.question: Which health tests should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for documented hip, eye, BAER hearing, autoimmune thyroiditis, and cardiac evaluations, reviewing any results with your veterinarian.

overview.summary: The Icelandic Sheepdog, celebrated as Iceland's native canine, is an agile Nordic spitz renowned for its cheerful demeanor, erect ears, and bushy tail curled over the spine. Developed to herd livestock across volcanic pastures, this devoted, vocal companion combines working grit with a gentle, people-focused household spirit.
overview.description: Slightly below medium stature, the Icelandic Sheepdog presents a sturdy rectangular frame clothed in a weather-resistant double coat with erect, highly mobile ears and a curled tail. The breed occurs in distinct short-haired and long-haired coat varieties, both bearing an insulating undercoat that easily deflects subarctic rain, wind, and snow. A cheerful, curious expression reflects its cooperative nature and keen sensory awareness. Historically trusted by Icelandic farmers to round up scattered sheep, cattle, and horses, it works with nimble agility and a melodious voice that guides stock through rugged volcanic terrain. In domestic settings, it forms devoted attachments to family members of all ages, greeting visitors with inquisitive enthusiasm. Because of its keen alert reflex and vocal working heritage, early guidance and structured daily activities are recommended to channel its natural energy.
overview.history: Arriving with Norse Viking settlers between AD 870 and 930, the ancestors of the Icelandic Sheepdog adapted over a millennium of geographical isolation to Iceland's unforgiving climate and rural farming practices. Developing as an indispensable pastoral worker, the dog tracked stray livestock across lava fields and sounded alarms to deter predatory birds from young lambs. Epidemics and natural disasters decimated the population in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, prompting rigorous preservation programs by Icelandic and international breeders to secure the breed's genetic foundation. Recognized worldwide as a cherished Nordic herding spitz, the breed continues to serve as an enduring symbol of Iceland's agricultural heritage.

funFacts: The Icelandic Sheepdog is recognised as Iceland's native dog breed.
Its ancestors are associated with dogs brought to Iceland by Norse settlers around AD 870–930.
The breed's traditional work included gathering and driving livestock on farms.

faq.question: Is the Icelandic Sheepdog a herding dog?
faq.answer: Yes. It developed as a farm herding dog in Iceland and was used to gather and move sheep and other livestock.

faq.question: How much exercise does an Icelandic Sheepdog need?
faq.answer: It generally needs daily walks, play and mental activity. The suggested 45–90 minutes per day in this record is a practical estimate, not an official requirement; needs vary with age, health and individual energy.

faq.question: Does the Icelandic Sheepdog bark a lot?
faq.answer: It is a naturally vocal breed and may bark to alert its household or during activity. Training, enrichment and rewarding calm behaviour can help manage unnecessary barking.

faq.question: Does it shed?
faq.answer: Yes. Its thick double coat sheds, with heavier seasonal shedding. Regular brushing helps remove loose hair and keep the coat in good condition.

faq.question: What colours can an Icelandic Sheepdog have?
faq.answer: The main colours include fawn, red, grey-shaded, chocolate brown and black. White markings accompany the main colour, and some coat patterns include coloured patches on a white background.

faq.question: What health checks should I ask a breeder about?
faq.answer: Ask for verifiable hip and eye screening results for the parents. A veterinarian can explain the results and advise which checks are appropriate for an individual dog.

faq.question: Is an Icelandic Sheepdog suitable for every apartment?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Suitability depends on the individual dog, daily activity, barking management, training and how long it would be left alone. The available sources do not establish a universal apartment-suitability answer.

overview.summary: The tallest of all spaniels, this rugged Irish water retriever stands out for its crisply curled purplish-liver waterproof coat, loose curly topknot, smooth tapering rat tail, and playful, devoted personality.
overview.description: The Irish Water Spaniel is a smart, upstanding, strongly built sporting dog with a slightly rectangular, barrel-chested frame engineered for swimming and retrieving in cold marshes. Its dense, naturally water-repellent liver coat forms tight, crisp ringlets across the neck, body, and legs, set off by a smooth short-haired face, a smooth V-shaped patch on the throat, a signature topknot of long loose curls peaking between the eyes, and a distinctive smooth-tipped rat tail. Large, well-haired, slightly spreading feet and powerful hindquarters drive a free, ground-covering stride with a mild rolling motion. Brave and tireless in the field, it brings an inquisitive, humorous, and affectionate nature into active family homes while remaining calmly discerning with strangers.
overview.history: Curly-coated, rat-tailed water dogs worked along southern Ireland's waterways by at least the late Middle Ages, with early mentions in Renaissance texts and historical names including Shannon Spaniel, Rat-Tail Spaniel, and Whip-Tail Spaniel. Although exact ancient ancestry was never formally recorded, modern standardization took shape in the 1830s through Dublin breeder Justin McCarthy and his influential foundation dog, Boatswain (born 1834). Recognized early in both Britain and North America during the late nineteenth century, the breed remains numerically rare today while continuing to shine as a versatile waterfowl retriever and spirited family companion.
overview.originalPurpose: Retrieving waterfowl and upland game birds across cold Irish marshes, estuaries, and rivers, and working in all types of shooting terrain.
currentRoles: Waterfowl and upland game retriever
Competitor in agility, dock diving, rally, tracking, flyball, and hunt tests
Loyal, playful companion for active outdoor households
Therapy and assistance partner suited to sensitive, people-focused temperaments

physical.coatType: Naturally water-repellent coat of dense, tight, crisp curls across the body, neck, and tail base, contrasted with short, smooth hair on the face, throat V-patch, front of the hind legs below the hocks, and tapering lower tail; crowned by a topknot of long, loose curls and long curled ear furnishings.
coatColors: Rich liver to dark liver with a purplish tinge (puce-liver), free of white markings aside from natural graying with age
physical.sheddingLevel: Low; the dense curly coat sheds very little and is often tolerated by allergy-sensitive owners, though dead hair must be brushed out weekly to prevent mats.
physical.droolingLevel: Low; fine, tight, dry lips keep drooling minimal.
distinctiveFeatures: Tallest of all spaniel breeds, strongly boned and slightly rectangular with a barrel-shaped rib cage and deep brisket reaching the elbows
Height at the withers of 53 to 59 cm for males and 51 to 56 cm for females, with adult working weights of 55 to 68 pounds for males and 45 to 58 pounds for females
Unmistakable rat tail set low and carried level with the back—thick and covered in short curls for the first 2 to 3 inches, then abruptly smooth and tapering to a fine point
High-domed skull crowned by a topknot of long, loose curls falling in a distinct peak between the eyes
Short, smooth facial coat accented by a curly beard at the back of the lower jaw and a smooth V-shaped patch on the throat
Rich puce-liver coat of tight, crisp, naturally water-repellent curls across the body and legs, with smooth hair on the front of the hind legs below the hocks
Strong underjaw with even white teeth closing in a scissor or level bite and a large dark liver nose
Comparatively small, almond-shaped eyes in medium-to-dark brown or dark amber (never yellow), framed by tight lids
Long, low-set lobular ears hanging close to the head and covered in abundant loose curls
Large, round, somewhat spreading, well-haired feet with thick pads and strong hindquarters driving a characteristic rolling gait

traits: Playful, humorous, and affectionately devoted to its family
Hardworking, brave, and eager in water and field work
Alert, inquisitive, and sharply intelligent
Eager to please once it clearly understands what is asked
Stable and discerning, often reserved with unfamiliar strangers without shyness or aggression
High-energy outdoors yet capable of settling calmly indoors after proper exercise
Sensitive to tone, responding far better to upbeat encouragement than harshness
Passionate natural swimmer with strong retrieving drive

exercise.level: High; an athletic, high-energy sporting retriever that needs substantial daily physical and mental activity to stay calm indoors.
activities: Long daily walks, trail hikes, and brisk jogging or safe bike runs
Swimming and water retrieving sessions
Backyard fetch and supervised play with other dogs
Dog sports such as agility, dock diving, rally, tracking, and flyball

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly at least once a week from puppyhood onward to clear loose hair and prevent matting in the dense curls, ears, and leg feathering.
grooming.bathing: Bathe as needed using a mild canine shampoo that respects the coat's natural water-repellent oils, allowing curls to dry naturally.
notes: Trim and shape the coat with scissors roughly every two months to keep it neat without obscuring the natural curl texture.
Start positive grooming habits early in puppyhood so brushing, nail trims, and ear checks stay stress-free.
Check and clean the long, curl-covered drop ears regularly—especially after swimming—to prevent moisture buildup.
Trim nails routinely and brush teeth regularly.

training.difficulty: Moderate; bright, reliable, and eager to please when sessions stay fun and varied, yet quick to bore under repetitive or heavy-handed drills.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based training and keep sessions interesting to prevent boredom.
Never use harsh or heavy-handed corrections, which backfire with this sensitive breed.
Give the dog a purposeful outlet through retrieving games, tracking, rally, agility, or dock diving.
Begin recall and polite greeting training early in puppyhood.
training.socialization: Introduce puppies early and gently to varied people, friendly dogs, everyday sights, and water environments so natural reserve around strangers matures into steady, polite confidence.

climates: Cool, wet, and temperate climates suited to its water-repellent curly coat
Warm climates, provided shade, fresh water, indoor cooling, and cooler-hour exercise are available
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply people-oriented and happiest when included in daily family activities.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced commercial or veterinarian-approved home-prepared diet matched to life stage (puppy, adult, or senior) and activity level.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily during early growth, transitioning to two meals daily on a balanced growth diet.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain active sporting energy and steady digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adjusted for lower activity and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal and monitor body condition closely, as some Irish Water Spaniels gain weight readily when overfed or given too many training treats. Divide daily food into two meals, keep clean fresh water available continuously, and consult a veterinarian on portion adjustments during heavy exercise or hunting seasons.
considerations: Watch calorie intake and budget training treats within the daily ration to avoid obesity.
Avoid high-fat table scraps and foods unsafe for dogs.
Allow rest around meals to support digestive comfort in deep-chested sporting dogs.
Transition gradually over five to seven days when changing foods.
nutrition.note: Caloric demands rise during active swimming or field work; verify exact portions with a veterinarian.

health.overview: Most Irish Water Spaniels are hardy, athletic dogs with a typical lifespan of 12 to 13 years, though owners and veterinarians must be alert to documented breed sensitivities to sulfa antibiotics (sulfonamides) and ivermectin, which can cause serious or fatal reactions. Responsible breeding programs prioritize pre-breeding screening for hip and elbow dysplasia, eye disease, thyroid function, and cardiac health, alongside diligent ear care for swimming dogs.
commonConditions: Medication sensitivities (sulfa antibiotics and ivermectin) — documented adverse and potentially fatal drug reactions in the breed; owners should ensure veterinary records carry a prominent warning
Hip and elbow dysplasia — developmental joint conditions monitored through pre-breeding radiographic evaluations
Thyroid disease (hypothyroidism) — endocrine concern monitored via pre-breeding thyroid screening
Ocular conditions — potential cataracts or eyelid issues (such as entropion or distichiasis) monitored through specialist veterinary ophthalmologist exams
Chronic ear infections (otitis externa) — common care risk in long, curl-covered drop ears exposed to frequent swimming without thorough drying
Allergies and skin/coat concerns — occasional reports of food or environmental allergies and follicular hair thinning
preventiveCare: Flag sulfa-antibiotic and ivermectin sensitivities clearly on your dog's veterinary chart before any medication is prescribed.
Ask breeders for published pre-breeding test results covering hips, elbows, eyes, thyroid, and heart.
Inspect and dry the long curl-covered drop ears thoroughly after every swim or bath.
Keep body weight lean to protect hip and elbow joints.
Maintain annual veterinary wellness checks, dental care, vaccinations, and year-round parasite prevention using breed-safe products.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow evaluation prior to breeding
Veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination prior to breeding
Thyroid panel evaluation prior to breeding
Cardiac evaluation prior to breeding
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with canine toothpaste and have a veterinarian inspect the scissor or level bite during routine wellness exams.
health.earCare: Check and gently clean the long, curl-covered drop ears regularly—especially after swimming—keeping canals dry to discourage infections.
health.skinCare: Part the dense curls during weekly brushing to check for burrs, ticks, mats, or irritation while preserving natural water-repellent oils.

idealFor: Active outdoor owners, swimmers, and hunters who enjoy vigorous daily exercise
Families with respectful children seeking a playful, loyal, low-shedding companion
Handlers interested in agility, dock diving, rally, tracking, flyball, or therapy work
Owners committed to weekly brushing, bimonthly trims, and post-swim ear care
notIdealFor: Sedentary households wanting a low-energy indoor companion
Apartments without convenient access to ample daily exercise and outdoor space
Owners unwilling to commit to regular curly-coat grooming and ear hygiene
Homes where the dog will be left alone for long stretches without family interaction

funFacts: Often dubbed the 'clown of the spaniel family,' the breed pairs a jaunty peak of curls between its eyes and a bare rat tail with an endearing, playful sense of humor.
It is the tallest of all spaniel breeds, bridging the size gap between medium and large sporting dogs.
Its signature smooth-tipped rat tail and dense, naturally water-repellent curls are functional adaptations for swimming through cold Irish marshes—not merely decorative styling.
Historical records from the late 1100s already referred to Irish water dogs by nicknames such as Shannon Spaniels, Rat-Tail Spaniels, and Whip-Tail Spaniels.
Owners must remind veterinarians to avoid sulfa antibiotics and ivermectin, as documented drug sensitivities in the breed can trigger severe reactions.

faq.question: What is an Irish Water Spaniel?
faq.answer: The Irish Water Spaniel is the tallest of all spaniel breeds—a sturdy Irish waterfowl retriever instantly recognized by its crisply curled purplish-liver coat, loose curly topknot, smooth tapering rat tail, and playful, loyal personality.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an Irish Water Spaniel?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 53 to 59 cm at the withers and weigh 55 to 68 pounds, while adult females stand 51 to 56 cm and weigh 45 to 58 pounds.

faq.question: How long does an Irish Water Spaniel live?
faq.answer: Typical life expectancy is 12 to 13 years with balanced nutrition, regular exercise, and routine veterinary care.

faq.question: Do Irish Water Spaniels shed, and how much grooming do they need?
faq.answer: They shed very little because their dense curls trap loose hair, making them a popular choice for some allergy-sensitive homes. They need thorough brushing at least once a week, shaping trims roughly every two months, and regular ear cleaning.

faq.question: Are there any special medication warnings for Irish Water Spaniels?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed has documented serious sensitivities to sulfa antibiotics and ivermectin, so owners should always ensure their veterinarian flags the dog's medical chart.

faq.question: Can an Irish Water Spaniel live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Their medium-to-large frame, high sporting energy, and love of running and swimming fit best in a house with a yard and active daily outings.

faq.question: Are Irish Water Spaniels easy to train?
faq.answer: They are smart and eager to please when training stays upbeat and varied, though harsh methods or repetitive drills quickly backfire.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Recommended pre-breeding evaluations include hip and elbow radiographs, specialist eye exams, thyroid panels, and cardiac checks.

overview.summary: The tallest of all sighthounds and a towering yet deeply serene Irish giant, uniting rough-coated athletic grace and historic wolf-coursing power with a famously gentle, patient, and dignified home temperament.
overview.description: The Irish Wolfhound is a commanding, colossal rough-coated sighthound built on the graceful, aerodynamic lines of a Greyhound—combining immense height and substantial muscle with effortless speed and agility rather than heavy mastiff bulk. Its long, level head is carried proudly atop a strong, muscular, dewlap-free arched neck, featuring dark oval eyes beneath wiry eyebrows, a coarse underjaw beard, a black nose and lips, and small, fine velvet rose ears folded neatly back. A remarkably deep chest, broad breast, long back, arched loins, and well-tucked belly flow into long, heavily boned straight forelegs and powerful hindquarters that drive an easy, ground-covering stride. Cloaked in a harsh, rough weatherproof coat in shades of grey, brindle, red, black, fawn, wheaten, or pure white, the Irish Wolfhound belies its intimidating size indoors: calm, sweet-natured, quiet, and devoted to its household, it embodies the classic 'gentle giant'—though its keen sighthound instinct to chase swift movement outdoors never fully sleeps.
overview.history: Few breeds boast a documented heritage as ancient as the Irish Wolfhound. Bred by Celtic peoples in Ireland to course wolves, Irish elk, and large game—and even to pull combatants from chariots in early warfare—giant Irish hounds entered recorded history in 391 AD, when Roman consul Quintus Aurelius Symmachus wrote of the astonishment in Rome upon receiving seven Irish hounds as a gift. Prized across medieval Europe as royal diplomatic presents, their numbers collapsed after wolves were hunted to extinction in Ireland by the late eighteenth century, compounded by widespread famine in the 1840s. By the mid-nineteenth century, the ancient breed stood on the brink of vanishing entirely. Beginning in 1862, Scottish army officer Captain George Augustus Graham dedicated decades to reviving the type by locating the last surviving Irish strains and carefully outcrossing them with Scottish Deerhounds, Great Danes, Borzois, and a Tibetan Mastiff-type wolfdog before line-breeding back to traditional form. The first formal breed description appeared in 1885, followed by international recognition in the mid-twentieth century. Today, the Irish Wolfhound is treasured worldwide as a serene family companion and lure-coursing athlete.
overview.originalPurpose: Coursing and bringing down wolves and large game by sight across Ireland, while also serving historically as a battlefield war hound and estate guardian.
currentRoles: Serene, devoted family companion
Lure-coursing and sighthound-sports competitor
Therapy dog
Deterrent household presence through imposing stature

physical.coatType: Rough, hard, wiry weatherproof coat covering the body, legs, and head, growing especially long and wiry over the eyes (eyebrows) and under the jaw (beard).
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; the harsh, wiry coat sheds moderately throughout the year and benefits from regular brushing and periodic hand-stripping of dead hair
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tight black lips and a strong, arched neck completely free of dewlap or loose throat skin keep drooling minimal, though the wiry beard easily drips water after drinking
distinctiveFeatures: Tallest of all coursing sighthounds, pairing colossal height and commanding presence with graceful, muscular Greyhound-like symmetry
Minimum height at the withers of 79 cm for males (desired average 81 to 86 cm) and 71 cm for females, with no formal upper height limit
Minimum expected weight of 54.5 kg for a 79 cm male and 40.5 kg for a 71 cm female, scaling proportionally upward with greater height
Long, level head carried high with a barely raised brow, minimal indentation between the eyes, a moderately pointed muzzle, black nose and lips, and a complete scissor bite
Dark, full, elliptical oval eyes framed by black rims and long, wiry eyebrows
Small, fine velvet-textured rose-shaped ears carried folded back like a Greyhound's
Rather long, very strong, muscular, well-arched neck completely free of dewlap or loose throat skin
Very deep chest, wide breast, long back, arched muscular loins, great breadth across the hips, and well-drawn-up belly
Long, slightly curved, well-coated tail of moderate thickness carried low with a gentle upward sweep near the tip
Heavily boned straight forelegs, long muscular thighs and second thighs, well-let-down hocks, and moderately large round feet with arched closed toes and strong curved nails

traits: Calm, dignified, gentle, and sweet-tempered indoors
Deeply devoted, loyal, and affectionate toward its human family
Remarkably quiet at home, rarely barking without good reason
Kind, patient, and tolerant around people, making a poor aggressive guard dog despite its intimidating presence
Sensitive and responsive to gentle guidance rather than harsh handling
Good-natured with respectful children, though its massive frame and swinging tail can easily bump toddlers unintentionally
Retains a powerful sighthound chasing instinct outdoors toward fleeing rabbits, wildlife, or small running animals

exercise.level: Moderate; calm and lounging indoors, adult Irish Wolfhounds need generous daily walks and safe opportunities to stretch their long strides in large fenced spaces—while puppies require strict exercise moderation to protect developing giant joints
activities: Long, steady daily walks on a sturdy leash across level ground or open countryside
Occasional free galloping inside a very large, securely fenced paddock or yard
Lure coursing and sighthound straight-racing for fit, fully mature adults
Calm obedience, therapy-dog visits, and mental enrichment

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly once or twice weekly with a stiff bristle brush and metal comb to remove dead wiry hair and prevent mats in the beard, eyebrows, and leg furnishings, hand-stripping dead coat twice a year if desired.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally when visibly soiled using a mild canine shampoo; wipe the wiry beard clean after meals and drinking.
notes: Provide thick, supportive orthopaedic bedding to prevent painful pressure sores and elbow calluses on bony giant joints.
Inspect the small rose ears weekly for wax buildup or debris.
Keep the strong, curved nails trimmed regularly so the round feet stay properly aligned under giant body weight.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate; eager to please and gentle-natured, though somewhat slower and more deliberate in responding to repetitive obedience drills than herding breeds—early leash manners are vital before the dog reaches giant size
tips: Begin loose-leash walking, polite greeting, and calm handling training immediately in puppyhood while the dog is still small enough to guide effortlessly.
Use warm, patient, reward-based methods with calm praise and food rewards; harsh scolding hurts this emotionally sensitive giant.
Never trust off-leash recall near unfenced roads or open wildlife areas—when a sighthound spots swift distant movement, coursing instinct can override verbal commands in seconds.
Practice calm counter-manners early, as an adult Irish Wolfhound can effortlessly reach kitchen countertops without even standing on its hind legs.
training.socialization: Early, calm, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, slippery indoor floors, vehicles, and veterinary clinics builds a composed, easily handled giant adult.

climates: Cool and temperate maritime climates, mirroring Ireland's damp, breezy weather where its rough wiry coat provides dependable protection
Cold winters are handled comfortably during active walks, though dry, draft-free indoor resting space with thick bedding is essential
Hot, humid summer weather requires shifting exercise to cool early-morning or evening hours with air-conditioned indoor rest and plenty of fresh water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate; serene and content napping indoors once exercised, though deeply attached to its family and unhappy if isolated outside in a kennel away from household company.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced giant-breed dog food, strictly using a controlled-calcium, moderate-calorie large/giant-breed puppy diet during rapid growth.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured meals daily during rapid skeletal growth, carefully moderated so puppies grow slowly and leanly without joint overload.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two (or three) measured smaller meals daily to support steady energy and help reduce acute stomach distension.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for older giant-breed cardiac, joint, and metabolic support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately—avoid overfeeding puppies in pursuit of maximum height, because excessive growth rates heighten developmental bone and elbow disorders. Keep mature adults lean and athletically muscled with ribs easily felt beneath the rough coat. Divide daily food into at least two smaller meals, enforce strict calm rest for an hour before and after eating, and keep clean water freely available without encouraging rapid gulping right after intense running.
considerations: Because Irish Wolfhounds are among the highest-risk giant breeds for life-threatening gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat), divide daily rations into two or more meals, restrict vigorous running around mealtimes, and discuss prophylactic gastropexy with a veterinarian.
Feed growing puppies a balanced giant-breed growth diet with controlled calcium and phosphorus—never add unprescribed calcium supplements.
Avoid high-impact jumping, long forced runs, or repetitive stair climbing until growth plates close around 18 to 24 months of age.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Giant-breed puppy growth nutrition and adult cardiac/bloat feeding strategies should always be tailored with a veterinarian familiar with giant sighthounds.

health.overview: The Irish Wolfhound is a beloved giant breed whose greatest heartbreak is its short life expectancy—typically 6 to 8 years (with peer-reviewed UK demographic data reporting a median age at death of 7.04 years). Major veterinary-documented causes of morbidity and mortality include inherited Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) and atrial fibrillation (AF), highly heritable bone cancer (osteosarcoma, estimated heritability 0.65), acute gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), recurrent bacterial pneumonia and rhinitis/bronchopneumonia syndrome, and congenital intrahepatic portosystemic liver shunts in puppies. Responsible breeding and veterinary care rely on early puppy serum bile acid screening, annual adult cardiac evaluations (ECG and echocardiography), radiographic hip and elbow screening, specialist eye exams, and careful sighthound anesthetic protocols.
commonConditions: Dilated Cardiomyopathy (DCM) and Atrial Fibrillation (AF) — the leading specific cause of cardiac death in Irish Wolfhounds, involving complex polygenic inheritance and weakened heart-muscle pumping; peer-reviewed clinical trials demonstrate that early preclinical detection via routine ECG/echocardiography and medical therapy (such as pimobendan) significantly delays congestive heart failure and sudden death

Osteosarcoma (bone cancer) — an aggressive malignant bone tumour primarily affecting the long leg bones, with a 2021 pedigree study of 5,110 Irish Wolfhounds estimating high heritability (0.65) and noting that 93% of osteosarcoma-related deaths occur before age 10
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — sudden, life-threatening gas distension and twisting of the stomach requiring immediate emergency surgery; a major risk in deep-chested giant hounds

Congenital intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (liver shunt) — an abnormal blood vessel allowing digestive-tract blood to bypass liver filtration, causing stunted growth and neurological signs; puppies should be screened via a dynamic (pre- and post-meal) serum bile acids blood test before placement

Rhinitis / bronchopneumonia syndrome and recurrent bacterial pneumonia — a well-documented breed predisposition to acute, rapidly progressing bacterial pneumonia (requiring prompt, prolonged antibiotic therapy) and young-dog nasal/respiratory inflammation
Hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, and developmental bone disorders — giant-breed orthopedic conditions monitored through pre-breeding radiographic hip and elbow evaluations

Hereditary eye disorders (including Progressive Retinal Atrophy / PRA), lymphoma, von Willebrand disease, and sighthound anesthetic sensitivity — requiring periodic specialist eye checks, awareness of lower anesthetic induction dosing requirements (often one-half to two-thirds standard calculated doses), and monitoring for delayed post-operative bleeding
preventiveCare: Insist on puppy dynamic serum bile acid test clearance for liver shunt prior to bringing a puppy home, and verify parental cardiac, eye, hip, and elbow screening clearances.

Schedule annual (or semi-annual in older adults) veterinary cardiac evaluations including an electrocardiogram (ECG) and board-certified cardiologist echocardiography to catch preclinical atrial fibrillation or DCM early.

Learn emergency warning signs of both bloat (unproductive retching, swollen tight abdomen, restlessness) and acute pneumonia (sudden high fever, laboured breathing, standing with head and neck extended), and discuss prophylactic gastropexy with your veterinarian.
Remind your veterinarian of giant sighthound physiology before surgery—Irish Wolfhounds typically require lower anesthetic induction doses and monitoring for post-operative bleeding.
Protect developing puppy joints from forced running and jumping until 18 to 24 months of age, maintain a lean body weight, and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention current.
recommendedScreenings: Dynamic (fasting and postprandial) serum bile acids test in puppies to screen for congenital intrahepatic portosystemic liver shunt
Cardiac evaluation by a board-certified veterinary cardiologist (echocardiogram and annual ECG screening for DCM and atrial fibrillation)
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (annual screening including PRA)
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental checks to keep the strong scissor bite and gums healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the small velvet rose ears weekly for wax buildup, dirt, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Check elbows, hocks, and bony pressure points regularly for calluses or sores (prevented by thick supportive bedding), and part the rough coat during brushing to check for ticks or skin irritation.

funFacts: In 391 AD, Roman consul Quintus Aurelius Symmachus wrote to his brother thanking him for a gift of seven Irish hounds, reporting that all of Rome gazed at them in amazement and imagined they must have been transported in iron cages.

Standing taller than any other coursing sighthound—with males desired to average 81 to 86 cm at the shoulder—an adult Irish Wolfhound can easily rest its chin on a dining table or reach over six feet tall when standing on its hind legs.

By the mid-nineteenth century the breed was nearly extinct after wolves vanished from Ireland; starting in 1862, Captain George Augustus Graham spent decades painstakingly rebuilding the breed using the last surviving Irish lines alongside Scottish Deerhound and Great Dane outcrosses.

A traditional motto long linked to the breed captures its dual nature: 'Gentle when stroked, fierce when provoked'—though modern Irish Wolfhounds are overwhelmingly serene, quiet, and friendly companions indoors.
The Irish Guards regiment of the British Army has maintained an Irish Wolfhound as its ceremonial regimental mascot since 1902, marching proudly at the head of parades.

faq.question: What is an Irish Wolfhound?
faq.answer: The Irish Wolfhound is an ancient, colossal rough-coated sighthound from Ireland—the tallest of all coursing hounds—originally bred to hunt wolves and large game and prized today as a calm, quiet, affectionate 'gentle giant.'

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an Irish Wolfhound?
faq.answer: Adult males stand at least 79 cm at the withers (with an average of 81 to 86 cm desired) and weigh at least 54.5 kg, while adult females stand at least 71 cm and weigh at least 40.5 kg, with weight increasing proportionally with greater height and no formal upper limit.

faq.question: How long does an Irish Wolfhound live?
faq.answer: Like many giant breeds, the Irish Wolfhound has a relatively short life expectancy of 6 to 8 years (with peer-reviewed UK studies reporting a median lifespan around 7 years).

faq.question: Can an Irish Wolfhound live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Although remarkably calm and quiet indoors, its colossal size, long stride, need for spacious stretching room, and avoidance of repetitive stairs during giant growth make a large house with a big securely fenced yard far more practical.

faq.question: Are Irish Wolfhounds good family dogs and good guard dogs?
faq.answer: They are wonderful, gentle, patient family dogs (with supervision around small toddlers who could be bumped by a giant body or tail). However, they are typically too friendly and serene to serve as aggressive guard dogs, relying mainly on their imposing size as a deterrent.

faq.question: How much grooming and shedding should I expect from an Irish Wolfhound?
faq.answer: They shed moderately and have a rough, wiry coat that is fairly straightforward to maintain: thorough brushing once or twice a week, occasional beard wiping, periodic hand-stripping of dead hair, and regular nail trims keep them tidy.

faq.question: Are Irish Wolfhounds easy to train?
faq.answer: They are gentle, sensitive, and willing to please with warm, patient positive training, though they can respond more deliberately than fast-paced herding breeds. Early loose-leash training is essential, and off-leash reliability near unfenced wildlife or roads should never be assumed.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for an Irish Wolfhound?
faq.answer: Major breed health priorities include inherited heart disease (Dilated Cardiomyopathy and atrial fibrillation), osteosarcoma (bone cancer), acute bloat (gastric dilatation-volvulus), congenital liver shunts in puppies (screened via serum bile acids), recurrent bacterial pneumonia, hip and elbow dysplasia, and hereditary eye conditions such as PRA.

overview.summary: A rough-coated Croatian scent hound, white with orange markings, built to hunt hare, fox and boar over stony, hilly ground in any weather, and gentle and devoted at home.
overview.description: The Istrian Coarse-haired Hound is a medium-sized, strongly built scent hound whose body is clearly longer than it is tall. Its most obvious feature is the coat: a harsh, dull, slightly wavy topcoat about 5 to 8 cm long over a shorter, dense undercoat that thickens in winter. The coat is snow white with even orange markings on the head and body, covering no more than about a third of the dog. The head is well proportioned, with a muzzle a little shorter than the skull, a black or brown nose, oval dark brown eyes with a serious look, and triangular ears that hang at eye level. By nature it is gentle and even-tempered, closely attached to its owner, and easy to train, yet keen and persistent in the field. It works its quarry from further away than the smooth-coated Istrian hound and gives a medium-toned voice with some deeper notes while trailing.
overview.history: The Istrian hounds are among Croatia's native hound breeds, shaped over centuries by practical hunting work. A manuscript written in 1719 by Bishop Petar Bakić describes these hounds as already known before the fourteenth century, and the earliest known picture of the breed is in the cathedral of St Mark in Makarska. The coarse-haired type shares its history with the smooth-coated Istrian hound but has always been depicted less often. Its rough coat made it the better choice for colder hunting grounds. The breed's first international standard was approved in 1955.

faq.question: Where does the breed come from?
faq.answer: Croatia, specifically the Istria region. It is one of the country's native hound breeds.

faq.question: How big is it?
faq.answer: Males stand 50 to 54 cm at the withers and females 48 to 52 cm, with 3 cm either way allowed for excellent dogs.

faq.question: How is it different from the smooth-coated Istrian hound?
faq.answer: It has a harsh, slightly wavy coat about 5 to 8 cm long, which suits colder hunting grounds. It also tends to work game further from the hunter and has a deeper voice.

faq.question: What colour is it?
faq.answer: Snow white with even orange patches on the head and body. Orange should cover no more than about a third of the dog, and lemon-yellow markings are not allowed.

faq.question: Is it a good family dog?
faq.answer: It is gentle and devoted at home, but it is a working hound with a strong hunting drive and suits experienced, active owners best.

faq.question: Are there known health problems?
faq.answer: Breed-specific health data is very limited, and no condition is known to be common. Routine care for an active hound, plus questions to the breeder about health checks, is the sensible approach.
