feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age to support steady musculoskeletal development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain field energy and keep digestion steady.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adjusted for reduced activity and joint health.

nutrition.guidelines: Weigh or measure daily portions consistently so the dog stays lean, sinewy, and agile without carrying excess weight over its joints. Active working hounds during autumn and winter hunting seasons require higher energy and protein density than companion dogs in lighter routines. Provide cool, fresh drinking water at all times.
considerations: Keep body condition athletic and well-muscled; excess weight reduces mountain stamina and increases joint strain.
Avoid vigorous sprinting immediately before or after large meals as a general deep-chested hound precaution.
Count all training treats inside the daily calorie budget.
Transition between food formulas gradually over five to seven days to prevent digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric requirements vary substantially between active hunting dogs and household companions. Consult a veterinarian for individualized feeding advice.

health.overview: The Polish Hunting Dog is generally a hardy, purpose-bred working hound, though formal breed-wide actuarial lifespan studies are not yet established. A peer-reviewed ophthalmic study of 193 Polish Hunting Dogs documented retinal lesions (8.3%), cataracts (2.6%), iris coloboma (1.6%), Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA, 1.6%), and isolated cases of Sudden Acquired Retinal Degeneration Syndrome (SARDS), retinal dysplasia, distichiasis, entropion, and ocular dermoid—leading veterinary researchers to recommend periodic specialist eye examinations. General medium-to-large active hound precautions—including orthopedic joint screening, drop-ear hygiene, and fieldwork injury checks—also apply.
commonConditions: Retinal lesions and Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA) — retinal changes (8.3%) and PRA (1.6%) documented in a veterinary ophthalmic study of 193 Polish Hunting Dogs, warranting periodic specialist eye checks

Cataracts and congenital ocular anomalies — cataracts (2.6%), iris coloboma (1.6%), and isolated cases of ocular dermoid, retinal dysplasia, distichiasis, entropion, and SARDS reported in screened Polish Hunting Dogs
Hip and elbow dysplasia — general developmental orthopedic precautions recommended for active, medium-to-large working hounds
Otitis externa (ear infections) — conformation-linked risk associated with low-set drop ears that can retain moisture and woodland debris
Fieldwork trauma — cuts, thorn punctures, paw injuries, or boar-hunting injuries sustained during rugged forest work
preventiveCare: Schedule periodic ophthalmological examinations with a veterinary eye specialist, especially for breeding stock and adult dogs.
Ask breeders for documented eye-examination certificates and orthopedic joint evaluations (hips and elbows).
Keep the dog lean and well-conditioned to reduce wear on joints during steep terrain work.
Inspect and dry the low-set drop ears after every wet outdoor outing to prevent ear infections.
Maintain consistent year-round protection against ticks, fleas, heartworm, and internal parasites—especially critical in forested hunting regions—alongside annual veterinary wellness exams.
recommendedScreenings: Periodic ophthalmological examination by a veterinary eye specialist (supported by peer-reviewed breed ophthalmic research)
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding (general working-hound orthopedic precaution)
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding (general working-hound orthopedic precaution)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly with canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental checks to keep the strong scissor bite and gums healthy.
health.earCare: Check the low-set, silky-haired triangular drop ears weekly for moisture, wax buildup, ticks, or redness, and clean gently with a veterinarian-recommended cleanser.
health.skinCare: Inspect the skin beneath the harsh coat and dense undercoat after every forest outing for ticks, burrs, scratches, or irritation.

funFacts: Although often confused abroad with the heavier Polish Hound (Ogar Polski), nineteenth-century Polish hunting treatises by Wiktor Kozłowski (1821) and Jan Szyttler (1839) already distinguished the lighter, faster, more trainable gończy as its own type.
During pursuit, the Polish Hunting Dog produces a distinctive, melodic bay with varied intonations, and females typically hunt with a noticeably higher-pitched voice than males.

The breed's modern survival owes much to Polish cynologist Józef Pawłusiewicz (1903–1979), who hunted with these mountain hounds in the Podkarpacie region, guided their systematic breeding, and wrote the first formal breed description.
Its athletic proportions are finely tuned for steep mountain forests: the body forms a 9:10 rectangle, and the distance from elbow to ground equals exactly half the dog's height at the withers.
The Polish Hunting Dog received definitive international recognition in November 2017, becoming Poland's fifth internationally recognized native breed.

faq.question: What is a Polish Hunting Dog?
faq.answer: The Polish Hunting Dog (Gończy Polski) is an agile, courageous medium-sized scenthound from southern Poland, bred to hunt wild boar and deer in mountainous forests and valued at home as a steady, protective companion.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Polish Hunting Dog?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 55 to 59 cm at the withers and females stand 50 to 55 cm. No single official weight range is published, though healthy adults maintain a lean, compact, well-muscled medium build.

faq.question: How is the Polish Hunting Dog different from the Polish Hound?
faq.answer: The Polish Hunting Dog (Gończy Polski) is lighter-boned, slightly smaller, faster, and more agile for mountain work than the heavier, deeper-throated Polish Hound (Ogar Polski).

faq.question: How long does a Polish Hunting Dog live?
faq.answer: No formal peer-reviewed actuarial lifespan study has established an official breed-wide lifespan range yet, though it is generally regarded as a hardy working hound when given proper nutrition and preventive veterinary care.

faq.question: Are Polish Hunting Dogs good family dogs?
faq.answer: Yes, for active households. They are stable, gentle, and deeply loyal to their families and patient with respectful children, while remaining naturally watchful and wary around strangers.

faq.question: Can a Polish Hunting Dog live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Its high outdoor energy, scent-tracking drive, and resonant hunting voice make it far better suited to a rural or suburban home with a securely fenced yard and daily forest or trail exercise.

faq.question: Are Polish Hunting Dogs easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent and notably more responsive to training than many traditional scenthounds, thriving on gentle, reward-based lessons—though their strong wildlife scent drive still requires diligent recall training.

faq.question: What health concerns should Polish Hunting Dog owners know about?
faq.answer: A veterinary study of 193 Polish Hunting Dogs documented retinal lesions, cataracts, iris coloboma, and Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA), so periodic specialist eye exams are strongly advised alongside general large-hound joint and ear care.

overview.summary: A sturdy, medium-sized Polish herding dog hidden under a long, shaggy coat, known for its sharp memory, watchful nature and lively but level-headed temperament.
overview.description: The Polish Lowland Sheepdog is a compact, muscular herder built slightly longer than it is tall, which gives it an agile, rectangular outline. Its whole body is covered in a long, dense, rough-textured coat over a soft undercoat, and the hair falling over the forehead often hides the oval, hazel eyes. The ears hang close to the head and are heart-shaped, and many dogs are born with a very short tail or none at all. Any coat colour is possible. In temperament the breed is alert and lively yet self-controlled, quick to learn and notably good at remembering people, places and routines. Bred to handle flocks and warn of intruders, it is still a capable working and watch dog, and with enough activity it settles well into family life, including in towns.
overview.history: Shaggy herding dogs have worked on the plains of Poland for centuries, and the breed is generally thought to descend from long-coated sheepdogs that reached Europe from Central Asia. A long-standing tradition says Polish traders took several of these dogs to Scotland in the early 1500s and exchanged some of them for sheep, and that they may have influenced British herding breeds such as the Bearded Collie, though this story cannot be confirmed. Interest in the breed grew after Poland regained independence following the First World War, and dogs were being shown in Warsaw by 1924. The Second World War halted breeding, and the population came close to disappearing. Afterwards, breeders searched farms for surviving dogs, and the veterinarian Danuta Hryniewicz played a central part in the recovery. Her male, Smok, sired the first ten litters of the 1950s, and every modern dog of the breed traces back to him. A breed standard was approved in Poland in 1959, the breed gained definitive international recognition in 1963, and it later spread across Europe and North America, being recognised in the United States in 2001. Because the breed was rebuilt from so few dogs, its genetic diversity remains among the lowest measured in any breed.

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb through to the skin every day, working in sections so mats do not form close to the skin, especially behind the ears, under the legs and on the belly.
grooming.bathing: Bathe when dirty, then dry the coat thoroughly; a damp, thick coat tangles quickly and can irritate the skin.

tips: Keep sessions varied and use food, toys and praise as rewards.
Set clear routines early; this breed remembers both good and bad habits.
Teach calm greetings and a 'quiet' cue to manage watchdog barking.
Redirect herding behaviours such as circling or nipping at heels into games or herding classes.
Avoid harsh corrections, which tend to make a confident dog more stubborn.
training.socialization: As a natural guard that is reserved with strangers, the puppy benefits from meeting many friendly people, children, calm dogs and new places from an early age. Regular positive outings help keep its watchfulness balanced rather than suspicious.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure meals and adjust portions so the dog stays lean. A thick coat can hide weight gain, so feel for the ribs and waist rather than relying on looks. Keep fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Extra weight adds strain to the hips, which matters in a breed where hip dysplasia occurs.
Count training treats as part of the daily food.
Change foods gradually over about a week.

health.overview: The Polish Lowland Sheepdog is a fairly hardy breed with a typical lifespan of more than 10 years. Hip dysplasia and a late-onset form of progressive retinal atrophy are the main inherited concerns, and breeders are advised to screen hips and eyes. Most cases of the eye disease studied in the breed carry the rcd4 gene variant, for which a DNA test is available. A rare but serious neurological disease, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, has been described in the breed. Because the modern population descends from very few dogs, genetic diversity is low, and breeding the least related dogs is recommended to protect future health.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: abnormal hip development that can lead to arthritis; about 16% of dogs in one screening registry sample were dysplastic

Progressive retinal atrophy (late-onset, mostly linked to the rcd4 variant): slow loss of night vision, then day vision, usually starting in middle age; a DNA test identifies affected and carrier dogs
Neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis: a rare inherited storage disease causing behaviour changes, poor coordination and blindness in young adult dogs
Other conditions reported in the breed: hypothyroidism, cataracts and patent ductus arteriosus (a congenital heart defect)
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for hip scores and current eye examination results for both parents.
Ask for rcd4 PRA DNA results, and avoid pairing two carriers.
Prefer breeders who consider genetic diversity and relatedness when choosing mates.
Keep the dog lean and avoid heavy, repetitive jumping while the puppy is growing.
Report night blindness, bumping into objects or clumsy movement to a vet promptly.
Keep up yearly health checks, vaccinations and parasite control; check under the thick coat for skin problems.
recommendedScreenings: Hip evaluation (official hip dysplasia scheme)
Eye examination under an official eye scheme or by a veterinary ophthalmologist
DNA test for progressive retinal atrophy (rcd4)
health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week with dog toothpaste and have the mouth checked at each vet visit.
health.earCare: Check the hanging ears weekly for wax, smell or redness, and keep the hair around the ear opening free of mats so air can circulate.
health.skinCare: Part the coat to the skin while grooming to look for mats, redness, hot spots or parasites. Dense mats trap moisture against the skin and should be worked out or carefully trimmed.

funFacts: According to a long-told story, Polish traders brought these dogs to Scotland in the early 1500s and swapped some of them for sheep, and they may have helped shape the Bearded Collie.
Every Polish Lowland Sheepdog alive today traces back to Smok, the dog who sired the breed's first ten litters after the Second World War.
A wartime legend tells of a PON named Psyche who barked before air raids on Warsaw, warning people to take shelter.
The first international show to include the breed took place in Czechoslovakia in 1965.
Many puppies of this breed are born with only a stub of a tail, or none at all.
Genetic testing has shown the breed's diversity to be among the lowest of all breeds studied, a legacy of its near-disappearance.

faq.question: How big is a Polish Lowland Sheepdog?
faq.answer: Males stand 45–50 cm at the withers and females 42–47 cm. The breed standards do not set a weight.

faq.question: How long do Polish Lowland Sheepdogs live?
faq.answer: They usually live more than 10 years with good care.

faq.question: How much grooming does the coat need?
faq.answer: A lot. The long, dense coat should be brushed through to the skin every day to prevent mats, and it needs thorough drying after baths.

faq.question: Do Polish Lowland Sheepdogs shed?
faq.answer: Yes. Daily brushing removes loose hair before it mats or ends up around the house, and shedding increases during coat changes.

faq.question: How much exercise do they need?
faq.answer: This is an active working breed that can need more than two hours of exercise a day, along with training or jobs that keep its mind busy.

faq.question: Are they good family dogs?
faq.answer: They are devoted to their family and usually good with children they are raised with. They are naturally watchful with strangers, so early socialisation is important.

faq.question: Are they easy to train?
faq.answer: They learn quickly and have an excellent memory, but they are also independent. Consistent, reward-based training works best.

faq.question: What health tests should a breeder do?
faq.answer: Responsible breeders screen hips and eyes and use a DNA test for the rcd4 form of progressive retinal atrophy. Choosing less related mates also helps, because genetic diversity in the breed is low.

faq.question: What colours do they come in?
faq.answer: Any colour or combination of patches is acceptable, although merle is not accepted under the UK standard.

overview.summary: A rare, rustic, and highly affectionate French pointing dog, famous for its curly, ruffled coat, striking topknot, and immense passion for hunting in marshlands and water.
overview.description: The Pont-Audemer Spaniel is a stocky, vigorous, and unique continental pointing dog that stands out for its delightfully rustic appearance. It is completely covered in curly, slightly ruffled hair that closely resembles a water spaniel, yet it functions primarily as a highly capable pointing breed. Its most defining physical characteristic is a curly topknot (a 'wig' of hair) on the top of the skull, which leaves the forehead bare and falls to frame the face alongside long, heavily feathered drop ears. The coat is generally brown or brown and white (frequently roan), exhibiting a beautiful dead-leaf shimmer that serves as excellent camouflage in dense, marshy environments. Because of its comical topknot and exceedingly cheerful, lively temperament, the breed earned the enduring nickname 'le petit clown des marais' (the little clown of the marshes). In the field, it is a hardy, tireless worker completely undeterred by cold water or brambles. At home, it is exceptionally gentle, profoundly affectionate, and makes a calm, devoted family companion.
overview.history: Originating in the Normandy region of France—specifically around the Marais Vernier and the town of Pont-Audemer—this rare spaniel traces its roots back to the seventeenth century. While its precise lineage is somewhat obscured, it is widely believed to have been developed by crossing old French pointing spaniels with the Irish Water Spaniel (or potentially an English water spaniel) to create a rugged, weather-resistant dog perfectly suited for hunting waterfowl in freezing marshes. Highly prized by local hunters for its stamina and staunch pointing ability, the breed remained a regional secret for many years. Like many European breeds, its numbers were devastated during the First and Second World Wars, bringing it dangerously close to extinction. Following World War II, dedicated French breed enthusiasts worked tirelessly to revitalize the population, though the Pont-Audemer Spaniel remains one of the rarest of all French pointing breeds today, cherished both for its immense working utility and its delightfully sweet disposition.

Deep, broad chest reaching the level of the elbows, providing excellent lung capacity for endurance
A moderately short, straight back and a slightly sloping croup
Tail that is traditionally docked in working regions (where permitted) or left natural, carried fairly straight and well-feathered with curly hair
Round, compact feet with thick pads and distinct hair growing between the toes for protection in rough terrain

traits: Exceptionally gentle, affectionate, and calm in a domestic setting
Hardworking, passionate, and energetic when hunting in the field or marshes
Highly intelligent and eager to please its handler
Cheerful and slightly comical, earning its 'little clown' nickname
Sociable and peaceable with children, strangers, and other household pets
Deeply bonded to its owners and highly sensitive to harsh corrections
Possesses a profound affinity for water and swimming
Generally quiet, utilizing its bark only when necessary

exercise.level: High; an athletic pointing breed built for marshland endurance that requires vigorous daily physical activity and mental stimulation, though it settles very calmly indoors
activities: Daily brisk leashed walks or long trail hikes
Extensive water retrieving and swimming in safe environments
Free running in a securely fenced, open field
Scent tracking, hunt tests, and interactive fetch games
Canine sports including agility and rally obedience

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly two to three times a week using a pin brush and a sturdy metal comb to detangle the curly, ruffled coat and prevent severe mats in the topknot and ear feathering.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally—every six to eight weeks or when visibly muddy—using a mild, moisturizing canine shampoo to preserve the coat's natural weather-resistant oils.
notes: The dense, curly coat acts like a magnet for burrs, twigs, and marsh debris; inspect and brush the coat immediately after woodland or water walks.
The heavy, fringed drop ears severely restrict air circulation. Inspect them weekly, wiping the canals gently with a veterinary-approved cleanser to prevent trapped moisture and bacterial infections.
Trim the excess curly hair between the foot pads regularly to prevent mud impaction and ensure solid traction.
Trim fast-growing nails every two to three weeks.
Brush teeth several times weekly with canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy; highly intelligent, naturally cooperative, and eager to please, making them exceptionally responsive to positive reinforcement
tips: Use exclusively positive, reward-based training; they are a deeply sensitive breed and will shut down completely if yelled at or treated harshly.
Begin basic obedience and leash training early to build confidence and establish a strong communicative bond.
Channel their natural pointing, scenting, and water-retrieving instincts into structured play to keep their minds engaged.
Although they are highly reliable, practice recall relentlessly to manage their hunting drive in unfenced rural areas.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy early, gradually, and positively to diverse people, friendly dogs, and novel environments. Their naturally sweet, cheerful disposition blossoms with proper early exposure, ensuring a confident and outgoing adult.

climates: Temperate climates
Cool and wet climates, where the dense, weather-resistant curly coat provides exceptional insulation
Warm climates, provided shade, cool indoor shelter, and fresh water are available, with intense exercise restricted to cooler hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low; they form incredibly deep, sensitive bonds with their human family and are prone to severe separation anxiety or depression if left isolated for long workdays without companionship.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for active medium-sized sporting breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age to support steady growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady energy and digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations strictly using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup, adjusting amounts to maintain a lean, athletic body silhouette beneath the ruffled coat. Divide daily food into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous running immediately before and after eating to mitigate bloat risk, and provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a strictly lean, well-muscled body condition to minimize mechanical stress on the joints.
Account for training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to prevent obesity.
Working dogs in active hunting seasons or freezing winter weather require a significant increase in caloric and protein density.
Transition between diet formulas gradually over five to seven days to prevent gastrointestinal upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary significantly based on exercise intensity, age, and outdoor temperature. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Pont-Audemer Spaniel is an exceedingly robust, rustic, and generally very healthy sporting breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years. Benefiting from a strict working heritage in demanding environments, the breed avoids many of the severe genetic diseases that plague highly commercialized dogs. Primary health priorities focus on maintaining orthopedic soundness and diligently preventing ear infections common to drop-eared water dogs.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints leading to osteoarthritis and stiffness, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Chronic otitis externa — bacterial and yeast ear infections promoted by heavy, curly-haired drop ears that restrict canal ventilation and trap moisture
Ocular conditions — minor occasional reports of inherited eye issues, monitored through routine veterinary ophthalmologist examinations
Alopecia (hair loss) — occasional reports of breed-specific hair thinning, particularly later in life, requiring veterinary dermatology assessment
Traumatic outdoor injuries — minor cuts, sprains, or thorn punctures sustained during vigorous fieldwork in dense marshes
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified radiographic clearances for hips and specialist eye examinations.
Thoroughly dry the heavily fringed drop ears and the dense coat after swimming, bathing, or wet weather walks to prevent moisture-induced infections.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition throughout life to minimize mechanical wear on joints.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms, especially for dogs highly active in rural and marsh environments.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has a complete 42-tooth scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the long, heavily feathered drop ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the curly coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, ticks, or brush scratches. Matting close to the skin can cause painful hot spots, so regular, deep combing is essential.

idealFor: Active individuals and families seeking an exceptionally calm, gentle, and highly affectionate sporting companion
Hunters or outdoor enthusiasts looking for a rugged, water-loving pointing and retrieving partner
First-time dog owners willing to provide consistent daily exercise to a highly biddable, eager-to-please breed
Homes with a securely fenced yard providing ample space for supervised running
Owners willing to commit to the time required for brushing and maintaining a thick, curly, and ruffled coat
notIdealFor: Sedentary individuals looking for a low-maintenance, low-energy indoor lap dog
Apartment dwellers without access to extensive outdoor running space
Owners who leave a dog home alone in isolation for long workdays, risking severe separation anxiety
Handlers who rely on harsh training methods or heavy-handed corrections
People seeking a fierce territorial guard dog

funFacts: In France, the breed's cheerful, lively temperament and comical appearance—featuring a distinct curly 'wig' on its head—earned it the enduring nickname 'le petit clown des marais' (the little clown of the marshes).

Despite having a curly coat that closely resembles a traditional water spaniel, the Pont-Audemer is classified as a pointing dog (like a setter or pointer) that also happens to be a superb water retriever.
The distinctive curly topknot leaves the forehead completely bare and short-haired, blending seamlessly into the heavily fringed ears.
The breed was heavily utilized in the Marais Vernier in Normandy, a massive, freezing wetland environment that demanded a dog with exceptional stamina and a highly weather-resistant coat.
The Pont-Audemer Spaniel is currently one of the rarest of all French pointing breeds, highly treasured by a small but fiercely dedicated group of European fanciers.

faq.question: What is a Pont-Audemer Spaniel?
faq.answer: The Pont-Audemer Spaniel (Epagneul de Pont-Audemer) is a rare, rustic pointing and retrieving gundog from Normandy, France, famous for its curly, ruffled coat, distinct topknot, and passion for hunting in marshes.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Pont-Audemer Spaniel?
faq.answer: Adult males and females both stand 52 to 58 cm at the withers and generally weigh between 20 and 27 kg, possessing a robust, stocky, and well-muscled silhouette.

faq.question: How long does a Pont-Audemer Spaniel live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular rigorous exercise, and preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Do Pont-Audemer Spaniels shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They are low shedders, as their curly coat traps loose hair. However, they require extensive grooming; thorough brushing and combing two to three times a week is necessary to prevent severe matting, especially in the ears and topknot.

faq.question: Can a Pont-Audemer Spaniel live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. While they are famously calm and gentle indoors, their high physical energy and need for vigorous daily exercise make them much better suited to a house with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Are Pont-Audemer Spaniels hard to train?
faq.answer: No, they are highly intelligent, cooperative, and very eager to please, making them easy to train. They are, however, deeply sensitive and require gentle, positive reinforcement.

faq.question: Are Pont-Audemer Spaniels good family pets and good with children?
faq.answer: Yes, they are outstanding family pets. They are exceptionally docile, sweet-natured, and cheerful (the 'little clown'), making them wonderful, peaceable companions for respectful children.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Pont-Audemer Spaniel?
faq.answer: They are a very robust and healthy breed. Primary health concerns are limited to conditions common in active, drop-eared sporting dogs, such as hip dysplasia and chronic ear infections.

overview.summary: An exceptionally bright, agile, and proud water-retrieving dog bred across multiple size varieties, combining keen athletic capability and strong trainability with devoted family companionship.
overview.description: The Poodle is a well-proportioned, square-leaning, and briskly moving dog celebrated worldwide for its sharp mind, lively spirit, and distinctive curly or corded coat. Rather than heavy or coarse in bone, it projects balanced elegance—carrying its head proudly atop a strong, slightly arched, dewlap-free neck, with an oval skull, straight muzzle measuring roughly nine-tenths of skull length, dark almond-shaped eyes, and flat pendant ears set along the cheeks. Its dense, springy coat comes in either tight, uniform, woolly curls or long, dense cords, traditionally styled in classic trims that leave joints free for movement while protecting vital areas. Across its size varieties—from the larger Standard down to Medium, Miniature, and Toy sizes—the Poodle is affectionate, people-focused, quick to learn, and eager to participate in daily family life, outdoor walks, swimming, and canine sports.
overview.history: Tracing its roots to skilled water-retrieving dogs in Western and Central Europe, the Poodle developed over centuries as a capable gun dog and swimmer used to retrieve waterfowl from lakes and marshes. Its name stems from the German word 'Pudel'—linked to splashing in water—while in France it is widely known as the 'Caniche' and celebrated as the national dog of France. Over time, breeders selected distinct size varieties—including Standard, Medium, Miniature, and Toy—adapting the breed's agility and intelligence from working marshes and trick performances into modern companion homes and competitive dog sports.
overview.originalPurpose: Retrieving waterfowl and game from water and marshland, alongside active companionship and trick/working roles.
currentRoles: Devoted family and household companion
Obedience, agility, rally, tracking, and dock-diving competitor
Water-retrieving and therapy dog

physical.coatType: Dense, springy double-style coat appearing either as profuse, fine, woolly, even curls elastic to the touch or as dense, heavy cords measuring at least 20 cm in length; traditionally groomed in structured trims.
physical.sheddingLevel: Low; the dense curly or corded coat traps loose hair rather than shedding freely around the home, requiring regular brushing or combing
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tight, well-fitting lips resting cleanly against the lower jaw and a dewlap-free neck keep drooling minimal
distinctiveFeatures: Balanced, lightly built yet muscular silhouette slightly longer than tall with withers height nearly matching croup height
Across size varieties, height at the withers spans 45 to 62 cm for Standard, 35 to 45 cm for Medium, 28 to 35 cm for Miniature, and 24 to 28 cm for Toy Poodles
Chiseled head with an oval skull slightly convex in profile, straight muzzle roughly nine-tenths of skull length, dark almond-shaped eyes, and close-fitting pendant drop ears
Strong scissor bite and a dewlap-free, slightly arched neck carried high and proudly
Upright, parallel limbs with a light, bouncy gait and naturally short-free tail set high at the loin
Profuse curly or corded coat with traditional grooming trims

traits: Highly intelligent, quick-witted, and eager to learn new cues and tasks
Affectionate, loyal, and deeply attached to its family household
Lively, playful, and alert with a light, buoyant energy level
Sociable and people-oriented, thriving on interaction, games, and mental engagement
Responsive to consistent, positive guidance and prone to boredom if left under-stimulated

exercise.level: High; an energetic, athletic dog across all size varieties that benefits from daily brisk walks, retrieve or swimming play, and mental enrichment
activities: Brisk daily walks and active outdoor play
Swimming, water retrieving, and dock-diving games
Agility, obedience, rally, and scent-work training
Interactive puzzle toys and trick learning

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly down to the skin several times a week—or daily for longer or corded coats—to prevent tangles and matting.
grooming.bathing: Bathe regularly with a mild dog shampoo and conditioner, detangling thoroughly before washing and drying completely.
notes: Schedule regular professional grooming trims every four to eight weeks depending on coat style and length.
Inspect pendant ears weekly for wax, moisture, or odour, and clean gently when needed.
Trim nails regularly and brush teeth several times weekly using dog-safe toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy; quick to grasp commands and enthusiastic when sessions are engaging and consistent
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based training with treats, praise, and play rather than harsh corrections.
Keep sessions varied and mentally stimulating so a sharp Poodle does not grow bored.
Practice recall and impulse control early, especially around water, wildlife, and busy areas.
training.socialization: Early, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, grooming routines, and everyday sights builds poise and confidence across every size variety.

climates: Temperate and four-season climates with appropriate coat grooming and warm shelter in cold weather
Warm weather requires avoiding strenuous midday exertion and providing shade and fresh water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; thrives on human companionship and can become restless or vocal if left alone for long stretches without enrichment.

nutrition.dietType: Complete and balanced commercial dog food formulated for the dog's life stage and size category.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to maintain steady energy and healthy body weight.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored to activity level, dental comfort, and joint care.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure portions according to size variety, age, and activity level to keep ribs easily felt without excess weight. Provide fresh drinking water continuously.
considerations: Monitor treat calories carefully to prevent weight gain, particularly in smaller or less active individuals.
In larger deep-chested Poodles, avoid vigorous exercise right before or after large meals and watch for signs of bloat.
Transition gradually between diets over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Exact calorie and nutrient needs vary by size variety (Toy, Miniature, Medium, or Standard) and activity level; consult a veterinarian for individualized guidance.

health.overview: Poodles across size varieties are generally active companions, though specific hereditary and age-related risks vary by size and lineage. Documented breed health priorities include sebaceous adenitis (an inflammatory skin condition affecting sebaceous glands that requires lifelong management and is not cured by a single treatment), progressive retinal atrophy (including prcd-PRA) and other ocular conditions, joint concerns such as hip dysplasia and patellar luxation, endocrine disorders including Addison's disease (hypoadrenocorticism) and Cushing's disease, and bloat in deep-chested larger individuals.
commonConditions: Sebaceous adenitis — a chronic inflammatory condition targeting sebaceous glands that can cause scaling, follicular casts, coat changes, and hair loss, requiring ongoing veterinary skin management
Progressive retinal atrophy and hereditary eye disorders — progressive vision loss and eye conditions monitored through DNA testing and periodic veterinary eye exams
Hip dysplasia and patellar luxation — joint developmental issues affecting hip sockets or kneecaps depending on size variety, screened via radiographs or clinical exams
Addison's disease (hypoadrenocorticism) and Cushing's disease — adrenal hormone imbalances requiring veterinary diagnosis and lifelong management
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) — an acute medical emergency most relevant to larger, deep-chested individuals
preventiveCare: Ask breeders for documented parental health evaluations (such as hip, patella, eye, and relevant genetic or endocrine screenings).
Maintain a lean body condition, regular exercise, dental hygiene, and routine ear and skin checks.
Seek prompt veterinary evaluation for persistent skin scaling, hair loss, vision changes, lameness, or sudden lethargy/vomiting.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (especially for larger varieties) and clinical patellar luxation evaluation
Periodic veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination and relevant DNA testing such as prcd-PRA
Elective thyroid, cardiac, or sebaceous adenitis evaluations as advised by a veterinarian or breeding programme
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using dog-safe enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental evaluations.
health.earCare: Inspect pendant ears weekly for wax, moisture, odour, or redness, cleaning gently with a dog-safe product when needed.
health.skinCare: Part the dense curly or corded coat regularly during grooming to check skin for dryness, scaling, irritation, tangles, or parasites.

idealFor: Active individuals and families wanting an intelligent, affectionate, trainable companion
Owners willing to commit to consistent brushing and regular grooming trims
Households that enjoy walks, games, swimming, or canine sports
notIdealFor: Owners looking for a low-grooming coat without regular brushing or professional trims
Sedentary households unable to provide daily physical and mental stimulation
People who leave a social dog alone for long periods without company

funFacts: The English name 'Poodle' comes from the German word 'Pudel,' linked to splashing in water, reflecting the breed's historic water-retrieving background.
In France, the Poodle is known as the 'Caniche' and is celebrated as the national dog of France.
Classic Poodle grooming clips originated for practical working reasons—leaving fur over joints and the chest while clipping elsewhere to reduce drag in water.
Poodles are recognized across multiple size categories—including Standard, Medium, Miniature, and Toy—while sharing the same core conformation and spirited intelligence.

faq.question: What is a Poodle?
faq.answer: The Poodle is a bright, agile, and affectionate dog breed originating in Western and Central Europe with roots in water retrieving, known for its curly or corded coat and multiple size varieties.

faq.question: How tall are Poodles?
faq.answer: Height at the withers depends on size variety: 45 to 62 cm for Standard, 35 to 45 cm for Medium, 28 to 35 cm for Miniature, and 24 to 28 cm for Toy Poodles.

faq.question: Do Poodles shed a lot, and how much grooming do they need?
faq.answer: Free household shedding is low because loose hair is held within the dense curly or corded coat, but grooming demand is high—requiring frequent brushing and combing plus regular trims to prevent matting.

faq.question: Can a Poodle live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes, if given daily walks, play, and mental enrichment suited to its size and energy level.

faq.question: Are Poodles easy to train?
faq.answer: Yes, Poodles are widely known for high intelligence and responsiveness to consistent, positive, reward-based training.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Poodle?
faq.answer: Key health topics include sebaceous adenitis, progressive retinal atrophy and other eye conditions, hip dysplasia or patellar luxation depending on size, endocrine disorders such as Addison's or Cushing's disease, and bloat in larger individuals.

overview.summary: An affectionate, robust, and highly intelligent pointing dog of Portuguese origin, renowned for its athletic stamina, short yellow coat, and supreme devotion as both an untiring bird hunter and a calm household companion.
overview.description: The Portuguese Pointer is a medium-sized, square-built, and harmonious sporting dog that radiates functional strength and rustic elegance. Designed to endure harsh terrain and long hours in the field, it possesses a deep chest, a sturdy back, and a remarkably solid bone structure. The breed is covered in a short, hard, and dense single coat—completely lacking an undercoat—that is typically found in beautiful shades of light, medium, or dark yellow, often accented by crisp white markings. Its distinct head features parallel planes, a broad skull, and large, expressive, oval-shaped brown eyes that reveal an incredibly docile, sweet, and highly intelligent nature. While it is a persistent, focused, and relentless worker outdoors, pointing staunchly at game, it transforms indoors into an exceptionally calm, quiet, and devoted family member that thrives on close human physical contact.
overview.history: Tracing its roots deep into the antiquity of the Iberian Peninsula, the Portuguese Pointer evolved alongside falconers as early as the twelfth century. In its homeland, the breed is famously known as the 'Perdigueiro Português'—a name directly derived from 'perdiz', meaning partridge, signifying its unmatched prowess in hunting this specific game bird. For centuries, it was an indispensable asset to local hunters and royal estates across Portugal. By the eighteenth century, the breed's reputation for keen scenting, steadfast pointing, and immense stamina drew the attention of British wine merchants trading in the region. It is widely documented that many of these dogs were exported to Great Britain, where they heavily influenced the development of the modern English Pointer. Despite facing challenges from modernization and shifting agricultural practices in the late nineteenth century, the breed was carefully preserved by dedicated Portuguese fanciers who formalized its written standard in the 1930s, ensuring this noble, rustic gundog continued to thrive.
overview.originalPurpose: Finding, scenting, and steadfastly pointing game birds—particularly partridge—for falconers and net hunters in the Portuguese countryside.
currentRoles: Versatile pointing and retrieving gundog
Canine athlete in field trials and scent work
Highly devoted household companion

physical.coatType: Short, hard, dense, and somewhat coarse single coat lying perfectly flat against the body, completely lacking an undercoat. The hair is noticeably finer and shorter on the head and ears.
coatColors: Yellow (fawn) in light, medium, or dark shades
Yellow featuring distinct white patches on the head, neck, chest, and lower limbs
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; the short single coat sheds consistently but is very easy to manage due to the lack of an undercoat
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tightly fitted, well-pigmented lips prevent excessive drooling
distinctiveFeatures: Solid, square-built, and harmonious frame where the length of the body equals the height at the withers
Height at the withers ideally 56 cm for males (limits 52 to 60 cm) and 52 cm for females (limits 48 to 56 cm)
Working weight ranging from 20 to 27 kg for males and 16 to 22 kg for females
Head characterized by parallel planes, a broad skull, and a distinct stop
Large, oval, and highly expressive eyes in shades of brown corresponding to the coat color
Drop ears that are thin, broad at the base, triangular with rounded tips, and hanging close to the cheeks
Complete and regular scissor bite
Deep, broad chest reaching down to the elbows, supporting excellent lung capacity
Short, broad, and slightly arched loin
Tail thick at the base and tapering toward the tip, carried horizontally or slightly raised in a gentle curve during action
Strong, well-boned limbs ending in round, tight toes with thick, dark pads

traits: Extremely affectionate, demonstrative, and deeply devoted to its human family
Highly intelligent, observant, and responsive to handler cues
Calm, docile, and remarkably unobtrusive when relaxing indoors
Energetic, focused, and persistent while working in the field
Sociable and gentle with children and familiar household members
Can be slightly reserved or aloof with strangers, but never sharp or aggressive
Eager to please, possessing a sensitive nature that thrives on positive guidance
Peaceable with other dogs when properly socialized

exercise.level: High; an athletic pointing breed that requires vigorous daily physical activity and mental stimulation, though it settles very calmly indoors afterward
activities: Daily brisk leashed walks or long trail hikes
Free running in a securely fenced, open field
Scent tracking, hunt tests, and interactive retrieving games
Canine sports including agility and rally obedience

grooming.brushing: Brush once a week using a soft bristle brush or a rubber hound glove to remove loose dead hairs, massage skin oils, and keep the coat bright and shining.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally when visibly soiled, using a mild canine shampoo to preserve the skin's natural protective oils.
notes: The short single coat is virtually self-cleaning and requires very little maintenance.
Inspect the drop ears weekly, wiping the canals gently with a veterinary-approved cleanser to prevent trapped moisture and infections.
Trim fast-growing nails every two to three weeks to maintain correct, tight foot alignment.
Brush teeth several times weekly with canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy; highly intelligent, naturally cooperative, and eager to please, making them highly responsive to positive reinforcement
tips: Use exclusively positive, reward-based training; they are deeply sensitive dogs that will shut down or become timid if yelled at or treated harshly.
Begin basic obedience and leash training early to build confidence and establish a strong communicative bond.
Channel their natural pointing and scenting instincts into structured play to keep their minds engaged.
Practice solid recall relentlessly to safely manage their strong hunting drive in unfenced rural areas.
training.socialization: Introduce the puppy early, gradually, and positively to diverse people, friendly dogs, and novel environments. Because they can be naturally reserved with strangers, proper early exposure ensures a confident, well-adjusted adult.

climates: Temperate climates
Warm climates, reflecting its Iberian Peninsula heritage, provided shade and fresh water are always available
Sensitive to extreme cold; the short single coat completely lacks an undercoat, so they require a warm dog jacket during freezing winter conditions
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low; they form incredibly deep, sensitive bonds with their human family and are prone to severe separation anxiety or depression if left isolated for long workdays without companionship.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for active medium-sized sporting breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support steady energy and digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations strictly using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup, adjusting amounts to maintain a lean, athletic body silhouette where the ribs are easily felt but not seen. Divide daily food into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous running immediately before and after eating, and provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a strictly lean, well-muscled body condition to minimize mechanical stress on the joints.
Account for training treats within the total daily caloric allowance to prevent obesity.
Increase protein and caloric density during active autumn hunting seasons or intense training periods.
Transition between diet formulas gradually over five to seven days to prevent gastrointestinal upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs vary significantly based on exercise intensity, age, and outdoor temperature. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The Portuguese Pointer is a highly robust, rustic, and athletic working breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years. Unspoiled by extreme cosmetic exaggerations, the breed generally enjoys excellent health. Primary health priorities focus on maintaining orthopedic soundness, preventing ear infections common to drop-eared dogs, and managing the dog's weight to protect joint longevity.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the coxofemoral joints leading to osteoarthritis and stiffness, monitored through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Elbow dysplasia — developmental abnormalities of the elbow joints that can cause forelimb lameness and secondary arthritis
Chronic otitis externa — bacterial and yeast ear infections promoted by drop ears that restrict canal ventilation and trap moisture
Ocular conditions — occasional reports of entropion (inward rolling eyelids) or ectropion (outward sagging eyelids), requiring veterinary monitoring
Traumatic outdoor injuries — minor cuts, sprains, or thorn punctures sustained during vigorous fieldwork in rough terrain
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding stock has certified radiographic clearances for hips and elbows, and specialist eye examinations.
Thoroughly clean and dry the drop ears after swimming, bathing, or wet weather walks to prevent moisture-induced ear infections.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition throughout life to minimize mechanical wear on joints.
Provide a warm dog jacket during freezing winter walks, as the breed lacks an insulating undercoat.
Administer consistent year-round parasite prevention against fleas, ticks, and heartworms, especially for dogs active in rural areas.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations, vaccinations, and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accredited national screening program prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong jaws with a complete scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the thin, triangular drop ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, or redness. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution, drying the leather thoroughly.
health.skinCare: Part the short, dense coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, ticks, or brush scratches. The single coat is very low maintenance and requires infrequent bathing.

idealFor: Active individuals and families seeking an exceptionally calm, gentle, and highly affectionate sporting companion
First-time dog owners willing to provide consistent daily exercise to a highly biddable, eager-to-please breed
Hunters or outdoor enthusiasts looking for a dedicated pointing and retrieving partner
Homes with a securely fenced yard providing ample space for supervised running
Owners who desire a deeply attached, short-coated dog that demands very little grooming
notIdealFor: Sedentary individuals looking for a low-maintenance, low-energy indoor lap dog
Apartment dwellers without access to extensive outdoor running space
Owners who leave a dog home alone in isolation for long workdays, risking separation anxiety and depression
Handlers who rely on harsh training methods or heavy-handed corrections
People seeking a fierce territorial guard dog

funFacts: In its native Portugal, the breed is known as the 'Perdigueiro Português'; the word 'perdigueiro' comes from 'perdiz', meaning partridge, highlighting the dog's historical specialty in hunting game birds.

The Portuguese Pointer is widely considered by canine historians to be a primary ancestor of the famous English Pointer, having been brought back to Britain by wine merchants in the eighteenth century.
The breed possesses a remarkable 'on/off switch', being a tireless, intensely focused hunter in the field, yet transforming into a remarkably calm, docile, and quiet companion inside the house.
Unlike many European pointing dogs, the Portuguese Pointer has absolutely no undercoat, which makes grooming incredibly easy but leaves them sensitive to freezing winter temperatures.
They are renowned for their highly demonstrative affection, often demanding physical contact and leaning against their owners to show devotion.

faq.question: What is a Portuguese Pointer?
faq.answer: The Portuguese Pointer (Perdigueiro Português) is a medium-sized, athletic pointing gundog from the Iberian Peninsula, famous for its short yellow coat, steadfast hunting ability, and incredibly affectionate, docile nature.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Portuguese Pointer?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 52 to 60 cm at the withers (ideal 56 cm) and weigh 20 to 27 kg. Adult females stand 48 to 56 cm (ideal 52 cm) and weigh 16 to 22 kg.

faq.question: How long does a Portuguese Pointer live?
faq.answer: With proper nutrition, regular rigorous exercise, and preventive veterinary care, the breed typically enjoys a healthy lifespan of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Do Portuguese Pointers shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They are low to moderate shedders. Their short, hard single coat has no undercoat, making grooming exceptionally easy—requiring only a quick weekly brush with a hound glove and very occasional baths.

faq.question: Can a Portuguese Pointer live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. While they are famously calm and quiet indoors, their high physical energy and need for vigorous daily exercise make them much better suited to a house with a securely fenced yard.

faq.question: Are Portuguese Pointers hard to train?
faq.answer: No, they are highly intelligent, cooperative, and eager to please, making them relatively easy to train. However, they are deeply sensitive and require gentle, positive reinforcement, as harsh corrections will damage their trust.

faq.question: Are Portuguese Pointers good family pets and good with children?
faq.answer: Yes, they are outstanding family pets. They are exceptionally docile, sweet-natured, and patient, making them wonderful, peaceable companions for children, provided they receive enough exercise.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Portuguese Pointer?
faq.answer: They are a very robust and healthy breed. Primary health concerns are limited to conditions common in many active sporting dogs, such as hip dysplasia and ear infections due to their drop ears.

overview.summary: A seafaring working companion developed along the rugged Atlantic shores of Portugal, the Portuguese Water Dog is renowned for its buoyant athleticism, webbed paws, and water-repellent single coat. Highly intelligent, affectionate, and spirited, it pairs a love for swimming and retrieving with a devoted, people-centered nature.
overview.description: Medium in stature with a robust, nearly square frame and powerful muscling, the Portuguese Water Dog is an aquatic athlete capable of a full day's work in surf and open sea. Its hair occurs in two natural varieties—tight cylindrical curls or gentle lustrous waves—completely lacking an undercoat and shedding very little hair into the home environment. Fully webbed toes and a strong, rudder-like tail provide propulsion and precise steering in rough water. In household life, the breed is famously friendly, eager to please, and deeply attached to its family circle, though its athletic stamina and keen intellect require structured daily exercise, interactive retrieving games, and consistent positive training to prevent boredom-driven mischief.
overview.history: Historically stationed aboard fishing trawlers along the coast of Portugal—most famously in the southern province of the Algarve—dogs of this ancient lineage served as versatile crew members. They plunged into the sea to herd fish into nets, retrieved lost tackle and overboard gear, guarded vessels in port, and swam courier messages between ships and coastal hamlets. When industrial fishing modernized in the early twentieth century, the breed faced near extinction until dedicated Portuguese preservationists gathered surviving working stock to re-establish the breed for international sport and companionship.
overview.originalPurpose: Assisting commercial fishermen along the Portuguese coast by herding fish into nets, retrieving lost tackle from the water, swimming couriers between boats, and guarding vessels in harbor.
currentRoles: Devoted family companion
Water rescue and water trials athlete
Agility, dock diving, and flyball competitor
Competitive obedience, rally, and tracking partner
Certified therapy and assistance dog
Conformation show competitor

physical.sizeCategory: Medium-sized, robust, squarely proportioned water dog
physical.coatType: Profuse, healthy single coat of strong hair lacking an undercoat, occurring in two distinct varieties: compact cylindrical curls with a lusterless texture, or hair falling gently in waves with a subtle sheen.
physical.coatLength: Continuously growing medium-to-long hair covering the entire body evenly, maintained in either a traditional lion clip (hindquarters and muzzle clipped close, leaving a full tail plume) or a practical all-over retriever clip.
physical.sheddingLevel: Low visible hair fallout; the single hair coat does not undergo seasonal undercoat blows, but loose strands remain trapped in curls or waves until removed through regular combing and professional clipping.
physical.droolingLevel: Low
distinctiveFeatures: Webbed skin between the toes extending to the tips, creating natural swimming paddles
Thick-based tail that tapers smoothly toward the tip, acting as an effective rudder in water
Two distinct natural coat varieties: compact cylindrical curls or loose flowing waves
Broad, domed topskull with a prominent central furrow and clean, heart-shaped drop ears
Traditional lion clip presentation or practical, uniform retriever clip
Bluish skin pigmentation under dark or white coat sections

traits: Intelligent and quick to learn
Spirited and energetic
Affectionate and devoted to family
Passionate swimmer and retriever
Eager to work cooperatively
Playful and enthusiastic
Alert watchdog manners
Naturally biddable yet occasionally self-willed

exercise.level: High
activities: Swimming, dock diving, and retrieving floating bumpers in safe water
Brisk daily neighborhood walks and off-leash romps in secure enclosures
Canine agility, flyball, and rally obedience courses
Interactive fetch, tug-of-war, and structured trick-training drills
Scent-work tracking puzzles and indoor food-dispensing games

grooming.brushing: Comb and line-brush down to the skin two to three times per week using a slicker brush and metal greyhound comb to prevent friction mats behind the ears, in the armpits, and around the thighs.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every 4 to 6 weeks or after ocean and lake swims, rinsing coat and skin thoroughly to remove chlorine or salt and blow-drying completely.
notes: Plan for professional or competent home clipping every 6 to 8 weeks in either the traditional lion clip or the retriever clip.
Rinse and dry the ear canals thoroughly after swimming sessions to prevent moisture-induced ear infections.
Check webbing between the toes for sand, debris, or small cuts after beach outings.
Trim nails every two to three weeks to maintain tight, functional foot structure.

training.difficulty: Moderate; exceptionally bright, eager to please, and responsive to praise, but possesses boundless energy and independent initiative if sessions become repetitive.
tips: Use positive, reward-based training with toys and high-value treats; avoid harsh or repetitive drills.
Teach reliable recall, loose-leash walking, and calm doorway manners from early puppyhood.
Provide constructive outlets for carrying items, as the breed naturally wants to hold objects in its mouth.
Introduce swimming and boat environments gradually with positive associations; never force a hesitant pup into deep water.
training.socialization: Provide ongoing positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, noisy public environments, and novel grooming tools throughout puppyhood to nurture an outgoing, steady adult temperament.

climates: Temperate and coastal climates
Cool climates with appropriate active exercise
Warm weather provided dogs have shade, fresh water, and access to cooling swim sessions
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply attached to family members and prone to separation anxiety or destructive chewing if left isolated for long hours without exercise.

nutrition.dietType: Nutritionally complete commercial kibble, wet food, or veterinary-formulated diet tailored to active, medium-sized sporting breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: 3 to 4 measured meals daily during growth, transitioning to 2 meals daily by six months of age
feedingFrequency.adult: 2 measured meals per day to maintain stable energy and lean muscle tone

nutrition.guidelines: Measure food portions accurately based on activity level and body condition score, regularly feeling the ribs and waist beneath the thick hair to prevent excess weight.
considerations: Avoid strenuous galloping or high-energy swimming immediately before and after meals.
Factor all training treats into the total daily caloric budget.
Provide clean, fresh water at all times, especially after swimming or rigorous exercise.
Consult a veterinarian if persistent digestive sensitivities, itching, or unexplained weight shifts occur.
nutrition.note: Caloric requirements vary with age, swimming workload, and metabolism; consult a veterinarian for personalized portion guidelines.

health.overview: The Portuguese Water Dog is generally a robust, active breed with an average lifespan of 10 to 15 years. Dedicated parent-club health programs emphasize pre-breeding DNA screening for inherited metabolic and ocular conditions—including GM-1 gangliosidosis, progressive retinal atrophy (prcd-PRA and EOPRA), microphthalmia, and juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy—alongside regular hip and eye evaluations.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: developmental laxity of the hip joints that can lead to osteoarthritis.
Progressive retinal atrophy (including prcd-PRA and early-onset EOPRA forms): inherited retinal degenerations causing progressive vision loss; detectable via DNA testing.
GM-1 gangliosidosis: a rare neurodegenerative lipid storage disease; controlled via established DNA screening.
Juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy (JDCM): a severe inherited heart-muscle failure in young dogs; preventable through genetic carrier screening.
Microphthalmia syndrome: a congenital developmental defect of the eyes.
Allergic skin disease and follicular dysplasia: sensitivities causing itching, hair thinning, or hot spots.
Hypoadrenocorticism (Addison's disease) and autoimmune thyroiditis.
Ear canal inflammation (otitis externa) related to moisture retention after swimming.
preventiveCare: Verify that puppy parents have certified DNA clearances for GM-1, prcd-PRA, EOPRA, and JDCM, plus certified hip and eye evaluations.
Dry ear canals carefully after swimming and clean weekly with veterinarian-approved solutions.
Maintain annual comprehensive veterinary checkups, core vaccinations, and routine parasite control.
Keep body condition lean to preserve joint health over years of active water sports.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation through an accepted screening scheme
Annual eye examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (CAER/CERF)
DNA test for GM-1 gangliosidosis (or verified clear by parentage)
DNA test for prcd-PRA and Early-Onset PRA (EOPRA)
DNA test for Juvenile Dilated Cardiomyopathy (JDCM)
DNA test for Microphthalmia syndrome

funFacts: Webbed toes with skin connecting the digits to the tips act as built-in swim fins, giving the breed incredible propulsion in heavy surf.
Two Portuguese Water Dogs, Bo and Sunny, famously served as the 'First Dogs' of the United States in the White House during President Barack Obama's administration.
A monk's chronicle written in 1297 contains the earliest historical account of a water dog rescuing a drowning sailor along the Portuguese coast.
The traditional lion clip was originally designed for working utility: clipping the rear legs gave swimming agility, while leaving chest hair protected vital organs from chilly Atlantic waters.
Their thick, rudder-like tails are carried high in a graceful curve when alert, acting as a steering paddle while diving and swimming.

faq.question: Where does the Portuguese Water Dog originate?
faq.answer: The Portuguese Water Dog originated along the Atlantic coast of Portugal, with strong historical roots in the southern Algarve region where fishermen relied on them as seafaring deckhands.

faq.question: How large do Portuguese Water Dogs get?
faq.answer: According to official measurements, males stand 50 to 57 cm at the withers and weigh 19 to 25 kg, while females measure 43 to 52 cm and weigh 16 to 22 kg.

faq.question: Are Portuguese Water Dogs hypoallergenic?
faq.answer: No dog is 100% hypoallergenic. However, because they have a single hair coat that does not shed an undercoat, they produce less dander fallout and are often well tolerated by people with mild pet allergies.

faq.question: What grooming do Portuguese Water Dogs require?
faq.answer: Their continuously growing coat requires line-brushing and combing several times weekly, along with professional clipping every 6 to 8 weeks in either a retriever clip or a lion clip.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Portuguese Water Dog need daily?
faq.answer: Healthy adults need 60 to 90 minutes of daily physical exercise and mental engagement. Swimming, fetch, agility, and dock diving are excellent outlets for their athletic energy.

faq.question: Are Portuguese Water Dogs good with children?
faq.answer: Yes, they are famously affectionate, playful, and friendly with family members and get along well with respectful children, though young puppies can be bouncy and benefit from supervision.

faq.question: What health tests should I look for in a Portuguese Water Dog?
faq.answer: Prospective owners should verify that both parents have certified hip and eye examinations, as well as DNA clearances for GM-1 gangliosidosis, prcd-PRA, EOPRA, and juvenile dilated cardiomyopathy (JDCM).

faq.question: Can a Portuguese Water Dog live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Their high athletic energy, working drive, and need for vigorous daily activity make them much better suited to homes with a securely fenced yard.

overview.summary: The Posavac Hound is a medium-sized Croatian scent hound built for endurance in the field. Recognizable by its rectangular frame, short reddish-wheaten coat, and crisp white markings, it pairs remarkable stamina and a resonant hunting voice with strong devotion to its handler. Prospective owners should plan for high scenting drive and daily outdoor activity.
overview.description: Muscular and slightly longer than tall at the withers, this sturdy hound moves with balanced, ground-covering efficiency. Its proportional head carries a broad skull, strong muzzle, dark brown oval eyes, and moderately long, rounded hanging ears. The dense, harsh, glossy coat comes in reddish-wheaten shades accented by clear white markings on the head, neck, chest, belly, lower legs, and tail tip. Gentle, lively, and eager to cooperate with familiar people, it can still lock onto an outdoor scent trail, making recall practice and secure lead management essential.
overview.history: An ancient Croatian hunting breed rooted in the Sava River valley (Posavina), the Posavac Hound traces back to red-and-white hounds depicted in a 1474 fresco, a 1719 manuscript, and nineteenth-century accounts by Franjo Bertić. Historically traded under the name 'boskini', dogs of this type were first exhibited in 1924, entered the Croatian stud book in 1929, and gained international recognition in 1955.
overview.originalPurpose: Scent hunting for hare, fox, and wild boar, as well as working as a leashed tracking hound.
currentRoles: Scent-hound hunting where lawful and appropriate

preventiveCare: Schedule regular veterinary exams and keep vaccinations and parasite prevention current.
Maintain a lean body condition and scale exercise to age and fitness.

health.earCare: Check hanging ears weekly for redness, odour, discharge, or head shaking. Clean gently with a veterinarian-approved solution only when needed.

faq.question: Where does the Posavac Hound originate?
faq.answer: It originates in Croatia, specifically the Posavina region along the Sava River valley.

faq.question: What was the Posavac Hound bred to do?
faq.answer: It was bred as a resilient scent hound for hunting hare, fox, and wild boar, and also excels as a leashed tracking hound.

faq.question: How tall is the Posavac Hound?
faq.answer: Adult males measure 50–56 cm at the withers and females measure 47–53 cm, with a ± 2 cm tolerance permitted for dogs of excellent type.

faq.question: How much does the Posavac Hound weigh?
faq.answer: Typical adult weight ranges from 16 to 25 kg, depending on sex, build, and conditioning.

faq.question: What does a Posavac Hound look like?
faq.answer: It is a medium-sized, rectangular hound with a short reddish-wheaten coat, crisp white markings, close-hanging rounded ears, and a sabre-shaped tail.

faq.question: Is the Posavac Hound easy to train?
faq.answer: Generally cooperative and devoted to its owner, it learns well with reward-based training, though strong scenting instincts make recall and long-line management important outdoors.

faq.question: What health problems is the breed known for?
faq.answer: No comprehensive breed-wide list of inherited conditions or formal screening protocol is established in consulted sources. Request parental health records from breeders and maintain regular veterinary check-ups.

overview.summary: A rugged, rough-coated, and exceptionally versatile German hunting pointer created strictly from hunting Poodles and English Pointers, blending keen open-field pointing speed and fearless cold-water retrieving with a calm, self-controlled, biddable character.
overview.description: The Pudelpointer is a dry, powerfully muscled, noble large German versatile gun dog whose conformation resembles a heavier, rough-coated Pointer built to conquer open plains, dense forests, and icy marshes alike. Nearly square in outline with a broad deep chest, short firm muscular back, and clean straight limbs, it moves with effortless range and endurance across demanding terrain. Its harmoniously proportioned head carries a pronounced stop, straight nasal bridge with a dark nose, large dark amber eyes radiating calm intelligence, medium-sized high-set hanging ears lying neatly against the cheeks, and distinctive rough facial furnishings—a strong beard, expressive bushy eyebrows, and a curling forelock. Wrapped in a closed, hard, flat-lying medium-length coat (4 to 6 cm at the withers) backed by a thick woolly undercoat in solid brown, dead-leaf, or black, the Pudelpointer shrugs off freezing water, rain, and thorny cover. Neither shy nor aggressive, it pairs intense upland pointing, tracking, and water-retrieving drive with an unusually calm, self-controlled, and eager-to-please nature—remaining primarily a dedicated hunting partner rather than a sedentary city companion.
overview.history: Unlike other rough-coated German pointing breeds, the Pudelpointer was crafted exclusively from two distinct foundation breeds—the traditional German hunting Poodle (Pudel) and the English Pointer—without any infusion from other pointing breeds. Beginning in 1881, German hunter and cynologist Sigismund Freiherr von Zedlitz und Neukirch (widely known by his pen name 'Hegewald') bred a black hunting Poodle bitch named Molly to a renowned English Pointer male named Tell, aiming to combine the Poodle's intelligence, love of water, retrieving passion, and protective coat with the Pointer's sensitive nose, fast ground-covering search, and rock-solid point. Although Poodles were used only during the initial foundation decades alongside a much larger number of Pointers, their water-working and retrieving traits remained permanently anchored in the breed. A dedicated German preservation society was founded in Darmstadt on July 17, 1897, definitive international recognition followed in November 1959, and German breeder Sigbot 'Bodo' Winterhelt introduced the first Pudelpointer to North America in 1956—helping shape modern North American versatile hunting dog testing. Even after targeted Pointer outcrosses in Germany during the 1980s before returning to pure breeding in 1990, the Pudelpointer has stayed comparatively rare and strictly working-focused worldwide.
overview.originalPurpose: Serving as a true all-purpose German versatile hunting dog—pointing upland game birds in open fields, tracking wounded game in forests, and retrieving waterfowl from cold lakes and marshes.
currentRoles: Versatile upland pointing, woodland tracking, and waterfowl retrieving gundog
Organised field-trial and hunting-test competitor
