overview.summary: A small, sinewy, and extraordinarily energetic French mountain herding dog from the Pyrenees, famed for its windswept facial hair, ground-skimming trot, and quick-witted devotion.
overview.description: The Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog packs remarkable stamina, agility, and intensity into a lean, light-boned, slightly rectangular frame. Its triangular head—reminiscent of a small bear or fox—features a flat skull, scarcely noticeable stop, and expressive dark almond eyes framed by black rims. Shorter hair along the end of the muzzle sweeps backward across the cheeks to produce a signature windswept look while leaving the eyes completely uncovered. Its dense long or semi-long coat blends coarse goat-like outer hair with woollier fur over the croup and thighs, occasionally forming natural cords called cadenettes or overlapping felted mats known as matelotes. In motion, this tireless little herder moves with a brisk, fluid trot that skims effortlessly across the ground. Fiercely devoted to its handler yet naturally suspicious of strangers, the breed thrives on constant mental engagement, vigorous exercise, and purposeful work alongside its owner.
overview.history: Emerging from humble pastoral roots in the high valleys of the French Pyrenees, the Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog remained largely unknown to formal dog circles until the early twentieth century. For generations, mountain shepherds relied on these agile, economical little herders to drive and gather flocks across steep alpine slopes, often working alongside the much larger Pyrenean Mountain Dog that guarded the sheep from predators. Because individual valleys remained isolated, coat length and build varied locally, yet the breed's resourceful, fearless herding temperament stayed remarkably uniform. During World War I, the French military recruited the breed in large numbers as liaison, search, and messenger dogs, valuing their speed, stealth, and independent initiative under fire. Formal written descriptions took shape between 1921 and 1925 and have changed very little since. Today, the Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog continues to herd flocks in its native mountains while excelling worldwide in agility, obedience, and herding sports.
overview.originalPurpose: Driving, gathering, and manoeuvring flocks of sheep independently across steep, rugged pastures in the Pyrenees Mountains.
currentRoles: Working sheep-herding dog
Elite agility, obedience, rally, and freestyle competitor
Alert household watchdog
Active companion for dedicated, sporty owners

physical.coatType: Long or semi-long, dense, almost flat or slightly wavy coat with a texture midway between goat hair and sheep wool. Hair is thicker and woollier on the croup and thighs—where it may naturally form cords (cadenettes) or overlapping felted plates (matelotes)—and shorter, windswept backward along the cheeks and muzzle without covering the eyes.
coatColors: Fawn (lighter or darker shades, with or without black overlay, occasionally with limited white on the chest and limbs)
Grey (lighter or darker shades, often with white on the head, chest, and limbs)
Harlequin or slate blue (blue mottled with black / merle)
Black, or black with limited white spotting (solid colours are preferred; black with tan points is not desired)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; the harsh outer coat sheds steadily and the woollier under-layers mat readily if not combed regularly
physical.droolingLevel: Low; thin, tight-fitting lips with black edges cover the lower jaw cleanly without loose corners
distinctiveFeatures: Small, lean, sinewy, and slightly rectangular silhouette (body length exceeds height at the withers)
Height at the withers of 42 to 48 cm for males and 40 to 46 cm for females (with a 2 cm tolerance either way for well-typed dogs)
Light-boned working weight typically ranging from 15 to 30 pounds
Triangular head with an almost flat skull, barely visible stop, and wedge-shaped muzzle
Shorter muzzle hair sweeping backward into a windswept facial frame that keeps the dark eyes clearly visible
Dark brown almond-shaped eyes with black eye rims regardless of coat colour (blue or wall eyes occur in harlequin/merle dogs)
Rather short, moderately broad-based ears set high; natural drop or semi-erect ears fold cleanly without hanging heavily
Moderately developed chest reaching to the elbow and a firm topline with prominent withers
Low-set, well-fringed tail of moderate length ending in a hooked tip, carried low or curving slightly forward when alert (natural bobtails also occur)
Low, effortless, ground-skimming trot ('shaving the earth') that conserves stamina across mountainous terrain
Coat capable of forming distinctive cords (cadenettes) or tile-like felted patches (matelotes) on the hindquarters

traits: Exceptionally lively, quick-witted, and brimming with nervous energy
Courageous, resourceful, and capable of independent initiative
Intensely devoted and closely attached to its primary handler
Alert, perceptive, and mischievous, making a sharp and vocal watchdog
Naturally wary and distrustful of unfamiliar strangers
Simultaneously headstrong and emotionally sensitive, requiring tactful yet firm guidance
Herds actively using nimble body movement and quick reactions rather than a quiet stare

exercise.level: Very high; a tireless mountain herder built to cover long distances across alpine slopes that requires substantial daily physical work and demanding mental challenges
activities: Fast-paced daily trail running, vigorous hiking, or off-leash work in safely enclosed rural spaces
High-speed canine sports including agility, obedience, rally, herding trials, and freestyle
Interactive scent-tracking games and advanced trick training
Structured fetch and body-awareness obstacle courses

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly at least once or twice weekly—paying special attention behind the ears, under the belly, and over the woollier hindquarters—to prevent tight mats unless deliberately maintaining separated cords (cadenettes).
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally with a mild canine shampoo; dry thoroughly down to the skin, especially if the coat is dense or corded, to prevent skin irritation.
notes: Never scissor the coat into a sculpted pet trim; the breed's rustic windswept texture should remain natural, with trimming limited to neatening the hair between the foot pads.
If allowing cords (cadenettes) to form on the hindquarters, separate them carefully by hand so they do not fuse into tight, painful skin-pulling mats.
Check the ears weekly for trapped hair, wax, or debris after outdoor runs.
Trim small, hard nails every two to three weeks.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging; whip-smart and deeply eager to work with its owner, yet headstrong and highly sensitive, punishing both lax indulgence and harsh corrections
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based methods such as clicker training, fast-paced games, and high-value treats; harsh scolding quickly undermines trust.
Establish calm, consistent boundaries from puppyhood—its mischievous charm makes it easy to spoil, which rapidly leads to pushy or noisy behaviour.
Channel its intense herding and chasing drive into structured dog sports so it does not herd joggers, bicycles, or running children.
Teach a dependable 'quiet' cue early to manage alert barking.
training.socialization: Thorough, positive, and continuous socialization from early puppyhood is non-negotiable. Because the breed is instinctively wary of strangers and sensitive to sudden sounds, gradual non-forced exposure to diverse people, calm dogs, and bustling environments prevents fearful reactivity.

climates: Cool and temperate mountain climates, where the dense, weather-resistant coat excels
Moderate climates with year-round outdoor access
Hot, humid climates are challenging; restrict heavy exercise to cool early mornings or evenings and provide reliable shade, ventilation, and cool drinking water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low; this is intensely a one-person or close-family working dog that tolerates solitude poorly and will very likely bark persistently or become destructive if left alone in an apartment or yard for long hours.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for small-to-medium, highly active working breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age to sustain rapid energy burn and steady bone growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to maintain steady blood sugar and athletic endurance.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adjusted for lower activity while preserving lean muscle mass.

nutrition.guidelines: Weigh or measure daily rations carefully to keep the dog lean and sinewy—ribs should remain easily palpable beneath the dense coat. Active herding or agility competitors burn far more calories than lightly exercised companions and require higher protein and energy density. Provide cool, fresh drinking water at all times.
considerations: Do not judge body condition by appearance alone; feel beneath the thick coat weekly so weight gain or loss does not go unnoticed.
Count all training treats inside the daily caloric budget, especially during intensive clicker-training sessions.
Avoid vigorous sprinting immediately before or after large meals.
Transition between food formulas gradually over five to seven days.
nutrition.note: Daily caloric needs vary widely depending on athletic workload, age, and ambient temperature. Consult a veterinarian to establish individual feeding quantities.

health.overview: The Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog is a remarkably hardy, long-lived working breed with a typical life expectancy of 17 to 19 years. While most individuals enjoy vigorous longevity, breeding-programme health data identifies specific orthopedic, ocular, cardiac, and neurological conditions—including hip dysplasia, patellar luxation, hereditary eye anomalies, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and epilepsy—that warrant conscientious pre-breeding screening.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia — developmental malformation and laxity of the hip joints that can progress to osteoarthritis, monitored closely through pre-breeding radiographic screening
Patellar luxation (or subluxation) — intermittent slipping of the kneecap out of the femoral groove, producing a skipping hind-limb gait
Hereditary eye diseases — congenital and late-onset ocular anomalies that can impair vision, monitored through early puppy eye checks (at 5 to 7 weeks) and annual specialist examinations
Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) — a congenital heart defect in which a foetal blood vessel fails to close after birth, screened via veterinary cardiac examination
Epilepsy — idiopathic seizure disorders reported in the breed, requiring long-term veterinary neurological management when present
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have certified radiographic hip clearances, clinical patella evaluations, recent specialist eye examinations, and cardiac clearances.
Ensure puppies receive a specialist veterinary eye examination between 5 and 7 weeks of age to catch congenital ocular anomalies early.
Keep the dog lean and well-muscled to reduce mechanical strain on the hips and kneecaps during high-speed agility and herding turns.
Maintain consistent year-round protection against ticks, fleas, heartworm, and internal parasites.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness check-ups and keep core vaccinations up to date.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Clinical patellar luxation orthopedic evaluation by a veterinarian
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (plus early puppy screening at 5 to 7 weeks of age)
Congenital or advanced cardiac evaluation by a veterinary cardiologist
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has strong jaws and a preferred scissor bite; regular veterinary dental checks help preserve tooth health well into its late teens.
health.earCare: Inspect the ears weekly for trapped coat hair, wax, redness, or moisture, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution.
health.skinCare: Part the dense double coat down to the skin weekly to check for tight mats, burrs, ticks, or skin irritation—especially across the woollier croup and thighs.

idealFor: Highly active, sporty individuals looking for a nimble partner in agility, obedience, rally, or herding
Experienced dog owners comfortable managing a sensitive, headstrong, and fiercely energetic herding temperament
Rural or suburban homes where the owner stays closely engaged with the dog throughout the day
Handlers prepared to invest consistent time in early socialization and natural long-coat maintenance
notIdealFor: First-time dog owners or passive handlers expecting an easygoing, low-maintenance lap dog
People who work long hours away from home and must leave a dog alone in an apartment or yard
Busy households with toddlers or frequent unfamiliar visitors unwilling to manage stranger wariness and heel-nipping herding instincts
Sedentary owners unable to commit to rigorous daily physical and mental exercise

funFacts: During World War I, the French Army recruited hundreds of Pyrenean Sheepdogs as courier and liaison dogs because their small size, speed, and independent wit enabled them to navigate muddy trenches and battlefields reliably.

In its native Pyrenees Mountains, the Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog traditionally worked as a team alongside the giant Pyrenean Mountain Dog: the agile little herder moved and gathered the flock while the massive mountain dog guarded it from wolves and bears.
The breed's dense coat over the hindquarters can naturally form distinctive rope-like strands called 'cadenettes' and overlapping tile-like felted plates called 'matelotes'.
When moving at a fast trot, the breed lowers its head level with its back and skims so close to the earth that French enthusiasts poetically say the dog 'shaves the ground.'
Despite its modest size, this hardy mountain sheepdog is one of the longest-lived herding breeds, frequently remaining active well into its late teens.

faq.question: What is a Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog?
faq.answer: The Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog (Chien de Berger des Pyrénées à poil long) is a small, agile, and fiercely energetic herding dog from the French Pyrenees Mountains, recognizable by its dense wavy coat, windswept facial hair, and intense devotion to its handler.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 42 to 48 cm at the withers and females stand 40 to 46 cm, with a 2 cm tolerance for well-typed dogs. Working weight typically ranges between 15 and 30 pounds, maintaining a lean, sinewy frame.

faq.question: How long does a Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog live?
faq.answer: This hardy mountain breed is remarkably long-lived, with a typical lifespan of 17 to 19 years when given proper nutrition, daily activity, and preventive veterinary care.

faq.question: Is the Pyrenean Sheepdog the same breed as the Great Pyrenees?
faq.answer: No. Although both originated in the Pyrenees Mountains and historically worked together on the same flocks, the Pyrenean Sheepdog is a small, fast herding dog whereas the Great Pyrenees (Pyrenean Mountain Dog) is a giant white livestock guardian.

faq.question: Can a Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Although small enough physically, this breed is far happier in active rural or suburban settings and will almost certainly bark excessively or become destructive if left alone in an apartment without intensive daily outdoor work.

faq.question: How much grooming does the long-haired coat need?
faq.answer: The dense long or semi-long coat should be brushed and combed at least once or twice a week to prevent tight matting—especially over the woollier croup and thighs—unless the owner deliberately maintains hand-separated cords (cadenettes).

faq.question: Are Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdogs good with strangers and children?
faq.answer: They are naturally wary of strangers and require thorough early socialization. With families, they do best alongside older, respectful children, as their quick herding instinct may lead them to chase or nip at running toddlers.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Long-Haired Pyrenean Sheepdog?
faq.answer: While generally robust and long-lived, the breed is screened for hip dysplasia, slipping kneecaps (patellar luxation), inherited eye disorders, congenital heart defects such as patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), and epilepsy.

overview.summary: The Rafeiro do Alentejo is a massive, self-assured Portuguese livestock guardian native to the sun-drenched plains of the Alentejo. Revered for its imposing bone, deliberate demeanor, and innate defensive vigilance, this ancient guardian combines quiet domestic tranquility with unyielding territorial dedication.
overview.description: Substantial, rustic, and powerfully proportioned, the Rafeiro do Alentejo carries a broad head with a gentle convex profile, small folded ears, and a dense, straight protective coat. Its rectangular frame, deep chest, and low-set tail convey formidable strength. Despite its imposing physical stature, it projects a self-assured, tranquil demeanor rather than nervous aggression or timidity. While peaceful and tolerant around familiar charges, its profound territorial awareness prompts immediate vigilance when strange animals or unfamiliar visitors approach. The breed possesses an independent intellect shaped by centuries of autonomous decision-making in the field. Consequently, successful stewardship demands extensive secure fencing, early desensitization, and patient, positive handling by experienced guardian-breed caretakers.
overview.history: Rooted in the agricultural heritage of southern Portugal, the Rafeiro do Alentejo descended from ancient Iberian pastoral molossers that accompanied nomadic herds along transhumance trails. Flocks shifted seasonally between highland summer pastures in central Portugal and winter plains in the Alentejo, exposing traveling livestock to wolves and large predators. Large guardian dogs guarded these trekking herds, establishing a unified rustic type along regional migration routes. By the late nineteenth century, rural estate owners formalized the regional name, valuing the dogs as night sentinels and flock protectors. Formal breed documentation confirms Portugal as its country of origin and celebrates its enduring role as a steadfast protector of livestock and rural estates.

tips: Initiate structured, positive reinforcement training during early puppyhood before rapid physical growth creates management challenges.

Introduce household guests under controlled, calm protocols without allowing unmonitored territorial entry.
training.socialization: Implement comprehensive, gentle socialization across early development, acquainting the pup with diverse sounds, footing surfaces, livestock, vehicles, and peaceful neutral strangers to nurture stable confidence without degrading legitimate guardian discernment.

nutrition.guidelines: Divide the daily caloric ration into two measured meals for adults to reduce gastric expansion risks. Provide fresh, clean drinking water at all times. considerations: Feed growing puppies diets formulated specifically for giant breeds to moderate growth velocity and support healthy skeletal mineralization.

Monitor adult weight vigilantly to preserve lean body condition and protect hip and elbow joints.

health.overview: The Rafeiro do Alentejo is an unexaggerated, robust working breed with an average lifespan of 12 to 14 years. As with other giant, deep-chested pastoral breeds, developmental joint conditions such as hip and elbow dysplasia, as well as acute gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), represent primary clinical considerations. Dedicated screening of breeding stock promotes long-term orthopedic soundness.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia
Elbow dysplasia

preventiveCare: Schedule yearly wellness checkups, advancing to semiannual veterinary exams during senior years.
Ensure puppies maintain slow, steady growth on controlled-energy diets to safeguard developing joints.
Discuss preventative gastropexy surgery with a veterinarian to protect against fatal gastric volvulus.
Seek emergency veterinary attention immediately if non-productive retching, abdominal distension, restlessness, or sudden collapse appears.
Maintain active parasite control, routine core immunizations, and oral dental prophylaxis.
recommendedScreenings: Hip radiographic evaluation

health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using pet-safe enzymatic toothpaste, scheduling periodic professional ultrasonic scaling during routine physical exams.
health.earCare: Examine folded ear canals weekly for redness, trapped plant matter, or yeasty odors, cleansing with an approved canine drying rinse as necessary.
health.skinCare: Part the dense coat regularly during grooming to check skin condition, inspecting for hot spots, ticks, or irritation after time in high pasture grass.

funFacts: The breed derives its name from the Alentejo province, a sweeping agricultural region occupying south-central Portugal.
Historically, these dogs accompanied livestock along seasonal migration routes called transhumance trails, defending flocks from wolves and bandits.
Unlike many herd-driving dogs that run constantly, this guardian conserves energy by resting quietly during daylight and assuming heightened alert vigilance after sunset.
Its characteristic gait is heavy and measured, displaying a distinctive rolling motion without exaggerated looseness.
The head possesses a distinctly convex profile and small folded ears, leading local shepherds to affectionately compare its profile to that of a bear.

faq.question: Where did the Rafeiro do Alentejo originate?
faq.answer: The breed originated in Portugal, particularly across the southern Alentejo plains, where it guarded moving flocks along historical transhumance routes between mountains and lowlands.

faq.question: How large does a Rafeiro do Alentejo get?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 66–74 cm at the withers and weigh 45–60 kg, while adult females measure 64–70 cm and weigh 35–50 kg.

faq.question: What was the breed's traditional working role?
faq.answer: It was bred as a steadfast livestock and property guardian, defending herds against apex predators such as wolves and guarding rural estates against nocturnal intruders.

faq.question: Can a Rafeiro do Alentejo thrive in an apartment?
faq.answer: No, this giant guardian is unsuited to apartment life; it requires substantial outdoor space, secure fencing, and a tranquil environment appropriate for its protective instincts.

faq.question: How does the breed react to strangers?
faq.answer: Naturally sober, watchful, and reserved, the breed assesses unfamiliar people with detached vigilance; it requires controlled introductions and does not welcome unannounced trespassers into its territory.

faq.question: How much exercise does it require each day?
faq.answer: A steady routine of approximately 45 to 60 minutes of low- to moderate-impact daily activity—such as leashed neighborhood walks and perimeter patrols around a securely enclosed acreage—helps maintain joint health and muscle tone without overtaxing heavy bones.

faq.question: What coat colors are typical for this breed?
faq.answer: Recognised coat shades include black, wolf grey, fawn, and yellow—either solid or brindled—always complemented by white markings, as well as white coats marked with patches of these colors.

faq.question: What health considerations should owners monitor?
faq.answer: Primary health priorities include screening for developmental hip and elbow dysplasia, managing bloat risk through proper feeding routines, and maintaining a lean, healthy adult body weight.

overview.summary: A compact, hard-muscled, and endlessly inquisitive American farm terrier offered in Miniature and Standard sizes, blending fearless vermin-hunting speed and dog-sport versatility with affectionate, easygoing family devotion.
overview.description: The Rat Terrier—fondly called the 'Rattie'—is a sturdy, athletic, smooth-coated American working terrier combining sleek elegance with tough, farm-ready grit. Built in two size divisions—Miniature (10 to 13 inches) and Standard (over 13 up to 18 inches)—it balances moderate bone and flat, hard musculature beneath taut skin, with chest depth at the elbow matching the leg length from elbow to ground. Its smooth, blunt wedge-shaped head features flat well-muscled cheeks, a moderate distinct stop, a strong tapering muzzle just shorter than the skull, tight lips, wide-set oblique oval eyes, and expressive matching ears carried erect, semi-erect and tipped, or button. Clad in a short, glossy, close-lying coat wearing crisp pied patterning in shades such as black, chocolate, red, apricot, or blue with white (and often warm tan points), the Rat Terrier carries a docked tail, natural bobtail, or tapered full tail without preference. Less combative than many traditional sparring terriers, it is bright, devoted, playful, and eager to please its family—excelling equally as a lively backyard companion, barn-hunt exterminator, or agile canine-sports competitor.
overview.history: An unmistakable American original, the Rat Terrier took shape across nineteenth-century family farms in the United States, where grain storage and henhouses depended on swift, fearless rodent hunters. Rural breeders combined small working terriers brought by British immigrants—such as early Smooth Fox Terriers, Manchester Terriers, and Old English White Terriers—with American feists and occasional crosses to faster or keen-scented breeds like Whippets and Beagles to enhance speed, agility, and hunting versatility. Popular folklore credits President Theodore Roosevelt with popularizing the 'Rat Terrier' name, and the breed became a fixture on American farms throughout the 1920s and 1930s before mechanized agriculture and chemical pest control reduced rural numbers. Historically, litters produced both longer-legged dogs ('Type A') and shorter-legged, heavier-boned dogs ('Type B'); in 1999, the shorter-legged variety became a separate breed named the Teddy Roosevelt Terrier, while a recessive natural hairless mutation born in a Rat Terrier litter in Louisiana later founded the American Hairless Terrier. Full American terrier-group recognition arrived in 2013, cementing the Rat Terrier's modern revival as a versatile family companion and dog-sport star.
overview.originalPurpose: Exterminating rats and other farm vermin, hunting small game, guarding henhouses and homesteads, and serving as a sturdy, multipurpose family farm companion.
currentRoles: Devoted, playful family and apartment companion
Versatile dog-sports competitor (agility, lure coursing, barn hunt, rally, obedience, and earthdog)
Alert household watchdog and small-farm ratter
Therapy dog

physical.coatType: Short, close-lying, smooth, shiny single coat over taut skin. Texture varies slightly, and a very faint ruff or wave along the back is permitted though undesirable; any kink, curl, or genetic hairlessness is unacceptable, and whiskers are never removed.
coatColors: Any variation of pied patterning—comparatively large patches of one or more colours combined with white—including predominantly black, chocolate, red, apricot, lemon, pearl/fawn, or blue, with or without tan points (cream to rust)
Extreme piebald 'solid white' coat showing mottled or spotted skin pigment

Badger markings, light speckling/ticking/mottling, and sabling are acceptable (solid non-white coats, bicolours without at least a one-inch white patch or strip, brindle, and merle patterns are disqualified)
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; the short, close-lying smooth coat sheds fine hairs steadily throughout the year with moderate seasonal increases
physical.droolingLevel: Low; clean, tight lips matching nose pigment or pink on flat cheeks and a dry arched neck keep drooling minimal
distinctiveFeatures: Compact, flexible, hard-muscled working terrier with moderate bone—neither rangy/toyish nor bulky/coarse—and body depth at the elbow matching elbow-to-ground height
Two distinct size divisions measured at the withers: Miniature (10 to 13 inches) and Standard (over 13 up to 18 inches); dogs over six months below 10 inches or above 18 inches are disqualified
Adult weight typically ranging from 10 to 25 pounds across both size divisions
Smooth, blunt wedge-shaped head widening gradually toward the ear base with flat well-muscled cheeks, moderate distinct stop, strong tapering muzzle just shorter than the skull, and tight clean lips
Fully pigmented nose matching body colour (seasonal fading allowed) and strong teeth meeting in a scissor bite (level bite acceptable)
Obliquely set, wide-apart oval eyes (not large) ranging from darkest brown to hazel in harmony with coat (grey eyes allowed in blue or blue-fawn dogs only; any blue eye colour is disqualified)
Matching ears set on line with the outer eye corner and carried erect, semi-erect and tipped, or button without preference (rose ears faulted; cropped ears disqualified)
Level firm back, short slightly arched muscular loin, moderately wide chest with discernible forechest, well-bent stifles, and oval compact toes with thick pads and strong nails
Tail set as a continuation of the spine—customarily docked between the second and third joint, born as a natural bobtail, or left naturally long tapering to the hock (length is unimportant)
Short, smooth, shiny pied coat with intact whiskers (genetic hairlessness, kinks, curls, brindle, and merle are disqualified)

traits: Keenly observant, curious, lively, playful, and full of energetic zest
Loving, deeply loyal, and devoted to its immediate family, craving regular time alongside its people
Generally friendlier and less combative with other dogs than traditional sparring terriers (a non-sparring breed, though supervised introductions remain wise)
Smart, responsive, and noticeably more eager to please and obedient to command than many harder-headed terriers
Alert and watchful around the home, barking mainly to announce visitors or unusual activity rather than incessantly
May be naturally reserved around unfamiliar strangers while remaining free of overt aggression or extreme shyness
Retains a fierce, fast-reacting vermin-chasing and digging drive outdoors toward rodents, squirrels, and small prey

exercise.level: Moderate to high; a sturdy, energetic farm terrier that thrives on brisk daily walks, vigorous play sessions, and stimulating dog sports while happily settling indoors beside its family afterward
activities: Brisk daily neighbourhood or trail walks on a secure leash
High-tempo canine sports including agility, lure coursing, barn hunt, rally, obedience, and earthdog trials
Interactive fetch, tug, and food-puzzle or scent-search games
Supervised vigorous running inside a securely fenced, dig-proof yard

grooming.brushing: Minimal coat upkeep—brush once a week with a rubber curry mitt or soft bristle brush to lift loose fine hairs and keep the short, smooth coat glossy.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only occasionally when visibly muddy or dusty from yard play or digging, using a mild canine shampoo.
notes: Never trim or remove the facial whiskers.
Inspect the erect, tipped, or button ears weekly for wax buildup, dirt, or redness.
Trim strong nails every two to three weeks so the compact oval feet stay neat and balanced.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste, as smaller terriers accumulate dental tartar readily.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate; clever, inquisitive, and eager to please, making it highly trainable for obedience and agility—though classic terrier curiosity and strong rodent-chasing drive demand secure containment and engaging sessions
tips: Begin consistent, upbeat basic obedience in early puppyhood using small treats, toys, and praise; Rat Terriers learn new cues rapidly and thrive on clear household routines.
Never allow an untrained Rat Terrier off-leash near unfenced roads or wildlife—its lightning-fast vermin-chasing instinct can send it darting after a squirrel or rabbit immediately.
Channel intense curiosity and digging energy into structured sports like barn hunt, agility, lure coursing, or scent puzzles.
Keep fences snug along the ground edge to discourage adventurous digging.
training.socialization: Generous, positive early exposure to varied strangers, public places, friendly dogs, and respectful children ensures its natural reserve around newcomers stays calm and confident.

climates: Temperate and four-season climates—adaptable across urban apartments, suburban homes, and rural farms
Warm sunny climates require shade, cool fresh drinking water, and sun protection over pale white-coated areas with minimal hair cover
Cold winter weather calls for a snug dog sweater or jacket on walks, as the short single coat offers limited insulation against freezing temperatures
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply bonded to its household and happiest spending active and relaxed time alongside its family, a bored Rat Terrier left alone all day can turn to digging, chewing, or alert barking.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced small-to-medium adult dog food suited to an active terrier.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age to support steady energy and balanced musculoskeletal growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily on a consistent schedule to maintain hard-muscled working condition.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for slower metabolism, dental comfort, and joint and cardiac wellness.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately with a scale or measuring cup to preserve the Rat Terrier's lean, hard-muscled silhouette without excess body fat—keeping weight strictly controlled protects kneecaps, hip joints, and heart health across its long 12- to 18-year lifespan. Count all training treats inside the daily caloric budget and provide clean fresh water continuously.
considerations: Match kibble size and caloric intake to whether the dog is a smaller Miniature (near 10 pounds) or a larger Standard (up to 25 pounds).
Maintain a lean body condition throughout life to minimise strain on patellas and hips.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric requirements vary substantially between 10-pound Miniatures and 25-pound athletic Standards. Consult a veterinarian to tailor daily portions.

health.overview: The Rat Terrier is generally a hardy, vigorous, and remarkably long-lived breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 18 years. Responsible breeding programmes actively screen for four core hereditary priorities: clinical patellar luxation, hip dysplasia (alongside developmental Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease in smaller lines), cardiac disease (ideally evaluated by a board-certified veterinary cardiologist), and autosomal-recessive Primary Lens Luxation (PLL, linked to ADAMTS17 and completely preventable via pre-breeding DNA testing). Additional health considerations include hereditary eye conditions monitored via specialist exams (and optional prcd-PRA DNA testing), elbow evaluations, and a peer-reviewed autosomal-recessive thyroid peroxidase (TPO c.331C>T) mutation shared with Toy Fox Terriers that causes congenital hypothyroidism with goiter (CHG) and central nervous system hypomyelination in affected puppies—also preventable via DNA screening.
commonConditions: Primary Lens Luxation (PLL, ADAMTS17-related) — an inherited weakness of the zonular eye ligaments causing painful dislocation of the lens, uveitis, and potentially blinding secondary glaucoma (typically surfacing between 4 and 8 years of age); completely preventable in breeding programmes through mandatory pre-breeding DNA testing
Patellar luxation — intermittent slipping of the kneecap out of the femoral groove, a well-known small-terrier orthopaedic concern actively evaluated prior to breeding

Hip dysplasia and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease — developmental hip-joint laxity (with one North American radiographic registry dataset showing 93.2% normal and 6.8% dysplastic/borderline across 74 evaluated dogs—a screened cohort rather than universal prevalence) alongside aseptic femoral-head necrosis in young small terriers

Cardiac disease — congenital or acquired heart murmurs and structural cardiac conditions prompting pre-breeding veterinary cardiac evaluations (with cardiologist exams preferred by knowledgeable breeders)

Congenital Hypothyroidism with Goiter (CHG, TPO-related) — a rare autosomal-recessive thyroid-hormone synthesis defect documented in peer-reviewed veterinary pathology research in Rat Terriers (caused by the TPO c.331C>T; p.Arg111* nonsense mutation shared with Toy Fox Terriers), leading to neonatal goiter, stunted growth, and CNS hypomyelination; preventable via DNA testing

Hereditary eye disorders (including prcd-PRA) and occasional allergies or dental disease — ocular conditions monitored via specialist veterinary ophthalmologist exams and elective DNA screening alongside routine small-terrier dental and skin care
preventiveCare: Insist on documented public pre-breeding clearances for both parents (bred at age 2 or older): clinical patellar luxation evaluation, radiographic hip (and ideally elbow) evaluations, veterinary cardiac exam (cardiologist preferred), specialist veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination, and DNA testing for Primary Lens Luxation (PLL)—plus elective DNA tests for prcd-PRA and TPO congenital hypothyroidism with goiter.
Keep the dog lean and well-muscled throughout its long lifespan to minimise stress on kneecaps and hips.
Brush teeth several times weekly, check ears weekly, and maintain core vaccinations and year-round parasite prevention.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations (semi-annually in senior years), watching promptly for any sudden eye redness, cloudiness, or squinting.
recommendedScreenings: Clinical patellar luxation orthopedic evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding (at 24 months of age or older; Legg-Calvé-Perthes screening in smaller lines)
Cardiac examination (preferably by a board-certified veterinary cardiologist)
DNA test for Primary Lens Luxation (PLL / ADAMTS17)
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist, plus elective radiographic elbow evaluation and DNA tests for prcd-PRA and Congenital Hypothyroidism with Goiter (TPO)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental cleanings to protect the strong jaws, scissor or level bite, and gums.
health.earCare: Inspect the erect, tipped, or button ears weekly for wax buildup, dirt, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Check the taut skin beneath the short, glossy coat regularly after yard play or digging for ticks, scrapes, allergies, or sunburn on pale white skin areas.

idealFor: Active singles, couples, families with respectful children, and energetic seniors wanting a portable, sturdy, affectionate, and long-lived American terrier
Apartment or house dwellers able to provide 45 to 60 minutes of daily brisk walks, interactive play, and secure leash/yard safety
Committed first-time dog owners looking for an eager-to-please, low-grooming, non-sparring terrier that responds rapidly to positive training
Dog-sport fans eager to try agility, lure coursing, barn hunt, rally, obedience, or earthdog trials
notIdealFor: Homes with free-roaming pet rodents, hamsters, rabbits, or small caged animals given its hardwired ratting drive
Owners wanting an off-leash hiker in unfenced wildlife areas or unwilling to dig-proof a backyard fence
Households leaving a deeply social, curious companion alone for long workdays without mental stimulation
Outdoor-only or freezing-kennel environments without cosy indoor shelter

funFacts: Popular American lore credits President Theodore Roosevelt—an admirer of hardy farm ratters—with giving the Rat Terrier its plain-spoken name, and when the breed's shorter-legged 'Type B' variety became a separate breed in 1999, it was named the Teddy Roosevelt Terrier in his honour.

The Rat Terrier is the direct parent breed of the American Hairless Terrier, which began from a single naturally hairless female puppy named Josephine born into a purebred Rat Terrier litter in Louisiana in 1972.
Unlike many traditional show terriers that are bred to spar head-to-head in the ring, the Rat Terrier is explicitly a non-sparring breed noted for being far friendlier with other dogs.
Every recognized Rat Terrier displays pied patterning (or extreme piebald white over spotted skin), while solid non-white coats, brindle, merle, curls, and genetic hairlessness are all excluded.
Rat Terriers are remarkably long-lived for a working terrier, routinely enjoying active lives of 12 to 18 years.

faq.question: What is a Rat Terrier?
faq.answer: The Rat Terrier ('Rattie') is a compact, athletic, smooth-coated American working terrier developed on nineteenth-century farms for rodent control and all-around companionship, known for its pied coat, keen curiosity, and friendly, trainable nature.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Rat Terrier?
faq.answer: The breed comes in two size divisions measured at the withers: Miniature (10 to 13 inches) and Standard (over 13 up to 18 inches). Adults typically weigh between 10 and 25 pounds across both divisions.

faq.question: How long does a Rat Terrier live?
faq.answer: Rat Terriers are notably long-lived, with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 18 years when kept lean and supported with routine veterinary care.

faq.question: Can a Rat Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes. Both Miniature and Standard Rat Terriers adapt well to apartment living as long as they receive 45 to 60 minutes of brisk daily walks, interactive games, and mental stimulation.

faq.question: Are Rat Terriers good with children, other dogs, and small pets?
faq.answer: They make sturdy, playful companions for families with respectful children and are generally friendlier with other dogs than many sparring terriers (with supervision). However, because of their strong vermin-hunting drive, they should not be trusted loose around pet rodents, rabbits, or similar small animals.

faq.question: How much grooming and shedding should I expect from a Rat Terrier?
faq.answer: Grooming is minimal: weekly brushing with a rubber mitt or soft brush manages moderate shedding and keeps its short, smooth, glossy coat clean, with baths only when dirty, regular nail trims, weekly ear checks, and frequent toothbrushing. Never trim its whiskers.

faq.question: Are Rat Terriers easy to train?
faq.answer: Yes—they are bright, inquisitive, and noticeably eager to please, excelling in agility, lure coursing, barn hunt, rally, and obedience with upbeat positive training. Consistent boundaries and secure leashes or fences are essential to manage their strong chasing and digging instincts.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Rat Terrier?
faq.answer: Generally a very healthy breed, its key documented health screening priorities include Primary Lens Luxation (PLL / ADAMTS17, preventable via DNA testing), patellar luxation, hip dysplasia, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, cardiac disease, hereditary eye conditions, and rare DNA-screenable Congenital Hypothyroidism with Goiter (TPO).

overview.summary: A powerful, athletic southern African hound distinguished by the symmetrical ridge of reverse-growing hair along its spine, great endurance, dignified reserve with strangers, and deep loyalty to its family.
overview.description: The Rhodesian Ridgeback is a handsome, muscular, symmetrically built hound combining high endurance with agile speed on a clean, slightly rectangular frame. Its unmistakable trademark is the dorsal ridge—a well-defined band of hair growing forward along the back, beginning directly behind the shoulders with two matching opposite whorls (crowns) and tapering neatly toward the hips. The short, dense, glossy coat spans wheaten shades from pale flaxen to deep red wheaten, paired with either a black nose and dark eyes or a brown (liver) nose and amber eyes. A flat skull, moderate stop, strong muzzle, clean tight lips, and high-set medium drop ears frame a calm, intelligent expression. Outdoors, it is a bold, fast-moving athlete with keen hunting drive; indoors, it is typically composed, affectionate, and quietly watchful.
overview.history: The only registered breed indigenous to southern Africa, the Rhodesian Ridgeback arose in the Cape Colony when early European settlers crossed their hunting and guardian dogs—including Greyhounds, Mastiffs, Terriers, and Great Danes—with the semi-domesticated ridged hunting dogs of the indigenous Khoikhoi people. In the late nineteenth century, big-game hunter Cornelius van Rooyen further refined these versatile hounds in Matabeleland (modern Zimbabwe) to track game in small packs of two or three and hold lions at bay through agile harassment—never attacking directly—until the hunter arrived. In 1922, breeder Francis Richard Barnes gathered enthusiasts in Bulawayo to draft the breed's first formal description, modeling its balanced proportions on the Dalmatian, with regional kennel approval following in 1926. Today the breed is prized worldwide as a devoted family companion, watchdog, and canine athlete.

health.overview: The Rhodesian Ridgeback is generally a healthy, sturdy hound with a typical lifespan of 10 to 12 years. Scientifically established inherited conditions in the breed include dermoid sinus (a congenital neural-tube skin defect linked to the 133-kilobase duplication of FGF3, FGF4, FGF19, and ORAOV1 that produces the dorsal ridge), Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (caused by a recessive 4-bp deletion in DIRAS1), and Early Onset Adult Deafness (associated with an autosomal recessive 12-bp deletion in EPS8L2). Other monitored or reported conditions include hip and elbow dysplasia, autoimmune thyroiditis, degenerative myelopathy (SOD1), hereditary eye anomalies, and gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat).
commonConditions: Dermoid sinus — scientifically established congenital neural-tube defect linked to the FGF3/FGF4/FGF19/ORAOV1 ridge duplication, forming a tubular tract along the dorsal midline that can become infected; puppies must be palpated carefully at birth

Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME) — scientifically established autosomal recessive seizure disorder caused by a 4-bp deletion in the DIRAS1 gene, producing myoclonic twitches and photosensitivity in young dogs; screenable via DNA testing
Early Onset Adult Deafness (EOAD) — scientifically established autosomal recessive hearing loss associated with a 12-bp in-frame deletion in the EPS8L2 gene; screenable via DNA testing
Hip dysplasia — monitored developmental malformation of the hip joint screened via pre-breeding radiographs
Elbow dysplasia — monitored developmental elbow abnormality screened via pre-breeding radiographs
Autoimmune thyroiditis — monitored immune-mediated thyroid disorder causing hypothyroidism, evaluated via blood antibody panels
Degenerative myelopathy (DM) — inherited late-onset spinal cord degeneration linked to the SOD1 variant, screenable via DNA testing
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) — reported acute emergency in deep-chested large breeds requiring immediate veterinary care
Hereditary eye anomalies — monitored through periodic veterinary ophthalmologist examinations
preventiveCare: Choose puppies from parents with verified hip, elbow, thyroid, and eye clearances plus DNA testing for JME, EOAD, and DM.
Ensure every puppy is palpated thoroughly along the neck, back, and tail base by an experienced breeder or veterinarian for dermoid sinus.
Feed two measured meals daily, keep body condition lean, and rest the dog before and after meals to help reduce bloat risk.
Check ears weekly, maintain nail length with a grinder or clippers, and schedule annual veterinary wellness visits.
recommendedScreenings: Physical palpation for dermoid sinus in puppies and breeding stock
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
DNA test for Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (DIRAS1 mutation)
DNA test for Early Onset Adult Deafness (EPS8L2 deletion)
Autoimmune thyroiditis blood panel and periodic veterinary ophthalmologist eye examination

funFacts: The breed's trademark dorsal ridge comes from a 133-kilobase genetic duplication spanning three fibroblast growth factor genes (FGF3, FGF4, and FGF19) along with ORAOV1, inherited from the ancient ridged dogs of the Khoikhoi people.
Despite its nickname 'African Lion Hound,' the breed never killed lions—small packs of two or three dogs used speed and agility to keep a lion at bay until the hunter arrived.
When Francis Richard Barnes drafted the first formal breed description in Bulawayo in 1922, he modeled its balanced proportions on the Dalmatian.
Hollywood actor Errol Flynn became the first breeder of Rhodesian Ridgebacks in the United States during the 1930s on his California ranch.
Although bred for endurance across the African veld, Ridgebacks are famous for lounging happily on warm sofas indoors once exercised—and for cleverly counter-surfing unattended food.
Rhodesian Ridgebacks appear in shades of wheaten with two distinct nose types: a black nose paired with dark eyes, or a less common brown (liver) nose paired with amber eyes.

faq.question: What is a Rhodesian Ridgeback?
faq.answer: The Rhodesian Ridgeback is a large, muscular hound indigenous to southern Africa, recognized by the symmetrical strip of backward-growing hair along its spine, its big-game tracking heritage, and its dignified, loyal nature.

faq.question: What causes the ridge on a Rhodesian Ridgeback's back?
faq.answer: The ridge is a strip of hair growing forward toward the head, caused by a dominant 133-kilobase genetic duplication involving FGF3, FGF4, FGF19, and ORAOV1; a classic ridge starts behind the shoulders with two matching opposite crowns and tapers toward the hips.

faq.question: Did Rhodesian Ridgebacks actually fight lions?
faq.answer: No. Working in agile groups of two or three, they tracked lions and kept them at bay through quick, elusive harassment without engaging in direct combat until the hunter arrived.

faq.question: How big does a Rhodesian Ridgeback get?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 63 to 69 cm at the withers and typically weigh 36 to 41 kg (ideal 36.5 kg), while adult females stand 61 to 66 cm and typically weigh 29 to 34 kg (ideal 32 kg).

faq.question: How long do Rhodesian Ridgebacks live?
faq.answer: With good nutrition, lean weight management, and regular veterinary care, Rhodesian Ridgebacks typically live 10 to 12 years.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Rhodesian Ridgeback need?
faq.answer: Very little. Weekly brushing with a rubber curry brush or hound mitt manages moderate shedding, paired with occasional baths, weekly ear checks, and regular nail trims (often easiest with a nail grinder).

faq.question: Can a Rhodesian Ridgeback live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Generally no. Although calm indoors after exercise, their large size, athletic drive, and need for secure running space make a house with a tall fenced yard a much better fit.

faq.question: Are Rhodesian Ridgebacks good family dogs?
faq.answer: Yes, in experienced, active homes. They are deeply devoted, protective, and affectionate with their own families, though their large size means play with young children should always be supervised.

faq.question: What is dermoid sinus?
faq.answer: Dermoid sinus is a congenital tube-like skin defect along the dorsal midline linked to the same genetic duplication that creates the ridge. Experienced breeders and veterinarians palpate newborn puppies carefully to detect it early.

faq.question: What health tests are recommended for breeding Rhodesian Ridgebacks?
faq.answer: Important pre-breeding checks include dermoid sinus palpation, radiographic hip and elbow evaluations, DNA tests for Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (DIRAS1), Early Onset Adult Deafness (EPS8L2), and Degenerative Myelopathy (SOD1), plus thyroid and ophthalmologist exams.

overview.summary: A diminutive, long-legged, finely boned Russian companion breed developed in smooth-haired and long-haired varieties, combining lively intelligence and cheerful athleticism with intense devotion to its household.
overview.description: The Russian Toy (Russkiy Toy) is one of the world's smallest dog breeds—an elegant, lively, high-stationed toy dog with fine bone, lean musculature, and a square body outline in which height at the withers equals body length. Its chest reaches the elbows, the height at the elbows is slightly more than half the withers height, and sexual dimorphism is only slightly defined. The breed exists in two coat varieties that can appear in the same litter: a sleek, shiny, close-lying smooth coat without undercoat, and a long-haired variety featuring a 3 to 5 cm body coat, feathered limbs and tail, and dramatic, butterfly-like ear fringes covering large, high-set triangular ears. Active, cheerful, curious, and keenly intelligent, the Russian Toy bonds closely with its family, loves both energetic play and lap snuggling, and may be slightly reserved with strangers while remaining neither timid nor aggressive.
overview.history: The Russian Toy traces its ancestry to English Toy Terriers imported into Russia as early as the eighteenth century—evidenced by a preserved short-haired terrier dated 1716–1725 in the Zoological Museum in Saint Petersburg that belonged to Emperor Peter the Great—and became a fashionable companion of the Russian aristocracy by the early twentieth century. Following the 1917 revolution and between 1920 and 1950, breeding of purebred toy terriers nearly ceased and numbers fell to a critical level. When Soviet breeders began reviving the stock in the mid-1950s in isolation, most surviving dogs lacked pedigrees and were not purebred, resulting in a distinct Russian type with a higher, rounder skull, flatter cheeks, and rounder eyes than the English Toy Terrier. On 12 October 1958, two smooth-coated dogs (one with slightly longer hair) produced a male puppy named Chikki with striking fringes on his ears and limbs. Acquired and bred in Moscow by Yevgueniya Fominichna Zharova—who mated him to a slightly long-coated female named Irma—this line became known as the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier. A first Russian standard for the two varieties was approved in 1966, and in 1988 both the smooth-haired Russian Toy Terrier and the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier were unified under a single breed standard, later dropping the word 'Terrier' to become the Russian Toy.

Nose-work and scent-detection games
Lure coursing for toy breeds

grooming.level: Low to moderate. Simple routine upkeep for both varieties, with extra brushing required for the long-haired variety's ear fringes and feathering.
grooming.brushing: Long-haired variety: brush or comb 2 to 3 times per week, paying special attention to the ear fringes and leg feathering. Smooth-haired variety: brush weekly with a soft bristle brush and wipe daily with a chamois cloth to maintain shine and minimize loose hair.
grooming.bathing: Bathe monthly (or every 1 to 2 weeks for show/companion maintenance) using a gentle, high-quality dog shampoo and conditioner or creme rinse; smooth-coated dogs can also be bathed occasionally as needed.
notes: Both varieties shed minimally, with noticeably less visible hair from the short smooth coat.
On long-haired dogs, comb out ear fringes and feathering gently to prevent tangles and keep them free of debris.
Long-coated puppies typically shed much of their puppy coat between 5 and 12 months of age; full adult coat develops after 1 year and full ear fringing may take until 2 to 3 years of age.
Keep nails clipped short and trim excess hair beneath the feet on long-coated dogs; no other coat trimming is needed (and trimmed coats are penalized in conformation).
Brush teeth regularly and inspect ears, eyes, and skin during routine grooming.

training.difficulty: Moderate. Keenly intelligent, agreeable, and eager to please, though capable of a terrier-like stubborn streak and trying to take charge if boundaries are inconsistent.
tips: Use upbeat, reward-based training with tiny treats and praise; keep sessions fun and engaging.
Enrol in puppy kindergarten and obedience classes early to channel the breed's intelligence and prevent bossy behaviour.
Take advantage of the breed's athleticism and nose by introducing agility, trick training, rally, or nose work.
Always walk the dog on a well-fitted harness rather than attaching a leash to a collar, protecting the delicate neck and trachea.
Remove collars and harnesses while the dog is inside the home so they cannot snag on household objects and cause injury.
Because of the breed's fine bone structure, prevent jumping from heights above 40 cm (such as high sofas or beds) and supervise interactions around large dogs.
training.socialization: Begin early, positive socialization in puppyhood with varied people, gentle handling, puppy kindergarten classes, and calm, size-appropriate dogs so natural reserve toward strangers does not turn into timidity or reactivity.

climates: Temperate climates
Indoor living with cold-weather protection (coats/sweaters or indoor litter/pad options during severe winter weather)
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Deeply attached to its human companions, the Russian Toy thrives on closeness and will quickly vocalize or become stressed if left isolated or neglected for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced, high-quality small-breed dog food (with extra-small kibble) or a veterinarian-supervised and approved home-prepared diet appropriate to life stage (puppy, adult, or senior).
nutrition.guidelines: Feed a nutritionally complete diet suited to the dog's age and activity level, selecting very small kibble that suits a miniature jaw. Because some Russian Toys have a poor sense of satiety and can easily become overweight—placing extra stress on delicate bones and patellas—measure daily portions carefully, limit training treats, avoid free-feeding, and keep fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Choose extra-small kibble sized for a toy breed weighing under 3 kg.
Monitor body condition and calorie intake closely, as excess weight strains slender legs and kneecaps.
Keep training treats tiny and deduct them from the daily food allowance.
Prepare home-cooked diets only with veterinary supervision and nutritional balancing.
Consult a veterinarian or breeder to set appropriate daily meal counts for puppies, adults, and seniors.
nutrition.note: Consulted kennel-club and breed-club sources do not prescribe fixed daily meal counts for puppies, adults, or seniors; feeding schedules should be tailored with a veterinarian.

health.overview: The Russian Toy is generally a healthy, long-lived toy breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years (and some individuals reaching 15 years or more). As in many diminutive breeds, dental issues are the most frequent everyday veterinary concern: most puppies retain deciduous (baby) teeth that require veterinary extraction by about nine months of age to prevent malocclusion, and tartar buildup with periodontal disease can begin by one year of age. Because of its fine bone structure, the breed is also vulnerable to limb fractures from falls or rough play and to tracheal injury if walked on a neck collar rather than a harness. For breeding stock, national breed-club and kennel-club health programs prioritize clinical screening for patellar luxation, inherited eye diseases (such as progressive retinal atrophy), and cardiac abnormalities, with optional evaluations for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip and elbow dysplasia, and congenital liver shunts.
commonConditions: Retained deciduous (puppy) teeth: most puppies fail to shed all baby teeth naturally as adult teeth erupt around 6 months of age, frequently requiring surgical extraction under anaesthesia by 9 months of age to prevent double rows of teeth, misalignment, and periodontal disease
Periodontal disease, plaque, and tartar buildup: can begin as early as 1 year of age without regular tooth brushing and routine veterinary dental care
Patellar luxation: a potentially inherited kneecap instability common to toy breeds and included in mandatory pre-breeding orthopedic screening

Inherited and traumatic eye conditions: progressive retinal atrophy (PRA, screened via ophthalmic exams and biobank research) as well as corneal ulcers and surface eye injuries due to large, prominent eyes
Cardiac conditions: monitored through pre-breeding veterinary cardiology evaluations

Traumatic bone fractures and open fontanel: fine limb bones can fracture from jumping off furniture or rough contact with large dogs, and an open fontanel (unclosed skull soft spot) past 9 months of age is a disqualifying developmental defect

Additional conditions monitored via optional breed-club screening: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (avascular necrosis of the femoral head), hip and elbow dysplasia, and congenital portosystemic (liver) shunts
preventiveCare: Brush the teeth regularly and have a veterinarian monitor tooth eruption between 6 and 9 months of age so retained baby teeth can be removed before they cause misalignment or gum disease.
Schedule routine veterinary dental examinations and professional cleanings as needed starting in young adulthood.
Walk the dog using a well-fitted harness rather than a neck collar to protect the fragile neck and trachea, and remove collars and harnesses indoors to prevent snagging accidents.
Prevent jumps from furniture or heights over 40 cm and supervise all interactions with large dogs or young children to avoid bone fractures.
Verify that breeding dogs have completed recommended orthopedic (patellar luxation), ophthalmic, and cardiac evaluations.
recommendedScreenings: Patellar luxation veterinary evaluation for breeding dogs
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (or accredited national eye-scheme examiner) for breeding dogs
Basic cardiac evaluation by a qualified veterinarian or veterinary cardiologist for breeding dogs

Optional additional breed-club evaluations: radiographic screening for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip dysplasia, and elbow dysplasia; paired serum bile acid testing for congenital liver shunts; and DNA biobank/panel participation
health.dentalCare: Most Russian Toy puppies retain deciduous (baby) teeth when their permanent teeth erupt, often requiring veterinary extraction by nine months of age so the jaw and bite develop normally. Because tartar and periodontal disease can start by one year of age, daily or frequent tooth brushing and regular veterinary dental checks are essential.
health.earCare: Inspect the thin, erect triangular ears during weekly grooming for wax, debris, or irritation. On long-haired dogs, comb the thick ear fringes two to three times a week to keep them tangle- and debris-free.
health.skinCare: The skin is thin and tight-fitting. On smooth-coated dogs, brush weekly with a soft brush and wipe daily with a chamois cloth to remove dead hair and prevent flaky skin; on both varieties, use a gentle dog shampoo and conditioner or creme rinse when bathing.

Careful, attentive households willing to brush teeth regularly, use a harness, and protect a finely boned toy dog from falls

funFacts: A preserved short-haired terrier named Lizetta dating from 1716–1725, which personally belonged to Russian Emperor Peter the Great, is displayed at the Zoological Museum in Saint Petersburg as early evidence of the breed's English-type ancestors in Russia.

The long-haired variety traces back to a single male puppy named Chikki, born on 12 October 1958 to two smooth-coated parents with slightly longer hair and developed in Moscow by breeder Yevgueniya Fominichna Zharova.
Both smooth-haired and long-haired puppies can be born in the same litter when two smooth-coated parents carry the recessive gene for long hair.
In long-haired Russian Toys, the signature butterfly-like ear fringes and full adult coat take two to three years to reach their full length.

Originally known separately as the Russian Toy Terrier (smooth-coated) and the Moscow Longhaired Toy Terrier (long-coated), the two varieties were united under one standard in 1988 and later had the word 'Terrier' dropped from the official breed name.

Despite standing only 22 to 27 cm tall (with 25 cm and 2.3 kg considered ideal in international standards), the Russian Toy competes enthusiastically in agility, rally, obedience, lure coursing, and nose work.

faq.question: How tall is a Russian Toy?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 22 to 27 cm for both males and females, with 25 cm preferred (and heights under 18 cm or over 29 cm disqualified). British standards list 20 to 28 cm (with a ±1 cm tolerance), and North American standards specify 8 to 11 inches (about 20.3 to 27.9 cm, with dogs under 7 inches or over 12 inches disqualified).

faq.question: How much does a Russian Toy weigh?
faq.answer: International standards specify a weight of up to 3 kg (6.6 lbs) for both sexes, with 2.3 kg (about 5 lbs) preferred, and disqualify dogs weighing under 1.5 kg or over 3 kg. North American standards specify a weight of up to 6 to 6.5 pounds (about 2.7 to 2.95 kg), with a preferred weight of 5 pounds and a disqualifying minimum of 2 pounds.

faq.question: What is the difference between the smooth-haired and long-haired Russian Toy?
faq.answer: The smooth-haired variety has a short, glossy, close-lying coat with no undercoat or feathering, and is often described as slightly more terrier-like in attitude. The long-haired variety has a 3 to 5 cm (1 to 3 inch) straight or slightly wavy body coat, distinct feathering on the legs and tail, and long, thick fringes on the ears that completely cover the ear edges and tips by three years of age. Both varieties share the same anatomy and can even be born in the same litter.

faq.question: Why do Russian Toy puppies often need baby teeth removed by a veterinarian?
faq.answer: Like several other tiny toy breeds, most Russian Toy puppies do not shed all of their deciduous (baby) teeth naturally when their permanent teeth erupt around six months of age. If retained baby teeth are not surgically extracted by about nine months of age, two teeth occupy the same socket, leading to bite misalignment, trapped food, rapid tartar buildup, and early periodontal disease.

faq.question: Why should a Russian Toy wear a harness instead of a collar on walks?
faq.answer: Because very small dogs have delicate necks and tracheas, pulling against a neck collar can cause throat or tracheal injury. Walking the dog on a well-fitted harness distributes pressure safely across the chest. Indoors, collars and harnesses should be removed so they cannot catch on furniture or vents.

faq.question: When does a long-haired Russian Toy get its full coat and ear fringes?
faq.answer: Puppies typically shed much of their puppy coat between 5 and 12 months of age. An adult coat does not develop until the dog is over a year old, and the full, dramatic ear fringing is often not complete until two to three years of age.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for Russian Toy breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Pre-breeding health programs recommend three core clinical evaluations—patellar luxation screening, an annual examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (or accredited eye-scheme examiner), and a basic cardiac evaluation—along with optional screenings for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, hip and elbow dysplasia, and paired serum bile acid testing for congenital liver shunts.

overview.summary: A large, athletic Dutch wolfdog created from German Shepherd and Eurasian wolf crosses, known for its unmistakable lupine appearance, deep family loyalty, independent will, and cautious flight instinct.
overview.description: The Saarlooswolfhond is a strongly built, long-legged, rectangular dog whose body shape, effortless ground-covering trot, and dense seasonal coat closely mirror a wild wolf. Its broad, wedge-shaped head carries firm upright ears and obliquely set yellow almond eyes with a watchful, reserved gaze. Coats appear in shaded wolf-grey, forest-brown, or rare cream-to-white. Despite its imposing presence, this breed is neither aggressive nor suited for guard duty; it meets unfamiliar people and environments with natural caution and prefers to retreat rather than confront. Within its trusted home pack, however, it forms an intense, devoted bond and thrives on steady companionship.
overview.history: In 1932 in the Netherlands, breeder Leendert Saarloos crossed a German Shepherd Dog male with a female Eurasian wolf from the Rotterdam Zoo, hoping to restore natural stamina and resilience he believed modern working dogs had lost. Through careful backcrossing to the German Shepherd line, he established a distinct wolfdog population originally called the European Wolfdog. Although Saarloos hoped the dogs would excel in police or guide work, their inherited wolf-like caution and strong tendency to avoid unfamiliar situations proved poorly matched to noisy city service. After his death in 1969, Dutch enthusiasts continued refining the breed, achieving national recognition in 1975 under the name Saarlooswolfhond in his honor and international recognition in 1981.
overview.originalPurpose: Created to restore natural endurance and resilience for working and guide duties, though its cautious temperament ultimately directed it into specialized companionship.

Medium-sized, sturdy, triangular upright ears with rounded tips and hair lining the inside

traits: Deeply devoted and dependable with its trusted owner and immediate family pack
Proud, independent, and inclined to follow its own judgment first
Naturally reserved and cautious around strangers, rarely seeking contact with unfamiliar people
Guided by a strong flight instinct—prefers to retreat from startling or unknown situations rather than confront them
Unsuited for protection or guard duty due to lack of territorial aggression
Lively and energetic in familiar, quiet outdoor spaces
Strongly pack-oriented and prone to severe distress when left isolated
Quiet overall, relying more on subtle body posture and occasional howling than barking

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a slicker brush and undercoat rake, shifting to daily sessions during heavy seasonal undercoat sheds.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when genuinely dirty so natural skin oils and weather-repellent coat texture stay intact.
notes: Expect heavy seasonal coat blows twice a year when winter undercoat lifts out in tufts.
Check the hairy upright ears weekly for dirt or burrs after outdoor walks.
Trim nails every few weeks if most exercise happens on soft trails.
Brush teeth several times a week with canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Very challenging; bright and observant, yet deeply independent and easily stressed by harsh pressure
tips: Rely strictly on gentle, reward-based training; scolding or physical pressure triggers shutdown, panic, or flight.
Keep lessons short, calm, and varied rather than drilling repetitive obedience routines.
Never attempt bite-work or guard training, which conflicts with the breed's cautious flight nature.
Keep on a secure leash or long line in unfenced areas, as independent roaming instincts make off-leash recall unreliable.
training.socialization: Early, gradual, lifelong socialization is essential: calmly introduce puppies to new surfaces, sounds, and polite visitors without forcing contact so natural reserve stays steady rather than fearful.

climates: Temperate climates
Cold climates, where the thick winter undercoat provides strong insulation
Warm climates when cool indoor rest, shade, and fresh water are always available
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Very low; intensely pack-oriented and prone to separation panic and escape attempts if left alone. Often settles much better alongside a calm, confident canine companion.

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced large-breed dog food with quality animal protein to sustain lean muscle and endurance.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured meals per day until six months of age to support steady large-breed growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals per day for steady energy and digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two controlled meals per day adapted for lower activity and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately with a kitchen scale or measuring cup to keep a lean, athletic silhouette. Split daily food into two meals, avoid intense running right before or after eating, and keep fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Maintain a lean, light-footed body condition to protect large-breed hips and spine.
Active dogs working in cold weather may need slightly higher daily calories.
Count training treats within the daily calorie allowance.
Switch diets gradually over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Work with a veterinarian to set tailored daily calories based on age, activity level, and season.

health.overview: Saarlooswolfhonds are generally athletic dogs that commonly live 12 to 15 years, though their narrow genetic foundation from German Shepherd and wolf ancestors leaves the breed vulnerable to specific inherited conditions. Peer-reviewed veterinary research highlights an unusually high carrier frequency (~31%) for autosomal recessive LHX3 pituitary dwarfism, alongside SOD1-linked degenerative myelopathy, hip dysplasia, and inherited eye disorders. Responsible breeding programs rely heavily on DNA screening and careful genetic diversity management.
commonConditions: Pituitary dwarfism (LHX3-related combined pituitary hormone deficiency) — scientifically established autosomal recessive disorder caused by a 7-bp deletion in intron 5 of LHX3 inherited from German Shepherd ancestry; European screening of 239 healthy breeding dogs found a 31% carrier rate, making pre-breeding DNA testing essential to prevent stunted growth, coat loss, and early mortality

Degenerative Myelopathy (DM, SOD1-related) — progressive late-onset spinal cord disease linked to an autosomal recessive SOD1 mutation with incomplete penetrance, causing gradual hind-limb weakness and paralysis in older dogs; screenable via DNA testing
Hip dysplasia — developmental hip-joint looseness that can progress to osteoarthritis in large breeds, monitored through hip radiographs
Inherited eye disorders — including Progressive Retinal Atrophy (PRA), cataracts, and glaucoma, monitored through routine specialist ophthalmic exams
Spondylosis — degenerative bone spurs along the spine occasionally noted in older large dogs
preventiveCare: Verify that both breeding parents are DNA-tested for LHX3 pituitary dwarfism (never mating two carriers) and SOD1 degenerative myelopathy.
Confirm pre-breeding hip dysplasia radiographs and specialist eye clearances.
Maintain a lean, fit body weight throughout life to reduce wear on hips and spine.
Provide a calm, predictable routine and secure fencing to prevent stress-related injury or escape.
Schedule yearly veterinary wellness exams and parasite prevention.
recommendedScreenings: DNA test for LHX3 pituitary dwarfism (combined pituitary hormone deficiency)
DNA test for SOD1 degenerative myelopathy (DM)
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly with canine enzymatic toothpaste and arrange routine veterinary dental checks to keep the strong jaws and scissor bite healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the upright, hair-lined ears weekly for burrs, wax, or irritation, wiping gently with a veterinarian-approved ear rinse.
health.skinCare: Part the thick double coat weekly to check for ticks or skin irritation, limiting baths so natural protective oils stay intact.
