overview.summary: A majestic, powerful, and vigilant white mountain sheepdog and livestock guardian native to the Slovakian Carpathians, celebrated for its imposing presence, fearless courage, dense weather-resistant double coat, and boundlessly faithful devotion to its family and flock.
overview.description: The Slovak Cuvac is an ancient, large mountain dog of sturdy constitution, imposing stature, and impressive power. Built in a moderately rectangular body format with a 9:10 height-to-length ratio on strong, rather tall legs, it combines formidable strength with light, agile movement across rugged mountain terrain. Beneath its dense, wavy white double coat—where guard hairs reach 5 to 15 cm and form a striking mane around the neck in males—lies strong bone and solid musculature. Its expressive, noble head features a broad skull, slight stop, dark brown oval eyes, black-pigmented lips and eye rims, and a complete, regular scissor bite. Bred strictly in pure white under ancient mountain tradition so shepherds could distinguish it from wolves and bears at night, the breed unites fearless protective vigilance with deep, loyal attachment to its human household. While composed and quiet at rest, it remains constantly watchful, making early socialization, clear boundaries, and experienced handling essential.
overview.history: The Slovak Cuvac descends from ancestral white flock-guarding dogs of the Eurasian mountain belt that accompanied human migration and pastoral settlement into the Carpathian Mountains and the High Tatras centuries ago. Living alongside Slovak shepherds on highland sheep pastures (known locally as 'salaš'), these dogs defended sheep, cattle, homesteads, and alpine borders from predatory wolves, brown bears, and marauders. The breed's name derives from the archaic Slovak verb 'čúvať' (meaning 'to hear' or 'to listen'), reflecting its acute auditory alertness. By the early twentieth century, modern agriculture, changes in predator populations, and the turmoil of the First World War threatened the breed with extinction. In 1929, veterinary medicine professor Antonín Hrůza from Brno initiated a systematic breeding and rescue program, recording the first official purebred litter on 4 June 1929 from surviving Tatra mountain stock. A dedicated breed club was established in 1933, leading to formal international recognition in August 1965. The breed's official name was revised from Tatranský Čuvač to Slovenský Čuvač to distinguish it from the closely related Polish mountain shepherd dog. In 2009, the breed was recorded into North American companion studbooks, continuing its role as an esteemed flock guardian and loyal family protector.

physical.coatType: Dense, weatherproof double coat with a wavy 5–15 cm harsh outer coat and a dense, downy undercoat
physical.sheddingLevel: High, with intense seasonal undercoat shedding in spring and autumn

distinctiveFeatures: Substantial, imposing mountain-dog build with strong bone, muscular limbs, and a moderately rectangular silhouette (withers height to body length ratio of 9:10)
Strong, elongated skull with a broad braincase, slight stop, and a powerful, straight muzzle measuring nearly half the total head length
Strong jaws with complete dentition and a regular scissor bite (pincer, overshot, or undershot bites are disqualifying faults)
Dark brown, oval-shaped eyes set straight, with tightly fitting black-pigmented lids conveying an alert and keen expression (wall or 'dragon' eyes are disqualified)
Medium-short, V-shaped ears set high, hanging flat and close to the head, with the lower tip reaching at most to the corner of the lips
Strong, dewlap-free neck carrying a striking, profuse mane in adult males
Broad chest with the sternum extending below elbow level, well-sprung ribs, and a straight, strong back with slightly arched loins
Low-set, cigar-shaped tail reaching the hocks at rest, carried in a graceful arch over the loins when alert or moving, without an upturned hook
Pure white coat consisting of 5 to 15 cm coarse guard hairs that form transverse waves across the back (tight curls or a parted spine are undesirable; yellow patches are disqualified)
Withers height of 62–70 cm (and weight of 36–44 kg) for males, and 59–65 cm (and weight of 31–37 kg) for females; rear dewclaws are undesirable

traits: Boundlessly faithful and loyal to family
Courageous and fearless when defending charges
Extremely alert, vigilant, and watchful
Independent and capable of autonomous decisions
Calm and steady in familiar surroundings
Reserved and naturally suspicious of unfamiliar strangers
Territorial with a deep, resonant warning bark
Gentle and protective with household children when properly socialized

exercise.level: Moderate to high. A sturdy mountain working dog that requires daily physical activity, perimeter patrols, and outdoor exploration in a securely fenced setting, though calm when at rest.
activities: Daily structured walks and countryside hikes on leash
Supervised patrolling and roaming in a securely fenced pasture or spacious yard
Farm chores, cart-pulling, and draft activities
Scent-tracking, nose work, and basic obedience games
Interactive outdoor play in cool weather or snow

grooming.brushing: Thorough brushing once or twice weekly using a pin brush and slicker to prevent matting, increasing to daily brushing during the twice-yearly seasonal undercoat blow
grooming.bathing: Occasional baths only as needed; the coarse white guard coat is naturally self-cleaning and repels dirt once dry
notes: Brush through the dense double coat once or twice weekly to remove loose hair, paying special attention to the neck mane, thigh feathering, and tail.
Expect heavy seasonal undercoat shedding in spring and autumn, during which daily combing with an undercoat rake prevents felted mats.
Never shave or clip the double coat; the dense coat serves as natural thermal insulation against both severe alpine frost and radiant summer heat.
Inspect the hanging ears weekly for dirt, wax, or moisture, and wipe gently with a veterinarian-recommended ear cleaner.
Check paw pads and claws after outdoor patrols, trimming nails regularly if they do not wear down naturally on rough terrain.
Brush teeth regularly with dog-specific toothpaste to preserve dental health.

training.difficulty: Moderate to challenging. Highly intelligent, courageous, and observant, but possesses strong independent guardian instincts and will not respond to harsh or purely mechanical drills.
tips: Establish calm, confident, and consistent leadership from early puppyhood using reward-based positive reinforcement and clear boundaries.
Avoid harsh physical punishment or angry confrontations, which undermine trust and cause a strong guardian breed to become defensive or shut down.
Teach loose-leash manners and reliable basic cues early before the puppy reaches its powerful adult weight of up to 44 kg.
Manage natural guarding instincts by teaching the dog to accept welcomed guests and settle quietly on cue.
Enclose exercise areas with sturdy, high fencing, as livestock guardians instinctively establish wide patrol territories if unconfined.
Provide mental enrichment and physical tasks to prevent boredom-induced nuisance barking or destructive outdoor digging.
training.socialization: Begin extensive, positive socialization during puppyhood, introducing varied people, friendly dogs, household noises, livestock, and diverse environments. Because the breed is naturally suspicious of strangers and protective of its territory, early socialization helps it distinguish normal everyday activity from genuine threats.

climates: Cold and snowy alpine climates (for which the dense double coat is naturally adapted)
Cool mountain and rural climates
Temperate climates
Warm climates only with abundant shade, air conditioning, cool indoor resting surfaces, fresh water, and exercise scheduled during cooler morning or evening hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate. Can calmly guard outdoor territory independently, but requires close daily human interaction and must not be left permanently isolated.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced canine diet formulated for large-breed dogs, adjusted for life stage, body condition, and workload
nutrition.guidelines: Provide measured portions of a nutritionally balanced large-breed food tailored to age and activity level. Large-breed puppies should grow at a steady, controlled rate on diets with balanced calcium and phosphorus levels to support healthy joint and bone development. Adult working guardians require higher energy density during cold winter months or active flock protection than during sedentary periods. Provide constant access to clean, fresh drinking water and divide daily rations into two smaller meals to help reduce the risk of bloat.
considerations: Avoid rapid growth and overfeeding during puppyhood to protect developing joints and cartilage.
Do not add unprescribed calcium or mineral supplements to an already complete commercial diet.
Divide adult food into two measured meals daily and restrict strenuous galloping immediately before or after eating to lower bloat (GDV) risk.
Monitor body condition regularly; ribs should be easily felt beneath the dense coat without excess fat.
Adjust portions to match seasonal outdoor temperatures and working demands.
nutrition.note: Consulted breed standards and club guidance do not prescribe fixed numerical daily meal counts across life stages; tailor feeding schedules and portion sizes with a veterinarian or breeder.

health.overview: The Slovak Cuvac is fundamentally a robust, hardy mountain guardian with an average lifespan of 11 to 13 years, shaped by centuries of natural selection in demanding alpine environments. The primary health priority in the breed is hip dysplasia (DBK / HD), a developmental orthopedic condition monitored through mandatory pre-breeding radiographic screening under parent-club breeding regulations (bonitácia). Radiographs are evaluated on the international A-to-E scale (earliest at 12 months, ideally at 20 months of age), with breeding restricted to dogs scoring no worse than C/C (grade 2/2). Responsible breeders also evaluate elbow dysplasia (DLK), maintain vigilance against gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat) common to deep-chested giant breeds, and ensure full dentition with a scissor bite and correct eyelid conformation as mandated by the breed standard.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia (DBK / HD): a multifactorial developmental malformation of the coxofemoral joints targeted by mandatory pre-breeding radiographic evaluation
Elbow dysplasia (DLK / ED): developmental joint incongruity monitored in breeding stock to maintain working soundness
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (GDV / bloat): an acute, life-threatening distension and twisting of the stomach in large, deep-chested dogs, manageable through divided meals and post-meal rest
Dentition irregularities: missing teeth or bite malocclusions (overshot, undershot, and pincer bites are strictly disqualified by the breed standard)
Ophthalmic conditions: eyelid anomalies such as entropion (inward-turning lid) or ectropion (outward-sagging lid), and pigment loss (wall or 'dragon' eyes, which are disqualified)
Traumatic joint strains and hygromas: potential bursal swellings or joint trauma from hard surfaces or high-impact jumping during rapid puppy growth
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents have documented radiographic hip clearances (RTG DBK) conforming to parent-club breeding standards (grade C/C or better).
Feed measured rations of a large-breed growth diet during puppyhood and avoid forced high-impact jumping or excessive stair climbing while bones and joints are developing.
Divide daily rations into two smaller meals and avoid vigorous exercise directly before or after feeding to minimize bloat risk.
Inspect and gently clean the ears regularly, and dry the coat thoroughly after heavy rain or snow.
Maintain a lean body condition throughout life to reduce mechanical stress on hips and elbows.
Keep core vaccinations, parasite prevention, and routine veterinary examinations up to date.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia radiographic evaluation (mandatory RTG DBK at minimum 12 months of age, ideally 20 months, evaluated under recognized veterinary scoring schemes)
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation (RTG DLK)
Pre-breeding conformation, dentition, and temperament evaluation (bonitácia)
Clinical ophthalmic examination for eyelid and cornea soundness
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth regularly with canine toothpaste and arrange routine veterinary dental inspections. Breed standards require strong jaws with full dentition of sound teeth meeting in a complete, regular scissor bite (pincer, overshot, or undershot bites are disqualifying faults).
health.earCare: Inspect the hanging V-shaped ears weekly for wax buildup, moisture, redness, or odour, and clean with a veterinarian-recommended cleanser as needed, keeping the ear canals dry.
health.skinCare: Part the dense double coat during weekly grooming to inspect for ticks, burrs, hot spots, or skin irritation, and examine paw pads after patrols over rough or icy ground.

funFacts: In ancient shepherd tradition, the Slovak Cuvac was bred strictly in white so shepherds could distinguish it from wolves and bears in the dark of night.
The breed's name comes from the archaic Slovak verb 'čúvať' (meaning 'to hear' or 'to listen'), reflecting its acute auditory alertness.
Modern pedigree breeding began on 4 June 1929, when Brno veterinary professor Antonín Hrůza registered the first official litter from surviving Tatra mountain stock.
Originally known as the Tatranský Čuvač, the breed's official name was updated to Slovenský Čuvač in the 1960s to distinguish it from Poland's Tatra shepherd dog.
In addition to protecting highland sheep flocks, the breed historically guarded 'salaš'—traditional alpine sheep-farming homesteads—and mountain borders.
Unlike many breeds that accept a pincer (level) bite, the official breed standard strictly disqualifies pincer bites, requiring a complete, regular scissor bite.

faq.question: What is a Slovak Cuvac?
faq.answer: The Slovak Cuvac (also known as the Slovenský Čuvač or Slovakian Chuvach) is a large, powerful white livestock guardian and sheepdog native to Slovakia's Carpathian and Tatra mountain regions. It is renowned for its courage, vigilance, thick weather-resistant coat, and deep loyalty to its family and flock.

faq.question: How big does a Slovak Cuvac get?
faq.answer: Conformation standards specify a withers height of 62 to 70 cm (24.4 to 27.6 inches) and weight of 36 to 44 kg (79 to 97 lbs) for males, and 59 to 65 cm (23.2 to 25.6 inches) and weight of 31 to 37 kg (68 to 82 lbs) for females.

faq.question: How long does a Slovak Cuvac live?
faq.answer: The typical life expectancy is 11 to 13 years when supported by responsible breeding, proper nutrition, joint care, and routine veterinary checkups.

faq.question: Why is the Slovak Cuvac always white?
faq.answer: Shepherds in the Slovak mountains historically selected for an exclusively white coat so they could instantly tell their guardian dogs apart from dark predators like wolves and bears in low light or at night.

faq.question: Is the Slovak Cuvac the same as the Polish Tatra Sheepdog or Hungarian Kuvasz?
faq.answer: No. While they share common Central European mountain livestock guardian ancestry and dense white coats, they are distinct breeds with separate standards and studbooks. The Slovak Cuvac was selectively bred in Slovakia's High Tatras, possesses distinct head proportions and body ratios, and was originally called Tatranský Čuvač before being officially named Slovenský Čuvač.

faq.question: Is the Slovak Cuvac suitable for first-time dog owners?
faq.answer: Generally no. Because of its large size, formidable physical strength, independent decision-making, and strong territorial instincts, it requires an experienced handler who understands livestock guardian behavior and provides consistent, positive guidance.

faq.question: How does the Slovak Cuvac behave around children?
faq.answer: When properly socialized and raised in a family setting, the Slovak Cuvac is typically gentle, patient, and fiercely protective of its household children. However, because of its large size, interactions with young children should always be actively supervised.

faq.question: Can a Slovak Cuvac live in an apartment?
faq.answer: No. Apartment living is unsuitable for this breed. It requires a home with a securely fenced yard or rural acreage where it can exercise, survey its surroundings, and express its natural guardian instincts without causing neighbor conflicts over alert barking.

faq.question: Does the Slovak Cuvac shed a lot?
faq.answer: Yes. The breed has a thick double coat that sheds moderately year-round and undergoes a heavy seasonal coat blow twice a year, during which daily brushing with an undercoat rake is needed to remove dead hair.

faq.question: What health tests are required for Slovak Cuvac breeding stock?
faq.answer: National parent-club regulations require pre-breeding radiographic hip dysplasia screening (RTG DBK) evaluated on the international A-to-E scale, with breeding restricted to dogs scoring grade C/C or better. Breeders also evaluate elbow soundness (DLK) and check dentition and eye health.

faq.question: Is the Slovak Cuvac friendly with strangers?
faq.answer: The breed is naturally reserved and suspicious of unfamiliar people. It will alert to visitors with a deep, resonant bark and watch carefully, requiring calm, managed introductions rather than expecting it to welcome strangers effusively.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Slovak Cuvac need?
faq.answer: It needs moderate to high daily physical activity, including leashed walks, secure yard patrols, and mental stimulation. Because it was bred to conserve energy while watching flocks, it is calm indoors when its daily exercise needs are met.

overview.summary: A rugged, noble Slovakian pointing and retrieving dog recognized by its weatherproof grey wire coat, eager trainability, and steady stamina across open fields, woods, and water.
overview.description: Built on clean, rectangular lines that balance moderate bone with athletic elegance, the Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer is an all-around hunting partner made for varied terrain. Its defining trait is a flat, harsh double coat about 4 cm long in brown-shaded sable—commonly called 'grey'—paired with a softer moustache and bold, slanted eyebrows. Almond-shaped amber eyes (blue in young puppies) lend an alert, thoughtful expression. Cooperative and quick to learn, this breed bonds tightly with its household and settles calmly indoors once its high daily exercise needs are met.
overview.history: This modern pointing breed was created in Slovakia (then part of Czechoslovakia) after World War II. Beginning in the 1950s, Slovak cynologist Koloman Slimák set out to develop a hardy, tractable all-purpose hunter suited to local field, forest, and water conditions by combining the Cesky Fousek (Czech Pointer), German Wirehaired Pointer, and Weimaraner. The resulting dogs paired the Weimaraner's distinctive grey tone and biddable temperament with a tough, protective wire coat. International recognition followed in 1982, and although numbers remain modest worldwide, the breed has earned a dedicated following among versatile hunters and active families.
overview.originalPurpose: Pointing, tracking, and retrieving game—including wounded game after the shot—across plains, forests, and water
currentRoles: Versatile pointing and retrieving hunting dog
Field trial, hunt test, and tracking competitor
Agility and obedience sport partner
Devoted companion for highly active households

physical.coatType: Harsh, straight, flat double coat with an outer coat about 4 cm long and a short, fine undercoat usually shed in summer; softer moustache on the lower muzzle and marked slanted eyebrows
coatColors: Brown-shaded sable ('grey') with lighter or darker shadings
Grey with white markings on the chest and legs
Grey with larger white markings or speckling
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate; sheds lightly most of the year with a heavier drop of the fine undercoat in summer
physical.droolingLevel: Low; neat, closely fitting dark lips keep drooling minimal
distinctiveFeatures: Sturdy, rectangular frame that is slightly longer than tall with noble, athletic lines
Harsh, flat grey wire coat paired with a softer muzzle moustache and distinct slanted eyebrows
Clean, moderately long head with clear brow ridges and a moderate stop
Large dark nose with wide nostrils
Almond-shaped amber eyes in adults; young puppies have blue eyes that darken with age
Broad, rounded drop ears set above eye level and covered in short, soft hair
Strong, level back with a deep chest and elastic, wrinkle-free grey skin
Well-coated tail hanging at rest and carried roughly level with the back when moving
Compact, rounded feet with well-arched toes and tough dark pads

traits: Cooperative, obedient, and quick to pick up training
Deeply affectionate and closely attached to family members
Energetic, tireless, and driven by strong scent and hunting instincts outdoors
Polite yet somewhat reserved when first meeting unfamiliar people
Sensitive to harsh handling; responds best to upbeat, consistent guidance
Generally sociable with other active dogs when well socialized
Alert and attentive around home without heavy guarding aggression

exercise.level: Very high; a hardworking pointing and retrieving dog that needs vigorous daily aerobic exercise paired with mental field tasks
activities: Brisk trail running, long hikes, and safe off-leash exercise in secure areas
Swimming and water retrieving
Tracking, scent games, and upland field work
Agility, rally, and obedience training

grooming.brushing: Brush once or twice a week with a stiff bristle brush or rubber hound glove, increasing brushing during the summer undercoat shed; occasional hand-stripping preserves the harsh outer texture.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when genuinely dirty so the weather-resistant wire coat does not soften.
notes: Check and dry the rounded drop ears after swimming or wet brushwork to prevent trapped moisture.
Rinse and comb the moustache and beard periodically to keep food debris from building up.
Trim nails every two weeks so toes stay compact for running.
Brush teeth several times a week with canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Easy to moderate; very bright and eager to work with its handler, yet sensitive enough that harsh corrections backfire
tips: Build lessons around positive reinforcement, play, and clear, calm consistency.
Channel hunting drive into structured retrieving, tracking, and steadiness exercises.
Reinforce solid recall early before allowing off-leash freedom in open country.
Keep workouts varied so this clever dog does not grow bored.
training.socialization: Provide calm, positive introductions to varied people, friendly dogs, traffic, and outdoor settings during puppyhood so natural reserve develops into steady confidence.

climates: Well suited to temperate climates
Handles cool and damp field weather comfortably thanks to its harsh double coat
Tolerates warm weather better after shedding its summer undercoat, provided exercise happens in cooler hours with plenty of water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; bonds closely with its people and can become anxious or restless if left alone for long daily stretches.

nutrition.dietType: Complete, balanced large-breed diet formulated for active sporting dogs, adjusted for seasonal fieldwork demands

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until about six months of age.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals per day to sustain lean muscle and reduce single-meal stomach load.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for lower activity and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily portions to keep the dog lean and hard-muscled, adjusting calories upward during heavy hunting or running seasons. Divide daily intake into two meals and avoid intense running immediately before and after eating to help reduce bloat risk.
considerations: Keep weight lean to protect hips, elbows, and athletic stamina.
Schedule calm rest periods around mealtimes to lower gastric dilatation-volvulus risk.
Count training treats within the daily calorie allowance.
Provide fresh water continuously, especially during warm-weather fieldwork.
nutrition.note: Confirm ideal daily calories with a veterinarian based on age, metabolism, and seasonal exercise load.

health.overview: The Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer is generally hardy and athletic, with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 15 years. Because the breed is rare worldwide, large-scale epidemiological data remain limited; responsible breeders prioritize screening for hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, and hereditary eye conditions such as progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) and cataracts. General large-breed and working-dog risks include gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat), moisture-related ear infections, and occasional field injuries.
commonConditions: Hip and elbow dysplasia — developmental joint conditions monitored through pre-breeding radiographic evaluations
Hereditary eye conditions — progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), cataracts, and eyelid conformation issues (entropion or ectropion) monitored via veterinary eye checks
Gastric dilatation-volvulus (bloat) — an acute, life-threatening stomach twisting risk associated with deep-chested large-breed conformation
Otitis externa (ear infections) — drop ears can hold moisture after swimming or wet fieldwork if not dried routinely
Field scrapes and sprains — minor cuts, paw-pad wear, or strains from dense brush and rugged terrain
preventiveCare: Confirm that breeding parents have documented hip and elbow evaluations and veterinary eye clearances.
Feed two smaller daily meals and keep vigorous running separated from mealtimes to help reduce bloat risk.
Dry the drop ears thoroughly after swimming or rain.
Keep weight lean and check paws and coat for thorns, burrs, or ticks after outdoor outings.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Annual eye examination by a veterinary ophthalmologist (screening for cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week with canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental checks to keep the scissor bite and gums healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the rounded drop ears weekly and after every swim for dampness, wax, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Part the wire coat weekly during brushing to inspect the elastic skin for ticks, burrs, or brush scratches.

idealFor: Hunters, runners, and outdoor enthusiasts who can provide 90 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily activity
Active families wanting a deeply loyal, cooperative, and versatile companion
Handlers interested in field trials, tracking, swimming, or agility
Homes with a securely fenced yard and direct access to trails or open countryside
notIdealFor: Sedentary households or owners wanting a low-energy indoor companion
Apartment living without extensive daily outdoor running outlets
Owners who leave a dog alone for long workdays
Anyone unwilling to manage strong hunting instincts and high exercise demands

funFacts: Because of its grey coloring and harsh wiry coat, the breed is often nicknamed a 'Weimaraner in a tweed jacket.'
Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer puppies are born with bright blue eyes that gradually shift to warm amber as they grow up.
The breed was developed in the 1950s by Slovak cynologist Koloman Slimák by blending the Cesky Fousek, German Wirehaired Pointer, and Weimaraner.
Its double coat has a harsh ~4 cm outer layer over a short, fine undercoat that is typically shed during the summer months.

faq.question: How big does a Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer get?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 62 to 68 cm at the shoulder and females stand 57 to 64 cm, with a typical working weight of 50 to 65 lb.

faq.question: How long does a Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer live?
faq.answer: With good nutrition, lean weight management, and regular veterinary care, the breed typically lives 12 to 15 years.

faq.question: How is it different from a Weimaraner or German Wirehaired Pointer?
faq.answer: It blends hallmarks of both ancestors: the distinctive grey coat color and cooperative sensitivity of the Weimaraner paired with the harsh wire coat, moustache, and rugged all-weather utility of wirehaired pointing breeds.

faq.question: How much exercise does a Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer need?
faq.answer: Plan on 90 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily exercise—such as trail running, swimming, retrieving, or scent work—to keep this athletic gundog calm and content indoors.

faq.question: Can a Slovakian Rough-haired Pointer live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Usually no. Its stamina, size, and strong drive to run and work outdoors suit a house with a securely fenced yard much better than apartment life.

faq.question: What health screenings are recommended for breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Recommended pre-breeding checks include hip and elbow dysplasia X-rays along with veterinary ophthalmologist eye exams to screen for cataracts and progressive retinal atrophy.

overview.summary: A robust, compact, and tireless medium-sized Swedish scenthound from the province of Småland, uniquely distinguished among Nordic hunting hounds by its nearly square frame, natural bobtail or full tail, and calm, devoted family nature.
overview.description: The Smålandsstövare—known in English as the Småland Hound—is a sturdy, athletic yet lightly elegant Swedish hunting hound bred for solo pursuit of hare and fox in all Nordic weather conditions. Unlike longer-bodied scenthounds, its body is almost perfectly square, combining strong bone without heaviness, a short powerful back, well-sprung ribs, and tightly closed feet densely packed with protective hair between the toes and pads to survive multi-day forest hunts. Its lean, medium-length head features equal skull and muzzle lengths, a well-defined stop, barely overhanging upper lips, calm dark brown almond eyes (or hazel in liver-brown dogs), and fairly high-set flat drop ears with rounded tips that lift slightly when alert. Wrapped in a harsh, close-lying medium-length double coat in rich black-and-tan or liver-brown-and-tan, the breed famously occurs with either a naturally born short stumpy tail, a half-length tail, or a full sabre tail. Quick to strike a trail and vocal with a dense, nuanced cry in the woods, it reliably seeks out its owner once a hunt concludes and settles peacefully at home as a steady, affectionate household companion—provided its intense hunting energy receives genuine outdoor work.
overview.history: During the nineteenth century, the wooded province of Småland in southern Sweden supported a colourful mosaic of local scenthounds. Their ancestry traced back to German, Polish, and Baltic hounds brought home by Swedish officers and soldiers returning from the great European wars between 1611 and 1718, which subsequently blended with local farmers' spitz-type homestead dogs and later English hunting hounds. Early Småland hounds varied widely in size, coat shade (black-and-tan, red, yellow, and white markings), and tail length, with many puppies born naturally short-tailed. In the early twentieth century, dedicated Swedish sportsmen worked systematically to restore the historic Småland type—placing particular emphasis on the traditional bobtailed line—and drafted the breed's first national written blueprint in 1921, recognizing both naturally short and full-length tails. New outcross blood of accepted type was last registered during the 1950s, and definitive international recognition arrived in January 1955. Today, the Smålandsstövare stands as one of Sweden's treasured national breeds, yet remains rare even in its homeland and relies on active hunting-focused conservation breeding.
overview.originalPurpose: Solo scenthunting with sustained, nuanced voice on hare and fox—and traditionally other small furred and forest game, though never deer—across Sweden's rugged woodlands.
currentRoles: Solo hare and fox hunting scenthound
Scent-tracking and woodland-trailing working dog
Loyal rural family companion for active hunting households

physical.coatType: Medium-length, harsh, straight, close-fitting outer coat growing coarser across the back and neck, backed by a short, dense, soft undercoat. Hair on the head, ears, and fronts of the legs is short and smooth, while longer guard hair may appear under the tail and along the backs of the thighs, with dense protective hair growing between the toes and pads.
coatColors: Black with clearly defined tan markings (ranging from amber to warm auburn over the eyes, sides of muzzle, throat, chest, legs, feet, under brisket and belly, inner thighs, under tail, and around anus)
Liver brown with clearly defined tan markings (paired with a dark brown nose and lighter, preferably hazel eyes)
Small white markings are permissible on the chest and toes
physical.sheddingLevel: Moderate; the harsh double coat sheds lightly year-round with moderate seasonal undercoat shedding
physical.droolingLevel: Low; lean cheeks, supple close-fitting neck skin, and upper lips that overhang only very slightly prevent drooling
distinctiveFeatures: Robust, compact, almost square medium hound frame (excessively rectangular bodies are faulted) with body depth nearly equalling half the height at the withers
Height at the withers of 46 to 54 cm for males (ideal 50 cm) and 42 to 50 cm for females (ideal 46 cm)
Occurs naturally with either a full tail barely reaching the hocks (straight or gently sabre-curved), a half-length tail, or a naturally born short stumpy tail (bear-tail also permissible)
Lean, medium-length head with equal occiput-to-stop and stop-to-nose lengths, straight nasal bridge parallel to the skull, well-defined stop, barely overhanging upper lips, and strong scissor bite
Almond-shaped dark brown eyes with a calm expression (lighter, preferably hazel eyes in liver-brown dogs; blue eyes disqualified)
Fairly high-set, flat-hanging drop ears with rounded tips that lift slightly above the skull line when attentive, reaching just short of halfway along the muzzle
Moderately long, strong neck with close-fitting skin, short powerful back, muscular slightly arched loin, and long broad gently sloping croup
Parallel, strong-boned straight forelegs with right-angled shoulder-to-upper-arm assembly and elbows tucked closely under the ribcage
Firm, tightly closed feet with well-knuckled toes and dense protective hair between the toes and pads built to endure multi-day hunting
Parallel, strong, long-reaching stride in black-and-tan or liver-brown-and-tan harsh double coat

traits: Calm, friendly, kind, and mentally stable in everyday household life
Deeply faithful and strongly bonded to its owner and family—reliably seeking out its handler after finishing a hunt
Keen, vigorous, tenacious, and remarkably enduring outdoors, capable of hunting for multiple consecutive days
Quick to pick up a scent trail and drives game with a dense, richly nuanced voice
Intelligent, social, and pleasant around people when properly raised
Driven by an intense solo hunting instinct for hare and fox, making it unsuited solely as an inactive companion pet

exercise.level: Very high; an extraordinarily enduring woodland scenthound built to hunt hare and fox across consecutive days that requires generous daily outdoor exercise and purposeful scent-tracking work
activities: Active solo forest hunting on hare and fox during hunting season
Structured scent tracking, mantrailing, and organised hunting trials
Long, brisk daily forest hikes and countryside trail runs on a secure leash or long tracking line
Supervised outdoor exploration inside a spacious, securely fenced rural yard

grooming.brushing: Easy-care harsh double coat—brush once a week with a firm bristle brush or rubber hound mitt to lift loose hair and woodland debris, increasing slightly during seasonal undercoat moults.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when genuinely dirty or odorous after forest work, using a mild canine shampoo.
notes: Preserve the dense protective hair between the toes and paw pads, checking after every woodland or snowy outing for ice balls, thorns, burrs, or pad scrapes.
Inspect the flat-hanging drop ears weekly—and after every wet forest hunt—for trapped moisture, wax buildup, ticks, or redness.
Trim strong nails regularly whenever rough outdoor terrain does not wear them down naturally.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate; intelligent, calm, and loyal to its handler, making it cooperative for scent work and hunting trials—yet its strong independent hunting drive demands patient recall and deer-avoidance training
tips: Use calm, consistent, reward-based training built on trust, food rewards, and structured scenting games; harsh pressure harms responsiveness in this kind-natured hound.
Begin recall, check-in habits, and wildlife-impulse control early on a long tracking line—traditional Swedish training specifically teaches the hound to focus on hare and fox while ignoring deer.
Provide genuine hunting or intensive tracking outlets so its high energy does not spill into boredom or restless barking.
Avoid assuming off-leash safety near unfenced roads or wildlife-rich suburbs.
training.socialization: Early, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, forest terrain, and everyday household noises supports its naturally calm, friendly, mentally stable temperament.

climates: Cold, snowy, and cool Nordic climates—its harsh weatherproof outer coat, dense soft undercoat, and densely furred paws are tailored for all-weather Scandinavian forest hunting
Temperate four-season countryside climates with woodland access
Warm summer weather requires shifting brisk exercise to cool early-morning or evening hours with reliable shade and cool drinking water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply bonded to its family and bred to spend hunting seasons actively in the forest rather than sitting confined in a kennel run or apartment.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for medium-sized, highly active sporting and hunting breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age to support steady musculoskeletal development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain multi-day hunting endurance and steady digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for reduced activity and joint health.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately to keep the dog strong, compact, and lean—never heavy or soft. Active hunting hounds working consecutive days in autumn and winter need higher energy and protein density than off-season dogs. Divide daily adult food into two meals, allow calm rest before and after eating, and keep clean fresh drinking water available continuously.
considerations: Keep growing puppies lean on a balanced medium-breed growth diet to minimise stress on developing hip joints.
Count all training treats inside the daily calorie allowance.
Avoid intense running immediately before or after large meals as a general deep-chested hound precaution.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric demands vary substantially between active autumn-winter hunting seasons and quieter off-season routines. Consult a veterinarian to establish individual feeding quantities.

health.overview: The Smålandsstövare is widely regarded as a relatively healthy, hardy working breed, though no formal breed-wide actuarial lifespan range is published by primary registries. Swedish national breeding documentation identifies epilepsy and hip dysplasia (HD) as conditions occurring in the breed, alongside occasional or isolated reports of Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) or other cardiac defects and cryptorchidism. Because the global population is numerically very small, modern Swedish breeding strategy balances strict exclusion of epileptic lines and repeat PDA-producing parents with careful genetic-diversity preservation—including controlled outcrosses with other Nordic scenthound breeds and lifting mandatory pre-mating hip-scoring requirements in 2020 to avoid overly narrowing the gene pool.
commonConditions: Epilepsy — documented as occurring in occasional cases; strict Swedish breeding rules exclude affected dogs, parents of affected offspring, offspring of affected parents, and full siblings from breeding while avoiding half-siblings whenever possible
Hip dysplasia (HD) — developmental laxity and malformation of the hip joints documented as occurring in the breed; monitored historically in Swedish breeding programmes

Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) and congenital cardiac defects — occasional/isolated cases documented in Swedish breed health records, with breeding guidelines excluding parents that produce more than one affected puppy
Cryptorchidism — occasional failure of one or both testicles to descend normally into the scrotum, noted in Swedish breed health monitoring

Otitis externa (outer ear infections) and fieldwork trauma — general conformation- and lifestyle-linked precautions for flat-hanging drop ears and multi-day forest hunting (ticks, thorns, and paw wear)
preventiveCare: Choose puppies from health-checked, hunting-tested parents and ask breeders for transparent multi-generation pedigree history regarding epilepsy, heart defects (PDA), and hip health.
Ensure breeding decisions respect genetic diversity and avoid mating two naturally short-tailed dogs without veterinary genetic guidance where dominant bobtail genetics could affect litter viability.
Inspect and dry the flat-hanging drop ears weekly—and after every wet forest hunt—to prevent moisture-related ear infections.
Check the densely furred paws, toes, and skin after woodland outings for ticks, thorns, or ice buildup, and maintain strict year-round tick, flea, and internal parasite protection.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness exams (including cardiac auscultation for murmurs in puppies and adults) and keep vaccinations current.
recommendedScreenings: Thorough multi-generation pedigree screening for idiopathic epilepsy history (affected dogs, parents, offspring, and full siblings excluded from breeding)
Veterinary cardiac auscultation in puppies and breeding adults to screen for Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) and other congenital heart defects
Elective radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding (monitored in the breed, though Sweden lifted its mandatory pre-mating requirement in 2020 to protect genetic diversity)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental checks to keep the strong scissor bite and gums healthy.
health.earCare: Inspect the fairly high-set, flat-hanging drop ears weekly for moisture, wax buildup, grass seeds, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution when needed.
health.skinCare: Run hands over the harsh medium-length coat and densely furred paws after every forest outing to catch ticks, burrs, scratches, or skin irritation early.

idealFor: Active hare and fox hunters with access to woodland hunting grounds seeking a tireless, fast-finding solo scenthound
Active rural hunting families wanting a calm, friendly, mentally stable dog that transitions warmly from forest work to home life
Dedicated countryside trackers able to provide 90 to 120 minutes of vigorous daily outdoor exercise and scent trials
Conservation-minded working-hound enthusiasts willing to train, trial, and help preserve one of Sweden's rare national breeds
notIdealFor: Apartment or city dwellers—this dedicated hunting hound should spend hunting seasons in the woods rather than confined indoors or in a small run
Households looking solely for a casual family pet without hunting or intensive scent-tracking outlets
Sedentary owners or first-time handlers expecting effortless off-leash walks around wildlife
Homes with free-roaming small pets such as rabbits or outdoor small livestock

funFacts: Among Sweden's native scenthounds, the Smålandsstövare is unique for naturally occurring with a born short bobtail ('stumpy tail' or bear-tail) alongside half-length and full-length tails—a heritage trait preserved since its first national blueprint in 1921.

Its lineage traces back to German, Polish, and Baltic hunting hounds brought home to Småland by Swedish soldiers returning from the great wars of 1611 to 1718, blended with local spitz-type farm dogs and English hounds.
Unlike many European scenthounds that hunt deer in packs, the Smålandsstövare is strictly a solo hound bred for hare and fox—never a pack dog and traditionally never used to hunt deer.
Its tightly closed feet grow dense protective hair between the toes and pads, acting as natural winter insulation so the dog can hunt over frozen or rough forest ground for several consecutive days.

Historically known mainly in classic black-and-tan, the 2017 update to its official description formally recognized liver-brown-and-tan dogs (complete with dark brown noses and hazel eyes) alongside black-and-tan.

faq.question: What is a Smålandsstövare?
faq.answer: The Smålandsstövare (Småland Hound) is a rare, robust, almost square medium-sized Swedish scenthound from the province of Småland, bred for solo hare and fox hunting and famous for occurring naturally with either a short bobtail or a full tail.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Smålandsstövare?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 46 to 54 cm at the withers (ideally 50 cm) and adult females stand 42 to 50 cm (ideally 46 cm). No official weight range is published, as healthy working hounds maintain a strong yet never heavy medium build proportionate to their height.

faq.question: How long does a Smålandsstövare live?
faq.answer: No official lifespan range or peer-reviewed actuarial longevity study is published by primary registries for the Smålandsstövare, though it is generally regarded as a hardy, relatively healthy working breed with proper veterinary care.

faq.question: Are all Smålandsstövare born with short tails?
faq.answer: No. Both naturally born short stumpy tails (including bear-tails), half-length tails, and full tails barely reaching the hocks are equally natural and accepted within the breed.

faq.question: Can a Smålandsstövare live in an apartment or purely as a family pet?
faq.answer: No. Although it has an excellent, calm, friendly temperament as a family dog indoors, it is a dedicated hunting hound with very high energy and strong hunting instincts that belongs in an active hunting or countryside tracking home rather than an apartment.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Smålandsstövare need?
faq.answer: Coat care is simple: weekly brushing clears loose hair from its harsh, close-lying medium-length double coat, with baths only as needed, paired with weekly drop-ear checks and regular paw and nail inspections.

faq.question: Are Smålandsstövare easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent, calm, faithful, and eager to partner with their owner—reliably returning to their handler after hunts—though their intense hare- and fox-chasing drive requires patient recall training and careful wildlife management.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Smålandsstövare?
faq.answer: Overall a relatively healthy working breed, its main documented health considerations are epilepsy (strictly managed through pedigree breeding exclusions), hip dysplasia, and isolated cases of congenital heart defects (such as PDA) and cryptorchidism, alongside careful management of its small global gene pool.

overview.summary: A sturdy, squarely built, and exuberantly friendly Irish farm terrier draped in a low-shedding, silky wheaten single coat, blending hardy working versatility with deeply devoted family warmth.
overview.description: The Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier is a medium-sized, compact, and agile working terrier whose soft, flowing single coat sets it unmistakably apart from harsh-coated terrier cousins. Built on a balanced square frame with solid bone, a deep chest, and powerful hindquarters, it carries a moderately long head with a flat skull, large black nose, dark hazel or reddish-brown eyes shaded by a neat fall of hair, and small-to-medium V-shaped ears breaking forward cleanly at skull level. Its single coat—occurring in lighter, silkier Irish-style waves or fuller, heavier coat lines—matures from a darker reddish or brownish puppy coat into any clear shade of ripening wheat by roughly two years of age. Though unmistakably a confident, self-reliant terrier with a strong vermin-chasing drive, the Wheaten is noticeably gentler, steadier, and more welcoming than many fiery terrier breeds, famous for greeting family and visitors alike with joyous, bouncy leaps.
overview.history: One of Ireland's oldest native terrier breeds, the Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier evolved over more than two centuries as the humble small farmer's all-around working dog across rural Ireland. While wealthy landowners kept sporting hounds and spaniels, tenant farmers relied on this tough, economical terrier to clear farms of rats, badgers, and otters, help move livestock, and guard rural cottages. Closely related to the Kerry Blue Terrier and the Irish Terrier, the Wheaten remained an unpretentious working dog without formal show records until the 1930s, earning formal recognition in Ireland in 1937 and definitive international acceptance in 1957, followed by North American recognition in 1973. Today, this lively Irish native thrives globally as an affectionate family companion and versatile competitor in agility, obedience, rally, and tracking.
overview.originalPurpose: All-purpose Irish farm dog used to exterminate rats and other vermin, assist with herding livestock, and guard rural homesteads.
currentRoles: Affectionate, lively family companion
Alert household watchdog
Canine sports competitor (agility, obedience, rally, tracking, and barn hunt)
Therapy dog

physical.coatType: Abundant, single-layered coat with no undercoat, feeling soft and silky with gentle waves rather than harsh wire or woolly curls. Coat density varies between lighter, silkier Irish-type coats and fuller, thicker coat lines; puppies are born darker and gradually clear to adult wheaten tones by 18 to 24 months.
coatColors: Clear wheaten in any shade from pale cream-wheat to warm golden-reddish wheaten (puppies are typically born reddish-brown, fawn, or mahogany with dark muzzle and ear tipping that gradually clears with maturity; blue-grey shading on the ears and muzzle may persist occasionally)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low; the single silky coat sheds very little loose hair around the home, though dead hair becomes trapped in the coat and mats rapidly without frequent combing
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tight, black-pigmented lips prevent drooling, though the long beard around the muzzle holds water after drinking
distinctiveFeatures: Medium-sized, sturdy, compact, square outline projecting athletic balance and strength
Height at the withers of 18 to 19 inches for males (ideal 18.5 inches) and 17 to 18 inches for females (ideal 17.5 inches)
Working weight of 35 to 40 pounds for males and 30 to 35 pounds for females
Soft, silky, gently waving single coat (no undercoat) maturing from dark puppy shades into clear ripening wheat
Moderately long rectangular head with a flat skull, defined stop, strong foreface, large black nose, and tight black lips
Large, clean white teeth meeting in a scissor or level bite
Dark reddish-brown or hazel, slightly almond-shaped eyes with black rims shaded by a characteristic facial fall of hair
Small-to-medium, high-set drop ears breaking level with the skull and dropping cleanly forward toward the cheek
Medium-length, strong, clean neck free of throatiness flowing into a level topline and deep chest
High-set tail carried upright at 90 degrees straight or with a slight curve forward (left natural in many countries, traditionally docked in some regions where legally permitted)
Compact, round feet with deep black pads and sturdy dark nails supporting a lively, free-striding gait

traits: Happy, exuberant, playful, and warmly sociable toward family and welcomed visitors
Deeply devoted and affectionate, thriving as an indoor family member
Alert, confident, and spirited without the sharp edginess of some harder terrier breeds
Intelligent and quick to learn, paired with a classic independent, mildly stubborn terrier streak
Famous for its enthusiastic vertical jumping greeting when meeting people ('Wheaten greetin'')
Retains an active farm-terrier prey drive toward squirrels, rodents, and small fleeing animals
Good, energetic playmate for respectful older children, though bouncy enthusiasm can knock down small toddlers

exercise.level: Moderate to high; a lively, sturdy farm terrier that thrives on brisk daily walks, energetic play, and mentally stimulating games to prevent boredom and rowdiness
activities: Brisk daily leashed walks or jogs through the neighbourhood, parks, or trails
Interactive games of fetch, tug, and scent puzzles
Supervised vigorous play inside a securely fenced yard
Canine sports such as agility, obedience, rally, tracking, and barn hunt

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb thoroughly down to the skin several times weekly—ideally daily in heavy-coated lines—using a medium-toothed metal comb and pin brush to prevent tight mats behind the ears, under the legs, and along the furnishings.
grooming.bathing: Bathe every four to six weeks using a gentle canine shampoo and light conditioner; always comb out every tangle before bathing because water tightens existing mats.
notes: Professional trimming every six to eight weeks keeps the silky single coat neat, manageable, and shaped without hiding the eyes completely.
Wipe the bearded muzzle after meals and drinks to prevent discolouration and skin irritation.
Inspect the folded drop ears weekly for trapped coat hair, wax, or moisture to prevent ear infections.
Trim dark nails every two to three weeks and brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Moderate; bright, willing, and eager to engage, yet independent enough to ignore repetitive drills unless training feels upbeat, fair, and consistent
tips: Use positive, reward-based training with small treats, toys, and lively praise; harsh corrections trigger stubborn shutdown.
Teach polite four-paws-on-the-floor greetings from early puppyhood to channel the breed's famous jumping greeting safely.
Practice solid recall and leash manners early, as squirrels, rabbits, and stray cats easily ignite its vermin-hunting drive.
Keep training sessions brief, fun, and varied to hold this clever terrier's interest.
training.socialization: Early, positive exposure to varied people, friendly dogs, children, grooming tables, and urban noises builds a confident, polite adult that handles busy environments and frequent combing calmly.

climates: Temperate and cool maritime climates, echoing the mild, damp conditions of Ireland
Moderate four-season climates
Warm climates are tolerated well indoors with air conditioning, provided the coat is kept comfortably trimmed and brisk walks are scheduled for cooler morning and evening hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; deeply people-oriented and social, Wheatens enjoy being part of household life and may bark or chew if left isolated for long workdays without exercise and mental enrichment.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for medium-sized active breeds, paying close attention to digestive tolerance and protein balance.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age to support steady musculoskeletal growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain steady energy and comfortable digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily tailored for lower caloric needs, kidney monitoring, and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal accurately using a scale or measuring cup to maintain a lean, solid waist—feel beneath the abundant coat weekly so gradual weight gain or unexpected weight loss does not go unnoticed. Because Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers carry a recognised predisposition to protein-losing kidney and intestinal disorders (PLN and PLE) as well as food sensitivities, monitor appetite, stool consistency, thirst, and urination closely and consult a veterinarian promptly if chronic digestive upset develops. Provide cool, fresh drinking water at all times.
considerations: Avoid abrupt dietary changes and rich table scraps; transition gradually between diets over five to seven days.
Count all training treats within the daily calorie budget to prevent excess weight.
Dogs diagnosed with food sensitivities, PLE, or PLN often require specialized veterinary therapeutic diets (such as hydrolysed, low-fat, or renal-support formulas).
Routine annual blood chemistry and urinalysis help detect early protein loss long before overt illness appears.
nutrition.note: Individual dietary needs can change significantly if food hypersensitivity, intestinal protein loss, or kidney disease develops; always consult a veterinarian before adopting therapeutic diets.

health.overview: The Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier has a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years and brings vigorous everyday energy, yet veterinary genetics research and breed health databases document several serious hereditary disorders that make responsible breeding and proactive annual veterinary screening essential. Key conditions include familial Protein-Losing Nephropathy (PLN)—strongly linked to variants in the NPHS1 and KIRREL2 genes—Protein-Losing Enteropathy (PLE), renal dysplasia, Addison's disease (hypoadrenocorticism), congenital microphthalmia caused by a unique maternally transmitted recessive RBP4 deletion, and a rare PIGN-related paroxysmal dyskinesia movement disorder.
commonConditions: Protein-Losing Nephropathy (PLN) — a serious familial glomerular kidney disease causing protein leakage into the urine, hypertension, blood clots, and eventual kidney failure (typically adult-onset); strongly associated with mutations in the NPHS1 and KIRREL2 genes, with homozygous dogs carrying markedly elevated risk (odds ratio 9.06) and screenable via DNA testing plus routine urinalysis

Protein-Losing Enteropathy (PLE) and chronic enteropathy — inflammatory intestinal disease causing abnormal protein loss through the digestive tract, chronic diarrhoea, fluid accumulation, or weight loss, sometimes linked to food hypersensitivities and occasionally occurring alongside PLN
Renal dysplasia (RD) — a congenital developmental malformation of the kidneys present from birth that can lead to early-onset kidney failure in young dogs

Hypoadrenocorticism (Addison's disease) — an immune-mediated adrenal hormone deficiency reported at elevated frequency in the breed, causing lethargy, vomiting, or acute collapse, and manageable lifelong with hormone replacement once diagnosed

Microphthalmia syndrome (RBP4-related) — a congenital eye malformation causing abnormally small eyes and severe vision impairment, inherited via a unique recessive maternal-effect deletion (c.282_284delGAA) in the RBP4 gene that manifests only when both the mother and puppy are homozygous; preventable through pre-breeding DNA screening

Paroxysmal dyskinesia (PxD, PIGN-related) — a rare autosomal-recessive movement disorder caused by a homozygous missense mutation (c.398C>T) in the PIGN gene (median onset around 2.25 years), producing recurring episodes of involuntary limb flexion and abnormal posture; preventable via DNA testing
Hip dysplasia and other hereditary eye disorders — monitored through pre-breeding radiographic hip certification and periodic veterinary ophthalmologist examinations
Degenerative myelopathy (DM) and ectopic ureters — additional conditions monitored in comprehensive breeding health programmes
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have certified pre-breeding clearances: radiographic hip evaluations, biennial specialist veterinary eye exams, PLN-associated DNA testing (NPHS1/KIRREL2), and baseline blood and urine protein screens, plus recommended DNA tests for microphthalmia (RBP4), paroxysmal dyskinesia (PIGN), and degenerative myelopathy.

Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations including a complete blood count, serum biochemistry panel, complete urinalysis, urine protein-to-creatinine (UPC) ratio, and blood pressure check—increasing urine protein monitoring to every 6 months in adult dogs carrying one or two PLN risk alleles.
Watch for early warning signs of PLN, PLE, or Addison's disease, including unexplained weight loss, increased thirst or urination, chronic vomiting or diarrhoea, lethargy, or fluid swelling.

Keep the folded ears dry and clean, maintain regular dental hygiene, and administer consistent year-round parasite prevention and vaccinations (including discussing leptospirosis vaccination with your veterinarian).
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding (permanent certification at 24 months or older)
Periodic ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (prior to first breeding and every 2 years up to age 10)
DNA test for Protein-Losing Nephropathy (PLN-associated NPHS1 and KIRREL2 variant alleles)

health.earCare: Inspect the small-to-medium folded drop ears weekly for trapped coat hair, wax, odour, or redness, cleaning gently with a veterinarian-approved solution.
health.skinCare: Part the silky single coat down to the skin during brushing to check for tight mats, moisture traps, fleas, ticks, or allergic skin redness.

funFacts: Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers are famous for their exuberant 'Wheaten greetin''—leaping enthusiastically straight up into the air to welcome family members and visitors face-to-face.

Puppies look surprisingly different from adults: they are born with darker reddish-brown, fawn, or mahogany coats and dark masks that gradually clear over 18 to 24 months into their mature golden-wheaten colour.
Unlike wire-coated terriers, the Wheaten has a single, silky, non-undercoated coat that sheds minimally—available in both a lighter, wavier traditional Irish coat and a fuller, heavier coat type.

In 2018, veterinary geneticists studying congenital microphthalmia in Irish Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers discovered a remarkable maternal-effect recessive deletion in the RBP4 gene: puppies only develop small eyes if both the mother and the puppy inherit two copies of the mutation, restricting vitamin A transport across the placenta.

In 2013, researchers identified NPHS1 and KIRREL2 gene variants associated with familial Protein-Losing Nephropathy (PLN) in the breed—the first molecular characterization of an inherited podocytopathy in dogs.

faq.question: What is a Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier?
faq.answer: The Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier (Irish Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier) is a medium-sized, squarely built farm terrier from Ireland, known for its silky, low-shedding wheaten single coat and happy, outgoing, deeply devoted temperament.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 18 to 19 inches at the withers and weigh 35 to 40 pounds, while adult females stand 17 to 18 inches and weigh 30 to 35 pounds.

faq.question: How long does a Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier live?
faq.answer: With attentive preventive veterinary monitoring, balanced nutrition, and daily exercise, the breed typically lives 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Do Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers shed, and how much grooming do they need?
faq.answer: They shed very little around the house because they have a single silky coat with no undercoat, but their grooming needs are high: they require thorough combing down to the skin several times a week to prevent painful mats, plus professional trimming every six to eight weeks.

faq.question: Can a Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes. Wheatens adapt happily to city apartments as well as country homes as long as they get 45 to 60 minutes of daily brisk walks, interactive play, and mental enrichment.

faq.question: Are Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers good with children?
faq.answer: Yes, they are warm, cheerful, and sturdy playmates for older, respectful children, though early training is helpful so their bouncy jumping greeting does not accidentally bowl over small toddlers.

faq.question: Are Soft Coated Wheaten Terriers easy to train?
faq.answer: They are smart and eager to engage, making them very trainable with upbeat, reward-based methods—though they retain enough independent terrier stubbornness to require patient, consistent follow-through.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Soft Coated Wheaten Terrier?
faq.answer: Key hereditary concerns include Protein-Losing Nephropathy (PLN, linked to NPHS1/KIRREL2 variants), Protein-Losing Enteropathy (PLE), renal dysplasia, Addison's disease, hip dysplasia, RBP4-related microphthalmia, and rare PIGN-related paroxysmal dyskinesia—making DNA screening, orthopedic/eye clearances, and annual blood and urine protein tests vital.

overview.summary: A large, powerful flock guardian from the southern steppes, wrapped in a long, harsh, mostly white coat and known for its calm confidence, independence and deep suspicion of strangers.
overview.description: The South Russian Shepherd Dog is a big, strongly built herding and guarding breed, somewhat longer than it is tall and never heavy or stocky. Its most striking feature is the coat: at least 10 cm long, harsh and shaggy, covering the whole dog, including the head and eyes, over a soft, thick, lighter undercoat. Colours are white or white with pale shading or patches of yellowish, grey, wheaten or ivory tones; puppies often change colour before reaching their adult shade at about 18 to 24 months. The head is long, the eyes are almond-shaped and brown, and the low-set triangular ears lie close to the cheeks under thick hair. By nature the breed is balanced, self-assured and independent. It forms a strong bond with its own family but treats strangers with wariness and reserve, a trait that comes from generations of guarding sheep, cattle and property with little human direction.
overview.history: The breed's ancestors are thought to include rough-coated, bearded sheepdogs that came from Spain to the steppes of southern Russia together with fine-wool sheep in the early nineteenth century; this movement is noted in the Russian Empire's law collection published in 1830. These lighter herding dogs were crossed with local shepherd dogs and sighthound-type dogs, producing a tougher, larger guardian suited to life on the open steppe. The dogs became known abroad, and at the Paris World's Fair of 1867 a Russian sheepdog won a gold medal for beauty. From 1898, systematic breeding on the Askania-Nova estate of Friedrich von Falz-Fein shaped the modern type and gave the breed its name. The first official standard was approved in the Soviet Union in the early 1930s. The breed received definitive international recognition in 1983 and was recognised in the United States in 1996, where its registered name changed from South Russian Ovcharka to South Russian Shepherd Dog in 2009. It remains rare outside its homeland.

grooming.brushing: Brush and comb the long coat through to the skin several times a week, and daily during seasonal shedding, to prevent felting and mats.
grooming.bathing: Bathe only when needed and dry the coat completely; a damp, dense coat can mat and irritate the skin.
notes: The undercoat sheds heavily at least once a year, needing extra combing.
Keep hair around the feet, hygiene areas and ears tidy to prevent soiling and mats.
Check the eyes under the facial hair and keep the area clean.
Trim the nails regularly; large dogs that walk mostly on grass may not wear them down.

training.difficulty: Challenging; intelligent but independent and dominant, so it needs an experienced, consistent handler
tips: Start training and handling early, before the puppy becomes large and strong.
Use calm, consistent, reward-based methods and clear household rules.
Teach reliable lead walking and a controlled greeting routine for visitors.
Never rely on off-lead control in public places.
Seek help from a trainer experienced with livestock guardian breeds if guarding behaviour becomes a concern.
training.socialization: Extensive, well-managed socialisation from puppyhood with people, other dogs and everyday situations is essential. Even well-socialised adults usually remain reserved with strangers, so visitors should be introduced under control.

feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals a day.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two smaller meals a day, adjusted for activity and body condition.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured meals and adjust portions to keep a lean, muscular body. The thick coat can hide weight gain, so check by feeling the ribs and waist. Keep fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Use a large-breed puppy diet so growth is steady rather than fast.
Avoid vigorous exercise just before and after meals.
Splitting the daily food into at least two meals is commonly advised for large, deep-chested dogs.
Change foods gradually over about a week.
nutrition.note: Calorie needs vary with age, neutering status and activity. A vet can recommend a target weight and portion size.

health.overview: Very little published health data exists for this breed, and no breed-specific health survey or screening programme was found. Owners should apply the usual precautions for large, heavy dogs: careful growth in puppyhood, keeping the dog lean, and hip and elbow screening of breeding dogs.
preventiveCare: Ask breeders whether the parents have had hip and elbow X-ray screening.
Keep the dog lean, especially while it is growing.
Avoid forced or repetitive high-impact exercise until the skeleton has matured.
Learn the signs of bloat, such as a swollen belly and unproductive retching, and treat them as an emergency.
Keep up yearly health checks, vaccinations and parasite control, and check under the coat for skin problems.

health.dentalCare: Brush the teeth several times a week with dog toothpaste and have the mouth checked at each vet visit.
health.earCare: Check the hair-covered ears weekly for wax, smell or redness and keep the hair around the ear opening free of mats.
health.skinCare: Part the coat to the skin while grooming to look for mats, redness, hot spots or parasites. Dense mats trap moisture and should be worked out or carefully trimmed.

faq.question: How big does a South Russian Shepherd Dog get?
faq.answer: Males should be at least 66 cm at the withers and at least 35 kg; females at least 62 cm and 30 kg. Larger dogs are preferred if they are well proportioned.

faq.question: Is this breed good for first-time owners?
faq.answer: Generally no. It is a powerful, independent guardian that needs an experienced, consistent owner and careful socialisation.

faq.question: How does it behave with strangers?
faq.answer: It is devoted to its family but naturally wary and reserved with people it does not know, and it will guard its home. Visitors should always be introduced under control.

faq.question: How much grooming does the coat need?
faq.answer: A lot. The long coat should be brushed through several times a week, and daily when the undercoat sheds, to prevent mats.

faq.question: What colours does the breed come in?
faq.answer: White, white with yellowish shading, or white with grey, wheaten or pale ivory patches. Puppies may change colour before they reach adulthood.

faq.question: How long does the breed live?
faq.answer: No reliable lifespan figure was found for this breed. As with other large dogs, good weight control and veterinary care help support a long life.

faq.question: What health problems does the breed have?
faq.answer: Breed-specific health data is very limited. Like other large breeds, it benefits from hip and elbow screening of breeding dogs, controlled growth and a lean body weight.

overview.summary: A giant, rustic Spanish livestock guardian known for its massive bone structure, abundant loose throat skin with a pronounced double dewlap, deep booming bark, and calm yet fearless defense of flocks and property.
overview.description: The Spanish Mastiff is an immense, powerfully muscled mountain guardian built slightly longer than tall, pairing heavy skeletal mass with flexible, balanced movement at a strong trot. Its dense, coarse, semi-long double coat covers thick, loose skin that forms a broad double dewlap along the neck. The large, truncated-pyramidal head has a slightly arched broad skull, a gentle stop, a wide straight muzzle in a 3:2 skull-to-muzzle ratio, and pendulous upper lips with black-pigmented gums and palate. Small dark hazel eyes set in thick black eyelids carry a quiet, noble expression that turns stern toward intruders, while medium triangular drop ears hang close to the cheeks. Calm, affectionate, and patient with its own family and livestock, the breed stands unwaveringly firm when defending its territory against predators or trespassers.
overview.history: Rooted in the ancient pastoral life of the Iberian Peninsula, the ancestors of the Spanish Mastiff arrived more than two millennia ago through early Mediterranean trade and developed alongside local herding stock. From the Middle Ages onward, the breed became inseparable from the Mesta, Spain's powerful association of sheep ranchers that moved vast Merino flocks seasonally between northern mountain pastures and southern lowlands. Wearing heavy spiked iron collars known as carlancas to protect their necks from wolf bites, these dogs guarded migrating herds and remote estates across Castile, León, and Extremadura. After traditional long-distance transhumance declined in the twentieth century, dedicated breeders and national clubs established formal breeding and health programs to preserve the breed's rustic build and working character.
