nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations carefully and feel the ribs through the thick double coat so excess weight does not accumulate—overweight/obesity was among the top five recorded clinical conditions (6.1%) in UK primary veterinary care for the breed.
considerations: Deduct training treats from the daily food allowance to prevent gradual weight gain.
For dogs with allergic skin disease, consult a veterinarian regarding diets rich in essential omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids or elimination trials.
Provide fresh drinking water at all times.
nutrition.note: General small-breed nutrition guidance; consult a veterinarian for individual portion sizes and dermatological diet advice.

health.overview: The West Highland White Terrier is a long-lived small breed with a typical life expectancy of 13 to 15 years—supported by a large UK primary-care veterinary study of 6,605 dogs that documented a median longevity of 13.4 years. In primary veterinary practice, the most frequently recorded routine conditions are periodontal disease (15.7%), otitis externa / ear disease (10.6%), overgrown nails (7.2%), allergic skin disorder / atopic dermatitis (6.5%), and overweight/obesity (6.1%), with cutaneous disorders as a group affecting 22.7% of dogs. Important breed-predisposed hereditary and chronic disorders include craniomandibular osteopathy (CMO / 'Westie Jaw'), canine idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis ('Westie Lung'), patellar luxation, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye), and rare globoid cell leukodystrophy (Krabbe disease).
commonConditions: Atopic dermatitis and allergic skin disease — chronic, heritable immune-mediated skin inflammation prevalent in the breed (6.5% specific prevalence and 22.7% overall cutaneous disorder prevalence in UK primary care), causing pruritus and secondary yeast or bacterial skin and ear infections
Periodontal disease and otitis externa — the two most frequently recorded clinical disorders in UK primary-care surveillance of the breed (15.7% and 10.6%, respectively)

Craniomandibular osteopathy (CMO / 'Westie Jaw') — painful, self-limiting proliferative bone enlargement of the mandible and tympanic bullae in puppies aged 4 to 8 months, associated with a leaky splicing variant (c.1332C>T) in the SLC37A2 gene on chromosome 5

Canine idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (CIPF / 'Westie Lung') — chronic, progressive interstitial lung fibrosis affecting middle-aged to older dogs of the breed, causing cough, exercise intolerance, crackles on auscultation, and secondary pulmonary hypertension
Patellar luxation and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease — orthopaedic hindlimb disorders involving kneecap displacement or aseptic necrosis of the femoral head in young dogs
Keratoconjunctivitis sicca (dry eye / KCS) and cataracts — ocular disorders monitored through regular ophthalmic examinations

Globoid cell leukodystrophy (GCL / Krabbe disease) — a rare, fatal autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by galactocerebrosidase deficiency (GALC gene mutation c.473A>C), preventable via carrier DNA screening
preventiveCare: Verify that breeding parents have DNA test results for craniomandibular osteopathy (SLC37A2) and globoid cell leukodystrophy (GALC), clinical patellar luxation evaluations, and specialist ophthalmic clearances.
Brush teeth several times a week and schedule regular veterinary dental checks, as dental disease is the single most common clinical diagnosis in the breed.
Inspect the skin and ears weekly during grooming and seek early veterinary dermatological care at the first signs of itching, redness, or ear odour.
Monitor breathing rate and exercise tolerance in middle-aged and senior dogs to detect chronic respiratory disease early.
Keep adult body weight lean (around 7 to 10 kg in males and 6 to 7 kg in females) and trim nails regularly.
recommendedScreenings: DNA test for Craniomandibular Osteopathy (SLC37A2 gene variant)
Clinical orthopedic evaluation for patellar luxation
Ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist
Radiographic hip evaluation for Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease and hip dysplasia
DNA test for Globoid Cell Leukodystrophy (GALC gene variant)
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times a week with canine enzymatic toothpaste and schedule regular veterinary dental assessments—periodontal disease was the most common disorder (15.7%) recorded in 6,605 UK West Highland White Terriers.
health.earCare: Check the small, erect, velvety-haired ears weekly for wax, redness, or odour and clean gently with a veterinarian-approved ear cleanser, as ear disease affects roughly 10.6% of dogs annually.
health.skinCare: Because cutaneous disorders affect more than one in five dogs of the breed—and conformation guidelines explicitly call for skin free from obvious skin problems—part the white double coat weekly to check the skin and bathe with gentle, non-drying shampoos.

funFacts: Colonel Edward Donald Malcolm of Poltalloch developed the pure-white strain in Argyllshire after one of his reddish working terriers was mistaken for a fox in thick cover and accidentally shot.

Before the name West Highland White Terrier was adopted in the early twentieth century, the breed was exhibited under regional names including the Poltalloch Terrier and the Roseneath Terrier (after the Duke of Argyll's estate).
Its straight, sturdy 13 to 15 cm tail—never docked—was bred strong enough for a huntsman to grip safely when drawing a wedged terrier out of an underground rock cairn.
The forefeet are purposefully larger than the hindfeet and thickly padded to give extra digging power in stony ground.
Despite its snow-white coat, the breed is never albino: the nose, lips, eye rims, paw pads, and nails are darkly pigmented in black.
Paired with a black Scottish Terrier, the breed became world-famous on James Buchanan's 'Black & White' Scotch whisky labels from the late Victorian era onward.

faq.question: What is a West Highland White Terrier?
faq.answer: The West Highland White Terrier—popularly called the Westie—is a small, sturdy Scottish earth dog with a pure-white harsh double coat, dark piercing eyes, erect pointed ears, a straight 13 to 15 cm tail, and a confident, friendly temperament.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is an adult West Highland White Terrier?
faq.answer: Adults stand approximately 28 cm at the withers, with typical weights of 7 to 10 kg for males and 6 to 7 kg for females.

faq.question: What is the typical lifespan of a West Highland White Terrier?
faq.answer: The breed typically lives 13 to 15 years; a large UK study of 6,605 West Highland White Terriers recorded a median lifespan of 13.4 years.

faq.question: Why was the West Highland White Terrier bred to be pure white?
faq.answer: Highland hunters needed a terrier that stood out clearly from foxes and badgers in dark rocks and heather; Colonel Edward Donald Malcolm of Poltalloch selected exclusively for white dogs after a dark-coated terrier was accidentally shot for a fox.

faq.question: How should a West Highland White Terrier's coat be groomed?
faq.answer: The double coat has a harsh, straight outer jacket about 5 cm long over a soft undercoat. Brush two to three times a week and either hand-strip the coat every few months to keep its wiry weather-resistant texture or clip it every four to six weeks.

faq.question: What are the most common health issues in the breed?
faq.answer: Routine veterinary care most often involves dental disease, ear infections, and allergic skin disease (atopic dermatitis). Breed-specific hereditary and chronic conditions include craniomandibular osteopathy ('Westie Jaw', testable via the SLC37A2 gene), canine idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis ('Westie Lung'), patellar luxation, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, dry eye, and rare globoid cell leukodystrophy (GALC gene).

faq.question: Can a West Highland White Terrier live in an apartment?
faq.answer: Yes. Its compact size suits apartments as well as houses with yards, provided it receives 45 to 60 minutes of daily walks and play and early training to moderate watchdog barking.

overview.summary: A rugged, highly versatile, and ancient hunting spitz from the Russian taiga, renowned for its wolf-like appearance, immense stamina, and specialized 'bark-pointing' hunting style.
overview.description: The West Siberian Laika is a medium-to-large, robustly built spitz breed that projects a distinctly primitive, wolf-like appearance. Forged by the harsh conditions of the Ural and Siberian forests, the breed features a lean, muscular, and slightly rectangular silhouette optimized for tireless endurance across difficult terrain. It is protected by a harsh, straight double coat that forms a noticeable collar around the neck and heavily fringes the tail, which is traditionally carried tightly curled over the back or hip. The wedge-shaped head is topped with pricked, highly mobile ears and dark, almond-shaped eyes that radiate an intense, observant, and independent intelligence. Renowned for its unique hunting method, the dog tracks game silently before aggressively barking to hold the quarry at bay and alert the hunter. While inherently wild in its hunting instincts and highly independent, it bonds deeply with its master, exhibiting a stable, even-tempered, and highly devoted nature within the home.
overview.history: The West Siberian Laika is one of the oldest aboriginal dog breeds in Russia, its roots intertwined with the indigenous Khanty and Mansi peoples of the Ural Mountains and Western Siberia. For centuries, these highly adapted, primitive hunting dogs were essential for survival in the dense taiga forests, used to hunt everything from small fur-bearing animals like sable and marten to massive, dangerous game such as wild boar, moose, and bear. Unlike specialized hounds, Laikas were bred for extreme versatility, requiring them to locate, track, and independently hold game at bay by barking (bark-pointing) until the hunter arrived. During the early twentieth century, Russian cynologists began to systematically categorize the vast, regional populations of Laikas, ultimately standardizing the West Siberian Laika from the finest Khanty and Mansi bloodlines. Today, it remains the most popular and widespread hunting dog in Russia, highly respected globally by serious outdoorsmen for its unmatched survival instincts, rugged health, and working drive.
overview.originalPurpose: Versatile, all-around hunting dog used by indigenous Siberian peoples to track, tree, and hold at bay a wide variety of game ranging from squirrel and sable to moose, boar, and bear.
currentRoles: Specialized bark-pointing hunting dog
Wilderness trekking and hiking companion
Vigilant property watchdog
Devoted household companion for highly active families

physical.coatType: Harsh, straight, and weather-resistant double coat. The guard hairs are stiff and stand off slightly from the dense, soft undercoat. The hair on the neck forms a distinct collar or ruff, and the tail is heavily feathered.
coatColors: Parti-color (white with patches of any of the aforementioned colors)
physical.sheddingLevel: High; sheds consistently year-round and intensely 'blows' its dense undercoat once or twice a year during seasonal changes
physical.droolingLevel: Low; tight-fitting, well-pigmented lips effectively prevent excessive drooling
distinctiveFeatures: Lean, athletic, and slightly rectangular silhouette (body length slightly exceeds height at the withers)
Height at the withers of 55 to 62 cm for males and 51 to 58 cm for females
Working weight ranging from 18 to 28 kg for males and 16 to 23 kg for females
Distinctly primitive, wolf-like facial structure and agile, light-footed movement
Wedge-shaped head forming an elongated triangle, with a gradual stop and a straight muzzle
Complete, strong scissor bite equipped to hold large quarry
Dark brown, almond-shaped eyes set slightly obliquely, projecting an alert and penetrating gaze
Erect, V-shaped, and highly mobile ears with pointed tips
Strong, muscular neck featuring a noticeable ruff of thicker hair
Tail set high and tightly curled into a ring over the back or hip, heavily coated
Deep, broad chest and strong, muscular legs designed for immense, prolonged endurance in deep snow

traits: Even-tempered, stable, and completely fearless in the presence of dangerous game
Intensely devoted, loyal, and affectionate with its master and immediate family
Highly independent, strong-willed, and naturally prone to making its own decisions in the field
Extremely high prey drive, hardwired to chase and tree small running animals
Highly alert and observant, functioning as an excellent, vigilant watchdog
Aloof, suspicious, and generally reserved around unfamiliar strangers, though never cowardly
Exceptionally vocal when working, utilizing a specialized, rhythmic bark to hold prey at bay
Requires clear, fair, and incredibly consistent leadership to manage its primitive instincts

exercise.level: Very high; a tireless aboriginal working breed requiring vast amounts of daily physical exertion and challenging outdoor tasks to prevent severe frustration and destructive behavior
activities: Extensive daily trail running, hiking, or wilderness trekking
Active hunting, tracking, and scent work in rural environments
Free running in a very large, highly secure, and deeply fenced enclosure
Mental enrichment focusing on natural exploration and problem-solving

grooming.brushing: Brush thoroughly two to three times weekly using an undercoat rake and a slicker brush, increasing to daily brushing during the heavy seasonal shedding periods (blowing coat).
grooming.bathing: Bathe rarely—only when visibly soiled—to preserve the harsh coat's natural weather-repelling and dirt-resistant oils.
notes: The dense undercoat is virtually self-cleaning, shedding dirt and mud naturally as it dries.
Inspect the erect ears weekly for dirt, debris, or ticks after wilderness excursions.
Trim the strong nails every few weeks, particularly if the dog is exercised mostly on soft earth, snow, or grass.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Challenging; highly intelligent but fiercely independent, lacking the eager-to-please nature of herding breeds and strongly inclined to obey its own survival instincts
tips: Use exclusively positive, reward-based training built on mutual respect; they will stubbornly ignore harsh corrections or repetitive obedience drilling.
Begin intensive recall training from early puppyhood, though they can never be fully trusted off-leash in unfenced areas due to their explosive prey drive.
Establish extremely clear boundaries regarding livestock and household pets, as their hunting instincts are exceptionally strong.
Channel their natural vocalization (bark-pointing) into controlled commands to manage excessive barking at home.
training.socialization: Extensive, continuous, and highly positive socialization is absolutely critical. Introduce the puppy early to varied people, calm dogs, and diverse environments to ensure its natural caution and aloofness do not develop into sharp, fearful defensiveness.

climates: Cold climates, where the incredibly dense, primitive double coat provides exceptional thermal insulation in freezing conditions
Temperate climates
Warm climates are tolerated poorly; the dog must have continuous access to cool indoor shelter, deep shade, and fresh water, with exercise strictly limited to cool early mornings
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low to moderate; despite their independence in the field, they are pack-oriented dogs that bond deeply with their owners and can become highly destructive or excessively vocal if left isolated and bored for long hours.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for highly active, medium-to-large working breeds, with a preference for high-protein formulations to support lean muscle.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three to four measured small meals daily until six months of age to support steady, robust growth.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to support sustained energy and digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic output.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure daily rations strictly using a digital kitchen scale or standard measuring cup. These dogs are highly efficient metabolizers due to their primitive origins and do not require excessive volume to maintain condition. Divide daily food into two distinct meals, restrict vigorous exercise immediately before and after eating, and provide cool, clean drinking water continuously.
considerations: Maintain a strictly lean, muscular body condition; excess weight severely compromises their stamina and mechanical joint health.
Working dogs in active hunting seasons or freezing winter weather require a significant increase in caloric and protein density.
Account for all training treats within the total daily caloric allowance.
Transition between diet formulas gradually over five to seven days to prevent gastrointestinal upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs fluctuate dramatically based on seasonal working activity, outdoor temperature, and age. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored daily feeding guidelines.

health.overview: The West Siberian Laika is an exceptionally hardy, primitive, and robust breed with a typical life expectancy of 12 to 14 years. Benefiting from centuries of brutal natural selection in the Siberian taiga, it possesses immense constitutional vitality and is virtually free of the severe genetic diseases that plague many highly domesticated breeds. Primary health concerns are typically related to physical injuries sustained during rigorous hunting rather than inherited conditions.
commonConditions: Traumatic outdoor injuries — cuts, sprains, torn ligaments, or thorn punctures sustained during vigorous hunting in rough terrain or encounters with dangerous game
Tick-borne diseases — infections such as Lyme disease or Anaplasmosis acquired from parasites in heavily wooded hunting environments
Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity of the hip joint, occurring very rarely in this robust breed but monitored as a general precaution for large working dogs
Cryptorchidism — occasional instances where one or both testicles fail to descend fully in male puppies
preventiveCare: Conduct thorough physical inspections of the dog's coat, skin, eyes, and foot pads immediately following every wilderness excursion or hunt to treat minor injuries early.
Administer rigorous, consistent, year-round parasite prevention against ticks, fleas, and heartworms.
Maintain a lean, athletic body condition to prevent unnecessary mechanical wear on the joints over the dog's lifetime.
Keep vaccinations fully up to date, particularly for dogs highly active in rural areas with wildlife exposure.
Schedule annual veterinary wellness examinations and routine health checks.
recommendedScreenings: Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation (generally recommended for breeding stock, though incidence is extremely low)
Routine ophthalmic evaluation by a veterinarian
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has powerful jaws and a complete scissor bite designed for grasping; periodic veterinary dental assessments preserve gum health.
health.earCare: Inspect the erect, pointed ears weekly for dirt, grass seeds, or tick attachments after outdoor work. Clean gently using a veterinarian-recommended ear solution.
health.skinCare: Part the dense, harsh double coat weekly during brushing to inspect the skin for external parasites, ticks, or burrs. The primitive coat requires minimal bathing and maintains its own healthy oils naturally.

idealFor: Highly active individuals, hunters, and wilderness enthusiasts requiring a tireless, robust outdoor partner
Experienced dog owners who understand primitive spitz breeds, extreme prey drive, and independent decision-making
Rural households with expansive, securely fenced acreage and immediate access to woodland or trails
Owners who appreciate a highly vocal, alert watchdog and an independent, wolf-like companion
notIdealFor: First-time dog owners, passive handlers, or those expecting a highly obedient, eager-to-please retriever temperament
Apartment, condominium, or dense urban dwellers where unavoidable noise and lack of space will cause the dog immense stress
Households with cats, small pet rodents, or poultry, given the breed's hardwired, explosive hunting instincts
Families seeking a highly sociable dog park companion that mixes freely with unfamiliar dogs and strangers
Sedentary individuals looking for a low-energy indoor pet

funFacts: The word 'Laika' translates literally from Russian to mean 'barker', perfectly describing the breed's specialized hunting technique of 'bark-pointing', where the dog finds game, trees it, and barks continuously to guide the hunter to the location.
The West Siberian Laika is the most numerous and popular hunting breed in all of Russia, deeply embedded in the survival and culture of the indigenous Khanty and Mansi peoples.
During the Space Race in the 1950s, the Soviet space program heavily favored Laika-type dogs for their intelligence, extreme hardiness, and resilience under pressure.

The breed retains many primitive, wolf-like traits, including an exceptionally high survival instinct, a naturally self-cleaning coat, and an incredibly efficient metabolism that requires less food than similar-sized domestic breeds.
Unlike hounds that track primarily by scent on the ground, the Laika utilizes a combination of scent, exceptional hearing, and sharp vision to locate game in dense forests.

faq.question: What is a West Siberian Laika?
faq.answer: The West Siberian Laika is a medium-to-large, primitive spitz breed from Russia, originally developed by indigenous hunters in the taiga forests for tracking, treeing, and holding dangerous game at bay through persistent barking.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a West Siberian Laika?
faq.answer: Adult males stand 55 to 62 cm at the withers and weigh 18 to 28 kg, while adult females stand 51 to 58 cm and weigh 16 to 23 kg, presenting a lean, highly athletic, and wolf-like silhouette.

faq.question: How long does a West Siberian Laika live?
faq.answer: Benefiting from centuries of strict natural selection, they are an exceptionally robust and healthy breed, typically enjoying a lifespan of 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Is the West Siberian Laika a good family dog?
faq.answer: They are deeply devoted and even-tempered with their own families, but they require a highly active, experienced household. They are not recommended for novice owners or homes with small pets due to their extreme prey drive and independence.

faq.question: Can a West Siberian Laika live in an apartment?
faq.answer: No. They are highly active, primitive hunting dogs that require vast amounts of daily exercise, mental stimulation, and open space, making them completely unsuited for apartment living.

faq.question: Do West Siberian Laikas shed a lot, and how are they groomed?
faq.answer: They are heavy shedders. While their harsh coat naturally repels dirt and requires little bathing, they heavily 'blow' their dense undercoat seasonally and require thorough brushing several times a week to manage the loose hair.

faq.question: Are West Siberian Laikas aggressive?
faq.answer: They are not inherently aggressive toward people, but they are highly alert, suspicious of strangers, and act as fierce watchdogs. They can, however, be highly aggressive toward small animals due to their hunting instincts.

faq.question: Are West Siberian Laikas hard to train?
faq.answer: Yes, they are highly intelligent but fiercely independent, preferring to follow their own instincts rather than human commands. Training requires immense patience, mutual respect, and positive reinforcement.

overview.summary: A sturdy, square-built, and fiercely determined water dog from Friesland in the Netherlands, distinguished by its tight, greasy curly coat, spiral tail, and watchful yet affectionate household nature.
overview.description: The Wetterhoun—widely known in English as the Frisian Water Dog—is a powerful, squarely proportioned working dog built for demanding, icy aquatic hunts without appearing clumsy. Except on the head and legs, which carry short smooth hair, the entire body is cloaked in dense, firm bundles of coarse, naturally greasy curls that insulate the dog in freezing canals and marshlands. Its robust head pairs a broad, slightly arched skull and parallel muzzle with slightly oblique oval eyes that give a serious, almost grim look, framed by smooth-hanging, mason's-trowel-shaped drop ears whose curls shorten toward the tips. A signature ornament of the breed is its long tail rolled tightly into a spiral over or beside the croup. At work, the Wetterhoun is persistent, self-willed, and eager to dispatch vermin. At home, however, it is remarkably calm, gentle, humorous, and deeply loyal—tolerant with family members while staying naturally reserved and quietly vigilant around strangers.
overview.history: Native to the northern Dutch province of Friesland, the Wetterhoun is believed to have descended from water-hunting dogs brought to the Low Countries by travellers or sailors from regions bordering the Baltic Sea. Throughout the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, Frisian farmers and hunters prized these rugged dogs for pursuing otters and small predators in frigid waterways, catching farm vermin, guarding rural homesteads, and even pulling small dog carts. Because the Wetterhoun and the neighbouring Stabyhoun were occasionally crossbred in the early twentieth century, dedicated Dutch enthusiasts stepped in to preserve both breeds separately. Today, the Wetterhoun remains a rare heritage breed found predominantly in the Netherlands, where carefully managed breeding and controlled outcross programmes work to safeguard its genetic health and traditional working resilience.

grooming.brushing: Minimal routine brushing is required—comb thoroughly during the two seasonal moults each year to remove dead hair, while avoiding frequent unnecessary combing between moults because over-brushing can stimulate excess shedding.
grooming.bathing: Avoid washing with shampoo as much as possible—especially for working water dogs—because detergents strip the coat's protective greasy oil layer and prevent the dog from drying quickly after swimming. Rinse with plain lukewarm water when muddy.
notes: Never clip or shave the dense curly coat; its natural oily texture is designed to shed cold water and protect the skin.
Inspect the smooth-lying, trowel-shaped drop ears weekly and dry them carefully after every swim to prevent moisture buildup and ear infections.
Check the round, strong feet and pads after wetland or woodland outings for thorns, mud plugs, or abrasions.
Trim strong nails every few weeks if they do not wear down naturally outdoors.
Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste.

training.difficulty: Challenging; intelligent and fully capable of learning obedience, yet strongly self-willed and prone to testing a handler's patience if commands feel repetitive or unfair
tips: Use calm, consistent, reward-based leadership built on mutual respect; heavy-handed corrections quickly provoke stubborn shutdown.
Keep training sessions brief, varied, and purposeful—this independent thinker obeys willingly when motivated, not like an automatic servant.
Start recall and impulse-control exercises early, particularly around small animals and waterways, to manage its strong vermin-hunting and aquatic instincts.
Stay patient and consistent through adolescence, when the breed's self-willed streak peaks.
training.socialization: Early, calm, and positive exposure to unfamiliar visitors, friendly dogs, urban noises, and everyday household sights helps balance its natural reserve toward strangers without dampening its steady watchdog instincts.

climates: Cool, damp, and temperate maritime climates, where the thick, naturally greasy curly coat provides outstanding insulation even in cold water
Moderate four-season climates
Warm or hot climates require keeping vigorous walks to cool morning and evening hours while offering shade, ventilation, and cool drinking water
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Moderate; calm and unhurried indoors once properly exercised, though it prefers spending time outdoors with its owner or keeping watch around a familiar family yard rather than enduring prolonged boredom.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality complete and balanced dog food formulated for medium-to-large, active working breeds.

feedingFrequency.puppy: Three measured small meals daily until roughly six months of age on a controlled large-breed growth diet to support healthy hip and elbow development.
feedingFrequency.adult: Two measured meals daily to sustain field stamina and steady digestion.
feedingFrequency.senior: Two portion-controlled meals daily adapted for lower metabolic needs and joint support.

nutrition.guidelines: Measure every meal carefully to maintain a solid, muscular working condition without carrying extra fat over the broad chest and joints. Adjust rations upward during heavy outdoor hunting or winter swimming seasons and dial them back during quieter stretches. Divide daily food into two meals, rest before and after eating, and provide cool, fresh drinking water at all times.
considerations: Keep puppies growing at a steady, moderate rate using a balanced medium-to-large-breed puppy formula to help lower developmental hip and elbow stress.
Count all training treats inside the daily calorie allowance to prevent excess weight.
Avoid intense running or swimming immediately before and after large meals.
Transition gradually between diet formulas over five to seven days to avoid digestive upset.
nutrition.note: Caloric needs differ noticeably between working water dogs and companion-kept adults. Consult a veterinarian to establish tailored portions.

health.overview: The Wetterhoun is a rugged working breed with an average lifespan of approximately 13 years, though its small global population creates heightened attention to genetic diversity and targeted health screening. Scientifically established hereditary priorities include an autosomal-recessive form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) caused by a nonsense mutation in the RAG1 gene—fully preventable through mandatory pre-breeding DNA screening—alongside orthopedic screening for hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia. Controlled outcross programmes are also employed to broaden the gene pool and strengthen long-term breed health.
commonConditions: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID, RAG1-related) — a fatal autosomal-recessive immunodeficiency caused by a nonsense mutation (c.2893G>T; p.Glu965*) in the RAG1 gene, resulting in a lack of functional B- and T-lymphocytes and high puppy mortality at 8 to 12 weeks of age; completely preventable via pre-breeding DNA testing
Hip dysplasia — developmental laxity and malformation of the hip joints that can lead to osteoarthritis and hind-limb lameness, monitored through mandatory pre-breeding radiographic screening
Elbow dysplasia — developmental abnormalities of the elbow joints that can cause forelimb lameness, monitored through radiographic screening prior to breeding
Otitis externa (ear infections) — conformation- and lifestyle-linked risk in swimming water dogs with smooth-hanging drop ears if moisture remains trapped in the ear canal
preventiveCare: Confirm that both breeding parents have certified DNA clearances for RAG1-related Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) so no affected puppies are produced.
Verify that breeding stock holds certified radiographic clearances for hip dysplasia and elbow dysplasia.
Keep the dog lean and avoid excessive high-impact jumping during puppyhood to protect developing hips and elbows.
Dry the drop ears thoroughly after every swim or wet-weather outing, and avoid stripping the natural protective coat oils with frequent shampooing.
Maintain annual veterinary wellness examinations, core vaccinations, and year-round parasite prevention.
recommendedScreenings: DNA test for Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID / RAG1 c.2893G>T mutation)
Radiographic hip dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
Radiographic elbow dysplasia evaluation prior to breeding
health.dentalCare: Brush teeth several times weekly using canine enzymatic toothpaste. The breed has a powerful, complete scissor bite; periodic veterinary dental evaluations help keep gums and teeth sound.
health.earCare: Check the moderately low-set, trowel-shaped drop ears weekly and after every swimming session for trapped water, wax, or redness, drying gently and using a veterinarian-approved cleanser when needed.
health.skinCare: Preserve the coat's natural slightly greasy protective layer by avoiding frequent shampoo baths and over-brushing outside seasonal moults; part the curls periodically to check for ticks or skin irritation.

idealFor: Active rural or suburban households with ample fenced yard space and immediate access to trails or water
Experienced, patient dog owners who appreciate an independent, humorous, self-willed working dog
Families with older children seeking a calm, tolerant indoor companion and quiet, watchful guardian
Hunters and outdoor enthusiasts wanting a low-grooming, weatherproof water dog
notIdealFor: Apartment or dense-city dwellers lacking generous outdoor space and daily countryside exercise
First-time owners or handlers expecting fast, eager-to-please, automatic obedience
Households with free-roaming small pets such as rabbits, ferrets, or rodents, given its keen vermin-catching drive
People who prefer heavily groomed dogs that are frequently shampooed or clipped

funFacts: In the West Frisian language, 'Wetterhoun' literally translates to 'Water Dog,' reflecting its centuries-old specialization in swimming through the icy canals and lakes of Friesland to hunt otters.
Its coat is meant to feel slightly greasy—washing a Wetterhoun with shampoo strips away the natural oil layer that keeps the dog waterproof and allows it to dry quickly after swimming.

The breed's drop ears are traditionally described as having the distinctive outline of a mason's trowel, covered in long curls near the base that shorten abruptly into smooth short hair over the lower third.
Historically, the Wetterhoun was not only a marsh hunter and homestead watchdog—in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries it was also harnessed to pull small utility dog carts.

In 2011, veterinary geneticists pinpointed the exact RAG1 gene nonsense mutation responsible for Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) in Frisian Water Dogs, enabling breeders to prevent fatal puppy losses with a simple DNA test.

faq.question: What is a Wetterhoun?
faq.answer: The Wetterhoun (Frisian Water Dog) is a rare, sturdy, square-built Dutch water dog from Friesland, known for its tight greasy curly coat, spiral tail, keen vermin-hunting drive, and calm, watchful loyalty.

faq.question: How tall and heavy is a Wetterhoun?
faq.answer: The ideal height at the withers is 59 cm for males and 55 cm for females, with typical working weights of approximately 34 kg for males and 28 kg for females.

faq.question: How long does a Wetterhoun live?
faq.answer: With balanced nutrition, generous daily outdoor exercise, and preventive veterinary care, the breed has an average life expectancy of around 13 years.

faq.question: How do you groom a Wetterhoun's curly coat?
faq.answer: Grooming is deliberately minimal. Comb out dead hair during the two annual moulting seasons, avoid frequent combing in between, and avoid shampooing whenever possible so you do not strip the natural greasy waterproofing oils.

faq.question: Can a Wetterhoun live in an apartment?
faq.answer: No. Although remarkably calm inside the house, the Wetterhoun is a sturdy outdoor yard and water dog that strongly prefers generous rural space, fresh air, and long daily walks.

faq.question: Are Wetterhouns good with children?
faq.answer: Yes. They are gentle, affectionate, and highly tolerant with children in their family, though their solid, heavy frame can make them a bit clumsy during excited play around toddlers.

faq.question: Are Wetterhouns easy to train?
faq.answer: Not for beginners. They are smart and capable of learning solid obedience, but their deeply self-willed nature tests an owner's patience and demands calm, respectful, unwavering consistency.

faq.question: What are the main health concerns for a Wetterhoun?
faq.answer: The primary hereditary concerns screened in breeding dogs are RAG1-related Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID, preventable through DNA testing), hip dysplasia, and elbow dysplasia, alongside routine ear care after swimming.

overview.summary: A sleek, medium-sized British sighthound bred for fast sprinting and agile coursing, known for its deep chest, arched loin, quiet indoor manners, and warm attachment to people.
overview.description: The Whippet combines lean muscular power with clean, graceful lines built for high-speed pursuit. Reaching bursts of up to 35 mph, this medium-sized sighthound has a deep chest for lung capacity, a smoothly arched loin, a tucked-up belly, and long, slender legs. Its head is long and lean with bright oval eyes, small rose-shaped ears folded neatly back, and a clean scissor bite. The short, fine coat lies close to the skin and appears in nearly every solid, brindle, or patched color pattern except merle. Indoors, Whippets are remarkably calm, quiet, and fond of soft bedding, yet outdoors they switch instantly into keen, fast-moving sprinters whenever motion catches their eye.
overview.history: Genetic research links the Whippet closely to the Greyhound, tracing back to ancient Celtic coursing hounds. During the 19th century, working families in northern England, Wales, London, and the Midlands developed this smaller, more economical runner for hunting rabbits and small vermin as well as weekend track racing. Breeders refined smaller Greyhounds with terrier lines to add quickness and grit, earning the dog nicknames such as 'Snap Dog' and 'the poor man's racehorse.' English textile mill workers later brought Whippets to Massachusetts, helping establish the breed in North America. Over time, the Whippet grew from a working-class racing and coursing dog into a widely loved companion and versatile canine sports competitor.

nutrition.guidelines: Feed measured portions to keep a trim sighthound silhouette rather than a heavy waist. A healthy adult Whippet should not look emaciated, yet two to four vertebrae should remain subtly visible and the hipbones should not be buried in fat. Avoid vigorous sprinting right before or right after a full meal.
considerations: High metabolism in active or racing dogs may require slightly higher calorie density than sedentary pets.
Maintain steady lean muscle without excess weight that strains slender joints and limbs.
Always provide fresh drinking water, especially after sprint sessions.

health.overview: Whippets are generally sturdy, long-lived sighthounds with a typical lifespan of 12 to 15 years. Two conditions have documented genetic links in the breed: a well-characterized myostatin gene deletion affecting muscle mass and racing speed, and mitral valve degeneration, where research has linked disease severity to a region on chromosome 15. Like other lean sighthounds, Whippets also require informed veterinary care regarding anesthetic protocols, athletic heart measurements, thin skin, and cold sensitivity.
commonConditions: Mitral valve degeneration (MVD) — age-related heart valve disease; genome-wide research in Whippets links disease severity to a genetic locus on chromosome 15

Myostatin (MSTN) gene mutation ('bully' Whippet syndrome) — established 2-base-pair deletion causing extra muscle and faster sprint times in single-copy carriers and extreme muscular hypertrophy with cramping in double-copy dogs
Anesthetic sensitivity — low body fat and sighthound liver metabolism increase sensitivity to certain older barbiturate anesthetics and heat loss under sedation
Thin-skin lacerations and toe injuries — minimal body fat and fine coat leave skin prone to small tears during rough play, while high-speed turns can sprain toes
Inherited eye disorders — cataracts and retinal degeneration monitored across breeding lines
Congenital deafness — unilateral or bilateral hearing loss reported in some lines
Cold sensitivity and hypothermia — fine single coat and minimal body fat offer little insulation in cold or wet weather
preventiveCare: Schedule annual wellness checkups that include careful heart auscultation, especially as the dog enters middle and senior years.
Work with a veterinarian familiar with sighthound anesthesia and normal athletic heart size when planning surgery or diagnostic imaging.
Provide soft, supportive bedding to protect bony elbows and hips from pressure calluses.
Use a fitted coat in chilly weather and supervise off-leash runs only inside tall, securely enclosed areas.
recommendedScreenings: Cardiac evaluation by a veterinary cardiologist
Ophthalmologist eye examination
Hearing evaluation (BAER test)
Myostatin (MSTN) DNA test for breeding dogs

health.earCare: Check the small folded rose ears weekly for wax buildup, redness, or odor, and wipe gently with a vet-approved ear cleaner when needed.
health.skinCare: Check the fine coat and thin skin after outdoor runs for small scratches, burrs, or tears, and protect against sunburn or frostbite during weather extremes.

funFacts: Whippets can accelerate to speeds of up to 35 mph using a flexible double-suspension gallop.
Because working-class miners and mill workers in 19th-century England raced them when full-sized Greyhounds were too expensive to keep, Whippets earned the nickname 'the poor man's racehorse.'
English textile mill workers brought some of the first Whippets to Massachusetts, helping introduce the breed to North America.
A single-copy variation in the myostatin (MSTN) gene gives carrier Whippets measurably greater muscle mass and faster racing times, while two copies produce the heavily muscled 'bully' Whippet.
Despite their track speed, Whippets rarely bark and spend much of their indoor time curled up under blankets or on soft cushions.

faq.question: Are Whippets good apartment dogs?
faq.answer: Yes. Whippets are quiet, clean, rarely bark, and love resting indoors, making them well suited to apartment living as long as they receive daily walks and regular safe opportunities to run.

faq.question: Can a Whippet be trusted off-leash in an open park?
faq.answer: No. Whippets have a powerful instinct to chase fast-moving objects and can reach up to 35 mph in seconds, so they should only run off-leash inside a tall, securely fenced enclosure.

faq.question: Do Whippets need coats in cold weather?
faq.answer: Yes. Their short, fine single coat and very low body fat provide little warmth, so a well-fitted dog coat or sweater helps keep them comfortable during cool, windy, or rainy walks.

faq.question: Are Whippets safe around cats and small pets?
faq.answer: Some Whippets learn to live peacefully with indoor cats they are raised alongside, but their strong sighthound chase drive makes outdoor cats, rabbits, and other small animals risky without close supervision.

faq.question: How much grooming does a Whippet need?
faq.answer: Very little. A weekly rubdown with a soft brush or rubber grooming mitt, occasional baths, regular nail trims, and routine dental care are usually enough.

overview.summary: A versatile, medium-sized Hungarian pointing and retrieving dog bred for field, forest, and icy water, distinguished from the smooth-coated Vizsla by its heavier bone, weather-resistant russet-gold wire coat, pronounced eyebrows, and harsh beard.
overview.description: The Wirehaired Vizsla (Drótszőrű Magyar Vizsla) is a lean yet robust, medium-sized multi-purpose gun dog that stands slightly taller and carries more substance than its smooth-coated relative while remaining a completely separate breed. Its close-lying, non-glossy wiry outer coat (about 2 to 3 cm long) and dense water-repellent undercoat protect the dog against rough cover and winter cold without hiding its athletic outline. Characteristic facial furnishings—pronounced eyebrows that highlight the stop and a harsh 2 to 3 cm beard on both sides of a blunt, muscular muzzle—combine with V-shaped neck brushes and self-coloured brown pigment on the nose, lips, and eye rims to create a clever, determined expression. Passionate, staunch on point, and determined to stay on a scent even while swimming, the breed is calm, gentle, loyal, and affectionate indoors, thriving on close handler contact and positive, varied training.
overview.history: Developed in the 1930s after the First World War by Hungarian and Austrian hunters and falconers—led initially by Vizsla breeder József Vasas of the Csabai kennel and German Wirehaired Pointer breeder László Gresznárik of the de Selle kennel—the breed was created to combine the golden-rust colour and close-working biddability of the smooth Hungarian Vizsla with a heavier frame and a dense, weatherproof wire coat suited to harsh winters and cold-water retrieving. Foundation crosses mated two working Vizsla females (Zsuzsi and Csibi) with a solid liver German Wirehaired Pointer sire (Astor von Potat), producing Dia de Selle, the first three-generation Wirehaired Vizsla ever exhibited, shown in Hungary on 6 June 1943. Stabilized in Hungary by 1950 and granted international recognition in 1963, the breed held its first dedicated Hungarian field trials in 1976 with 26 entries, reached North America in the 1970s (earning Canadian recognition in 1978 and North American field recognition in 1986 with female Palotásmenti Jutka), and achieved full conformation recognition in the United States in 2014.
overview.originalPurpose: Versatile gun and falconry dog bred to point, track, and retrieve feathered and furred game across field, dense forest, and cold water, including European deerstalking
currentRoles: Versatile hunting companion for upland game birds, waterfowl, furred game, and deerstalking
Falconry dog
Pointing, retrieving, water-test, and blood-tracking competitor
Agility, obedience, rally, tracking, nose work, dock diving, barn hunt, and lure coursing participant
Therapy dog and active household companion

physical.coatType: Close-lying, strong, dense, non-glossy wiry outer coat over a dense, water-repellent undercoat, with shorter, softer hair on the lower legs, chest, and belly and characteristic facial and neck furnishings
physical.coatLength: Outer coat 2 to 3 cm (0.75–1.25 in; about 2.5 cm / 1 in in American standards and 3–4 cm / 1.25–1.5 in in Canadian standards) on the body, with a harsh 2 to 3 cm beard on the muzzle, pronounced eyebrows, V-shaped brushes on both sides of the neck, and feathering brushes along the backs of the legs
coatColors: Dark sandy gold (semmelgelb / dark sandy yellow)
Golden rust (with or without a white forechest/throat patch up to 5 cm / 2 in in diameter and white toe markings)
physical.sheddingLevel: Low to moderate
physical.droolingLevel: Low
distinctiveFeatures: Dense, close-lying wiry outer coat (2–3 cm) and water-repellent undercoat that protect against briars and icy water without obscuring the body outline
Pronounced bushy eyebrows accentuating the stop and a harsh 2 to 3 cm beard on both sides of the blunt, muscular muzzle
V-shaped coat brushes on both sides of the neck and distinct hair brushes along the backs of the forelegs (absence of undercoat or leg brushes is a disqualifying or eliminating fault)
Self-coloured dark brown nose, lip, and eye-rim pigment that harmonizes with the russet-gold coat (any black on the nose or a spotted butterfly nose is a disqualification)
Rounded V-shaped pendulous ears set at medium height and hanging close to the cheeks, slightly shorter than those of the smooth Vizsla

Slightly rectangular body (length from breastbone to buttocks exceeding withers height in roughly a 10:9 ratio) with brisket depth slightly less than half the withers height and elbows level with the sternum
Complete, regular scissor bite of 42 teeth; slightly oval feet with tough slate-grey or dark pads; rear dewclaws are a disqualification

Withers height of 58–64 cm for males and 54–60 cm for females internationally (58.4–63.5 cm [23–25 in] and 54.6–58.4 cm [21.5–23 in] in the United States; 57–64 cm and 53–60 cm in Canada), and typical adult weights of 25–29.5 kg (55–65 lbs) for males and 20–25 kg (45–55 lbs) for females (or 22–30 kg / 48.5–66.25 lbs across both sexes in Canadian standards)

traits: Affectionate, loyal, and closely bonded to its handler and family
Calm, gentle, and tractable indoors
Intelligent, self-confident, and eager to learn
Sensitive and intolerant of harsh handling or physical punishment
Passionate, determined, and staunch on point in the field and water
Can display a stubborn streak or bore easily with repetitive drills
Outgoing and friendly, though occasionally reserved with strangers
Possesses a well-developed protective and watchdog instinct

exercise.level: High
activities: Field hunting, pointing, tracking, and land or water retrieving
Swimming and dock diving (a natural, low-impact outlet for puppies and adults)
Hiking, jogging, and cycling with an active owner once skeletally mature
Off-leash running in a securely fenced area (essential due to strong prey drive)
Nose work, blood tracking, barn hunt, agility, rally, obedience, and lure coursing
Interactive puppy games such as 'wing on a string', toy retrieving, and hidden-treat scent searches

grooming.brushing: Routine brushing with a slicker brush or grooming mitt removes dirt and loose hair; wiping with a damp cloth suffices between baths. Dogs with longer wire coats benefit from periodic hand-stripping (by hand or stripping knife, working small sections at a time) to pull dead hairs and stimulate coarse wire regrowth.
grooming.bathing: Monthly or only as needed using a mild dog-safe shampoo; excessive bathing softens the harsh wire texture.
notes: Never clip or shave a correct wire coat; clipping damages the weather-resistant wire texture and is penalized as a fault in conformation.

Coat expression varies genetically within the breed: alongside the ideal rough wire coat (up to about 2–5 cm), some puppies inherit almost no furnishings ('smooth' wires requiring minimal upkeep), while others develop a long, soft, woolly coat that does not strip out and requires specialized care.
Use a grooming mitt or shedding blade during seasonal shedding to reduce loose hair indoors.
Trim toenails every four weeks (many owners do this during the dog's monthly bath).
Clean and dry the hanging ears regularly—especially after swimming—and wipe the beard after meals.
Begin regular tooth brushing early in puppyhood.

training.difficulty: Moderate
tips: Enrol in puppy kindergarten early and use upbeat, reward-based positive reinforcement; because the breed has a soft, sensitive temperament, harsh words or physical corrections are counterproductive and damaging.
Keep training lessons short, varied, and engaging—always ending on a positive note—as these clever dogs bore quickly with repetitive drills and can show a stubborn streak.
Provide calm, consistent household boundaries and gradually condition puppies to alone time so their close attachment to family does not develop into separation anxiety.

Avoid strenuous forced exercise—such as long-distance running, high-impact jumping, or excessive stair climbing—until the growth plates close at skeletal maturity; let puppies regulate their own play and rest after training lessons.
Ensure off-leash running takes place in a securely fenced area until field conditioning and recall are solid, as natural prey drive is strong.
training.socialization: Provide early, ongoing positive exposure to diverse people, children, dogs, surfaces, and field environments. Properly socialized adults are outgoing, steady, and adaptable in the home and field, neither timid nor aggressive.

climates: Cold and snowy winter climates (for which the dense wire coat and undercoat were specifically bred)
Cool and temperate climates
Warm climates when provided with shade, fresh water, and exercise during cooler hours
livingEnvironment.aloneTimeTolerance: Low. Deeply people-oriented and bred to maintain close contact with its handler, the Wirehaired Vizsla thrives as an indoor family member and can develop separation anxiety, restlessness, or destructive habits if isolated for long periods.

nutrition.dietType: High-quality, complete and balanced commercial dog food or veterinarian-supervised home-prepared diet matched to life stage (puppy, adult, or senior) and workload
nutrition.guidelines: Active hunting and sporting dogs require a nutrient-dense ration during working seasons that differs substantially from the diet needed by a growing puppy or a less active companion. Because Wirehaired Vizslas are strongly food-motivated, measure daily portions carefully, deduct training treats from the daily calorie allowance to prevent obesity, and keep clean, fresh water available at all times.
considerations: Adjust caloric density and portion sizes to match seasonal hunting, training, or companion activity levels.
Watch treat consumption closely during reward-based training, as the breed is food-oriented and can gain excess weight if overfed.
Prepare home-cooked diets only with veterinary supervision and approval.
Ensure constant access to fresh water—especially important for dogs carrying or at risk for hyperuricosuria.
Consult a veterinarian to establish individualized meal schedules for puppies, adults, and seniors.
nutrition.note: Authoritative kennel-club and parent-club sources do not prescribe fixed numerical meal counts per day for puppies, adults, or seniors; consult a veterinarian for life-stage feeding frequency.

health.overview: The Wirehaired Vizsla is generally a sturdy, long-lived hunting breed with a typical lifespan of 12 to 14 years, supported by parent-club health surveillance and mandatory pre-breeding screening. Under the national breed club's Code of Ethics (amended October 2025), all breeding parents must hold hip dysplasia clearances (radiographic certification at 24 months or older and/or a hip distraction-index score of 0.70 or better without degenerative joint disease), a current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye clearance, and documented DNA testing for Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE, requiring at least one parent of every litter to test Clear/Normal). A second autosomal recessive disorder with a validated DNA test in the breed is canine hyperuricosuria (HUU, caused by an SLC2A9 mutation), which predisposes affected dogs to urate bladder and kidney stones. Breeders also screen for elbow dysplasia and cardiac disease (such as subaortic stenosis), and monitor for inherited eye conditions, cancer, hypothyroidism, idiopathic epilepsy, and reported breed sensitivities to anaesthesia and combined vaccine/flea-medication protocols.
commonConditions: Hip dysplasia: a primary orthopedic screening focus required prior to breeding (in 2025 orthopedic registry testing of 19 dogs, 21% scored Excellent/Normal, 68% Good, and 11% Fair)

Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE): an autosomal recessive chronic cutaneous lupus caused by a missense variant in the UNC93B1 gene (c.1438C>A / p.Pro480Thr on chromosome 18), recently confirmed by biopsy and DNA testing in Wirehaired Vizslas; causes scaling, crusting, and hair loss beginning on the ears, muzzle, and back and spreading to the limbs and ventrum, along with joint pain/lameness, intermittent fever, lymphadenopathy, and possible proteinuria (often presenting around age 3 in this breed with symptoms that require lifelong management)

Hyperuricosuria (HUU): an autosomal recessive purine metabolism defect caused by a missense mutation in exon 5 of the SLC2A9 gene (c.563G>T / p.Cys188Phe on chromosome 3), leading to elevated urinary uric acid and predisposition to urate bladder and kidney stones that often require surgical removal

Ophthalmic disorders: hereditary cataracts, progressive retinal atrophy (PRA), glaucoma, persistent pupillary membranes (PPM), entropion, ectropion, and distichiasis (double row of eyelashes; both entropion/ectropion and distichiasis are disqualifying or eliminating faults in conformation standards)
Elbow dysplasia and subaortic stenosis (SAS): orthopedic and congenital cardiac conditions included in parent-club elective pre-breeding screening

Additional conditions tracked in breed health surveys and advisories: cancer, autoimmune diseases, hypothyroidism, idiopathic epilepsy, moisture-related outer ear infections in swimming dogs, sensitivity to vaccines or combined vaccine/flea-medication administration, and delayed recovery from anaesthesia
preventiveCare: Verify that both parents of any prospective puppy hold hip clearances (at ≥24 months or distraction index ≤0.70), current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist certificates, and ECLE DNA test documentation showing at least one Clear/Normal parent, along with recommended HUU, elbow, and cardiac results.

Discuss vaccination schedules, parasite preventives, and anaesthetic protocols with your veterinarian in advance, as sensitivity to combined vaccine/flea-medication treatments and slow recovery from anaesthesia have been reported in the breed.

Protect growing joints by avoiding forced long-distance running, repetitive jumping, or excessive stairs until skeletal maturity, and consult your veterinarian regarding the timing of spaying or neutering.
Clean and thoroughly dry the pendulous ears after swimming or wet field work to prevent otitis externa.
Monitor urinary habits (straining, hematuria, or frequent small voids), especially in dogs not cleared of hyperuricosuria.
recommendedScreenings: Hip dysplasia evaluation (radiographic certification at 24 months of age or older and/or hip distraction-index score of 0.70 or better; mandatory under parent-club Code of Ethics)
Annual ophthalmic examination by a board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist (mandatory under parent-club Code of Ethics)
Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE / UNC93B1 c.1438C>A) DNA test (mandatory under parent-club Code of Ethics that at least one parent of a litter be tested Clear/Normal)
Hyperuricosuria (HUU / SLC2A9) DNA test via buccal swab or blood sample (recommended by the parent club)
Elbow dysplasia radiographic evaluation and veterinary cardiac evaluation (recommended by the parent club)
Optional coat-genetics DNA testing (furnishings and coat length) for breeding planning
health.dentalCare: Begin a regular tooth-brushing routine with dog-safe toothpaste at an early age and schedule routine veterinary dental checks. Conformation standards require strong jaws with a complete, regular scissor bite of 42 teeth.
health.earCare: Inspect the rounded V-shaped hanging ears weekly for redness, debris, or odour, and dry them carefully after every swim or bath to prevent moisture-related ear canal infections.
health.skinCare: Maintain the wiry coat and skin through regular brushing and periodic hand-stripping rather than clipping. Watch for uncharacteristic scaling, crusting, or hair loss on the ears, muzzle, and back (which warrant veterinary evaluation for ECLE or other dermatoses), and discuss separated timing for vaccines and flea/tick medications with your veterinarian.

idealFor: Upland bird, waterfowl, and deerstalking hunters or falconers seeking a cold-hardy, versatile pointing and retrieving dog
Active families and outdoor enthusiasts who hike, jog, swim, or cycle and want their dog closely involved in daily life
Handlers interested in hunt tests, field trials, water tests, nose work, tracking, agility, rally, obedience, or dock diving
Owners who use gentle, reward-based training and can provide daily physical and mental stimulation
notIdealFor: Sedentary households or owners unable to provide vigorous daily exercise and mental work
Homes where the dog would be left isolated for long workdays or kept in an outdoor kennel away from the family
Heavy-handed trainers who rely on harsh verbal or physical corrections
Owners unwilling to manage a strong hunting prey drive around small animals or provide secure fencing

funFacts: Created in the 1930s by Hungarian Vizsla breeder József Vasas (Csabai kennel) and German Wirehaired Pointer breeder László Gresznárik (de Selle kennel), the breed was designed for hunters and falconers who needed a heavier-boned, cold-hardy dog for winter field and icy water work.
The first three-generation Wirehaired Vizsla ever exhibited at a dog show was a female named Dia de Selle, shown in Hungary on 6 June 1943.
In 1976, the first dedicated field tests exclusively for Wirehaired Vizslas were held in Hungary, drawing 26 entries.

The first Wirehaired Vizsla recorded in North American versatile hunting dog testing (#WV-000001) was a female named Palotásmenti Jutka, owned by Sándor Arany, who earned the breed's first Utility Prize II in 1986.

Although closely related to the smooth-coated Vizsla, the Wirehaired Vizsla is a completely separate breed that stands slightly taller and heavier, and cross-breeding between the two is not permitted by any major registry.

Because of the breed's natural affinity for water and determination to stay on a scent while swimming, it is eligible to compete not only in pointing breed hunt tests and water tests, but also in retriever hunt tests.

Conformation standards prize a natural working dog: a Wirehaired Vizsla is shown with minimal stripping and is explicitly never penalized in the show ring for sinewy working muscle or 'honorable scars' earned in the field.

faq.question: What is a Wirehaired Vizsla, and is it just a coat variety of the smooth Vizsla?
faq.answer: No. Although developed in the 1930s by crossing smooth-coated Hungarian Vizslas with German Wirehaired Pointers, the Wirehaired Vizsla (Drótszőrű Magyar Vizsla) is a completely separate breed with its own conformation standard and studbook. It is slightly taller, heavier-boned, and more robust than the smooth Vizsla, and cross-matings between the two breeds cannot be registered.

faq.question: How big does a Wirehaired Vizsla get?
faq.answer: International conformation standards specify a withers height of 58 to 64 cm (22.75–25.25 in) for males and 54 to 60 cm (21.25–23.75 in) for females. American standards specify 23 to 25 inches (58.4–63.5 cm) for males and 21.5 to 23 inches (54.6–58.4 cm) for females, while Canadian standards allow 57 to 64 cm for males and 53 to 60 cm for females. Typical adult weights are 25 to 29.5 kg (55–65 lbs) for males and 20 to 25 kg (45–55 lbs) for females, or 22 to 30 kg (48.5–66.25 lbs) across both sexes in Canadian standards.

faq.question: How long does a Wirehaired Vizsla live?
faq.answer: The typical lifespan is 12 to 14 years.

faq.question: Why do some Wirehaired Vizslas have smooth or woolly coats?
faq.answer: Coat texture and length vary within the breed due to coat-furnishing and coat-length genetics. While the ideal coat is a harsh, close-lying wire topcoat (about 2–4 cm long) with a dense undercoat, beard, and eyebrows, some puppies inherit almost no wire furnishings and appear nearly smooth, whereas others inherit a longer, soft, woolly coat that cannot be hand-stripped and is faulted in the show ring.

faq.question: How should a Wirehaired Vizsla's coat be groomed?
faq.answer: For everyday care, the coat is nearly 'wash and wear': routine brushing with a slicker brush or grooming mitt and wiping with a damp cloth between occasional baths keep it clean. Dogs with longer wire hair benefit from periodic hand-stripping—pulling dead outer hairs by hand or with a stripping knife in small sections—to encourage coarse new growth. A correct wire coat should never be clipped with electric clippers.

faq.question: What health screenings and DNA tests are required for Wirehaired Vizsla breeding dogs?
faq.answer: Under the national breed club's Code of Ethics, breeding dogs must have hip dysplasia clearance (radiographic certification at 24 months or older and/or a hip distraction-index score of 0.70 or better), a current annual board-certified veterinary ophthalmologist eye exam, and DNA testing confirming that at least one parent of the litter is Clear/Normal for Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE / UNC93B1). Breeders are also encouraged to test for Hyperuricosuria (HUU / SLC2A9), elbow dysplasia, and cardiac health.

faq.question: What is Exfoliative Cutaneous Lupus Erythematosus (ECLE) in the Wirehaired Vizsla?
faq.answer: ECLE is an autosomal recessive autoimmune skin and systemic disorder caused by a missense mutation in the UNC93B1 gene. It causes scaling, crusting, and hair loss starting on the ears, muzzle, and back and spreading to the legs and underside, sometimes accompanied by joint pain, lameness, fever, and proteinuria. Although cases identified in Wirehaired Vizslas have often appeared later (around age 3) and been less severe than in German Shorthaired Pointers, it is a painful, life-altering condition that breeders prevent through mandatory DNA screening.

faq.question: Are there any special veterinary precautions for Wirehaired Vizslas?
faq.answer: Yes. The national breed club's health statement notes that Wirehaired Vizslas have been reported to be sensitive to vaccines and combined vaccine/flea-medication treatments, and some dogs have experienced difficulty or slow recovery when waking from anaesthesia. Owners should discuss these sensitivities with their veterinarian before procedures.

faq.question: How much exercise should a Wirehaired Vizsla puppy get?
faq.answer: Puppies have abundant energy and need daily play and mental stimulation—such as retrieving games, 'wing on a string', hidden-treat scent games, and swimming—but they should not be taken on forced long-distance runs, high-impact jumps, or excessive stairs until their growth plates close at maturity. Let puppies self-regulate their activity and rest after training sessions.

faq.question: Are Wirehaired Vizslas easy to train?
faq.answer: They are intelligent, intuitive, and eager to please, but they have a sensitive ('soft') temperament and bore quickly with repetitive drills. Short, fun, reward-based sessions with clear, calm boundaries work best, whereas harsh verbal or physical punishment should never be used.

overview.summary: A diminutive, spirited toy terrier originating in northern England, the Yorkshire Terrier is famous for its shimmering, floor-length steel blue and tan coat and bold, vivacious persona. Despite its compact lap-dog stature, this feisty canine retains the tenacious drive, inquisitive mind, and alert instincts of its industrial rat-catching ancestors. It thrives as a devoted household companion when provided with daily mental enrichment, interactive play, and dedicated coat and dental care.
overview.description: Carrying itself with an upright, self-important carriage, the Yorkshire Terrier presents a compact, neat silhouette with a flat-parted, glossy mantle of fine silk. Its skull is moderately flat and small, accentuated by erect V-shaped ears, dark sparkling eyes, and a confident, inquisitive expression. Adult coats showcase a distinct two-tone coloration: a cool, dark steel blue spanning from the occiput to the tail base, complemented by warm, golden-tan points on the head, chest, and legs. While wonderfully adaptable to compact city living, the breed is far from an inert accessory; it possesses quick reflexes, an eager watchdog alertness, and an affectionate, feisty charm that responds best to gentle, positive training and patient socialisation.
overview.history: The breed emerged during the mid-nineteenth century in the industrial counties of Yorkshire and Lancashire, where Scottish textile weavers brought ancestral working terriers south to English coal mines and textile mills. Crossbreeding between early Paisley, Clydesdale, Waterside, and English Black and Tan Toy Terriers produced a small, fearless ratter capable of dispatching rodents in cramped spaces. As the Industrial Revolution progressed, the dog's dramatic silky mantle caught the attention of fashionable Victorian society, swiftly transforming it into an iconic companion of the British aristocracy while preserving its bold, tenacious spirit.
overview.originalPurpose: Controlling vermin and catching rats in coal pits, textile mills, and crowded industrial workshops.
currentRoles: Devoted family companion
Conformation show dog

physical.droolingLevel: Low; tight, clean lip conformation prevents noticeable salivation.
